title: Does P equal NP?
importance_reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.
focus_reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.
formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove P=NP or P≠NP in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
context:
A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. P=NP would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. P≠NP would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.
why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.
status_note: The Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved, checked on 11 September 2026. The cited restricted-circuit lower bounds and proof-method barriers do not resolve the uniform decision problem.
progress: 1971–1973: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation. | 1975–2009: Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions. | 2011: Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove P≠NP. | 2026-09-10: The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

working_summary: P versus NP asks whether every problem with efficiently checkable solutions also has an efficient deterministic decision algorithm. Boolean satisfiability is a representative test case because all NP problems reduce to it. Checking one assignment is easy, while deciding whether any assignment works requires accounting for all possibilities. The target concerns worst-case polynomial time on arbitrarily large inputs. A resolution would establish a fundamental relationship between searching and verifying, without by itself determining practical exponents or average-case difficulty.

title: Does P equal PSPACE?
importance_reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.
focus_reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.
formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most C(n+1)^k work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form Q₁x₁⋯Qₘxₘ φ(x₁,…,xₘ), where each Qᵢ is ∃ or ∀, quantified variables are distinct, and φ is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over {0,1}. The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove P=PSPACE or P≠PSPACE. The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
context:
Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, ∀x∃y (y=x) is true because y may depend on x, whereas ∃y∀x (y=x) is false. Both variables range over {0,1}. A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion P⊆PSPACE is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. P≠NP would imply P≠PSPACE because NP⊆PSPACE. A proof of P=NP, however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem IP=PSPACE characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds t(n)≥n, a time-t multitape computation can be simulated in O(√(t log t)) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time n^(2−ε) for every ε>0. The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.
why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.
status_note: Primary-source review and a search for subsequent results on 11 September 2026 found no resolution. Williams’ 2025 simulation and August 2026 MFCS survey concern time-space bounds; neither states an equality or separation of P and PSPACE.
progress: 1970s–1981: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time. | 1992: Shamir proves IP=PSPACE, giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation. | 2025 conference / 2026 journal: Williams proves the O(sqrt(t log t)) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old O(t/log t) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages. | 2026-08: Williams’ MFCS invited survey discusses this simulation and further space-complexity developments. It supplies no separation of the unions P and PSPACE.
working_summary: Polynomial space permits a computation to reuse its memory while exploring potentially enormous collections of possibilities. The question asks whether every problem solvable with that memory budget is also solvable in polynomial time. Truth of quantified Boolean formulas supplies a concrete complete problem. Alternating existential and universal choices describe strategies that can be much larger than one ordinary certificate. The project tests whether repeated reuse of a modest workspace gives strictly more decision power than any polynomial-time computation.

title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be solved in logarithmic space?
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.
focus_reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.
formal: Is L=P? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses O(log(n+2)) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most C log₂(n+2) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in O((n+2)ᶜ) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove L=P or L≠P in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
context:
A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about log₂ n bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

L⊆NL⊆P, where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that L≠NL would therefore separate L from P, but L=NL would not itself settle L=P. Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in O(√(t log t)) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller O(log n) target unresolved.
why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.
status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.
progress: 1975: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question. | 2005–2008: Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems. | 2025–2026: Williams obtains the O(√(t log t)) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case. | 2026: Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.
working_summary: Logarithmic-space computation can retain only a few input indices and counters while repeatedly rereading the input. The question asks whether that memory always suffices for every polynomial-time decision problem. Evaluating a supplied Boolean circuit is a representative complete task. Shared dependencies make naive recomputation expensive, while storing all intermediate gate values exceeds the space budget. The project tests whether efficient computation fundamentally needs substantial working memory or can always reorganize its information into an extremely small state.

title: Is nonuniform TC⁰ strictly smaller than nonuniform NC¹?
importance_reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.
focus_reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.
formal: Is TC⁰⊊NC¹ for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family f=(f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1}) in NC¹ such that for every fixed depth d≥1, exponent k≥1, and constant M≥1, there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing f_n exactly has size greater than M(n+1)^k?
definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes x_1,…,x_n, optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than m/2 inputs equal 1. TC⁰ consists of all families with such circuits of size M(n+1)^k and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. NC¹ consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size M(n+1)^k, and depth at most b log_2(n+1), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove TC⁰⊊NC¹ or TC⁰=NC¹ for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single NC¹ family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every NC¹ family admit such a family.
context:
The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. NC¹ permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives TC⁰⊆NC¹. The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰ circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the NC¹ side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group S_5, capture NC¹ under very simple reductions. S_5 consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform NC¹ using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform TC⁰. Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in E^NP. Here E^NP allows deterministic time 2^{O(n)} with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to NC¹. The target here concerns an NC¹ family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.
why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.
status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in E^NP and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.
progress: 2002: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰, demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth. | 2018–2019: Chen and Tell show how improvements in the depth dependence of superlinear wire lower bounds for certain NC¹-complete problems would yield superpolynomial TC⁰ lower bounds. | 2025-12-09: Dawar and Evans characterize uniform NC¹ with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open. | 2026: Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an E^NP function; the result does not supply an NC¹ separation against every constant depth.
working_summary: TC0 circuits use a constant number of layers of powerful majority gates. NC1 circuits use logarithmically many layers of ordinary bounded-input Boolean gates. The question asks whether the former nonuniform class is strictly weaker than the latter. Many arithmetic tasks already fit in TC0, so their familiar sequential implementations do not provide separating examples. The project seeks a function whose nested logical dependencies cannot be compressed into a fixed-depth network even when each gate can aggregate many inputs at once.

title: The Berman–Hartmanis isomorphism conjecture
importance_reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.
focus_reason: A defining structural-complexity conjecture about the entire NP-complete degree, stronger than P≠NP and supported by substantial restricted-model theorems and oracle barriers.
formal: For every pair of languages A,B⊆{0,1}* that are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, does there exist a bijection f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that f and f⁻¹ are computable in deterministic polynomial time and, for every string x, x∈A if and only if f(x)∈B?
definitions: A language is a set of finite binary strings, including a specified membership decision for every string; malformed encodings are therefore part of the language convention. NP consists of languages L for which x∈L exactly when some witness of length polynomial in |x| is accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. A many-one reduction from L to A is a total deterministic polynomial-time function g with x∈L iff g(x)∈A. A is NP-complete if A∈NP and every L∈NP reduces to A in this sense. The desired f is a permutation of all finite binary strings, taking members to members and nonmembers to nonmembers. Its running time is polynomial in its input length, and its inverse has a polynomial bound in the inverse input length. The algorithms and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed pair A,B, but not on the particular input string. No advice, oracle, randomness or length-preservation requirement is allowed. This is the unconditional conjecture; P≠NP is not an assumption.
answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: P≠NP is not an added hypothesis.
context:
NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies P≠NP, but its negation does not automatically imply P≠NP. To see the first point, suppose P=NP. Then the nontrivial languages {0} and 0{0,1}* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on P≠NP.

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform AC⁰ reductions, with nonuniform depth-three AC⁰ circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here AC⁰ means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.
why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.
status_note: The 2022 primary-author problem column states that the full conjecture is open. A later-source search on 11 September 2026 located the 2025 recovery-reduction preprint, which still uses it as a conjectural hypothesis, and found no resolution. Its truth-table recovery consequence is conditional.
progress: 1977: Berman–Hartmanis prove isomorphism for paddable complete languages and formulate the unrestricted conjecture. | 1989: Kurtz–Mahaney–Royer present random-oracle counterexamples at STOC; a journal treatment follows in 1995. | 1996: Fenner–Fortnow–Kurtz publish an oracle relative to which the conjecture holds. | 1998: Agrawal–Allender–Rudich prove the nonuniform AC⁰ isomorphism and gap theorems. | 2009: Agrawal–Watanabe give conditional nonuniform structural results involving one-way functions and easy cylinders. | 2022: The Hartmanis open-problems column retains the full conjecture and discusses the remaining cylinder and reduction questions. | 2025: Nareddy and Mishra’s recovery-reduction preprint states the isomorphism conjecture and derives a random-corruption recovery consequence conditional on it.
working_summary: Polynomial-time reductions show that NP-complete problems can simulate each other, but may erase information. The Berman-Hartmanis conjecture asks whether every pair instead admits a polynomial-time computable bijection with a polynomial-time inverse. That bijection must preserve yes and no instances across the entire string space. Padding provides evidence for familiar complete problems without covering all possible complete languages. The project asks whether completeness forces one efficiently reversible organization of instances, reaching beyond ordinary mutual reducibility.

title: Is the polynomial hierarchy strict at every finite level?
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.
formal: Is $\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}$ for every integer k≥0? Here Σ₀^P=P, and Σₖ^P for k≥1 consists of languages definable by k alternating blocks of polynomially bounded Boolean quantifiers, beginning existentially, followed by a deterministic polynomial-time predicate.
definitions: A language L is in Σₖ^P if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R such that, for every binary input x, $x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1$, where Qₖ is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Each yᵢ is an entire string, so k counts quantifier blocks, not individual bits. The predicate is polynomial-time in the combined input length. k is fixed for a class membership claim and cannot grow with |x|; p and R may depend on k and L. Let Πₖ^P consist of complements of Σₖ^P languages, and let PH=⋃ₖ≥0Σₖ^P. In particular Σ₁^P=NP and Π₁^P=coNP. These are uniform, unrelativized classes of total decision languages. Strictness at level k means that some language in Σₖ₊₁^P is absent from Σₖ^P. The separating language may depend on k. All classes use ordinary Turing computation with no advice or external oracle.
answer_criterion: Prove strict containment at every finite level, or prove equality Σₖ^P=Σₖ₊₁^P for some fixed k. Equality at any adjacent pair collapses all higher levels to that level, so a collapse at even one finite level answers no. Proving strictness for finitely many levels or relative to an oracle does not answer yes.
context:
NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.
why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.
status_note: Explicitly conjectured in the primary-source survey and Wigderson’s hierarchy discussion. Research through 10 September 2026 yielded no unrelativized proof of infinitude or finite collapse. Random-oracle infinitude and conditional Karp–Lipton collapses are not recorded as resolutions.
progress: 1970s: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy; Stockmeyer develops its structural properties and complete problems. | 1980s: Oracle constructions show that all levels can be distinct in a relativized world. Karp–Lipton-type theorems connect small circuits for NP to a collapse of the unrelativized hierarchy. | 2015: Rossman, Servedio, and Tan establish infinitude relative to a random oracle with probability one. Their proof comes from an average-case lower bound separating consecutive constant circuit depths. | 2025–2026: Hirsch and Volkovich study the Linear Ordering Principle, related small complexity classes, and Karp–Lipton-style conditional collapses. These are implications under hypotheses, not an unconditional collapse or separation of PH.
working_summary: The polynomial hierarchy adds successive alternating blocks of efficiently bounded existential and universal choices. Its first levels already include polynomial-time computation and ordinary NP verification. The question asks whether every additional fixed level strictly increases computational power. Equality of neighboring levels would collapse all higher finite levels as well. The project studies whether increasingly nested candidate-and-challenge reasoning creates an endless hierarchy of difficulty, a stronger issue than separating P from NP at the first step.

title: Does NP contain a language without polynomial-size Boolean circuits?
importance_reason: A foundational strengthening of P≠NP and the central target of general Boolean circuit lower bounds. Its consequences and methods reach across complexity, derandomization, learning, and cryptography.
formal: Is $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}$? Precisely, does there exist one language L∈NP such that, for every integer k≥1, real C>0, and integer N≥1, some n≥N satisfies $\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k$, where Lₙ is the characteristic function of L on n-bit inputs and CC is minimum Boolean circuit size?
definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n input bits, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and one output bit. There are no depth or fan-out restrictions; a gate output may be reused arbitrarily. Size counts AND, OR, and NOT gates. Lₙ must be computed exactly on every n-bit string. A family {Cₙ} is nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct Cₙ from n, and the circuit may depend arbitrarily on the input length, but not on the particular input of that length. P/poly consists of languages having circuits of size at most C(n+1)^k for some fixed constants C,k and every n. NP consists of languages L with a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that x∈L iff some y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. The existentially chosen language L is the same for every exponent k. The lower bound need only hold at arbitrarily large lengths for each k; an eventual bound at every sufficiently large length would be stronger. Equivalently, ask whether the NP-complete language SAT has no polynomial-size circuit family under an ordinary explicit binary formula encoding.
answer_criterion: Prove NP is not contained in P/poly, or prove the containment. A positive separation requires one NP language escaping every polynomial circuit-size bound. Proving that, for each exponent k, a possibly different language requires more than n^k gates does not suffice. Containment can be established by giving polynomial-size circuits for SAT at every input length; an efficient uniform circuit generator is not required.
context:
A polynomial-time algorithm yields a polynomial-size circuit for each input length by unrolling its computation. The converse fails because a different circuit may be selected for every length without any effective way to generate those circuits. The conjecture asks whether NP retains hard problems even after granting this substantial extra freedom. A separation would imply P≠NP, while P≠NP alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting arguments show that most truth tables need exponentially many gates. They do not produce the required language in NP: an arbitrary sequence of hard truth tables need not have efficiently verifiable membership certificates. This is the central explicitness difficulty. It is also why enumerating hard functions at a few fixed lengths cannot satisfy the quantified statement on this card.

The Karp–Lipton theorem gives a consequence of the opposite outcome: if NP has polynomial-size circuits, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. This is evidence linking nonuniform algorithms to uniform complexity, but it is not a contradiction because the hierarchy is not known to be infinite.

The natural-proofs theorem identifies a conditional obstacle to a broad family of circuit lower-bound techniques. Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, a property of truth tables that is both efficiently recognizable and sufficiently common cannot distinguish all hard functions from polynomial-size circuits in the required way. The theorem constrains a method, not every possible proof.

Williams’ separation for nondeterministic exponential time and constant-depth modular circuits demonstrates that faster satisfiability algorithms can yield nonuniform lower bounds. It leaves two restrictions relative to this target: the hard language may lie above NP, and the competing circuits have constant depth.
why: This is the main unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound conjecture for efficiently verifiable problems. Circuits remove issues of uniform program construction and expose a finite combinatorial object, making the problem a central route toward unconditional computational lower bounds. It connects complexity classes, pseudorandomness, learning, and limitations of proof techniques.
status_note: Explicitly posed by Wigderson and identified as the flagship unresolved circuit target in the March 2026 primary paper. Checked through 10 September 2026; no unconditional resolution of NP versus general polynomial-size circuits located. Restricted-depth or conditional lower bounds do not settle this card.
progress: 1980s: The Karp–Lipton theorem shows NP⊆P/poly implies PH=Σ₂^P. Wigderson’s Theorem 5.5 records this consequence next to Conjecture 5.4. | 1997: Razborov and Rudich prove the natural-proofs barrier under a strong cryptographic hardness assumption. This does not establish the desired circuit lower bound or its impossibility. | 2011 conference / 2014 journal: Williams proves that NEXP lacks polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits. ACC has fixed depth and allows modular counting gates; the result does not handle unrestricted circuits for an NP language. | 2026-03: Chen, Tal, and Wang obtain n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds against depth-two linear-threshold circuits for a function in E^NP, for every ε>0. Their introduction identifies NP⊄P/poly as the flagship open target.

working_summary: Nonuniform Boolean circuits may choose a separate computational design for each input length. The question asks whether some language in NP requires more than polynomially many gates despite that freedom. A uniform running-time lower bound would not automatically establish this stronger claim. Counting shows that most functions have large circuits but does not supply the necessary NP language. The project seeks explicit hardness robust to arbitrary length-specific preprocessing and would connect circuit lower bounds to the structure of the polynomial hierarchy.

title: Does every unsatisfiable Boolean formula have a short efficiently checkable certificate?
importance_reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a fixed polynomial p such that, for every Boolean CNF formula F, $F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\iff\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|F|)}:V(F,\pi)=1$, with V never accepting a certificate for a satisfiable formula? Equivalently, is NP=coNP? The verification algorithm and polynomial are fixed for all formulas.
definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals x or NOT x. Variables take values in {0,1}; unsatisfiable means that no assignment makes all clauses true. The formula is encoded explicitly in binary, and |F| is its total bit length, including variable names and all literal occurrences. Empty clauses and an empty conjunction have their usual false and true meanings. V halts in time polynomial in |F|+|pi| on every pair of strings and rejects malformed formula encodings. Certificates may be arbitrary binary strings; they are not restricted to any particular inference calculus. NP is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked in deterministic polynomial time. coNP consists of complements of NP languages. No randomization, oracle, advice, or interaction with a prover is allowed.
answer_criterion: Construct a sound verifier and one polynomial length bound covering every unsatisfiable formula, or prove that no such verifier and bound exist. Equivalently, prove NP=coNP or NP≠coNP. A lower bound for a particular proof system is insufficient for separation, and an efficient algorithm for finding certificates is not required for equality.
context:
A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when NP=coNP. The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.
why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.
status_note: The unrestricted certificate question remains a research target in the August 2026 primary workshop description. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. Lower bounds for individual proof systems do not establish the universal separation.
progress: 1979: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between NP=coNP and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system. | 2026-08: The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.
