working_summary: An unsatisfiable formula has no assignment that makes every clause true. The question asks whether one fixed efficient verifier can always check a polynomial-length certificate of that impossibility. The certificate format is unrestricted as long as it is sound for every formula. This is equivalent to asking whether NP equals coNP. The project concerns the possibility of universally concise explanations for the failure of all candidate solutions, rather than lower bounds for any one particular set of proof rules.

title: An explicit function with no linear-size Boolean circuits
importance_reason: A fundamental lower-bound milestone for unrestricted computation, with connections to matrix complexity, proof techniques and the limitations of nonuniform algorithms.
formal: Does there exist a total function F:{0,1}*→{0,1}*, computable by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and satisfying |F(x)|=|x|, such that its unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not O(n)? Explicitly, for every C>0 and N≥1, must some n≥N satisfy CC(Fₙ)>Cn?
definitions: Fₙ is the restriction of F to n-bit inputs, with n output bits. CC(Fₙ) is the least number of gates in a directed acyclic Boolean circuit computing all these outputs exactly on every input. Each gate may compute any Boolean function of at most two input bits: the full B₂ basis, including AND, OR, XOR and negation. Input nodes, constants 0 and 1, and designated output wires are free; gates have unrestricted fan-out and there is no depth bound. Gates may be shared among outputs. The family of competing circuits is nonuniform: the circuit at one input length need have no effective relationship to circuits at other lengths. In contrast, explicitness of F means a single deterministic Turing machine outputs F(x) in at most p(|x|) steps for one fixed polynomial p, with no advice. The empty input has empty output. This card fixes a polynomial-time interpretation of the source’s broader word “explicit” and preserves its allowance of n output bits. Changing between B₂ and the usual bounded-fan-in AND/OR/NOT basis changes size by at most a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Exhibit one such polynomial-time function and prove that CC(Fₙ)/n is unbounded along arbitrarily large input lengths, or prove that every polynomial-time length-preserving function has O(n)-size nonuniform circuits, with the hidden constant allowed to depend on the function. A fixed bound such as 10n is insufficient. The precise target is not O(n); it does not additionally require the ratio to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. A superlinear single-output example would also settle the question after padding the output with zeros.
context:
A circuit is a finite computation with a separate design for each input length. Intermediate results can be used many times, and different output bits can share the same work. This sharing is a central source of power: a lower bound for formulas, which cannot freely reuse intermediate results, need not hold for circuits. The target here leaves depth, fan-out and Boolean operations unrestricted apart from the two-input gate bound.

The explicitness requirement prevents a counting argument from solving the problem. There are vastly more Boolean functions than small circuits, so most functions require exponentially many gates. But describing one by its entire truth table takes exponential space, and selecting the first hard truth table by exhaustive search need not yield a polynomial-time function. We need an efficiently specified computation and a proof that every circuit for it exceeds every fixed linear bound.

Multi-output functions make the question especially concrete. A fixed, efficiently constructible binary matrix Aₙ defines Fₙ(x)=Aₙx over the two-element field. Its n outputs are parity sums of selected inputs. Computing every output separately can cost Θ(n²), yet a clever circuit may share partial sums across rows. Counting proves that some matrices need Ω(n²/log n) gates, but an explicit superlinear lower bound remains unknown even for this linear-algebra setting. A lower bound against XOR-only circuits would not automatically rule out smaller circuits that use nonlinear Boolean gates.

The polynomial-time convention also separates this question from NP versus P/poly. The desired F already has polynomial-size circuits because its algorithm can be simulated by circuits. Showing that it lacks linear-size circuits would separate two size scales within efficient nonuniform computation; it would not establish P≠NP. Conversely, proving superpolynomial circuit lower bounds for an NP language would address a stronger resource barrier but would not by itself make that language a polynomial-time example for this card.

For one output bit, Li and Yang obtain a 3.1n−o(n) lower bound over the full two-input basis. Their functions are affine dispersers, meaning that they remain nonconstant on every sufficiently large affine subspace of the Boolean cube, and suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. The proof refines gate elimination: restrict inputs so that gates disappear while retaining enough difficulty in the restricted function. Raising the constant was a substantial advance, but any fixed constant still falls short of the present target.

Cavalar and Oliveira’s 2025 work develops another route through the fusion method and combinatorial covering problems. It translates circuit lower-bound questions into suitably defined two-dimensional covers and proves strong bounds for random graphs. The remaining challenge is obtaining the necessary explicit cover lower bounds. A reformulation that can express the desired hardness is valuable, but does not yet provide the hard polynomial-time function.

Two 2026 developments clarify proof techniques. Carmosino, Dang and Jackman formalize convergent gate simplification in selected bases and construct efficient refuters for a classical parity lower bound. Their constructive proof notion concerns finding errors in proposed small circuits; it is additional structure on a lower-bound proof, rather than a superlinear size bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision studies natural proofs specifically for linear maps represented by matrices. Under the stated cryptographic assumptions, pseudorandom matrices with unusually small circuits obstruct large, efficiently recognizable classes of hard matrices. Different constructions yield barriers above near-linear or linear size. These are conditional restrictions on a defined proof strategy, not an impossibility theorem for proving the desired lower bound by other means.
why: This asks for the first unbounded improvement over linear size for an efficiently computable unrestricted circuit task. It isolates a basic gap between knowing that hard functions abound and proving hardness for one explicitly computable function.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No superlinear unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bound for a polynomial-time length-preserving function was located. The question fixes the source’s explicitness convention; recent gate-simplification, covering and conditional natural-proofs results do not furnish such an example.
progress: 2018: Wigderson’s Open Problem 5.8 asks for an explicit n-input, n-output function with circuit complexity not O(n). | 2021–2022: Li–Yang improve the general B₂ single-output lower bound to 3.1n−o(n). | 2025-03-21: Cavalar–Oliveira publish a fusion and graph-cover framework for Boolean circuit lower bounds. | 2026-02-20: Carmosino–Dang–Jackman give constructive gate-elimination proofs for a classical linear lower bound in selected bases. | 2026-07-23: Raz’s revision adds a conditional natural-proofs barrier for superlinear lower bounds on explicit linear maps.
working_summary: A multi-output Boolean function can share intermediate computations among all its output bits. The question asks for one polynomial-time computable family whose unrestricted Boolean circuits exceed every fixed linear size bound. The saved formulation uses as many output bits as input bits. An arbitrary hard truth table does not satisfy the explicitness requirement. The project seeks a modest but fundamental lower bound demonstrating that some efficiently specified transformations intrinsically need more than a constant amount of circuit work per input bit.

title: Exponential circuit lower bounds for 3-SAT
importance_reason: A sweeping quantitative lower-bound target for the canonical efficiently verifiable problem, directly connected to nonuniform complexity and the foundations of exponential-time algorithms.
formal: For the explicitly encoded n-variable 3-SAT function SATₙ defined below, do there exist constants c>0 and n₀ such that CC(SATₙ)≥2^{cn} for every n≥n₀?
definitions: For each n≥1, enumerate all clauses on variables x₁,…,xₙ containing zero, one, two or three distinct variables, each with either sign. A zero-literal clause is false. There are M(n)=Σⱼ₌₀³2ʲ·binom(n,j) such clauses, with binom(n,j)=0 when j>n. Order them first by length, then by the increasing tuple of variable indices, then by their sign bits, with 0 meaning positive and 1 negated. The input is b∈{0,1}^{M(n)}; its jth bit says whether clause j is included. Let Φ_b be the conjunction of included clauses, with an empty conjunction true, and define SATₙ(b)=1 iff some assignment in {0,1}ⁿ satisfies Φ_b. Thus every input is valid. CC counts gates in a directed acyclic circuit with one output, arbitrary Boolean gates of at most two inputs, constants 0 and 1, unrestricted depth and fan-out, and exact correctness on every b. Inputs, constants and output wires are not gates. Circuits may be chosen nonuniformly for each n. The exponential parameter is the number n of variables, while the circuit has M(n)=Θ(n³) input bits. This fixed encoding and the restriction to 3-CNF are an editorial variable-parameter formulation of the source’s exponential SAT circuit question.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed eventual exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits, or prove its negation: for every c>0 and N≥1 there exists n≥N with CC(SATₙ)<2^{cn}. A circuit family of size 2^{o(n)} at all lengths would suffice for the negative direction, but that is stronger than the exact negation. A lower bound only against bounded-depth, monotone, formula, uniform or proof-system models does not settle the question. A circuit upper bound 2^{αn} for one fixed α>0 remains compatible with a smaller positive lower-bound exponent.
context:
SAT asks whether a collection of local constraints admits a simultaneous Boolean assignment. Here each selected clause prohibits one pattern on at most three variables. An assignment can be checked efficiently, but the conjecture says that deciding whether any assignment works requires exponentially many gates even when a different circuit may be designed separately for every n. It is a quantitative strengthening of the question whether NP has polynomial-size circuits.

Fixing the representation is essential. An n-variable 3-CNF can have Θ(n³) distinct clauses; writing a list of literals instead introduces binary variable names and a different bit length. These encodings are polynomially interconvertible, but a claim exponential in the literal number of input bits is not invariant under polynomial changes of encoding. This card therefore fixes both the representation and the variable parameter. The target is 2^{Ω(n)}, which is 2^{Ω(M^{1/3})} in the number M of circuit inputs.

There is a simple matching exponential scale for an upper bound. For each of the 2ⁿ assignments, form an AND requiring bⱼ=0 for every clause that assignment would falsify. OR these tests over all assignments. The resulting circuit decides SATₙ and has O(M(n)2ⁿ) gates. This is an explicit construction showing what exhaustive search means in the chosen nonuniform model. The conjecture allows substantial improvements in the exponential constant, while ruling out the absence of every positive eventual exponential lower bound.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis concerns uniform algorithms and the number of variables. Impagliazzo, Paturi and Zane’s sparsification lemma relates general fixed-width CNFs to disjunctions of sparse CNFs, with at most 2^{εn} branches for each fixed ε>0. This explains why variable and clause parameters are closely connected in exponential-time reductions. It does not automatically turn a uniform hypothesis into a lower bound against arbitrary circuits, and the precise almost-everywhere quantifiers on this card are part of its target.

Even much weaker general-circuit lower bounds remain elusive. Li and Yang prove 3.1N−o(N) gates for particular explicit single-output functions of N input bits. That is a theorem about carefully chosen affine dispersers, not an exponential lower bound for SAT. A counting argument can prove that most truth tables are exponentially hard, but it cannot identify SAT among those hard functions.

There has been important progress by linking faster satisfiability algorithms to lower bounds for other circuit classes. Williams proves that nondeterministic exponential time has languages without polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC restricts depth while allowing unbounded-fan-in Boolean and modular gates. The distinction matters in two places: the hard language need not be in NP, and the competing circuits are not unrestricted. This theorem demonstrates a powerful strategy without resolving this card.

Algorithmic progress continues within the exponential regime. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint refines the analysis of the existing PPSZ algorithm, reporting a randomized general-3-SAT running-time base of 1.307031578 and a slightly smaller base under uniqueness. The authors retain the same algorithm and unique-to-general lifting theorem; their improvement comes from a sharper combination of inequalities with rational certificates. These are upper bounds, with randomness and success guarantees, rather than lower bounds for exact circuits. A constant base above one remains compatible with the target.

A positive answer would rule out polynomial-size circuits for this NP decision problem and therefore imply P≠NP. A negative answer would not imply P=NP: circuits of size 2^{√n}, for example, would refute an eventual exponential bound while still being superpolynomial in the input size, and a nonuniform circuit family need not be constructible by one efficient algorithm.
why: A precise worst-case formulation of the belief that satisfiability retains exponential complexity even with arbitrary nonuniform preprocessing by input size. It separates exponential hardness from polynomial hardness and from bounds tied to a restricted computational model.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unconditional exponential lower bound for unrestricted circuits deciding variable-parameterized 3-SAT was located. The card specifies an almost-everywhere bound, an explicit total clause-incidence encoding, and n as the variable count; it does not assert exponential hardness in the Θ(n³) encoding length.
progress: 1998–2001: Impagliazzo–Paturi–Zane develop sparsification and reductions preserving subexponential complexity in variable parameters. | 2011–2014: Williams establishes NEXP lower bounds for constant-depth ACC circuits using satisfiability algorithms. | 2018: Wigderson states the exponential SAT circuit conjecture; this card makes its parameter and encoding explicit. | 2021–2022: Li–Yang prove a 3.1N−o(N) general-circuit bound for explicit functions; it is neither exponential nor a SAT bound. | 2026-07-12: Jiang–Cai report a small improvement in the randomized PPSZ upper exponent for general 3-SAT.
working_summary: The saved 3-SAT family uses a fixed encoding of which clauses on n variables are present. The conjecture asks for circuit size exponential in n, even when every input length gets its own arbitrary circuit. Its scale is stronger than merely excluding polynomial-size circuits. The variable count differs from the total number of encoded clause bits, so the parameter must remain explicit. The project aims to prove that searching for a satisfying assignment retains essentially exponential difficulty even under nonuniform computation.

title: Does PH equal PSPACE?
importance_reason: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
formal: Is PH=PSPACE? Equivalently, is there a fixed integer k≥0 such that the truth problem for fully quantified Boolean formulas belongs to Σᵖ_k?
definitions: Languages are subsets of {0,1}*. PSPACE contains the languages decided by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input of length n while using at most C(n+1)^a work-tape cells, for constants C,a depending on the machine. The read-only input tape is not charged, and there is no polynomial time limit. Set Σᵖ₀=P, the deterministic polynomial-time languages. For k≥1, a language L lies in Σᵖ_k if there are a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when ∃y₁∀y₂∃y₃⋯Q_k y_k R(x,y₁,…,y_k)=1, where each y_i ranges over {0,1}^{p(|x|)} and Q_k is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Set PH=⋃_{k≥0}Σᵖ_k. The integer k is fixed for an entire language; it cannot grow with an input. Machines and predicates are uniform and have no advice or oracle. A fully quantified Boolean formula is an explicit Boolean formula using AND, OR and NOT, preceded by quantifiers binding every variable exactly once; variable names and the entire formula are binary encoded. Its truth uses the ordinary successive quantifier semantics over {0,1}. The language TQBF consists of its true well-formed encodings; malformed strings are rejected. The number of quantifier blocks in TQBF inputs is unrestricted.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves PSPACE⊆PH; the reverse inclusion is already known. Equivalently it places TQBF in one fixed Σᵖ_k, which would put every PSPACE language in that same level by polynomial-time reductions. A negative resolution proves that some PSPACE language, equivalently TQBF, is outside every fixed level. A separation at one fixed level or an oracle-relative result alone does not answer the question.
context:
Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

The formula ∀x∃y (x=y) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula ∃y∀x (x=y) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some Σᵖ_k and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore PH=PSPACE would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation PH≠PSPACE alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.
why: Separates unbounded polynomial-space computation from a bounded number of polynomial-time alternations.
status_note: No established resolution found in the primary-source search through 11 September 2026. The checked 2026 results concern completeness and relativized class relationships. Historical preprint claims of equality or non-collapse are not counted as settled theorems; their proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2007: The cited textbook draft states TQBF completeness, PH⊆PSPACE and the collapse consequence of equality. | 2026-02: New multilevel optimization completeness theorems preserve the bounded-level versus PSPACE classification without separating the classes. | 2026-02: A sparse-oracle construction separates PH from PSPACE while allowing PH to collapse; the result is explicitly relativized.
working_summary: Does every polynomial-space decision problem lie in the polynomial hierarchy? PH allows a fixed number of alternating quantifier blocks for each language. PSPACE also describes polynomial-time alternation with no fixed bound on the number of alternations. Equality would put TQBF in one finite level and hence collapse PH to that level. Completeness and oracle results illuminate the distinction without settling the ordinary class equality.

title: Does NEXP require superpolynomial constant-depth threshold circuits?
importance_reason: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
formal: Is there a language L∈NEXP such that, for every fixed circuit depth d≥1, every fixed exponent k≥1, every constant C≥1 and every N≥1, some n≥N has no depth-at-most-d Boolean circuit of size at most C(n+1)^k with AND, OR, NOT and majority gates that computes L correctly on every n-bit input? Equivalently, is NEXP⊄TC⁰ for nonuniform TC⁰?
definitions: NEXP=⋃_{a≥1}NTIME(2^{n^a}): a language is accepted by one nondeterministic Turing machine whose every computation branch halts within exponential time 2^{n^a}, up to a constant factor, for some fixed a. An input is in the language exactly when at least one branch accepts. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, constants 0 and 1 and one output. AND and OR may have any positive fan-in; NOT has one input. A majority gate on m inputs outputs 1 when at least ⌈m/2⌉ of them are 1, including a tie when m is even. Fan-out is unrestricted. Size is the number of operation gates plus wires. Repeated connections count individually, so their multiplicities cannot encode uncharged weights. Depth is the maximum number of operation gates on an input-to-output path. All circuits compute exactly on every input; no average-case correctness or randomness is allowed. TC⁰ consists of languages having one fixed depth bound and one polynomial size bound across all input lengths. The family may be nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct its nth circuit. NEXP machines are uniform and have no oracle or advice. The formal quantifiers permit the lower bound to be witnessed at infinitely many input lengths, rather than requiring failure at every sufficiently large length.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves that one language in NEXP has no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family, with depth and polynomial exponent both unrestricted constants. A negative resolution proves NEXP⊆TC⁰. A bound ruling out only n^k gates for one fixed k, or only one fixed circuit depth, does not by itself establish the displayed separation.
context:
A constant-depth circuit applies only a bounded number of layers, but a majority gate can inspect many inputs at once. For three bits it returns 1 on 110 and 111, while returning 0 on 100. Thus majority is not a bounded-fan-in local operation. TC⁰ permits many such gates in parallel and lets their outputs feed later layers. The depth bound stays fixed as input length grows, while the number of gates and wires may be any fixed polynomial.

Parity is difficult for constant-depth circuits using only AND, OR and NOT, but it is easy for majority circuits. A threshold test for whether an n-bit input has at least t ones is implementable with a majority gate and suitable constants. Two adjacent threshold tests identify an exact number of ones, and taking an OR over odd counts gives parity with a polynomial number of gates in constant depth. This example shows why a lower bound for the weaker gate set cannot simply be reused after majority is added.

The hard language need only have a nondeterministic exponential-time algorithm; it need not be in P or NP. That is a generous uniform computation budget, making the lack of a known separation striking. Nevertheless, counting the truth tables that have no small circuits does not automatically identify one language within this budget. The assertion requires one language that defeats every fixed polynomial size and every fixed depth, rather than a different unrestricted truth table for each desired bound.

Williams proves that NEXP does not have polynomial-size ACC circuits. ACC allows constant-depth Boolean circuits with gates testing the number of 1 inputs modulo a fixed integer. TC⁰ can implement these modular tests by combining threshold comparisons. It is therefore a more permissive class, and excluding ACC does not exclude TC⁰. The original 2011 reference supports this nearby theorem, not the stronger conclusion asked here.

Chen, Tal and Wang prove super-quadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits, with a hard function in E^NP, exponential time with an NP oracle. Their n^(2.5−ε) bound is still a fixed polynomial and addresses depth two. A September preprint claims near-cubic wire bounds in that setting; its source also carries a critical comment, and it is not independently verified here. Wire counts and gate counts are different quantitative parameters. Ren and Williams obtain near-maximum general circuit bounds with a promise-Merlin–Arthur oracle and one bit of advice. None of these statements supplies the required ordinary NEXP language outside all of nonuniform TC⁰.
why: Tests whether the algorithmic approach to circuit lower bounds can cross the threshold-gate barrier.
status_note: No NEXP⊄TC⁰ resolution found through 11 September 2026. The checked March, July and September results retain different hard-language models or fixed depth and polynomial quantitative bounds. The September preprint has a source comment raising concerns and is recorded as an unverified claim.
progress: 2011: Williams separates nondeterministic exponential time from polynomial-size ACC circuits, a subclass of TC⁰. | 2026-03: Chen–Tal–Wang prove n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two threshold circuits and a hard function in E^NP. | 2026-07: Ren–Williams prove near-maximum unrestricted bounds for a class with a promise-MA oracle and advice. | 2026-09: Near-cubic depth-two wire bounds are claimed in a preprint with a critical source comment; this is not a TC⁰ separation.
working_summary: Does some NEXP language escape all polynomial-size constant-depth majority circuits? Majority gates make this circuit class substantially more powerful than constant-depth AND/OR circuits. Williams established the corresponding separation for ACC circuits with fixed-modulus gates. Recent threshold-circuit bounds still restrict depth or polynomial size and use different hard-language classes. The target requires one ordinary NEXP language outside the entire nonuniform class TC⁰.

title: NL versus UL
importance_reason: A basic class equality tying directed reachability, isolation, pseudorandomness and the structure of low-memory witnesses.
formal: Is NL=UL? Equivalently, is there a single nondeterministic Turing machine that decides directed s–t reachability using O(log N) work space and polynomial time, has exactly one accepting computation on every reachable instance, and has no accepting computation on every unreachable instance, where N is the explicit input length?
definitions: An input consists of a finite directed graph with labelled vertices and explicitly listed edges, together with vertices s,t. Reachability asks whether a directed path from s to t exists; the length-zero path is allowed when s=t. A machine has a read-only two-way input tape, O(log(N+2)) read/write work-tape cells over a fixed finite alphabet, and a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation. Every computation branch must halt within a polynomial in N. NL permits any positive number of accepting branches on yes inputs; UL permits exactly one. On no inputs both classes require zero accepting branches. A branch is a sequence of transition choices, not merely its endpoint or output. Rejecting branches need not be unique. Machines are uniform finite programs without advice, randomness, oracle access or additional catalytic storage. The equality asks whether every NL language has some equivalent UL machine; it does not require a computable compiler converting descriptions of arbitrary machines. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logspace reductions, so its UL membership suffices.
answer_criterion: Prove a uniform O(log N)-space unambiguous algorithm for all directed reachability inputs, or prove that some NL language is not in UL. Any positive construction must remain unambiguous on every input without assuming that the supplied graph itself has a unique path. A polynomial-time algorithm using O((log N)^{3/2}) space, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, or an unproved hardness hypothesis is progress rather than a solution.
context:
A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, NL=UL would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing L=NL. A proof that NL≠UL would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since L⊆UL⊆NL.

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary NL=UL question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using O((log N)^{3/2}) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue NSPACE[n]⊆USPACE[O(n)], under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length ℓ, without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude 2^{Ω(log w·log ℓ)}, so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.
why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.
status_note: The checked general unconditional simulation still uses O(log^{3/2} N) space. The 2025–2026 hardness-based results remain conditional, catalytic results use additional resources, and Hoza’s July 2026 lower bound excludes only oblivious isolation. No settlement of uniform NL=UL found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1997–2000: Reinhardt–Allender show that min-isolation supports unambiguous reachability and prove the nonuniform equality NL/poly=UL/poly. | 2017–2019: Van Melkebeek–Prakriya obtain a polynomial-time unambiguous simulation using O((log N)^{3/2}) space; CCC 2017 and SICOMP 2019. | 2025-06-18: Doron–Pyne–Tell–Williams derive linear-space unambiguity from substantially weakened but still unproved uniform circuit lower bounds. | 2026-02-06: Arvind–Chakraborty–Datta’s revised catalytic isolation result uses extra restorable memory and UL oracle access. | 2026-03-30: Pyne–Tell survey recent isolation results, distinguishing the classical conditional NL=UL theorem from newer conditional linear-space simulations. | 2026-07-23: Hoza proves that deterministic oblivious min-isolation for all layered digraphs requires quasipolynomial-size weights in the general parameter regime.
working_summary: An ordinary nondeterministic reachability algorithm can have many accepting paths of computation. UL requires at most one accepting computation for each input while retaining logarithmic workspace. The question asks whether this unambiguity restriction changes the class NL. The machine may still have many rejecting branches, so this is weaker than demanding determinism. The project seeks to isolate a unique successful witness efficiently, clarifying whether ambiguity itself is a source of computational power in small-space graph problems.

title: Can directed reachability be decided in deterministic logarithmic space?
importance_reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices {1,...,n} and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to L=NL.
definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so s=t is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic O(log N) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has N=Theta(n^2) bits, O(log N)=O(log n). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
context:
A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within n−1 edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses O(log² n) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, NL=coNL shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.
why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly retains the directed logspace question, and the February 2026 hardness result concerns restricted graph classes without resolving it. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution of L versus NL.
progress: 1970: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in O(s²) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an O(log² n)-space algorithm. | 1987–1988: Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular NL=coNL, so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms. | 2005–2008: Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem. | 2025: Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to O(log n). | 2026: Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

The question asks for a deterministic algorithm using the same tiny workspace on an explicitly stored graph. Repeated input scans are allowed, but a full visited array or search frontier is not. title: The inverse-polynomial-soundness sliding-scale PCP conjecture
importance_reason: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
formal: Do constants a,b,c>0 and q≥1 exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a log₂(N+2) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most (N+2)^b symbols over an alphabet of size at most (N+2)^b, with perfect completeness and soundness at most (N+2)^(−c)?
definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with O(log N) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most (N+2)^(−c). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.
why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2015: The source achieves inverse-polynomial soundness with O(polyloglog N) queries rather than a constant number.

title: P_R versus NP_R in the Blum–Shub–Smale model
importance_reason: The defining complexity-class question for exact computation over the reals, connecting TCS to algebraic geometry and numerical computation.
formal: Is P_ℝ=NP_ℝ for the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered field of real numbers?
definitions: Inputs are finite tuples x∈ℝ^n, with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. It can store and copy real numbers, perform +, −, ×, and division by a nonzero number, and branch on the sign or equality to zero of a stored real, at unit cost per operation; the ordinary BSS input, output and register-shift operations are included. P_ℝ consists of subsets of the disjoint union of the spaces ℝ^n decidable by one such deterministic machine in polynomially many steps as a function of n. NP_ℝ consists of sets for which membership of x is equivalent to existence of a real witness y of length bounded by a polynomial in n that is accepted by one deterministic BSS verifier in polynomially many steps. Machine constants are finite and independent of input length; witnesses may contain arbitrary reals. The target is equality of these classes, not equality in a finite-precision or bit-cost model.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The BSS model treats exact field operations and order tests as elementary computation. Its version of nondeterminism allows real witnesses and captures basic real algebraic feasibility problems.

This separation is a foundational question about algebraic computation over a continuum. Classical P versus NP does not by itself answer it: the input representation, cost model and certificates differ.
why: The defining complexity-class question for exact computation over the reals, connecting TCS to algebraic geometry and numerical computation.
status_note: Open target supported by the dated sources. Literature was checked on 11 September 2026, with the limits recorded here; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The full real-constant BSS convention is explicit. This is not a duplicate of the atlas’s classical P versus NP target.
progress: 1997: The survey develops the model and its central P_ℝ versus NP_ℝ question; the literature check found no established resolution.

title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
importance_reason: Determines the representation-size cost of determinism when compiling knowledge into a form supporting exact model counting.
formal: Is there a family of polynomial-size DNF formulas for which every equivalent deterministic decomposable negation-normal-form circuit has superpolynomial size?
context:
This is a SIZE lower bound, not a polynomial-time conversion question; #P-hardness already rules out a generic efficient conversion under standard assumptions. DNNF versus d-DNNF separation alone does not settle it.

Prior addition asks about deterministic equivalence testing of d-DNNF. TCS-0306 concerns complementation, and TCS-0496 concerns database lineages. None is the DNF versus d-DNNF size separation. TCS-0308 is the general Boolean formula-versus-circuit size gap (full linked section read); it does not require either DNF inputs or d-DNNF outputs.
why: Determines the representation-size cost of determinism when compiling knowledge into a form supporting exact model counting.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. This is a SIZE lower bound, not a polynomial-time conversion question; #P-hardness already rules out a generic efficient conversion under standard assumptions. DNNF versus d-DNNF separation alone does not settle it.
working_summary: A DNF formula describes satisfying assignments as a union of conjunctions, whose cases may overlap. The proposal asks whether some polynomial-size DNFs require superpolynomial-size deterministic decomposable circuits for the same Boolean function. Determinism requires disjoint alternatives, while decomposability requires conjunctions to separate their variables. A separation would show that imposing these useful structural restrictions can force an inherent representation-size increase. The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

title: The Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
importance_reason: Connects the arithmetic nature of numbers to an elementary resource bound on computing their digits.
formal: For every integer b≥2 and every real x∈[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
definitions: Write x=∑_{n≥1}d_n b^(−n), where d_n∈{0,…,b−1}, using the unique expansion that is not eventually all b−1; a terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means x=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. Algebraic means P(x)=0 for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant C≥1 such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing t_n for the step at which d_n appears, 1≤t_(n+1)−t_n≤C for every n≥1. The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.
context:
For example, 1/7=0.142857142857… in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, √2−1 is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies x²+2x−1=0. The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from b^n supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.
why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.
status_note: Explicitly open in the checked 2024 research paper and June 2026 thesis abstract. The May 2026 automata paper uses a different input representation. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. A June 2026 listing titled “FIS Application: Hartmanis-Stearns” supplied no theorem statement or full text at https://uvsmpublications.com/publications/fis-application-hartmanis-stearns/ and is not evidence of a resolution. Proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1970: Linear-time and real-time sequence generation are shown to coincide for multitape machines. | 2020: The published revisiting paper proves transcendence restrictions for pushdown and exponential-growth morphic models. | 2024: ICALP work proves additional word-based transcendence results while explicitly retaining the full conjecture. | 2026: Automata compute digits from specially represented inputs; a June thesis abstract still describes the general conjecture as open.
working_summary: The question concerns a fixed machine that prints all digits of a real number with bounded delay between outputs. Every rational number permits this because its expansion is eventually periodic. The conjecture says that any irrational number generated this quickly must be transcendental. It quantifies over unrestricted deterministic multitape machines, beyond the restricted automata covered by known partial results. A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.

title: Do stable ternary compaction functions have linear-size Boolean circuits?
importance_reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.
formal: Is there an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every integer n≥1, the function S_n:{0,1,2}^n→{0,1,2}^n that removes all symbols 2 and appends the same number of 2s on the right, preserving the order of the other symbols, is computed by a Boolean circuit with at most Cn gates in the model below?
definitions: Encode symbols 0,1,2 as 00,01,10 respectively. The circuit has 2n input bits and 2n output bits, with arbitrary fan-out, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and optional Boolean constant gates. Size counts all non-input gates, including constants; wires and output designations cost nothing. Correctness is required only on concatenations of the three valid encodings; output on inputs containing 11 is unrestricted. If i_1<...<i_m are exactly the indices with a_i≠2, the required decoded output is a_(i_1)...a_(i_m) followed by n−m copies of 2. In particular, 0s and 1s retain their relative order. The circuit may depend on n; no uniform construction algorithm, depth bound, monotonicity restriction or indivisible-record model is imposed. The constant C is independent of n.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A sequential scan can retain the 0s and 1s and place the dummy symbols at the end. The circuit question asks whether this global rearrangement can also be implemented with only linearly many bounded-fan-in Boolean operations.

Stability makes the retained binary string part of the answer. Counting how many symbols of each kind occur, or outputting all 0s before all 1s, would discard the required order and compute another function.

Small unstable-compaction circuits do not resolve the stable version. Lower bounds in indivisible-record models and results conditional on network-coding conjectures must likewise be distinguished from an unconditional lower bound in this unrestricted Boolean model.
why: Test linear circuit size for a concrete, sequentially simple function whose stability requirement preserves substantial information.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional resolution of Regan’s exact stable ternary Boolean-circuit target was found. The cited unstable-compaction and conditional results do not settle this model.
progress: 2007: Regan poses linear Boolean-circuit size for stable ternary compaction. | 2020–2021: Asharov, Lin and Shi obtain small circuits for unstable compaction and short-key sorting while distinguishing the stable task.
working_summary: Stable ternary compaction moves every 2 to the end while preserving the order of all 0s and 1s. The question is whether every input length admits a Boolean circuit of size proportional to that length. The circuits use a fixed bounded-fan-in basis and may have arbitrary depth and fan-out. Stability retains the original binary sequence, so ordinary ternary sorting is insufficient. The target supplies a concrete function for studying the limits of linear-size circuits.

title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
importance_reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.
formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants c_M >= 1 and an integer d_M >= 1 so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair (x,M(x)), uses at most c_M S_M(x) tape cells, and takes at most c_M T_M(x)^{d_M} steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here S_M counts total storage including input and output, and T_M is at least the input length, as defined below.
definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. S_M(x) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. T_M(x) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and M(x), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
context:
Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with O(S) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.
why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.
status_note: The cited 2001 and 2005 works document the unresolved general tradeoff. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of the simultaneous polynomial-time/O(S)-space target, but no recent primary source explicitly certifying this precise target was located. Current openness remains less well verified than the historical formulation.
progress: 1989: Bennett proves reversible simulation in O(T^{1+epsilon}) time and O(S log T) space for fixed positive epsilon, among other tradeoffs. | 2001: Buhrman, Tromp, and Vitányi interpolate between low-space exponential-time and higher-space polynomial-time simulations. | 2005: Vitányi identifies simultaneous time and space efficiency as the main unresolved general-simulation question.

title: Doubly efficient IP = PSPACE for the full time range
importance_reason: Tests the efficiency limits of the IP = PSPACE phenomenon when both verifier and prover costs matter, across the full time range.
formal: Suppose a language is decided in polynomial space and time $T(n)$. Does it have an interactive proof with a $\operatorname{poly}(n)$-time verifier, a $\operatorname{poly}(T(n))$-time honest prover, and a constant completeness–soundness gap? Soundness must hold against arbitrarily powerful cheating provers. The target includes $T$ beyond the quasipolynomial range.
definitions: Use uniform classical randomized verification with completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3. For every polynomial-space decider with time-constructible bound T(n) at least n, a protocol with the stated bounds is sought. Polynomial exponents may depend on the decider, but not on n.
answer_criterion: Prove the specified verifier/prover time guarantees for every polynomial-space language and its time bound, or prove the negation of that universal statement. Improving only a restricted range of T is partial progress.
context:
IP = PSPACE alone does not guarantee that producing the proof costs only a polynomial in the original computation time.

Interactive proofs separate the effort of checking a computation from the effort of producing a convincing transcript. The usual class equality allows an honest prover to use enormous resources. That is enough for a complexity-class statement, but does not establish that proof generation is efficient relative to the computation being certified.

The target compares the honest prover directly with the original running time T. A prover using a polynomial in T would have controlled overhead even when the verifier has only polynomial time in the input length. Soundness still has to hold against a cheating prover of unlimited power; restricting the honest prover does not weaken the adversary in the definition.
why: This asks whether a long, space-efficient computation can be verified without hiding an excessive cost in the honest prover.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: FOCS 2025: The previous range cited in the paper was $T(n)=n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}$. | 2026-06-21: The direct construction extends the range to $T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}$. It does not cover arbitrary polynomial-space computation times.
working_summary: An interactive proof lets a verifier check a claim through conversation with a prover. The question asks whether polynomial-space computations taking time T can be verified in polynomial input time using an honest prover running in polynomial T time. The requirement extends across the full time range, beyond quasipolynomial computations. This would make proof generation efficient relative to the computation being certified, strengthening the resource content of IP=PSPACE. The saved review stresses that soundness must still withstand arbitrarily powerful cheating provers, despite the efficiency requirement imposed on the honest one.

title: Does the two-input formula noise threshold also govern general circuits?
importance_reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.
formal: For p in [0,1/2), let Reliable(p) mean that there exists a constant delta>0 such that for every n>=1 and every Boolean function f:{0,1}^n->{0,1}, some finite circuit C of the kind below satisfies Pr[C(x)=f(x)]>=1/2+delta for every input x. Is Reliable(p) true exactly for p<(3-sqrt(7))/4? In particular, is it false at the boundary as well as above it?
definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input sources x_1,...,x_n, constant sources 0 and 1, gates of fan-in at most two, and one designated output wire. Any Boolean function of a gate's input bits is allowed. Each gate is evaluated once in topological order and independently flips its correct Boolean output with probability exactly p. All outgoing wires from that gate carry the same resulting bit; reuse does not generate fresh independent copies. Inputs, constants, and wires are noiseless. Every computational gate, including the output gate when present, obeys the noise rule; there is no extra noiseless decoder. Fan-out is unrestricted, and different incoming paths may share gates. C may depend on p,n,f but not on x. Its size and construction time are unrestricted. The probability is solely over independent gate failures. Delta may depend on p but is common to all n,f,x. A formula is the restricted case in which computational gates have fan-out at most one, with input variables still allowed to occur repeatedly.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated equivalence for the full interval 0<=p<1/2, including p=(3-sqrt(7))/4. A proof or refutation must use the specified independent gate-flip model and a uniform positive correctness advantage across all functions.
context:
The success advantage must be fixed before choosing a function or its number of inputs. Allowing it to shrink with the function would describe a much weaker task. The noisy output itself is read, so the target does not assume an unlimited perfect final computation.

Unger establishes the exact threshold for two-input formulas, extending the earlier NAND-gate result, and conjectures the same threshold for circuits. Shared subcomputations correlate wire values even though the underlying gate failures are independent.

Later work studies asymmetric noise on AND and XOR gates and relates reliability to amplification. Its different gate-specific error assumptions and formula bounds do not settle the common-noise, unrestricted-fan-out proposition here.
why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.
status_note: The circuit-threshold conjecture is explicit in Unger's 2008 paper. The later asymmetric-noise paper was checked as a different model. Searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution, but did not locate a recent primary source explicitly reaffirming this exact conjecture. Historical openness should not be read as a fresh status certification.
progress: 2008: Unger proves the formula threshold (3-sqrt(7))/4, including impossibility at equality, and states the circuit extension as a conjecture. | 2023-05-01: Version 5 of Shutty, Wootters, and Hayden develops asymmetric-noise results and distinguishes formulas from general circuits.

title: Is d-DNNF closed under negation with only polynomial size growth?
importance_reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.
formal: Do a constant c>0 and an integer k>=1 exist such that, for every finite variable set X and every d-DNNF circuit C over X of size s, there is a d-DNNF circuit D over X of size at most c(s+1)^k computing the Boolean complement of C on every assignment X->{0,1}? No algorithm for finding D within that bound is required.
definitions: An NNF circuit is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph whose leaves are constants 0,1 or literals x,not-x for x in X, and whose internal nodes are AND or OR gates. Edges run from a gate to its inputs. The variable set of a subcircuit comprises the variables occurring in its reachable literals. Decomposable means that the input subcircuits of every AND gate have pairwise disjoint variable sets. Deterministic means that no assignment to X makes two different inputs of any OR gate both true. A d-DNNF satisfies both properties. Size is the total number of vertices plus edges; fan-in is arbitrary and part of that size. Evaluation has the usual Boolean meaning. No negation gates above leaves, additional variables, or requirement of compatibility with a common variable decomposition tree is allowed. Constants c,k are independent of X and C. The output D may use any decompositions meeting these conditions.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal polynomial size bound, or prove that no constants c,k satisfy it. Algorithmic difficulty of producing a small complement alone does not refute this size-existence statement.
context:
Decomposability prevents conjunctions from sharing variables and determinism prevents disjunctions from sharing satisfying assignments. Negating a circuit syntactically need not preserve both properties.

Structured d-DNNFs additionally respect a variable decomposition tree. The 2024 negative result for that restricted class cannot be transferred automatically to unrestricted d-DNNF, since a complementary circuit here may use other decompositions.

The STACS 2026 discussion retains complementation as an open question. The separate algorithmic question asks for a polynomial-time procedure producing the complement. Such a procedure implies the size bound on this card; the converse is not established. Both targets are retained because an existence theorem would settle a representation barrier without necessarily supplying the algorithmic transformation.

The stronger polynomial-time construction question is retained as TCS-0306. The existence of small complementary circuits does not by itself give an efficient algorithm for constructing them.
why: Deterministic decomposable circuits represent Boolean solution sets while supporting exact counting. Closure under complement asks whether a compact representation of satisfying assignments necessarily gives a comparably compact representation of nonsatisfying assignments, independently of construction time.
status_note: Explicitly open in the 2026 STACS discussion and in the maintained primary question list accessed 11 September 2026. The structured-class impossibility is distinct. The existing algorithmic-negation card TCS-0306 asks a stronger uniform construction question, so it is not replaced by this nonuniform size question.
progress: 2024: Vinall-Smeeth proves that structured d-DNNF is not closed under polynomial-size negation. | 2026: Amarilli and coauthors identify unstructured d-DNNF complementation as an open issue in their STACS paper. | 2026-09-11: Amarilli's maintained question list explicitly distinguishes the unresolved polynomial-size question from polynomial-time construction.

title: Supercubic uniform formula lower bounds for SAT
importance_reason: Improving explicit formula or depth-three circuit lower bounds would go beyond established lower-bound techniques.
formal: Does there exist a constant ε>0 such that no LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family computing SATₙ for every n has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves?
definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for xᵢ, 1 for ¬xᵢ), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: ⌊log₂i⌋ zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
importance_reason: Stronger time-space or uniform circuit lower bounds would constrain natural satisfiability and graph problems in standard resource regimes.
formal: For every space-constructible function s:ℕ→ℕ with s(n)≥⌈log₂(n+2)⌉, is every language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) decidable deterministically in o(s(n)²) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an O(s(n))-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace g_D(n) on n-bit inputs satisfies lim(n→∞) g_D(n)/s(n)²=0?
definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. NSPACE(O(s(n))) denotes languages with such a machine using at most C s(n) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on 1ⁿ can output 1^s(n) using O(s(n)) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving s^(2−ε) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of s(n)². Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in s(n)², a simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.
context:
A nondeterministic machine can choose among several next moves and accepts if some sequence of choices succeeds. A deterministic simulation must decide the same question without those choices. Savitch’s theorem shows that squaring the workspace is enough, even though the simulation may take much longer.

If a nondeterministic computation uses about s cells, the target is a deterministic simulation whose memory divided by s² tends to zero. A bound such as s²/log(s+2) would qualify, while 0.01s² would not. These expressions illustrate the meaning of little-o; the question imposes no particular rate of improvement.

For s(n) of order log n, the target becomes deterministic o(log² n) space for every language in nondeterministic logarithmic space. This includes directed reachability: given a directed graph and two vertices, decide whether there is a directed path between them. The full card quantifies over all admitted s and does not restrict inputs to a special graph family.
