title: Is weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
definitions: A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
context:
Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.
why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.
status_note: Open in the original 2024 question and the maintained list accessed 10 September 2026. Searches did not locate a polynomial algorithm or hardness resolution. TCS-0485 is a duplicate seminar pointer to the same formulation, not a separate open question.

The project tests whether the strong disjointness promise still helps when every term must be defeated simultaneously while optimizing an additive objective over the complement.

title: Do unrestricted weights make polynomial-size linear decision lists stronger?
importance_reason: Asks whether numerical weight magnitude remains a source of expressive power once threshold decision lists may have unrestricted alternation, linking list complexity to threshold-circuit barriers. The existing numerical score is retained.
formal: Is LDL_polywt a proper subset of LDL, where both classes allow polynomially many linear-threshold queries and arbitrary alternation depth, but LDL_polywt requires every integer weight and threshold to have polynomially bounded magnitude?
definitions: A Boolean function family is f=(fₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1})_{n≥1}. A linear decision list consists of s ordered pairs (qᵢ,bᵢ) and a default bit b_{s+1}. On input x, it returns bᵢ at the first i for which qᵢ(x)=1, or the default if all tests fail. Each query is qᵢ(x)=1 iff wᵢ,₀+∑_{j=1}^n wᵢ,ⱼxⱼ>0, with integer weights wᵢ,ⱼ, including the offset wᵢ,₀. Allowing a test for qᵢ(x)=0 is equivalent on integer-valued sums to another query of this form. Size is the number s of queries; weights’ bit lengths are not charged as extra queries. LDL consists of all families admitting, for some fixed constants c,C>0, lists of size at most C(n+1)^c at every n, with no bound on integer weights. LDL_polywt requires in addition constants b,B>0 such that every weight in every list has absolute value at most B(n+1)^b. Constants are uniform across input lengths and queries, but may depend on the family. Neither class requires an algorithm generating the lists. Polynomial magnitude is stronger than polynomial bit length: a weight 2ⁿ has n+1 bits but is not polynomially bounded in magnitude. There is no additional bound on the number of changes in the output sequence (b₁,…,b_{s+1}); it may grow as large as the list length. Proper inclusion means that some family lies in LDL but not LDL_polywt. Equivalently, for that family, every pair of fixed polynomial size and weight bounds fails at some input lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove that some family has polynomial-size unrestricted-weight lists but has no family of polynomial-size, polynomial-magnitude-weight lists, or prove LDL_polywt=LDL by establishing such bounded-weight representations for every LDL family. A lower bound that applies only while alternation depth is restricted does not settle this target.
context:
A threshold test can compare a weighted sum of input bits with a threshold. A decision list checks several such conditions in order, and the first success chooses the output. This model permits branching by the order of tests, even though it is simpler than an arbitrary decision tree.

An individual threshold can use exponentially large integer weights. The question asks whether polynomially many tests with polynomially bounded weights can always reproduce the behavior of a polynomial-size list that uses those large numbers. Merely proving that one threshold requires large weights is insufficient.

A list returning 0,1,0,1 in successive branches switches output value several times. The paper proves weight-sensitive separations under a bound on such alternation. Once that restriction is removed, additional changes in output value may increase the power of bounded-weight lists.

For the greater-than function, the paper gives an exponential-in-n/k lower bound for bounded-weight lists at bounded alternation parameter k, while an unrestricted-weight threshold suffices. This does not exclude polynomial-size bounded-weight lists with much larger alternation, so the full-class inclusion remains the distinct question.
why: Tests whether numerical weight magnitude is an intrinsic source of power in threshold decision lists, or whether enough branching in a polynomial-length list can eliminate it. The answer would clarify the role of weights in a model closely connected to threshold circuit lower bounds.

title: Does Nephew resist efficient decision-tree reductions to Lossy-Code?
importance_reason: A concrete candidate separating natural total randomized query search from lossy compression. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Prove or refute the source’s concrete conjecture Nephew ≰dt Lossy-Code. In Nephew, given oracle access to two total functions f,g:V→V on an arbitrary finite nonempty set V, output v∈V such that f(f(g(v)))≠f(v) or f(g(v))=v. The relation ≼dt is the deterministic polylogarithmic-complexity reduction defined below; replacing it with randomized or white-box reductions changes the question.
definitions: Encode V by integer labels and encode the two function tables in binary. Let N=|V| and let n denote the total table bit length, Θ(N log(N+1)); the tables are accessed through queries, not supplied for free as readable circuit descriptions. A function-value query can be simulated by O(log(N+1)) bit queries, so either interface gives the same polylogarithmic scale. Lossy-Code_{M→2M} supplies oracle functions e:[M]→[2M] and d:[2M]→[M] and asks for z∈[2M] with e(d(z))≠z. The letters e,d denote expansion and compression; they are unrelated to Nephew’s f,g. For search relations R on n input bits and S on m input bits, an S-formulation of R has a deterministic decision tree F_i computing each target bit i from the source input x, and, for every possible target solution o, a decision tree G_o decoding a source output. It must satisfy (F(x),o)∈S⇒(x,G_o(x))∈R for every x and every valid target solution o. If d_* is the maximum depth of these trees, the reduction’s complexity is log m+d_*. R≼dt S means that this is at most (log(n+2))^{O(1)} for the entire family, with a fixed exponent. The reduction is nonuniform in input length and may describe a target table of quasipolynomial or larger-than-polynomial size as long as log m is polylogarithmic; it cannot inspect that whole table. TFZPPdt consists of total search families with polylogarithmic verification-query complexity and randomized polylogarithmic-depth query algorithms which never return an invalid solution, may return failure, and fail with probability at most 1/3 on each input.
answer_criterion: Show that no family of Lossy-Code formulations of Nephew has complexity bounded by any fixed power of log n; or refute the candidate by giving such a formulation and proving that every target solution decodes correctly. A failure of a particular attempted reduction is not a separation. An efficient reduction would refute the Nephew candidate without settling whether some other natural TFZPPdt problem lies outside LOSSY.
context:
Think of f(v) as v’s parent and g(v) as its designated nephew. The two allowed outputs expose either an incorrect grandparent or the fact that the designated nephew is actually a child. Arbitrary function tables need not be genuine family trees; the equations, not the terminology, define a valid answer.

If V={v}, both functions must fix v, so f(g(v))=v and v is a valid answer of the second kind. At larger sizes, the source proves totality for every pair of function tables, not just acyclic parent structures.

The composition e∘d has at most M possible outputs but there are 2M possible inputs. Consequently at least M strings fail exact reconstruction. This explains why Lossy-Code has a simple zero-error randomized search algorithm, while an adversarially chosen valid failure can still be difficult to decode into another search problem.

A valid reduction must handle every z for which the target compression fails. Showing that one specially selected loss reveals a Nephew witness is insufficient. The universally quantified decoding requirement is central to the conjecture.

title: Can efficient randomized evidence lack a comparably short certain proof?
importance_reason: A foundational comparison of randomized mathematical evidence, deterministic decision and proof length. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Are there properties of growing families of finite mathematical objects that can be certified efficiently with arbitrarily high probabilistic confidence, yet have no comparably short certain proofs? The source poses this as a broad question about mathematical evidence; an object encoding, randomized guarantee and proof system must be fixed before it defines a separation to prove.
definitions: For a complexity-theoretic formulation, encode an object by a binary string x of length n and represent the property by a language L. A bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decider gives the correct membership answer with probability at least 2/3 on every input; independent repetition can reduce this error to δ with O(log(1/δ)) repetitions. A deterministic polynomial-time decider instead always gives the correct answer. A different notion is a polynomially checkable certificate: a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p satisfy x∈L iff there exists a string π of length at most p(n) with V(x,π)=1. This asks for certificate existence and efficient checking, not for efficiently finding the certificate. A proof-length question in a particular formal calculus additionally fixes that calculus, its axioms and proof encoding. A bound on the probability that an experiment issues a false certificate is a sampling guarantee; it is not automatically a posterior probability that a fixed mathematical statement is false. For one fixed finite object, asymptotic proof-length claims require a growing parameter or a family, since a single statement can be treated as a constant-size instance.
answer_criterion: Select one precise family, evidence protocol, resource scale and sound proof notion, then prove or refute the resulting separation. A large experiment, a small p-value, practical difficulty finding a proof, or a lower bound only for one proof method does not by itself establish absence of all short certificates in a broader model.
statement_review_issue: The source does not specify an asymptotic family of encoded objects, the randomized certification interface or soundness error, which truths require certificates, a sound proof system and proof-length measure, or whether “efficient” and “short” mean polynomial size or a practical resource bound. BPP versus P, BPP versus NP-style certification, and lower bounds in a fixed formal proof system are different questions. No one is silently selected as equivalent to the source’s discussion.
context:
The diameter of a fixed puzzle graph has one definite value. Random sampling can nevertheless provide a reliable procedure for drawing conclusions about it without exploring the entire graph. The randomness belongs to the procedure, not to the underlying mathematical fact.

The paper uses random Rubik states and a solver to support a 36-move upper bound with a controlled sampling-error probability. Its abstract also recalls the independently established 20-move bound. This illustrates the cost of reproducing evidence, rather than an example known to have no short certain proof.

Randomized primality testing illustrates the practical usefulness of randomness, but PRIMES is also decidable in deterministic polynomial time by the Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena theorem. It therefore supplies no asymptotic separation of randomized and deterministic polynomial-time decision.

A certificate may be short and easy to verify even when nobody knows how to find it quickly. Replacing “no short proof” with “no fast deterministic decision algorithm” changes the question, just as replacing a general certificate with a proof in one fixed calculus does.
why: Asks how probabilistic computational evidence compares with certain verification of finite mathematical facts. Its significance depends on distinguishing practical reproducibility, derandomization and proof complexity rather than merging them into one undefined obstacle.
status_note: Full source discussion, primality comparison and subsequent searches checked through 11 September 2026. The source does not formulate one proof system or asymptotic separation, so its broad question cannot receive a single verified open/closed disposition.

The source asks whether such evidence can be efficient even when a comparably short certain proof is unavailable. title: Explicit superlinear circuit lower bounds with polynomially growing depth
importance_reason: A strong circuit lower-bound target underlying barriers for distributed subgraph detection. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Construct an explicit family f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1} and constants δ₁,δ₂>0 such that no family of bounded-fan-in, bounded-fan-out Boolean circuits with depth O(n^{δ₁}) and size O(n^{1+δ₂}) computes every f_n exactly. The numerical circuit target is fully recovered; the uniform resource bound meant by “explicit” still needs to be specified.
definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n Boolean inputs, Boolean gates and one output. Size counts gates, and depth is the longest input-to-output path. Bounded fan-in and fan-out mean a constant bound independent of n on the number of incoming and outgoing wires at a gate; standard bounded bases, such as AND, OR, NOT and copy gates, differ by constant-factor size and logarithmic/additive depth overheads immaterial to positive polynomial exponents. The circuits are deterministic and nonuniform: different input lengths may use unrelated circuits, with no efficient construction algorithm for the circuits assumed. Exact computation requires C_n(x)=f_n(x) for every x∈{0,1}^n. Once δ₁,δ₂ are fixed, exclusion of the family means that for every fixed fan bound and constants A,B>0, there are arbitrarily large n for which no circuit of depth at most A n^{δ₁} and size at most B n^{1+δ₂} computes f_n. This is a simultaneous depth-and-size restriction; the circuit is not required to be shallow or small separately. An explicitness convention would impose a resource bound on one uniform procedure specifying or evaluating the f_n. Merely asserting that a hard truth table exists does not provide such a convention.
answer_criterion: Fix the intended explicitness requirement, construct a family satisfying it, and prove the simultaneous size/depth exclusion for some positive constants δ₁,δ₂. A counting argument giving unnamed hard functions, a constant-depth lower bound only, or a superlinear bound with no fixed polynomial exponent saving does not meet the stated target.
statement_review_issue: The full source gives the circuit resource bounds but does not define “explicit”: polynomial-time evaluation, membership in NP or E, or another uniform construction bound lead to different benchmark classes. A complete formulation must choose and source that requirement. The nonuniform circuit quantifiers and exact computation target are recovered below; no particular uniformity requirement is silently substituted for the source’s term.
context:
For illustration, δ₁=0.01 and δ₂=0.01 would exclude all exact circuits having depth O(n^{0.01}) and size O(n^{1.01}) for the constructed family. These values are illustrative: any fixed positive pair would suffice. A circuit may escape the claimed lower bound by exceeding either limit.

There are far more Boolean truth tables than circuits with these resources, so counting proves that hard functions exist. The challenge is to identify a uniformly describable family within a meaningful complexity class and establish its lower bound.

Theorem 29 shows that sufficiently strong round lower bounds for ordered induced-path detection or quantum induced-cycle detection would imply this circuit result. That is a conditional implication between lower bounds, not a circuit separation already proved by the paper.

title: Does the n/2-Ramsey search problem belong to TFAP?
importance_reason: A structural classification of Ramsey search by robustness of totality. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Does the total search problem that, given adjacency-query access to a simple graph on 2^n vertices, asks for a clique or an independent set of size ⌊n/2⌋ belong to TFAP in the source’s black-box sense, namely the closure of robust total search problems under low-depth decision-tree many-one reductions?
definitions: Take n≥4, vertex set {0,1}^n and one input bit for each unordered pair of distinct vertices; let N=binom(2^n,2) be the number of these bits. A solution lists ⌊n/2⌋ distinct vertices and identifies whether all pairs are edges or all are nonedges. Each solution can be verified with O(n²)=poly(log N) queries. A black-box TFNP problem is a family R_N⊆{0,1}^N×O_N, with finite solution sets O_N, total on every input, and with a decision tree of depth poly(log N) verifying each proposed solution. A partial input a∈{0,1,*}^N is witnessing if some one output o is valid for every complete input extending a. A function h(N) is negligible in log N when, for every constant c>0, h(N)≤(log N)^{-c} for all sufficiently large N. A problem is robust if for every such nonnegative h, all sufficiently large N have the property that every partial input fixing at least (1−h(N))N bits is witnessing. A deterministic decision-tree many-one reduction R_N→Q_M has one depth-poly(log N) tree computing each target input bit and, for every target solution o, one such tree decoding a source solution; log M is poly(log N). For every source input x and every valid target solution o of the constructed target, decoding must give a valid source solution. No uniform circuit-construction condition is imposed on these decision trees. TFAP^dt consists precisely of problems reducible in this sense to a robust black-box TFNP problem. The source’s circuit-input TFAP definition assigns membership through this oracle counterpart: an explicit succinct adjacency circuit does not authorize a stronger, arbitrary white-box reduction. The floor fixes the harmless integer convention for the source’s n/2 notation.
answer_criterion: Prove a low-depth decision-tree many-one reduction from this Ramsey search family to a robust total search family, with the required target-size bound and correctness for every target solution, or prove that no such reduction exists. Showing merely that every graph has many Ramsey sets, or proving membership for the smaller n/10 target, does not resolve this membership question.
context:
The input describes 2^n vertices, but an answer contains only about n/2 of them. Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of that size in every graph. Checking a proposed answer needs only its pairwise adjacency bits.

A robust problem still has one definite valid answer after almost all input bits have been fixed, regardless of how the few missing bits are completed. This is stronger than counting many answers on each complete input: different completions could have entirely different valid sets.

TFAP includes reductions to robust problems. Membership can therefore hold without proving that this particular adjacency-bit presentation has the robustness property. The reduction must preserve validity for every solution returned by the target.

The source places weak pigeonhole search and several other abundant-solution tasks in TFAP and proves black-box separations from several standard TFNP subclasses. It conjectures Ramsey membership as a way to locate its totality principle more precisely.

The source asks about n/10-Ramsey if n/2-Ramsey is not in TFAP. Finding a set of size n/10 is easier as an output requirement, so membership of that variant would not establish membership for the larger set requested here.

title: An unconditional hierarchy for uniform NAND depth

formal: Can the source’s input-aware polylog-time uniform NAND-depth classes be separated unconditionally: NDepth[a log₂n] ⊊ NDepth[b log₂n] for every pair of admissible constants a<b? definitions: A NAND gate takes two bits u,v and outputs ¬(u∧v). A NAND formula is a rooted binary tree of such gates whose leaves are input bits, their negations or Boolean constants; depth is the largest number of gates on an input-to-output path. For c≥0, the source writes NDepth[c log₂n] for languages decided by uniform NAND formulas with depth at most (c+o(1))log₂n; the o(1) tends to zero as input length n grows. The coefficient c is therefore meaningful and is not hidden in O(log n). In Definition 1.5 a single random-access machine A receives n, an n-bit input x, and a binary address b describing a path from the root (0 for left, 1 for right). It must describe the gate at that address in time (log n)^O(1). The source calls this input-aware uniformity and says it can select subformulas using bits of x. Its displayed definition still denotes the formula by φ_n rather than φ_{n,x}; that distinction is left explicit here. Strict class containment means that some language belongs to the larger-depth class and to no formula family in the smaller-depth class. It is a separation of deterministic NAND computations, not a comparison of nondeterministic time bounds.

title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
importance_reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.
focus_reason: A foundational algorithmic primitive whose optimal complexity tests the computational power of the word RAM and would affect many tasks built on ordering integer keys.
formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.
why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.
status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in [n] concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.
progress: 2002: Han–Thorup achieve O(n√log log n) expected time and linear space for arbitrary word-sized integer keys. | 2004: Han’s journal paper gives deterministic O(n log log n) time and linear space, following STOC 2002. | 2014: Belazzougui–Brodal–Nielsen extend expected linear time to w=Ω((log n)² log log n). | 2025: The CMU integer-sorting lecture retains linear sorting for arbitrary word lengths as an open question and distinguishes polynomial-size universes.
working_summary: Integer sorting can inspect the bits of keys instead of treating them only as objects to compare. The question asks for one always-correct randomized word-RAM algorithm taking expected linear time for every permitted word length. The constant must remain uniform when keys occupy much more than logarithmically many bits. Ordinary radix sorting handles smaller universes but its number of passes can grow. This tests whether powerful word operations can completely remove the asymptotic overhead of ordering an arbitrary list of machine words.

title: Can all pairwise sums X+Y be sorted in quadratic time?
importance_reason: A long-standing structured sorting question: only 2n real parameters generate n² values, yet converting known comparison savings into optimal total time remains unresolved. Documented geometric reductions and connections to convolution give the question significance beyond one sorting routine.
focus_reason: Sorting all pairwise sums is a classical structured comparison problem: the output is quadratic, but exploiting the inherited order with equally efficient total computation remains the target. It adds real-key comparison algorithms alongside word-RAM integer sorting and data structures.
formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer n≥2 and every X=(x₁,…,xₙ), Y=(y₁,…,yₙ)∈ℝⁿ, A outputs a permutation ((i₁,j₁),…,(i_{n²},j_{n²})) of [n]×[n] satisfying x_{i_r}+y_{j_r}≤x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}} for 1≤r<n², in at most Cn² unit-cost operations?
definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
context:
The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.
why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The 2017/2018 decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.
progress: 1976: Fredman proves an O(n²) comparison bound for sorting X+Y; this does not provide quadratic total running time. | 1992–1995: Lambert and Steiger–Streinu give algorithms combining O(n²) comparisons with O(n² log n) total time. | 2014: The necklace/convolution paper explicitly retains quadratic-time sorting on the real RAM as open while proving faster algorithms for more limited convolution outputs. | 2017 / STOC 2018: Kane–Lovett–Moran obtain O(n log² n) depth using 8-sparse linear tests. The bound concerns decision-tree queries and excludes output and general computational costs.
working_summary: Given two lists of n numbers, form every sum consisting of one number from each list. The task is to sort these quadratically many sums as quickly as possible. They have substantial inherited order, so they are not an arbitrary collection of unrelated values. The source distinguishes having few comparisons from implementing those comparisons with equally small total running time. Removing avoidable overhead would improve both structured sorting and geometric problems whose events are ordered by pairwise sums.

title: Does every hypergraph have a cut sparsifier with O(n/ε²) hyperedges?
importance_reason: The question concerns the general power of sparsification, linear sketches, or adversary-robust summaries, which are widely reused algorithmic tools.
focus_reason: A universal cut-preserving reduction of hypergraphs to few weighted hyperedges is a broad compression target supporting many downstream algorithms. Its focus is the size of a combinatorial sparsifier, with no query-interface guarantee.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C>0 such that, for every integer n≥2, every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph H on V=[n], and every real ε∈(0,1/2), there is a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph H′ on the same V with at most Cn/ε² hyperedges and (1−ε)cut_H(S)≤cut_H′(S)≤(1+ε)cut_H(S) for every S⊆V simultaneously?
definitions: A hypergraph H=(V,E,w) has E⊆{e⊆V:|e|≥2} and weights w:E→ℝ_{≥0}. Its cut value is cut_H(S)=Σ_{e∈E: e∩S≠∅ and e∩(V\S)≠∅}w(e): a crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. H′=(V,E′,w′) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set E′ need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |E′|, not Σ_{e∈E′}|e|, weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of n, ε, edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence statement with one constant C, or prove that the minimum required number of hyperedges times ε²/n is unbounded over the permitted inputs and accuracies. For a negative answer, the lower bound must allow arbitrary nonnegative hyperedges on the original vertex set. A growing logarithmic factor or a counterexample only to a particular sampling method does not resolve the target.
context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.
why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No Cn/ε² existence theorem or matching refutation was located. The old quadratic upper bound has been superseded by O(n log n/ε²). The original source permits an arbitrary weighted hypergraph on the same vertices; this card preserves that scope. Later near-optimal storage statements do not remove the logarithmic edge-count gap.
progress: 2012: Batson–Spielman–Srivastava achieve the graph edge-count benchmark through spectral sparsification. | 2018: Krauthgamer poses the O(n/ε²) same-vertex hypergraph existence question. | 2020: Chen–Khanna–Nagda obtain O(n log n/ε²) hyperedges, eliminating the prior rank dependence. | 2024: Near-optimal sketching addresses bit complexity, with logarithmic factors retained. | 2025 / 2026: Insertion-only streaming space improves without proving the exact edge-count target.
working_summary: A hypergraph cut counts the total weight of hyperedges meeting both sides of a vertex partition. A cut sparsifier replaces the hypergraph by a smaller weighted hypergraph that approximately preserves every cut at once. The question asks whether O(n/epsilon squared) hyperedges always suffice for multiplicative error epsilon. This matches the natural target from ordinary graphs, while a hyperedge can involve arbitrarily many vertices. The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.

title: Can reachability diameter be approximated within a constant in near-linear time?
importance_reason: Relates directed reachability structure to near-linear algorithms and isolates a basic obstruction behind shortcutting and parallel graph computation.
focus_reason: A constant-factor estimate of the largest finite directed distance in near-linear time is a broad algorithmic target alongside sorting, sparsification and offline comparisons. It is the highest-ranked remaining candidate in this category; its saved importance score and statement are preserved.
formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least 2/3 in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving D(G)=0 on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.
answer_criterion: Give a randomized algorithm and one absolute constant C meeting the displayed guarantee in near-linear time on every directed graph, or prove that no constant approximation is possible with that time bound.
context:
A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.

The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.
why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.
progress: 2026: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved. | 2026: Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.
working_summary: Reachability diameter measures the largest finite shortest-path distance in a directed graph. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted so that disconnected directions do not make the answer automatically infinite. The question asks for a constant-factor estimate in near-linear time on every unweighted directed graph. Simple searches from arbitrary pivots can miss a long directed route. A successful method would summarize the extent of reachable routes without computing distances from every vertex or imposing strong connectivity.

title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
importance_reason: A general multiplicative sparsification conjecture linking support size to a structural invariant, with consequences for cuts, codes and CSPs. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C>0 such that for every integer m≥1, every family S⊆2^{[m]}, every weight vector w∈ℝ≥0^m and every 0<ε<1, there is a reweighting w̃∈ℝ≥0^m with at most C·CL(S)/ε² nonzero coordinates and satisfying (1−ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ≤∑_{i∈A}w̃ᵢ≤(1+ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ simultaneously for every A∈S?
definitions: Here [m]={1,…,m}, and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is {i:w̃ᵢ>0}; coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as ∑wᵢ=1 is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length ℓ consists of distinct coordinates a₁,…,a_ℓ and distinct sets A₁,…,A_ℓ∈S with aᵢ∈Aᵢ for every i and aⱼ∉Aᵢ whenever i<j. CL(S) is the maximum possible ℓ, allowing ℓ=0. Equivalently, take the union-closure U(S)={⋃T:T⊆S}, including the empty union; CL(S) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from ∅ in U(S). Thus CL(S)=0 when S is empty or contains only ∅. It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A (1±ε) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and ε. The source allows ε>0; values ε≥1 admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to 0<ε<1 preserves it.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than C·CL(S)/ε² coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.
context:
A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so CL(S)=m. With unit original weights and ε<1, every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

The paper gives support O(CL(S)·log²(CL(S)/ε)·(log log(CL(S)/ε))²/ε²), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.
why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.
status_note: Published definitions, main bound and Conjecture 23 checked through 11 September 2026, together with the related May 2026 report and subsequent searches. No matching logarithm-free universal bound or counterexample was located.
progress: 2026-07: The ICALP paper proves a universe-size-independent bound with logarithmic overhead and poses the O(CL(S)/ε²) bound as Conjecture 23. | 2026-05-15: A related CSP sparsification report still states its broad characterizations with polylogarithmic and accuracy factors; its abstract does not settle the sharper conjecture.
working_summary: A sparsifier retains and reweights a few coordinates while approximately preserving every set’s total weight. The conjecture asks for a support bound proportional to chain length divided by ε². Chain length is measured through the union-closure, so even an incomparable collection of singleton sets can have large chain length. The published upper bound has extra logarithmic factors, which are precisely the remaining loss in the question. A resolution would establish whether this structural parameter completely controls multiplicative sparsification up to a universal constant.

title: Maximum-weight independent set with no long induced claw or large clique
importance_reason: An exact-algorithm boundary for maximum-weight independent set in hereditary graph classes. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every fixed pair of integers t≥1 and r≥2, is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a vertex-weighted graph containing neither an induced S_{t,t,t} nor a clique K_r, computes the maximum possible weight of an independent set?
definitions: The input is a finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E), with n=|V|, and integer weights w:V→N. An independent set I⊆V contains no adjacent pair, and its weight is Σ_{v∈I}w(v), with the empty set having weight zero. S_{t,t,t} is the tree formed by three paths of t edges sharing one common endpoint and otherwise having disjoint vertices; it has 3t+1 vertices and one degree-three center. An induced copy requires exactly the edges of that tree among its selected vertices. K_r is the complete graph on r vertices, so excluding it means every clique has size at most r−1. The algorithm is promised both exclusions. For each fixed t,r its running time must be at most n^{c(t,r)} times a constant depending on t,r, with arithmetic and comparisons on weights counted at unit cost as in the source. No bounded maximum degree, excluded biclique, or supplied graph decomposition is assumed. This is polynomial time for each fixed t,r, not necessarily a fixed-parameter bound f(t,r)n^C with universal C.
answer_criterion: Give such an exact polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed t,r, or refute the universal algorithmic assertion, for example by an appropriate conditional hardness result for one fixed pair. Approximation or an algorithm requiring an additional bounded-degree or biclique exclusion promise does not establish the conjecture.
context:
For t=1, S_{t,t,t} is the ordinary four-vertex claw K_{1,3}. Increasing t allows longer arms. Edges between selected arm vertices can destroy an induced copy, so the exclusion is different from forbidding the tree as any subgraph.

The source proves polynomial-time maximum-weight independent set when S_{t,t,t} is excluded as an induced subgraph and some fixed complete bipartite graph K_{s,s} is excluded as a subgraph. The conjecture asks to retain only a bound on clique size.

For t≥2, arbitrarily large complete bipartite graphs satisfy these induced-tree and triangle exclusions while having quadratically many edges. The conjectured class therefore extends beyond the sparse graph setting of the proved result.

Weights can make a smaller independent set preferable to a larger one. The target is the maximum sum of weights, not only the maximum number of mutually nonadjacent vertices.
why: Would extend exact independent-set algorithms from degree- or biclique-restricted graphs to a substantially broader hereditary class defined by a branching pattern and clique size.

title: Recognizing and constructing mim-width-one decompositions
importance_reason: A foundational recognition problem for using small-mim-width graph algorithms. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on any finite graph G, either outputs a branch decomposition of mim-width at most one or correctly reports that no such decomposition exists?
definitions: G=(V,E) is a finite undirected simple graph with n=|V|. For A⊆V, the cut graph G[A,V∖A] keeps exactly those edges with one endpoint in each side; edges internal to either side are discarded. An induced matching in this bipartite graph is a set of vertex-disjoint edges whose endpoints induce exactly those matching edges. Let mim_G(A) be its maximum size. A branch decomposition (T,L) consists of a tree T whose internal nodes have degree three and a bijection L from V to the leaves of T. Deleting a tree edge splits its leaves and hence V into A and V∖A. The decomposition width is the maximum mim_G(A) over its tree-edge cuts. The graph’s mim-width is the minimum over all such decompositions. The target is a decomposition of width ≤1, including width zero for edgeless graphs; empty and one-vertex graphs have the trivial width-zero convention. Runtime is polynomial in the ordinary explicit graph input size. No decomposition or bounded-width promise is supplied. The tree need not be a caterpillar: restricting it to one would instead ask about linear mim-width.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm that returns a valid width-at-most-one decomposition on every yes-instance and rejects every no-instance in polynomial time, or establish an obstruction to this guarantee. Algorithms using a supplied decomposition, recognizing only a subclass, or deciding width at most two do not settle the question.
context:
Across every cut in the chosen tree, there cannot be two disjoint crossing edges with both cross-pair edges absent. Edges inside a side do not affect this test. Equivalently, every cut graph must be a bipartite chain graph.

Many graph problems become tractable when a small-mim-width decomposition is available. The source even shows new polynomial-time algorithms at width one, but those guarantees assume the decomposition is supplied.

Testing the cuts of one given tree is different from finding a tree whose every cut is good. The recognition question must succeed or reject on an arbitrary input graph.

The ICALP 2026 paper proves NP-completeness for recognizing mim-width at most two and for width-one recognition of several related parameters. It explicitly leaves ordinary mim-width one open, so those results do not settle this card.

title: Černý conjecture: a reset word of length at most (n−1)²
importance_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
focus_reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.
formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n≥1 states have a reset word of length at most (n−1)²?
definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system A=(Q,Σ,δ), with |Q|=n, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, and a total function δ:Q×Σ→Q. Extend δ to words by δ(q,ε)=q and δ(q,wa)=δ(δ(q,w),a). A word w is a reset word when |{δ(q,w):q∈Q}|=1. The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold rt(A) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles n=1. No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models.
answer_criterion: Prove that rt(A)≤(n−1)² for every synchronizing complete deterministic n-state automaton, or exhibit such an automaton with rt(A)>(n−1)² and prove that strict inequality. Alphabets and state counts are unrestricted as specified above.
context:
Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. A proof of the conjecture must match this obstruction exactly.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.
why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.
status_note: Szykuła’s survey posted 25 August 2026 explicitly states the unrestricted conjecture as open and records the cubic upper bound. Sources and later work were checked on 11 September 2026. The July one-cluster preprint is a restricted-class claim whose proof was not independently verified.

working_summary: A reset word drives a finite automaton to one common state, regardless of where it started. The project asks whether every synchronizing complete deterministic automaton with n states has such a word of length at most (n−1)². Explicit automata attain this length, so the proposed bound cannot be reduced. The difficulty is coordinating successive mergers of possible states without paying a cubic total cost. A solution would identify the exact worst-case effort required to regain control of an unknown finite-state system.

title: Can every two-way NFA be determinized with polynomially many states?
importance_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
focus_reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.
formal: Do universal constants C,k≥1 exist such that, for every n≥1, every finite nonempty input alphabet Σ and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over Σ with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most C(n+1)^k states satisfying L(D)=L(A)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word w∈Σ*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in {−1,0,+1}; moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most C(n+1)^k states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over {0,1}, consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least 2^r states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses O(r) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with n^{O(log n)} states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to NL⊆L/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with L=NL.

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in a_1*⋯a_t* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.
why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.
status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. The STACS 2026 paper explicitly retains ordinary two-way determinization as open. Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision supplies a quadratic lower bound, still compatible with polynomial determinization. Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.
