title: Are one-clock timed Büchi–Landweber games determined?
importance_reason: A foundational strategy-existence question for timed reactive synthesis. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Is every game in the source’s one-clock timed model determined: for any finite nonempty move alphabets T,M, any one-clock nondeterministic Büchi timed automaton A over T×M, and either choice of the player who owns L(A), does Timer or Monitor have a winning strategy? The question includes both ordinary one-clock automata and the source’s 1-resetting extension, with the clock semantics specified below. Strategies may use unlimited memory and need not be computable.
definitions: In round i≥1, Timer chooses a_i∈T and a nonnegative rational delay τ_i; after observing this move, Monitor chooses b_i∈M. Put t_i=∑_{j≤i}τ_j. The resulting infinite timed word is ((a_i,b_i),t_i)_{i≥1}. Timestamps may be equal or bounded above: no non-Zeno requirement is imposed. A has finitely many locations, sets of initial and accepting locations, one clock x initially zero, and finitely many transitions (ℓ,(a,b),g,Y,ℓ′), where g is a finite conjunction of x⋈c tests with ⋈∈{<,≤,=,≥,>} and c a nonnegative integer, and Y either resets x to zero or leaves it unchanged. In the ordinary model, delay τ adds τ to the clock before checking g and applying the optional reset. In the 1-resetting extension, the value checked is frac(x+τ), its fractional part; that value is retained unless the transition resets it. A word belongs to L(A) iff some run visits accepting locations infinitely often. Neither player controls this accepting-run existential quantifier. The designated owner wins exactly words in L(A), and the other player wins its complement. A Timer strategy maps finite Monitor histories to the next pair (a,τ); a Monitor strategy maps nonempty histories of Timer’s letters and timestamps to the next b. Each player can reconstruct its own past moves from its strategy. A strategy wins if every opposing response sequence yields a winning word. Determinacy requires the existence of one such strategy; a finite-state controller or synthesis algorithm is an additional requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove that at least one player has a winning unrestricted strategy in every game for both specified clock variants, or give a game in one of these variants in which neither player has a winning strategy. Undecidability of deciding the winner, or failure of finite-memory strategies, is not a nondeterminacy example.
context:
Timer announces a letter and how much time has elapsed. Monitor sees that information before answering. The automaton evaluates their combined infinite timed word. This is a perfect-information turn-based game, rather than a game in which both players simultaneously choose delays.

For any completed play, membership in L(A) decides the winner. Determinacy asks for a stronger statement: before the opponent’s future choices are known, can one player choose a rule that wins against all of them?

Let both alphabets be {0,1}, let Monitor own the language of words in which a_i=b_i in every round, and let A ignore its clock. Monitor wins by replying with the observed a_i. General nondeterministic timed winning languages need not have such an immediate response rule.

The source proves undecidability across its synthesis variants, already with one clock, and studies when a finite controller suffices. It explicitly leaves determinacy unresolved. An undecidable winner problem can still have a winner for every individual game.

Replacing rational delays by arbitrary real choices, forbidding convergent time sequences, restricting strategies to controllers, or assigning control of nondeterministic runs to a player changes the game. The 1-resetting extension also has its own transition semantics and is included explicitly.
why: Would establish whether these timed synthesis models always give one player a mathematically winning strategy, independently of whether that strategy can be computed or implemented with finite memory.
status_note: Full game and clock semantics, the synthesis/determinacy distinction and the January arXiv record checked with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching determinacy theorem or nondetermined example was located.
progress: 2026-02-25: The STACS paper proves the synthesis undecidability and memory results but states that determinacy of its games remains unknown.

title: The complexity of reachability for two-dimensional branching VASS
importance_reason: Importance has not been individually assessed. This draft shares the provisional midpoint with other unassessed drafts; its position is not evidence that the question is less important.
formal: Determine the computational complexity of reachability for a two-dimensional branching vector addition system with states and binary-encoded numerical data. The decidability part of the original question is settled; the remaining target is the complexity classification, whose required time/space precision is not specified in the source.
definitions: Use the direct two-counter extension of the 2017 model. An instance consists of a nonempty finite state set Q={1,…,s}, a finite transition list Δ⊆Q×Q×ℤ²×Q, initial states I⊆Q, and a target (q,v)∈Q×ℕ², with ℕ={0,1,2,…}. A transition (q_L,q_R,z,q_P) combines child configurations (q_L,u) and (q_R,w) into the parent configuration (q_P,u+w+z), provided both coordinates of the resulting vector are nonnegative. All vector arithmetic is componentwise. A complete run is a finite rooted tree in which every internal node has exactly two ordered children and obeys one transition, every node carries a configuration with nonnegative counters, and every leaf is labeled (i,(0,0)) for some i∈I. A one-node initial run is allowed. The target is reachable precisely when it labels the root of some complete run. States may repeat, both children may have the same state, and their vectors need not be equal. No separate zero-test operation is available. The system, initial-state list and target are explicit finite inputs; state indices, signed displacement coordinates and nonnegative target coordinates are encoded in binary with separators, and N denotes the resulting bit length. Dimension is fixed at two, while s, the number of transitions and numerical magnitudes vary with the input. Algorithms must give the exact yes/no reachability answer and halt on every valid input. Quantitative bounds should state whether they measure worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time or workspace as a function of N; the source does not select the desired classification or matching-bound precision.
answer_criterion: The surviving research task is to obtain an explicit complexity classification for this binary-encoded reachability problem, beyond the known decidability result and inherited PSPACE hardness. The source does not fix the cost measure or precision needed to count matching upper and lower bounds as a complete answer; this remains a formulation issue. Merely proving decidability again would not settle the original request for precise complexity.
statement_review_issue: The original asks for precise computational complexity without fixing time versus space, a target class, or the precision required of matching bounds. This revision spells out the natural binary-encoded two-counter extension of its model but does not invent a PSPACE-completeness, elementary-time or other sharper conjecture.
context:
Ordinary counter-system reachability follows one sequence of configurations. A branching run is a tree: two independently justified configurations are combined, their resources are added, and a transition applies a fixed displacement. Every leaf must start with zero counters in an allowed initial state. The question asks how difficult it is to recognize whether such a finite justification tree exists.

For example, let i be initial and include transitions (i,i,(1,0),a), (i,i,(0,1),b), and (a,b,(−1,−1),t). The first two create a(1,0) and b(0,1) from zero leaves; the last combines them into t(0,0). Replacing its displacement by (−2,−1) would make that combination invalid because one counter becomes negative. Branching adds the child vectors; it does not copy one vector into both children.

Numerical encoding matters even with only one counter. The original paper proves PSPACE completeness for binary displacements, contrasting it with polynomial-time completeness for unary displacements. The two-counter problem inherits PSPACE hardness by setting every second coordinate to zero. This lower bound alone does not establish PSPACE membership in dimension two.

The 2025 result proves that the reachable configurations in two dimensions have a computable semilinear description. A semilinear set is a finite union of sets b+{k₁p₁+⋯+k_rp_r : k₁,…,k_r∈ℕ}, with fixed nonnegative integer base and period vectors. Such a description gives a terminating reachability decision procedure. The paper explicitly leaves its computational cost unbounded by any stated complexity estimate.

The 2025 presentation permits rules with zero, one or several input states and uses distinct states within each rule. The original binary-tree model fits this setting: zero leaves become initial rules, and a repeated child state can be represented by a fresh copy with the same reachable vectors. This preserves the two counter coordinates. The decidability result therefore applies to the imported problem despite the notational difference.

The original concluding paragraph asked for both decidability and precise complexity. Only the first part is settled by the two-dimensional theorem. This card retains the remaining classification question, while marking its unresolved precision requirement; it is not a new claim that two-dimensional reachability might be undecidable.

A July 2026 preprint claims decidability in general dimension and explicitly leaves complexity upper bounds open. That wider claim is not needed to justify the published two-dimensional result, and it does not provide the missing classification here.
why: Two counters are the first dimensional increase beyond the known one-counter complexity classification. Determining the cost of exact reachability would separate the power of a terminating symbolic procedure from usable bounds on resources needed to analyze branching computations.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The original decidability conjecture is settled by the published MFCS 2025 theorem. The broader request for precise two-dimensional complexity remains open in the checked sources: MFCS 2025 explicitly supplies no upper bound, FoSSaCS 2026 confirms the distinction, and the July 2026 general-decidability preprint also leaves complexity bounds open. The whole card is therefore not marked resolved. No independent proof audit was performed.

title: An elementary upper bound for vector-addition-system reachability
importance_reason: Historical elementary-complexity threshold for exact counter reachability, with broad consequences for verification lower bounds. The imported numerical score is retained to preserve ranking history; the question is now resolved and ineligible for active selection.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing-machine algorithm A and fixed integers h≥0 and c≥1 such that, for every explicitly encoded vector-addition-system reachability instance of bit length N, A decides exact reachability correctly within E_h((N+2)^c) steps, where E_0(x)=x and E_{j+1}(x)=2^{E_j(x)}? The constants and the single algorithm must work for all input dimensions and numerical values. This historical proposition is false.
question_excerpt: Despite intense investigation during the last four decades, it is still an open problem whether an elementary complexity upper bound for the reachability problem exists.
definitions: An instance is a dimension d≥1, a nonempty finite list T of displacement vectors in ℤ^d, and initial and target vectors a,b∈ℕ^d, with ℕ={0,1,2,…}. A configuration is any vector in ℕ^d. From u one may take displacement t∈T exactly when every coordinate of u+t is nonnegative, obtaining u+t. The target is reachable if a finite sequence t₁,…,t_k∈T has a+∑_{i=1}^j t_i∈ℕ^d for every 0≤j≤k and a+∑_{i=1}^k t_i=b. Length k=0 is allowed. The input explicitly lists all coordinates, using binary integers with signs and separators; N is the total bit length. Dimension and list length are input parameters. A is one finite deterministic program and must halt with the exact yes/no answer on every valid instance. No random error, counter bound, polynomial-growth promise, zero-test instruction, or branching operation is included. An elementary running-time bound has some fixed tower height h as defined in the statement; the height cannot depend on the instance. Binary encoding fixes the presentation without changing whether any elementary bound exists, since translation to unary data has at most elementary size growth.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute existence of the single uniform elementary-time decision algorithm quantified above. A refutation must exclude every fixed tower height and polynomial bottom exponent; showing that one algorithm or one fixed resource bound fails is insufficient. The published non-elementary lower bound supplies the negative resolution.
context:
A counter vector can describe the quantities of several resources in a concurrent system. Every transition makes a fixed change, but cannot consume resources that are absent. The reachability question asks whether the system can finish with exactly the specified quantities, after any finite number of transitions.

For example, start at (2,0) with the single displacement (−1,2). The reachable vectors are (2,0), (1,2) and (0,4). The target (0,3) is not reachable, although (0,4) is coordinatewise at least as large. Replacing exact equality by that weaker comparison gives coverability, a different task.

Polynomial time, exponential time and a fixed stack of several exponentials are all elementary. Allowing the stack height to grow with input size is a qualitatively stronger resource bound. The old question asked whether some fixed height would suffice for every instance, rather than whether a particular implementation could be made faster.

The quoted 2018 question concerns unrestricted vector addition systems. The paper’s title refers to a special polynomial-growth subclass studied later in the article; imposing that restriction here would change the question. Likewise, a bound for one fixed low dimension would not establish the required uniform bound over all dimensions.

Czerwiński and coauthors proved a lower bound excluding elementary complexity, first presented at STOC 2019 and developed in a 2021 journal article. This is a limitation of the decision problem itself, not merely a demonstration of long runs or poor performance by an existing algorithm.

Subsequent work classified ordinary VAS/VASS reachability as Ackermann-complete. Finite control states and the state-free vector presentation are polynomially interreducible, so this later classification concerns the same unrestricted reachability task. The simpler non-elementarity theorem already settles the historical yes/no question recorded here.
why: Exact resource reachability is a basic verification problem that other decision tasks can encode. Its non-elementary complexity shows that decidability can coexist with worst-case costs beyond every fixed-height exponential tower, and that exact target matching can be much harder than merely accumulating enough resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The elementary-upper-bound proposition is false by the STOC 2019 / JACM 2021 non-elementarity result of Czerwiński, Lasota, Lazić, Leroux and Mazowiecki. The accepted journal manuscript’s Section 1 model and Theorem 6 match the unrestricted VAS reachability question on the original 2018 page. The later Ackermann-completeness result strengthens this resolution. Source and theorem matching were checked; proofs were not independently audited or formalized.

working_summary: A vector addition system repeatedly adds permitted integer vectors while keeping every counter nonnegative. Exact reachability asks whether a given initial vector can reach a specified target after finitely many such steps. The historical question asks whether one algorithm can decide all instances within a fixed-height tower of exponentials in the input length. The non-elementary lower bound published at STOC 2019 and in JACM 2021 rules out every such bound. The card therefore records a resolved negative answer, with the general model kept separate from the polynomial-growth subclass named in the original paper.

title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be efficiently parallelized?
importance_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
focus_reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.
formal: Is P=NC, where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For L∈NC there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family (Cₙ)ₙ≥0 such that Cₙ decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most C(n+2)ᶜ gates, and has depth at most C(log₂(n+2))ᵏ. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic O(log(n+2))-space transducer given 1ⁿ must output the description of Cₙ; its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish P≠NC.
context:
Circuit evaluation makes the apparent obstacle concrete. A sequential algorithm visits the gates in their supplied topological order and computes every value in polynomial time. The question is whether the Boolean function described by an arbitrary such circuit always has an efficiently constructible, much shallower evaluation circuit. Depth of the supplied circuit and depth of an algorithm that evaluates it are different quantities.

For example, a long chain that successively ANDs input bits can be replaced by a balanced tree of AND gates with logarithmic depth. Thus a long chain in the input is not by itself a lower bound on the time needed to evaluate it. Circuit Value allows arbitrary sharing and combinations of gate types, rather than promising this particular associative form.

Ladner proved Circuit Value complete for P under logarithmic-space reductions. These reductions themselves admit NC computation, and NC is closed under their composition. An NC algorithm for this one problem would therefore parallelize every problem in P. P-completeness supplies this conditional consequence; it does not already prove the absence of a parallel algorithm.

The resource tradeoff is polynomial total circuit size against polylogarithmic dependency depth. The exponent of the polynomial work budget may be large, so a positive answer would not automatically provide nearly linear work or useful speedups on a small machine. Logspace uniformity prevents the circuit descriptions from supplying arbitrary nonuniform information. The union over all fixed depth exponents also makes this broader than asking whether P equals NC¹.

Restricted circuit models reveal real obstructions. Raz and McKenzie separate monotone NC from monotone P, and separate consecutive levels of the monotone NC hierarchy. Their lower bounds restrict the computing circuit to AND and OR. A monotone function can still have a substantially more powerful circuit when NOT gates are allowed, so the restriction cannot be removed from the conclusion.

Recent matching lower bounds sharpen this caution. Cavalar and coauthors prove a stretched-exponential monotone circuit-size lower bound for perfect matching, a problem with polynomial-time general algorithms. The separation measures the cost of forbidding negation. It supplies progress in circuit lower bounds while leaving the general uniform parallel-computation question untouched.
why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.
status_note: The primary P-completeness monograph and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No unrestricted resolution of P versus logspace-uniform NC was found. The 2025/2026 matching lower bound concerns monotone circuits and therefore does not resolve the stated AND/OR/NOT model.
progress: 1975: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization. | 1995: Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations. | 1999: Raz and McKenzie prove monotone NC≠monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits. | 2025–2026: Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size 2^{n^{Ω(1)}}, improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.
working_summary: NC describes computations with polynomial total circuit size and only polylogarithmic dependency depth, under a uniformity requirement. The question asks whether every problem solvable in polynomial sequential time belongs to this parallel class. Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem: given a circuit and its input, compute the designated output. An NC algorithm for circuit evaluation would therefore parallelize every problem in P. The challenge is to distinguish a long chain in the supplied circuit from an unavoidable chain in every possible algorithm for evaluating its behavior.

title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
importance_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
focus_reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.
formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most Cn(log(n+2))^a bits of memory and C(log(n+2))^b passes, with success probability at least 2/3 for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous O(n logᵃ(n+2))-bit space and O(logᵇ(n+2))-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least 2/3 on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
context:
Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most n−1 scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and n^{1/2+o(1)} depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc (u,v) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires Ω(log n/log log n) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that o(√log n) passes require n^{2−o(1)} space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the Ω(log n/log log n) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies n^{1/2+o(1)} as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.
why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.
status_note: The primary survey, cited multipass bounds and the revision of 9 September 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. The recent paper explicitly retains the n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass upper benchmark. No polylogarithmic-pass algorithm or lower bound ruling out every polylogarithmic pass bound in the stated memory model was found. This check covers decision with adversarial fixed order, rather than a changed stream or a path-output requirement.
progress: 2013–2016: Guruswami–Onak establish multipass superlinear space lower bounds for directed reachability decision; these imply Ω(log n/log log n) passes in semi-streaming space. | 2019: Jambulapati–Liu–Sidford develop nearly linear-work, approximately square-root-depth parallel reachability and its sparse shortcut construction. | 2021: Chen and coauthors prove almost-quadratic space is necessary for o(√log n) passes, strengthening the few-pass space tradeoff. | 2022: Assadi and coauthors state and explain the n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming implementation, including path recovery, in Proposition 4. | 2023-09: Assadi’s survey records the gap and explains the transition from search lower bounds to reachability-decision lower bounds. | 2026-09-09: The revised streaming-monotonicity paper retains the square-root reachability benchmark and reduces faster approximation to faster reachability.
working_summary: Directed reachability in a stream asks whether one vertex can reach another when graph edges arrive in an adversarial order. Nearly linear memory in the vertex count cannot store every edge of a dense graph. The question asks for a randomized algorithm using only polylogarithmically many passes and n times a polylogarithmic number of memory bits. Simple repeated scans can propagate reachability one step at a time, taking many passes on badly ordered paths. The project is to combine a small memory footprint with far fewer scans without relying on favorable edge order.

title: Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?
importance_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
focus_reason: A canonical deterministic parallel-algorithm and derandomization question for a basic graph optimization problem.
formal: Do there exist constants C,a,b>0 and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most C(n+2)^a gates and depth at most C(log₂(n+2))^b?
definitions: The input is the n×n binary adjacency matrix of a graph on [n], with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an n×n binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the n² output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input 1^n writes the description using O(log₂(n+2)) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the stated logspace-uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth search circuits on all simple undirected graphs, or prove that no such family exists. A negative answer rules out every fixed choice of the size and depth exponents and constants. An algorithm only for bipartite graphs, or one using quasipolynomial circuit size or catalytic auxiliary memory, does not meet the specified positive criterion.
context:
A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits n^{O(log² n)} processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.
why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.
progress: 1987 / background: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it. | 2017: Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap. | 2026-06-01: Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC. | 2026-06 / revised 2026-07-15: The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.
working_summary: Perfect matching seeks pairwise disjoint edges that cover every vertex of a graph. The question asks for a deterministic parallel algorithm on general graphs with polynomially many processors and polylogarithmic running time. Sequential polynomial-time algorithms do not supply this bound because their matching updates may depend on earlier choices. General graphs also contain odd cycles, which require coordination beyond the constraints that suffice in bipartite graphs. The saved card distinguishes this target from the nearby bipartite advance and asks whether compatible matching decisions can be organized efficiently in parallel without randomness.

title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in O(log log n) rounds
importance_reason: The bounded-degree distributed LLL is a central conflict-resolution primitive and a benchmark for the randomized LOCAL complexity hierarchy. Its connection to locally checkable labeling and its use in coloring algorithms give a precise reason to seek the log-logarithmic bound.
focus_reason: A canonical obstacle to resolving local conflicts rapidly, with consequences for many distributed graph algorithms.
formal: Does there exist an integer c≥2 such that, for every fixed integer d≥2, a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm A_d and a constant K_d solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with p·d^c<1/2, within K_d(1+log₂log₂(n+2)) rounds, with probability at least 1−n^(−3) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
definitions: There are n≥2 bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]; shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor 1/2 removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer c≥2 admits, for every fixed d≥2, algorithms A_d and constants K_d with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.
context:
The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability 2^{1−k}. Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability (1−p)^n, which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition p·d^c<1/2 is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form O(d/log d + (log log n)^{O(1)}) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an O(log log_{1/p} n) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same O(log log n) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.
why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.
status_note: The original conjecture, primary distributed bounds, the 2025 locality result and the August 2026 resilient-LLL paper were checked on 11 September 2026. No result settling the exact bounded-degree O(log log n) worst-case target was found. The fixed factor 1/2 and order of slack/degree quantifiers preserve the saved precise interpretation. Node averages and results for stronger communication models are not substituted for this guarantee.
progress: 2016: Brandt and coauthors prove Ω(log log n) lower bounds for sinkless orientation and distributed LLL under the stated criterion hypotheses. | 2017: Fischer–Ghaffari obtain 2^{O(√log log n)} rounds at low dependency degree under polynomial slack and explicitly record the Chang–Pettie O(log log n) conjecture. | 2023: Davies gives O(d/log d + (log log n)^{O(1)}) rounds under polynomially strengthened criteria, with a broader probability-versus-degree tradeoff. | 2025: Davies-Peck improves node-averaged LOCAL complexity and complexity in other models; Theorem 3 retains a separate, larger worst-case LOCAL bound. | 2026-08: Davies-Peck and Zhang extend efficient resilient-LLL applications to triangle-free coloring. Their general-degree discussion does not resolve the fixed-degree linear-log-log target.
working_summary: The distributed Lovasz Local Lemma seeks an assignment avoiding many bad events, each depending on only a bounded number of other events. Processors know local portions of this dependency structure and communicate in synchronous LOCAL rounds. The question asks for O(log log n) rounds with high probability when the dependency degree is constant and the probability criterion has sufficiently strong constant polynomial slack. The guarantee must bound the worst finishing time over all nodes. An algorithm that achieves only a small average finishing time would leave the central coordination issue unresolved for the last remaining bad events.

title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
importance_reason: Exact weighted distances are a basic distributed optimization primitive. Matching the bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark, or proving an additional obstacle, would resolve a central gap between exact algorithms and communication lower bounds, with consequences for other distributed graph constructions.
focus_reason: A basic distributed graph primitive with an unresolved gap between algorithms and communication lower bounds.
formal: For every fixed integer b≥1, do there exist constants K,c>0 and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with n≥2 vertices, integer edge weights in [0,n^b] and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most K(√n+D)(log₂(n+2))^c rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least 1−n^(−3)? Here D is the diameter of the unweighted graph.
definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]. Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for dist(s,v), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated O((√n+D)polylog n) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous 1−n^(−3) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an n^{o(1)} overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.
context:
Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only O(log n) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in O(log n) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The √n term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores dist(s,v). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound Õ(√n D^{1/4}+D), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra D^{1/4} factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, Õ(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+√n+D), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For D≈n^{1/2}, its displayed terms give n^{3/5+o(1)}, while the target is Õ(n^{1/2}). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires n^{3/5} rounds.

The notation n^{o(1)} allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for (1+ε)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed ε they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as n^{b+1}, forcing exactness by taking ε extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its ε dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.
why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.
status_note: Primary exact CONGEST bounds, randomized distance lower bounds, the approximation result and later-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No algorithm or impossibility theorem settling the full stated polylogarithmic-overhead target was found. The inherited 2026 paper is retained as related-work provenance, rather than used alone as evidence of the current best bound.
progress: 2011 / 2012: Das Sarma and coauthors establish randomized communication lower bounds for exact and approximate distance problems, giving the Ω̃(√n+D) lower-bound benchmark. | 2020 / 2022: Chechik–Mukhtar obtain Õ(√n D^{1/4}+D) rounds for exact weighted SSSP. | 2022: Rozhoň and coauthors give near-optimal deterministic distributed algorithms for (1+ε)-approximate undirected distances, with accuracy-dependent complexity. | 2023: Cao–Fineman give Õ(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+√n+D) rounds for polynomially bounded weights, including an improvement in the intermediate-diameter comparison. | 2026-04-18: The programmable-matter article retains a CONGEST gap in related work. Its own communication model and theorems are different, and that summary does not include the 2023 bound above.
working_summary: Single-source shortest paths asks every vertex to learn its exact distance from one source in a weighted network. In CONGEST, each edge carries only a logarithmic number of bits per communication round. The target is a randomized algorithm using roughly sqrt(n) plus the hop diameter D rounds, ignoring polylogarithmic factors. The graph is undirected and connected, with nonnegative polynomially bounded integer edge weights. Achieving this bound would combine global distance propagation with the bandwidth limits of the network at the scale identified by the saved problem statement.

title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
importance_reason: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on [n], decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity R_A(n)=ω(1)? Only node 1 is required to output the decision bit, and the input, bandwidth and limiting convention are fixed below.
definitions: For each n≥2, the communication network is the complete graph on processors 1,…,n. The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the n−1 adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most ceil(log₂ n) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with P(G) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. R_A(n) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement R_A(n)=ω(1) means that for every integer B≥1 there is N such that R_A(n)>B for every n≥N; it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within C(n+1)^k steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the ω(1) target.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed ω(1) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.
context:
Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an Ω(log log n) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker ω(1) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.
why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.
status_note: The checked primary literature leaves explicit superconstant unicast bounds as a central challenge. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution of this polynomial-time, one-bit target. The latest checked revision of the one-round MST result is January 2024; it is not presented as a new 2026 status theorem.
progress: 2014: Circuit simulations explain barriers to explicit lower bounds and separate unicast from broadcast communication. | 2018: A uniform congested-clique time hierarchy is proved through hard-function selection, without the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time guarantee. | 2023 / 2024: The MST lower bound excludes one round with logarithmic link bandwidth; it does not establish a diverging lower bound for a one-bit graph predicate.
working_summary: Can a graph predicate that is easy to compute centrally require a number of congested-clique rounds tending to infinity? Each processor initially knows its incident graph edges and can send a different logarithmic-size message to every other processor in each round. Only one decision bit is required, and local computation is unrestricted. Known hard-function counting and hierarchy arguments do not provide the required centrally polynomial-time predicate. Broadcast bounds and the known two-round MST limitation do not resolve this unicast one-bit target.

title: Can directed reachability have near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth?
importance_reason: Combining near-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for directed reachability would resolve a major barrier in efficient parallel graph algorithms.
formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm meeting the work, depth, and error guarantees simultaneously on all directed inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the specified PRAM model. Work measured by transitive-closure size is insufficient.
context:
A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”
why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 closure-sensitive algorithm. Near-linear input work with polylogarithmic depth remains the target.
progress: 2019: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability. | 2026-05: Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density. | 2026-08: Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.
working_summary: A parallel reachability algorithm must identify every vertex reachable from a source in a directed graph. The target combines nearly linear total work in the input size with polylogarithmic depth, using randomization and high-probability correctness. Ordinary graph search does little work but can expose a long sequence of dependent frontiers. Highly parallel transitive-closure methods may perform far more work than this one-source task requires. The question is whether shortcuts or another representation can remove long dependencies while accounting for the cost of constructing all auxiliary information.

title: Is finding a depth-first-search tree in deterministic NC?
importance_reason: Asks whether the search structure produced by an apparently sequential graph traversal can be computed efficiently in parallel.
formal: Does there exist a logspace-uniform family of deterministic Boolean circuits of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth that, on the adjacency matrix of every finite simple undirected graph, outputs a valid depth-first-search forest? The roots and the order of visiting neighbors may be chosen freely for each input.
definitions: For n≥1 the input is the n×n symmetric zero-diagonal adjacency matrix of a graph G on V={1,…,n}. The output is a parent array p∈{0,…,n}^n, with 0 denoting a root. If p(v)≠0, require {v,p(v)}∈E(G); repeatedly taking parents must reach 0 from every vertex. These parent edges define a rooted forest, and each connected component of G must be spanned by one of its trees. A vertex u is an ancestor of v if u lies on the tree path from v to its root. The forest is a DFS forest if, for every edge {u,v}∈E(G), one endpoint is an ancestor of the other. For undirected graphs this is exactly the class of forests produced by recursive depth-first search under some choices of roots and neighbor orders. Encode each parent entry in ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ bits. Each circuit C_n has n² input bits and n⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ output bits, uses AND and OR gates with at most two inputs and NOT gates with one input, and has size at most O(n^c) and depth at most O((log₂(n+2))^k), for fixed constants c,k independent of n and G. Logspace uniformity means that one deterministic Turing machine, given 1^n, writes the description of C_n while using O(log(n+2)) working space, excluding its read-only input and write-only output tapes. Correctness is required on every valid adjacency matrix; behavior on other bit strings is unrestricted. The empty graph has the empty output. No randomness or input-length-specific advice is supplied. NC here refers to computing a valid encoded output, rather than deciding a Boolean language.
answer_criterion: Construct one circuit family satisfying all the stated correctness, uniformity, size and depth requirements, or prove that no such family exists. The output may be any valid DFS forest. A randomized algorithm, a quasipolynomial-size circuit family, an algorithm only for a restricted graph class, or a lower bound for one prescribed traversal order does not settle this question.
context:
Depth-first search explores an unvisited neighbor, completes the recursive exploration from that neighbor, and only then tries another neighbor of the current vertex. The resulting parent pointers form a spanning forest. The question asks whether that structure can always be assembled in a small number of parallel stages, even though the familiar sequential procedure follows one exploration at a time.

Being a spanning tree is not enough. In a triangle with vertices 1, 2 and 3, a tree rooted at 1 with children 2 and 3 fails: edge {2,3} joins different branches. The path with parent pointers p(1)=0, p(2)=1 and p(3)=2 is a valid DFS tree. The ancestor condition makes this distinction explicit without prescribing a traversal order.

The height of the output tree is not the running time being bounded. A path graph may require a DFS tree of height n−1, yet its n parent entries may be computed in parallel. Conversely, a sequential algorithm with linear running time need not have polylogarithmic parallel depth.

The freedom to choose a valid output matters. Reproducing the lexicographically first DFS order under fixed choices is P-complete according to the cited source. That hardness result does not exclude efficient parallel computation of a different valid DFS forest.

The general undirected problem has a randomized NC algorithm, and a deterministic parallel algorithm with quasipolynomially many processors is known. The latter exceeds the polynomial resource bound in this question. Deterministic NC algorithms are also known for several restricted graph families. The 2025 source still leaves general deterministic NC open.

There is a separate goal of keeping total work close to the input size. The 2023 algorithm obtains work Õ(m+n) and depth Õ(√n), where m is the number of edges and Õ suppresses factors polynomial in logarithms. Its depth bound is sublinear but does not establish the polylogarithmic depth required here.

Uniformity requires one small-space procedure to describe the circuits for every input length. The circuits cannot be unrelated choices supplied separately for each n. Both this requirement and the polynomial size bound belong to the target; merely showing that suitable circuits exist with larger resources leaves a different question.
why: DFS is a basic graph structure whose standard construction has a long chain of sequential choices. Resolving this question would determine whether randomness can always be removed from its efficient parallel construction while retaining polynomial total resources.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves deterministic NC construction for general graphs open while proving results for restricted classes. Targeted searches found no later general resolution. Randomized NC, deterministic quasipolynomial resources, and the 2023 near-linear-work algorithm have distinct guarantees. The cited proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 1988: Aggarwal and Anderson give a randomized NC algorithm for undirected DFS, as documented in the 2025 paper’s introduction. This permits randomness. | 2023: Ghaffari, Grunau and Qu give a randomized algorithm with Õ(m+n) work and Õ(√n) depth; this addresses work efficiency with a larger depth bound. | 2025-12-09: Chauhan, Datta and Praveen prove deterministic parallel bounds for bounded-genus and undirected single-crossing-minor-free graphs, and a logspace bound for bounded treewidth. The general question remains open in their statement.
working_summary: A depth-first-search forest records the parent choices of recursive graph exploration. For an undirected graph, it is a rooted spanning forest in which every graph edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. The problem asks for a deterministic, uniformly specified parallel computation that constructs any such forest with polynomial resources and polylogarithmic depth. Randomized NC algorithms and deterministic results for restricted graph classes are known, but those guarantees do not settle the general target. A solution would show whether this basic search structure can always be built efficiently in parallel without random choices.

title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in o(log* n) rounds
importance_reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.
formal: Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every n≥3 and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least 1−1/n in $T(n)=o(1+\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from [n²], and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.
definitions: The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |0⟩ ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |0⟩ registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in {1,2,3}. Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. T(n) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is T(n)/(1+log* n)→0 as n→∞; log* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.
answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.
context:
A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is Θ(log* n).

Naor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs Ω(log* n) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.

There is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.

The August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.

A separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.
why: This is a canonical test of quantum advantage for a natural distributed symmetry-breaking task. A faster protocol would improve one of the basic local coordination primitives; a lower bound would have to explain a limitation of quantum realizability that mere causal consistency does not capture.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves high-probability cycle 3-coloring open. Its new theorem is for anonymous nodes and success probability exactly 1, so it is not recorded as resolving this identified, bounded-error protocol question. No later resolution located through 10 September 2026.
