progress: 1980s–1990s: Cole–Vishkin and subsequent algorithms give O(log* n) classical coloring. Linial proves a matching deterministic lower bound. These classical bounds also give a quantum upper bound by running a classical protocol. | 1991: Naor proves the classical randomized ring-coloring lower bound, preserving the log-star obstruction when small failure probability is allowed. | 2016: Holroyd and Liggett construct finitely dependent colorings. These establish the barrier to deriving the desired quantum lower bound solely from finite dependence or causality. | 2026-07: Fraigniaud, Magniez, and Ziccardi give quantum lower bounds for rooted-tree 3-coloring and even-cycle 2-coloring. Their rooted-tree lower bound uses degree as a growing parameter. | 2026-08: Coiteux-Roy and coauthors prove that for any fixed c≥3, anonymous quantum-PN c-coloring of an even directed n-cycle with probability 1 needs more than floor(n/2)−2 rounds. They explicitly leave high-probability correctness open.
working_summary: Processors arranged on an oriented cycle must choose three classical colors so that adjacent processors receive different colors. The question allows quantum communication and asks for a round bound asymptotically smaller than log-star n. Nodes have distinct identifiers and know the cycle size, while their initial quantum registers are unentangled. The complete coloring must be valid with probability at least one minus one over n. A successful algorithm would beat the classical symmetry-breaking threshold, whereas a lower bound must handle quantum correlations without relying only on coarse causality constraints.

title: Can distributed MIS be solved in sublogarithmic time on every graph?
importance_reason: A basic randomized symmetry-breaking question on arbitrary graphs whose resolution would sharpen the global locality frontier.
formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.
answer_criterion: Give one randomized LOCAL algorithm with a uniform o(log n) round bound and the stated success probability on all graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A degree restriction does not settle the proposition.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?
why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. General-graph sublogarithmic elapsed-round complexity remains open in the checked literature; awake-time and high-girth results have different guarantees.
progress: 2016: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$. | 2025: Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier. | 2025: Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.
working_summary: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent vertices and leaves every unselected vertex next to a selected one. The question asks for a randomized LOCAL algorithm that finds such a set in o(log n) rounds on every graph with high probability. Message sizes and local computation are unrestricted, so the resource measures the distance over which decisions must be coordinated. The running-time improvement must hold uniformly even for graphs of very large degree. Degree-sensitive algorithms already improve some cases, but the target requires a mechanism that also avoids logarithmically many phases on unrestricted graphs.

title: One cycle versus two: is logarithmic time necessary in low-memory MPC?
importance_reason: A small connectivity promise problem serves as a basic round-complexity benchmark for low-memory massively parallel computation.
formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint (n/2)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is O(n) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.
answer_criterion: Prove the logarithmic lower bound for every fixed sublinear-memory exponent and every admissible randomized algorithm, or refute that universal lower bound. An o(log n)-round algorithm for one fixed exponent would suffice for a refutation.
context:
Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.
why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.
progress: 2022: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here. | 2025: Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.
working_summary: The one-cycle-versus-two problem distinguishes a single n-vertex cycle from two disjoint cycles of half that size. In the low-memory MPC model, edges are spread across machines with sublinear local memory and linear total memory. The conjecture says randomized algorithms require Ω(log n) communication rounds under these resource bounds. Both input types have identical vertex counts, edge counts, and degrees, so only their global connectivity distinguishes them. A lower bound must handle arbitrary communication between machines and arbitrary encodings, rather than assuming information can travel only along graph edges.

title: Nearly quadratic bit complexity for perfectly secure asynchronous Byzantine agreement
importance_reason: Close a basic communication gap for agreement without computational trust assumptions.
formal: Is there a randomized asynchronous binary Byzantine-agreement protocol tolerating every t<n/3 with perfect security and expected Õ(n²) communication bits, using private authenticated channels and no setup?
definitions: There are n processes with binary inputs and reliable asynchronous point-to-point channels. Byzantine processes may deviate arbitrarily; honest processes must agree, and if all honest inputs equal b then their decision must be b. Perfect security requires zero probability of a safety violation against computationally unbounded adversaries, with almost-sure termination under fair delivery. Communication is to be measured for honest processes; faulty processes cannot be charged a bounded number of arbitrary transmissions.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Fix adaptive-corruption and erasure conventions, the adversary’s access to honest channel traffic and randomness, admissible fairness, logarithmic factors and termination-time requirements.
context:
Byzantine agreement is a basic fault-tolerance primitive. Nearly quadratic communication with optimal resilience and information-theoretic security would combine the strongest correctness guarantee with a fundamental efficiency scale.

ABEL obtains efficient multivalue extension given a binary agreement primitive. Its extension overhead is not a complete binary protocol with that communication bound. The candidate keeps the underlying binary agreement question separate from the solved extension result.
why: Close a basic communication gap for agreement without computational trust assumptions.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2025: The paper solves the multivalue extension overhead relative to an assumed binary agreement protocol.

title: Robustness of the deterministic consensus hierarchy
importance_reason: Determine whether a central measure of synchronization power behaves consistently under composition.
formal: Can combining deterministic shared-object types yield a wait-free consensus number strictly larger than the maximum consensus number of the types used separately?
definitions: The intended hierarchy permits any number of instances of a type and atomic read/write registers. Its consensus number is the largest process count for which deterministic wait-free binary consensus can be implemented; it is infinite when all finite counts are possible. Combining types means allowing instances of each type in one implementation. Wait freedom requires completion after finitely many steps of each participating nonfaulty process regardless of other process speeds or crashes. The target excludes nondeterministic shared objects.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Copy the refined consensus-number definition, allowed object initializations, deterministic type semantics and process-access restrictions; the older one-object hierarchy is not interchangeable with this model.
context:
Consensus number measures the synchronization power of a shared-memory primitive. Robustness asks whether that power composes: can several individually weak primitive types jointly become stronger?

The book distinguishes the refined hierarchy used here from an earlier nonrobust version. Counterexamples using nondeterministic objects also do not settle the deterministic question. The hierarchy’s definition is therefore part of the mathematical problem, not a terminology choice.
why: Determine whether a central measure of synchronization power behaves consistently under composition.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2018: The discussion separates known nonrobust variants and nondeterministic counterexamples from the deterministic refined-hierarchy question.

title: Can deterministic LOCAL algorithms find an MIS in O(log n) rounds?
importance_reason: Matching a logarithmic deterministic bound for MIS would settle a central gap in local symmetry breaking.
formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be O(log n) uniformly over degrees.
answer_criterion: Give one deterministic LOCAL algorithm with a uniform O(log n) bound over all graphs and valid identifiers, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Constants must not depend on maximum degree.
context:
Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.
why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is solved; the O(log n) target remains open in the checked literature.
progress: 2019: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor. | 2020: Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS. | 2024: Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$. | 2026: Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve Δ-coloring; their result does not give an O(log n) MIS algorithm.
working_summary: Deterministic maximal independent set algorithms must coordinate their choices using the graph and vertex identifiers alone. The question asks whether O(log n) LOCAL rounds suffice on every graph and every valid identifier assignment. The output must be independent and dominate all unselected vertices, without requiring maximum cardinality. Network decomposition already supports polylogarithmic deterministic algorithms, so the target is a sharper dependence on network size. Reaching the logarithmic bound would require organizing deterministic progress efficiently even when identifier patterns defeat simple greedy local rules.

title: Sketching vs. Streaming
importance_reason: Separating sketching from general streaming would identify the power and limitations of a widely used algorithmic abstraction.
formal: Sketching vs. Streaming
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question compares the power of models or representations. Resolving it would identify whether their difference changes what can be computed, rather than only the implementation cost.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: A streaming algorithm compresses an input while processing it sequentially, whereas a sketch supports computation from independently prepared summaries. The source asks whether efficient streaming for symmetric functions can generally be converted into efficient sketching. It frames the issue through one-way communication versus simultaneous messages to a referee. The concrete challenge is to find natural functions with a substantial gap or establish a transformation under suitable symmetry assumptions. This would clarify when the ability to adapt a summary to previously processed data offers more power than independently summarizing the pieces.

title: Compact routing at stretch 2k−1 and n^(1/k) storage
importance_reason: Reach a basic space-versus-route-quality frontier for distributed network representations.
formal: For every integer k≥2, do universal graph-routing schemes exist with stretch at most 2k−1 and Õ(n^(1/k)) words of routing information per vertex, without a preliminary handshake?
definitions: A routing scheme preprocesses a connected undirected weighted graph and assigns local routing tables and destination labels. During a route, each vertex chooses an outgoing port using only its local table, the destination label and a bounded packet header. Stretch bounds routed length divided by shortest-path distance for every ordered pair. The intended model permits topology-dependent labels; it is not name-independent routing, and a global distance oracle alone is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Specify weight encoding, word size, admissible destination labels and header length, preprocessing costs and constants depending on k; confirm the exact no-handshake model.
context:
Compact routing asks how much global network knowledge must be stored locally to deliver paths close to shortest. The proposed space-stretch curve is a central target connecting routing with sparse distance representations.

Chechik improves the achievable stretch in this storage range while retaining a gap to 2k−1. The existing TCS-5770 instead extracts an extremal girth-construction question; that graph-existence target does not provide routing tables, labels or packet forwarding.
why: Reach a basic space-versus-route-quality frontier for distributed network representations.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2013: The source improves routing guarantees without attaining this universal space-stretch endpoint.

title: Does sublinear deterministic volume always collapse to O(log* n)?
importance_reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.
formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with V_A(n)=o(n) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with V_B(n)=O(1+log* n)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in {1,…,|V(G)|²}. Here V_A(n) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed Δ≥2, a fixed verification radius r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree Δ, possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, Π and the exact |V(G)|, and visited set {v}. It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. log* n is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no O(log* n)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every C>0 and every n₀, some n≥n₀ satisfies V_B(n)>C(1+log* n). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
context:
A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.
why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.
status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.
progress: 2020: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume. | 2021: Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below o(√log n) can be sped up to deterministic O(log* n). title: Quadratic expected message complexity for asynchronous crash consensus
importance_reason: Determine the fundamental message cost of randomized agreement under adversarial asynchrony.
formal: Does a randomized asynchronous binary consensus protocol exist with expected O(n²) messages against a strong adaptive adversary, tolerating every t<n/2 crash failures?
definitions: The n processes communicate by reliable asynchronous point-to-point messages and start with binary inputs. A crashed process takes no further steps. Every process that does not crash must eventually decide with probability one under fair scheduling; all decisions agree, and when all initial inputs are b every decision is b. A strong adversary observes past states, messages and revealed random outcomes and chooses subsequent process steps, message deliveries and crashes without seeing future coins. The bound counts all messages sent before protocol termination and must hold in expectation for every admissible adversary. It does not impose a bit bound on each message.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Reconcile the precise t-dependent constants, stop condition and validity convention with the journal model; specify whether the protocol knows n and t and whether computation and message sizes have additional constraints.
context:
Randomization makes asynchronous agreement possible despite crash failures, but robustness to a strong scheduler affects its communication cost. A quadratic bound would reach a central efficiency frontier in the standard message-passing model.

Alistarh, Aspnes, King and Saia give nearly quadratic expected communication against a strong adversary. Their logarithmic overhead is not a proof of the exact quadratic target. This question concerns crash failures, separately from Byzantine behavior or private-channel security.
why: Determine the fundamental message cost of randomized agreement under adversarial asynchrony.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2017: The source gives O(n² log² n) expected messages in its model, leaving the quadratic endpoint unresolved.

title: Is two-dimensional single-grain sandpile prediction in NC?
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved parallel-complexity question for a simple two-dimensional dynamical system, connecting computational prediction with statistical physics.
formal: Is the following decision problem in logspace-uniform NC? An input gives positive integers W,H, an explicit W-by-H array c with entries in {0,1,2,3}, and two cells p,q in that rectangle. Extend c by zero to the whole integer square lattice and add one grain at p. Answer YES exactly when q eventually topples under the four-neighbor parallel sandpile dynamics defined below. The input length N includes every array entry, not a compressed representation.
definitions: The four neighbor displacements are E={(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)}. Set c_0(v)=c(v)+1 if v=p, and c_0(v)=c(v) otherwise. At each integer time t>=0 every vertex v with c_t(v)>=4 topples once, losing four grains and sending one to each neighbor. Equivalently, c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4 I[c_t(v)>=4]+sum_{e in E} I[c_t(v-e)>=4], where I is the indicator. The question is whether c_t(q)>=4 for some t>=0. The array is row-major with binary dimensions and cell coordinates; invalid encodings are rejected. The zero extension is an infinite lattice, not a periodic boundary or a boundary that absorbs grains. A supplied rectangle may contain extra zero rows or columns to include p and q. Finite initial mass eventually stabilizes. NC here means that for some fixed integers a,k the decision has Boolean circuits of size O(N^a) and depth O((log N)^k), with fan-in at most two, whose description is generated from 1^N in O(log N) work space. There is no requested time t in the input and the answer is exact, without random error.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute membership of the specified language in logspace-uniform NC. Any complexity assumption used in a negative result must be stated explicitly.
context:
The initial configuration is stable, so all activity comes from the extra grain. The requested output is a single eventual-toppling bit; computing the entire final configuration or a toppling at a specified time are related but different tasks.

The classical dimension-dependent results provide efficient parallel prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three. They leave the planar case as a distinct question.

Recent work still separates the standard four-neighbor lattice from weighted or nonuniform grids. NC membership and P-completeness are not an unconditional exclusive dichotomy: a P-completeness result rules out NC only under NC != P.
why: A local deterministic physical process can have a long cascade after a single perturbation. This problem asks whether its outcome permits an efficient parallel computation, addressing the boundary between prediction and sequential evolution.
status_note: The 2025 primary source and the introduction of the 25 June 2026 preprint explicitly leave the standard planar case open. Checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 preprint is used for dated status and variant separation, not as an independently verified proof. This card fixes the NC-membership side of the proposed parallel-complexity question.
progress: 1998 / 1999: Moore and Nilsson obtain NC^3 prediction in one dimension and P-completeness in dimensions at least three, leaving dimension two open. | 2025-06-26: Concha-Vega and Perrot explicitly define single-grain eventual prediction on the infinite lattice and retain the von Neumann-neighborhood problem as open. | 2026-06-25: A new preprint studies weighted and nonuniform crossing constructions and continues to state the standard two-dimensional complexity question as open.

context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.

status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Distance sketching compresses vectors so that their dissimilarity can be approximated from small summaries. The source asks which distances admit such sketches and whether sketchability essentially forces a norm-like dependence on the vector difference. title: What is the deterministic round complexity of maximum independent set in the congested clique?
importance_reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
context:
The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.
why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.
status_note: The 2025 seminar source asks for the optimal round complexity. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate matching bounds for this exact task. Randomness and bandwidth are fixed explicitly here; results for maximal MIS, broadcast cliques, or edge-restricted CONGEST do not resolve this formulation.
progress: 2014: Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman establish circuit-simulation connections and distinguish unicast from broadcast congested cliques. Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task. | 2025: Chechik explicitly asks for the communication rounds necessary to compute a maximum independent set in the congested clique.
working_summary: Maximum independent set asks for a largest collection of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. Here each vertex is a processor in a congested clique, whose communication links exist even between nonadjacent input vertices. The question asks for the optimal deterministic number of rounds, with unlimited local computation and storage. Collecting the full graph at one processor gives an elementary upper bound, after which even exhaustive local optimization costs no communication rounds. The challenge is to determine how much information must move to identify an exact optimum, independently of the usual centralized NP-hardness barrier.

title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
importance_reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.
formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 and one deterministic VOLUME algorithm that computes a maximal matching on every bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Δ, inspecting at most C(Δ+1)^k distinct vertices per queried vertex, independently of the number n of graph vertices? A proper input two-coloring specifying the bipartition is supplied. Answers to all vertex queries must describe the same matching.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph, arbitrary local port orders, a supplied proper two-coloring, distinct identifiers in [n²], and known integers n and Δ≥1 bounding its size and degrees as stated. A query at v must output either ⊥ for unmatched or the local port of its matching edge. If v names u then u must name v. Every edge must have at least one matched endpoint, which is equivalent to maximality by inclusion. Initially the algorithm sees only v’s identifier, degree, color, ports, n, and Δ. It may adaptively follow a port at any already visited vertex; doing so reveals the neighbor’s identifier, degree, color, and reciprocal port. Count all distinct visited vertices, including v. The explored set is connected: arbitrary jumps to identifiers are forbidden. Each query starts afresh, with no preprocessing or memory retained between queries. Repeating a query must give the same answer regardless of other queries or their order. Local computation and temporary memory are unrestricted but finite, and only the number of distinct visited vertices is charged. One finite deterministic program must work for all n, Δ, graphs, identifiers, and port orders; the constants C,k are universal. There is no additional log n or log* n term in the allowed volume.
answer_criterion: Construct the uniform polynomial-in-Δ algorithm with globally consistent matching answers, or prove that every correct deterministic algorithm violates every such polynomial bound on some valid input and query. A randomized bound, expected volume, an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal, or a polynomial bound containing a factor depending on n does not settle this formulation.
context:
A matching is maximal when there is no edge that can be added while keeping its endpoints disjoint from the current matching. It can be much smaller than a maximum matching. The local output is only one port or an unmatched symbol, so the difficulty is the information needed to make this small answer consistent with answers elsewhere.

The supplied bipartition lets the two sides play different roles. A simple distributed procedure has unmatched vertices on one side propose along a new incident edge, while vertices on the other side accept at most one proposal and remain matched thereafter. After O(Δ) rounds this yields a maximal matching. Gathering a whole neighborhood to simulate those rounds can inspect Δ raised to a linear-in-Δ power many vertices.

Volume asks whether that exploration can be made much narrower. A vertex may follow a few carefully chosen dependencies far into the graph, instead of collecting every branch of a large ball. But it cannot simply choose a convenient partner in isolation: when that partner is queried separately, the answers must agree. The lack of shared mutable query state makes this coordination part of the algorithm itself.

The independence from n is essential. For each fixed Δ, even an enormous function such as Δ^(2Δ) is constant as n grows. This question compares those constants uniformly as Δ grows, asking for a single polynomial. It is therefore different from obtaining logarithmic dependence on n for fixed degree or from studying only a single fixed-degree LCL.

Known round lower bounds force at least linear dependence on Δ when n is sufficiently large. They leave a large interval between that obstruction and full-neighborhood simulation. Suomela conjectures an exponential degree dependence for volume, so even deciding whether a polynomial is possible would determine which side of that major gap is achievable.
why: This is a basic test of whether a fast distributed symmetry-breaking algorithm can be evaluated locally without exploring an exponentially branching dependency structure. A polynomial bound would give a small deterministic oracle for a fundamental graph primitive; a superpolynomial lower bound would expose an information cost that round complexity alone does not capture.
status_note: Explicitly open in the February 2026 primary problem list. Review through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic degree-only polynomial-volume algorithm or superpolynomial lower bound. The bipartition, connected probes, stateless consistency, and worst-case deterministic guarantee are fixed explicitly.
progress: 2020: rounds: Brandt and Olivetti sharpen the degree dependence of bipartite maximal matching in LOCAL. In the identifier model, the deterministic Ω(min{Δ,log n/log log n}) lower bound gives an Ω(Δ) obstruction to any degree-only volume bound by choosing sufficiently large n. | 2020: volume model: Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive exploration and explain why an f-round LOCAL algorithm gives a Δ^O(f)-volume algorithm. Combining this with the bipartite O(Δ)-round procedure gives the baseline Δ^O(Δ) volume. | 2026-02: Suomela explicitly asks whether bipartite maximal matching admits polynomial volume in Δ, and conjectures 2^Θ(Δ) as the correct dependence. The conjecture is not a proved lower bound.
working_summary: A maximal matching is a collection of disjoint edges to which no further edge can be added. The question asks for a deterministic local-query algorithm on bipartite graphs whose inspected volume is polynomial in the maximum degree and independent of graph size. A proper two-coloring identifying the bipartition is supplied. Simulating a distributed proposal algorithm by exploring whole neighborhoods can incur an exponential dependence on degree. The project is to follow a much smaller dependency structure while ensuring that separately answered vertex queries describe the same matching.

title: Lifting sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
importance_reason: A general comparison between streaming models could transfer algorithms or lower bounds across a large set of problems.
formal: Lifting sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Streaming approximation for a constraint satisfaction problem estimates the best fraction of constraints that one assignment can satisfy. Sketches impose additional structure by requiring independently processed summaries to combine consistently. The conjecture asks whether resistance to nontrivial approximation by o(sqrt(n))-space sketches implies resistance to all o(n)-space streaming algorithms. Thus the proposed implication both broadens the algorithm model and raises the memory threshold. A proof would greatly extend existing sketching classifications, while a simple counterexample would expose a useful algorithmic distinction between sketches and more general streams.

title: How many rounds does triangle detection require in CONGEST?
importance_reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.
formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.
answer_criterion: Determine a function f(n) with an O(f(n))-round randomized algorithm and an Omega(f(n)) worst-case lower bound for every randomized algorithm in the stated model, up to constant factors. Either a faster algorithm or a stronger lower bound alone is partial progress.
context:
Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.
progress: 2021: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound. | 2025: Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round. | 2025-10: Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks a distributed network to report whether any three vertices are pairwise adjacent. In CONGEST, each edge transmits only O(log n) bits per round, even though vertices initially know all their own neighbors. The saved card asks for the optimal randomized round complexity between the stated doubly logarithmic lower bound and roughly n^(1/3) upper bound. Detection needs only one positive witness somewhere in the network, unlike listing every triangle. The challenge is to exploit that smaller output requirement while still communicating enough information to discover an edge between two neighbors.

title: Can a congested clique find a maximal independent set in constant rounds?
importance_reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.
formal: Is there a randomized algorithm that, on every n-vertex simple input graph, finds a maximal independent set in O(1) rounds in the Congested Clique model, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for every requested fixed $c>0$? Processor v initially knows its identifier and incident input edges. Every ordered pair of processors may exchange an O(log n)-bit message per synchronous round, whether or not the input edge exists. Each processor outputs whether it belongs to an independent set that dominates every vertex outside it. The algorithm must be uniform across inputs; it cannot be chosen after seeing the graph.
definitions: Here $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of the input graph, not of the communication network. Messages to different recipients may differ. Local computation is unrestricted. $O(1)$ means independent of both $n$ and $\Delta$, with constants allowed to depend on the requested failure exponent. This is the unicast Congested Clique, rather than the weaker broadcast variant.
answer_criterion: Construct one randomized algorithm whose round bound is constant on every input graph, with the stated high-probability guarantee, or prove that constant rounds cannot suffice for all graphs in this model.
context:
This changes the communication network while leaving the graph problem unchanged. A vertex can contact a distant processor immediately, so graph distance no longer limits the spread of information. Bandwidth still matters: one processor can receive only $O(n\log n)$ bits per round, whereas a general graph can contain $\Theta(n^2)$ independently specified edges. Sending the entire input to one leader is therefore not a constant-round solution.

That bottleneck is not itself a lower bound for MIS. A complete graph has many edges but is easy: a designated vertex can join the independent set and all others can stay out. The sought algorithm only needs enough information to coordinate a valid answer; it need not reconstruct every edge in one place.

Known algorithms exploit this by solving suitably sparse sampled subgraphs and reducing the remaining degrees. The general upper bound is $O(\log\log\Delta)$ rounds. The central question is whether a bounded number of communication phases can remove the need for repeated sparsification.

A closely related relaxation is already possible in constant rounds: a 2-ruling set remains independent but only has to put every vertex within distance two of a selected vertex. MIS requires distance one. This supplies a precise nearby success case against which to assess the unresolved target.
why: I include this beside the LOCAL MIS problem because it tests a different limitation of distributed computation: restricted bandwidth despite universal communication. A constant-round algorithm would show that exact local domination needs only a bounded number of global exchanges. A lower bound would have to explain why distributed processing cannot avoid the bottleneck.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Constant-round MIS on arbitrary input graphs remains open in the checked literature.
progress: 2018: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović, and Rubinfeld obtain the $O(\log\log\Delta)$-round MIS bound using sparsification. | 2023: Cambus, Kuhn, Pai, and Uitto obtain constant rounds for the 2-ruling-set relaxation. | 2025: Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin, and Halldórsson obtain constant rounds, for example, when average degree is at most $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$. They also identify graph families on which existing sparsification methods require $\Omega(\log\log n)$ iterations. That restriction applies to those methods, not to all Congested Clique algorithms.
working_summary: A maximal independent set is independent and places every excluded vertex next to a selected one. In the congested clique, processors can send separate short messages directly to every other processor. The question asks whether a randomized algorithm can solve this task in a constant number of rounds on every input graph with high probability. Collecting all edges at one leader is too expensive, but the algorithm need not reconstruct the entire graph to choose a valid set. The target is to replace repeated sparsification and degree-reduction phases with a bounded amount of globally coordinated communication.

title: Graph Matchings
importance_reason: MIS and graph matching are fundamental graph primitives whose local or streaming complexity has broad algorithmic consequences.
formal: Graph Matchings
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns algorithmic solvability in a specified model. Its structural value is to locate the boundary between an effective procedure and a computational or logical obstruction.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Maximum weighted matching chooses disjoint edges with the greatest total weight. The source asks for a streaming approximation arbitrarily close to optimal using O(n log n) space and a number of passes depending only on the accuracy. title: Can deterministic (Delta+1)-coloring beat square-root dependence on degree?
importance_reason: Breaking the square-root degree barrier for the canonical coloring task would improve a broadly reused distributed primitive.
formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
context:
A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.
why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is deterministic and uniform in both degree and graph size; fast randomized coloring is not a resolution.
progress: 2020: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette. | 2026-02: Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence. | 2026-01: The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.
working_summary: A proper coloring with Delta plus one colors always exists for a graph of maximum degree Delta. title: A general 3/2 communication lower bound for reliable broadcast
importance_reason: Would determine the optimal leading communication constant for Byzantine reliable broadcast. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Must every Byzantine reliable-broadcast protocol in the source’s asynchronous authenticated point-to-point model have worst-case large-message communication overhead at least 3/2 asymptotically, when n=3t+1 and up to t parties can be Byzantine, even without a three-round delivery bound or a sublinear-in-n first-round sender load? This selects the source’s version with both restrictions removed.
definitions: There are n=3t+1 parties with pairwise authenticated channels and a designated sender holding a message m of ℓ bits. Honest-to-honest messages are eventually delivered, with no upper bound on delay; Byzantine parties may deviate arbitrarily. Validity requires every honest party eventually to deliver m when the sender is honest. Agreement requires all honest deliveries to have the same value. Integrity allows each honest party at most one delivery, and totality requires that if one honest party delivers, all honest parties eventually do so. A Byzantine sender may cause no delivery. Let C_A(n,ℓ) be the worst-case total number of bits sent by honest parties in one execution of protocol A, over admissible inputs, faults and delivery schedules. Faulty-party transmissions are not charged. For a faulty sender, the source measures the effective message length by the largest payload fragment an honest party sends under the protocol’s declared encoding. The large-message overhead is L_A(n)=limsup_{ℓ→∞} C_A(n,ℓ)/(nℓ). This uses the upper limit to include protocols without a limiting coefficient; it agrees with the source’s limit whenever that limit exists. The proposed bound is liminf_{t→∞}L_A(3t+1)≥3/2; equivalently, no constant improvement below 3/2 is possible uniformly for all sufficiently large n and sufficiently long messages. The source permits collision-resistant hashing and, for signature-based protocols, signature setup, counting their transmitted bits through a security parameter κ. The payload comparison discards lower-order terms in ℓ, such as O(κn²log n), and uses the source’s cryptographic correctness convention. There is no bound of three on the number of rounds and no restriction that the sender’s first-round total be o(nℓ).
answer_criterion: Prove the universal 3/2 lower bound in the stated unrestricted asynchronous model, or give a correct protocol with a strictly smaller asymptotic worst-case payload coefficient. An upper bound of 3/2 or a lower bound only for three-round, weakly balanced protocols does not resolve this question.
context:
Sending an ℓ-bit payload to n parties naturally costs on the order of nℓ bits. The open question concerns the leading constant caused by fault tolerance, rather than whether communication can be linear in payload length.

The original theorem applies even to synchronous crash faults, but requires delivery within three rounds and only o(nℓ) first-round bits from the sender. It does not establish the lower bound for protocols that use more rounds or concentrate the load on the sender.

MiniCast attains leading coefficient 3/2 in the worst case. The later Locher–Shoup work reduces its good-case latency to three rounds and also gives signature-based two-round variants. These constructions strengthen the evidence for optimality but do not prove the general lower bound.

A protocol may use approximately nℓ bits when everything goes well and still need 1.5nℓ bits in its worst execution. The conjecture is about the latter, counting all communication sent by honest parties even when a faulty sender prevents delivery.
why: Would settle the leading bandwidth cost of reliable broadcast, a primitive used inside many fault-tolerant distributed protocols.
status_note: Original restrictions and overhead definition checked against MiniCast, the October 2025 full follow-up and the OPODIS 2025 failure-case paper. No general lower-bound resolution was located through 12 September 2026. The question here concerns the unrestricted asynchronous version, not an unrestricted synchronous crash-fault claim.
progress: 2024: Locher proves a 3/2 lower bound for three-round protocols with restricted first-round sender load and asks to remove these restrictions. | 2025: MiniCast provides a general worst-case 3/2 upper bound; subsequent protocols improve latency while retaining that coefficient. | 2025-10-03: The revised Locher–Shoup follow-up still invokes optimality only under the restricted lower-bound conditions.
working_summary: Reliable broadcast must give all honest parties a consistent outcome despite Byzantine behavior. New protocols can do this with leading worst-case communication cost 1.5 times n times the payload length. The open question asks whether that constant is unavoidable for all protocols. The proved lower bound still restricts latency and first-round sender communication. Removing both restrictions is different from improving a protocol’s failure-free cost.
