title: Dimension-independent polyhedral sparsifiers for stochastic integer programs
importance_reason: An extension of polyhedral stochastic sparsification to more general integer optimization models. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Can the source’s (1−ε)-approximate stochastic sparsification framework be extended to a specified class of general integer linear programs with degree polynomial in 1/p, 1/ε and explicitly identified structural parameters, but independent of the total number of variables and constraints? The source does not select those structural parameters or formalize the general-ILP activation model.
definitions: In the source’s packing framework, E is a finite set of items, F⊆2^E is the downward-closed family of feasible item sets, and P_F=conv{1_S:S∈F} is their feasibility polytope. Here 1_S is the 0–1 indicator vector of S; P_F is the convex hull of integer feasible sets, not an arbitrary linear-programming relaxation. Each item independently becomes active with the common known probability p∈(0,1], producing R⊆E. A nonadaptive sparsifier chooses a possibly random query set Q⊆E before seeing R and learns which queried items are active. Degree at most d means 1_Q∈d P_F for every realization of Q; the empty query set can have degree zero. Given a nonnegative objective f on feasible item sets, put OPT(R)=max{f(S):S∈F,S⊆R}. The approximation requirement is E_{Q,R}[OPT(Q∩R)]≥(1−ε)E_R[OPT(R)], with Q independent of the unknown activation realization. For assignment problems, F records which item sets admit some feasible assignment to bins; the actual assignment is chosen after activation is revealed. An ILP ordinarily has integer variables, linear constraints and a linear objective. How such a general instance supplies E,F and independent activation is part of the extension still to be specified.
answer_criterion: Name an ILP class, activation model and structural invariants, then give an efficiently constructible query set with the claimed polyhedral-degree and expected-value bounds independent of dimension, or establish an obstruction within that same specification. A bound allowed to depend on a structural parameter that simply encodes the entire instance size does not give the intended dimension-independent conclusion.
statement_review_issue: A general-ILP extension needs to specify how integer variables become independently activated items, the admissible coefficient signs and domains, the feasibility polytope/projection, and the allowed intrinsic structural parameters. The phrase “intrinsic structural parameters” does not name an invariant or bound its dependence; permitting a parameter that itself equals the dimension would make dimension independence vacuous. The intended efficient construction model and expected versus stronger approximation guarantee must be preserved when selecting a complete extension.
context:
If every subset of E is feasible, then P_F=[0,1]^E. Querying all n items has degree one, even though it makes n queries. Thus constant degree does not mean a constant number of probes; it means the query set fits into a constant scaling of the feasible-set polytope.

The sparsifier preserves the expected optimum available among queried active items. Computing that optimum may remain hard. An efficient construction of Q therefore does not imply a polynomial-time near-optimal solution algorithm for every resulting integer program.

Knapsack, multiple knapsack and generalized assignment admit sparsifiers of degree polynomial in inverse activation probability and inverse accuracy, independent of item and constraint counts. The query degree is defined in item space, so assignments and item indicators cannot be interchanged.

Some rare activation realizations may lose much of their optimum. The definition compares expected optimal values under independent activation. Requiring a multiplicative approximation for every realization would be a different and stronger problem.

A parameter might describe restricted interaction between constraints and variables, but the source’s open question does not pick one. Until it does, there is no proposed universal bound whose validity can be proved or disproved.
why: Would extend query-efficient stochastic optimization beyond specialized packing and assignment constraints. The polyhedral measure can capture useful redundancy even when feasible solutions have very different cardinalities.
status_note: Source definition, guarantees, item projection and general extension question checked with the preprint abstract and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No single invariant or general-ILP benchmark is selected in the source, and no matching universal resolution was located.

working_summary: A sparsifier chooses which items to query before learning which independently become available. It must preserve nearly the full expected optimum while its indicator fits inside a small scaling of the feasible-item polytope. title: High-precision approximation of a log-sum-exp minimizer
importance_reason: A basic precision distinction in convex optimization and computational invariant theory. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given integer vectors ω_1,…,ω_n∈Z^d with 0 in the full-dimensional interior of their convex hull, nonzero Gaussian rationals v_1,…,v_n and a precision p≥1, outputs x∈Q^d with ||x−x*||₂<2^{−p}, where x* is the unique minimizer of f(x)=log(Σ_{i=1}^n |v_i|² exp(ω_i·x))? The time must be polynomial in the input dimensions, coefficient bit lengths and p.
definitions: Let M∈Z^{d×n} have columns ω_i, and let P=conv{ω_1,…,ω_n}={Σ_i a_iω_i: a_i≥0, Σ_i a_i=1}. The promise 0∈int(P) uses interior in R^d, not relative interior in a smaller affine space. A Gaussian rational v_i has the form a_i+b_i√(−1), with a_i,b_i∈Q; v_i≠0 ensures q_i=|v_i|²=a_i²+b_i²>0. The logarithm and exponential in f are the real natural logarithm and exponential. Under the promise, f is strictly convex, attains its minimum, and has exactly one minimizer x*∈R^d. Integers and rational numerators/denominators are encoded in binary. If B and b are the respective total encoding lengths of M and v, the target bit complexity is poly(d,n,B,b,p), including the rational output. Precision is supplied as an integer p and the running time is polynomial in its numerical value. This standard dyadic-accuracy convention spells out the source’s log(1/ε) dependence for ε=2^{−p}; a general binary rational accuracy request also incurs the cost of reading that request. No bound on a Hessian condition number or on the numerical magnitudes of the integer weights is an additional promise.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with the stated bit-complexity and Euclidean error guarantee on every promised input, or establish an obstruction to this guarantee. A small value of f(x)−min f, a small gradient, or convergence without the polynomial dependence on coefficient bit lengths and requested precision does not suffice.
context:
Two points can have almost identical objective values while remaining far apart in a very flat direction. This card asks for the actual coordinates of the unique minimum to a prescribed Euclidean accuracy.

The source cites polynomial-time algorithms producing points of nearly optimal objective value. Example 7.4 shows a family where a point remains distance one from x* despite a value gap doubly exponentially small in the coefficient encoding length.

An integer exponent weight can be exponentially large relative to its number of bits. An algorithm polynomial in that numerical weight would not provide the requested polynomial bit complexity.

For a diagonal torus action, the squared norm after scaling is Σ_i |v_i|² exp(ω_i·x). Its minimizing location specifies a distinguished scaling associated with the Kempf–Ness orbit. The numerical formulation above states the target without requiring group-action notation.
why: Separates efficient approximation of convex objective values from efficient recovery of minimizers, with consequences for canonical scaling and orbit comparison in invariant theory.
status_note: Full conjecture, coordinate normalization and flatness example checked, together with the source version record and the 2026 interior-point theorem. No polynomial-bit-time Euclidean minimizer approximation was located through 12 September 2026.
progress: 2024: The source states Conjecture 7.3 and gives an explicit separation between very small value error and small distance to the minimizer. | 2026-07-07: The manifold interior-point theorem gives objective-value guarantees for Kempf–Ness functions; its stated conclusion does not resolve this point-approximation problem.
working_summary: The input defines a strictly convex logarithm of a weighted sum of exponentials. Its minimum exists and is unique, but the question asks to locate that minimum accurately. The required running time is polynomial in coefficient bit lengths and the number of desired accuracy bits. Existing small-objective-error guarantees can leave the point far from the minimizer. The related 2026 optimization theorem still supplies a value guarantee rather than this distance guarantee.

title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?

formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.

context:
The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant C_H≥1 such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric d_G admits a map f:V(G)→ℝᵐ into some finite-dimensional ℓ₁ space satisfying d_G(u,v)≤‖f(u)−f(v)‖₁≤C_H d_G(u,v) for all vertices u,v?
definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and d_G(u,v) is the minimum path length. In ℝᵐ, ‖x−y‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ |xⱼ−yⱼ|. The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant C_H may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |V(G)|, the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and ℓ₁ embeddings.

The target ℓ₁ space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an ℓ₁ embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their ℓ₁ distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is O(√log n) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by γ faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion O(√log(γ+1)). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed γ and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of K₂,ₙ as (3k−2)/(2k−1), where k=⌈n/2⌉. The values approach 3/2. This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.
why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded ℓ₁ distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.
status_note: The planar constant-distortion case remains explicitly open in the checked May 2026 notes. Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for K₂,ₙ, do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. The inherited fixed-treewidth approximation theorem uses a stronger relaxation and expressly does not prove a flow–cut-gap bound. No general settlement found through 11 September 2026.

The graph may have arbitrary positive edge lengths, and every pair of vertices must be preserved within a constant factor. This constant may depend on the excluded minor but cannot grow with the graph. Because ℓ₁ metrics decompose into weighted cuts, the question also governs multicommodity flow–cut gaps. Even the planar case tests whether a strong topological restriction is enough to remove all growing distortion.

title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
importance_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
focus_reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in O((N+1)^c) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into S³; the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of S³ starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has O(n log(n+1)) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in NP∩coNP and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply NP=coNP. Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most (236n)¹¹ Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form exp((log N)^{O(1)}), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.
why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.
status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.

This review has not independently validated the proof.
working_summary: Unknot recognition asks whether a closed loop represented by a finite crossing diagram can be deformed into a circle without cutting. A complicated drawing may still represent an unknot, so simplifying visible crossings is not a complete decision method. The target here is a deterministic algorithm whose bit complexity is polynomial in the diagram encoding. The saved card records a September 2026 preprint claiming such an algorithm, with its proof not independently validated. This description therefore preserves the uncertainty around that claim while explaining the computational target.

title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture for edge-path diameter
importance_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
focus_reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.
why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.
status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.
progress: 1992: Kalai–Kleitman establish a quasipolynomial general edge-diameter bound; Todd’s paper records and sharpens the recurrence-based result. | 2010–2012: Santos disproves the original linear Hirsch conjecture with a 43-dimensional bounded polytope having 86 facets. | 2014: Todd proves the upper bound (n−d)^{log₂d}. | 2018–2019: Sukegawa’s asymptotic improvement lowers the exponent by log₂log d up to an additive constant, still quasipolynomial. | 2025: The ETH geometry notes retain the polynomial problem; Wulf establishes Π₂^p-hardness of computing diameters even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes. | 2026-02-10: Natura’s revised manuscript proves polynomial circuit diameter, including monotone circuit walks; ordinary edge diameter remains open.
working_summary: The vertex-edge graph of a convex polyhedron records which feasible vertices can be joined by a single edge move. Its diameter is the largest shortest-path distance between any two vertices. The polynomial Hirsch conjecture asks for one polynomial bound in the number of facets and dimension that works uniformly for every pointed polyhedron. Counterexamples to the original linear Hirsch bound do not refute this weaker polynomial target. Resolving it would constrain the combinatorial geometry of linear programs, although short undirected paths would still not supply an efficient improving simplex rule.

title: How many k-element subsets can a line separate from a planar point set?
importance_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
focus_reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.
formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. K₂(n,k) and the uniform constant-factor target are defined, but the admissible representation of the answer F(n,k) is not. Allowing arbitrary functions admits F=K₂ itself, while an arbitrarily imposed expression grammar or computational bound would change the question. An answer representation must be selected before this is a closed benchmark specification.
statement_review_issue: K₂(n,k) and the uniform constant-factor target are defined, but the admissible representation of the answer F(n,k) is not. Allowing arbitrary functions admits F=K₂ itself, while an arbitrarily imposed expression grammar or computational bound would change the question. An answer representation must be selected before this is a closed benchmark specification.
context:
A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.
why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.
status_note: The June 2025 problem entry retains the gap. The 2024 halving-line improvement changes lower-order terms rather than the exponent. No matching asymptotic bound was located in the status search through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1997–1998: Dey proves K₂(n,k)=O(n k^(1/3)) for 1≤k≤n/2 through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an O(n^(4/3)) upper bound. | 2000–2001: Tóth constructs planar point sets with n exp(Ω(√log k)) k-sets for n≥2k>0, improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows. | 2008: Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce n^(1+ε) halving edges for any fixed positive ε. | 2024-07: Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains 4/3. | 2025-06: The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.
working_summary: A k-set is a selection of k points that a line strictly separates from all remaining points of a planar configuration. The problem asks for the largest possible number of distinct k-sets among n points in general position. The desired estimate must remain sharp when k grows with n, including nearly balanced cuts. Duality turns this into a question about levels in arrangements of lines. Closing the gap between constructions and upper bounds would clarify the complexity of geometric selection and related optimization problems.

title: Lang–Plaut problem
importance_reason: Asks whether intrinsic metric dimension permits Euclidean dimension reduction.
formal: Does every doubling subset of a Hilbert space admit a bi-Lipschitz embedding into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, with dimension and distortion depending only on the doubling constant?
context: This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: Asks whether intrinsic metric dimension permits Euclidean dimension reduction.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls. The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space. It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor. Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant. The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.

title: Is PL four-sphere recognition decidable?
importance_reason: A longstanding and precisely isolated computational-topology problem connecting finite combinatorial input with fundamental four-dimensional topology.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine which, on every finite simplicial complex K promised to be a closed combinatorial 4-manifold, halts and decides whether K is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the boundary of a 5-simplex?
definitions: A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite family of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets; its maximal sets are its facets. The input lists all facets with integer vertex labels in binary. K is pure of dimension 4 when all facets have five vertices. The link of a vertex v consists of the faces σ not containing v for which σ∪{v} is a face of K. A closed combinatorial 4-manifold here is a nonempty pure 4-dimensional complex in which each vertex link is a PL 3-sphere; connectedness is not promised. The standard PL d-sphere is the boundary complex of a (d+1)-simplex. Two complexes are PL homeomorphic when they admit finite simplicial subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic, equivalently when their geometric realizations admit a homeomorphism affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions. A simplicial subdivision triangulates the same realization by smaller simplices contained in the old simplices. Correctness and termination are required on every promised input; no behavior is required on other inputs. There is no time or space bound beyond termination.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A triangulation is finite data, but deciding the global space it describes may exceed the power of every algorithm. Sphere recognition is decidable in low dimensions and undecidable from dimension five onward; dimension four is the exceptional unresolved case in this PL formulation.

The category matters: a topological homeomorphism need not supply a PL equivalence. The practical study explicitly distinguishes a homology four-sphere, a topological four-sphere and the standard PL four-sphere. This card asks for recognition of the last object.

Successful recognition on large test collections does not establish termination on every promised manifold. The question is about the existence of a decision procedure, rather than the speed or reliability of a particular implementation.
why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 presentation and 2022 research paper support the unresolved PL four-dimensional target; no later resolution was found.
progress: 2022: The computational study distinguishes recognizing the standard PL sphere from detecting a topological sphere and reports inconclusive four-dimensional instances. | 2025-07-15: The research presentation retains dimension four as the unresolved recognition boundary.
working_summary: The input is a finite triangulation promised to be a closed combinatorial four-dimensional manifold. The task is to recognize the standard piecewise-linear four-sphere. The question asks for a terminating decision algorithm, with no polynomial-time requirement. Recognizing a topological sphere or checking its homology would answer a different question. The problem marks the exceptional dimension between established decidability and undecidability results for sphere recognition.

title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
importance_reason: Asks how far network and metric representations can be compressed while preserving distances.
formal: Does every weighted graph with designated terminals have a suitably reweighted minor on exactly those terminals whose terminal distances lie between the original distances and a universal constant times those distances?
context: This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: Asks how far network and metric representations can be compressed while preserving distances.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.

title: The optimal complexity of Klee's measure problem in higher dimensions

definitions: An input is a list of n≥0 closed boxes B_i=∏_{j=1}^d [a_i,j,b_i,j], specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with a_i,j≤b_i,j. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have O(log(n+2)) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. The requested precision is a Θ bound: logarithmic factors count, and constants may depend on d. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied.

An improved upper bound alone, a conditional lower bound, a restriction to particular box shapes, or a result only for approximate or dynamic volume does not complete the classification.
context:

title: The complexity of SEFE for two graphs
importance_reason: A central simultaneous graph-drawing problem about making overlapping structures geometrically consistent.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given any two finite simple planar graphs G₁=(V,E₁) and G₂=(V,E₂) on the same labeled vertex set, decides in polynomial time whether they admit planar topological drawings that coincide on every shared vertex and every shared edge?
definitions: The input gives n≥0, V={1,…,n}, and two symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is H=(V,E₁∩E₂), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points p(v)∈ℝ² to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints p(u),p(v), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same p(v) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in E₁∩E₂. Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,c≥1 with at most C(N+1)^c bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

G₁ is planar, and G₂ can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to G₁. This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph K₅. Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

The checked 2025 papers report polynomial-time algorithms when H is connected. This is connectivity of the shared edges and vertices, not merely connectivity of each input graph. Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

title: Find a simple closed quasigeodesic in polynomial time

definitions: A convex polyhedron here is a compact convex polytope K⊂ℝ³ with nonempty interior, whose boundary ∂K is a polyhedral sphere. A simple closed curve is a continuous injective map γ:S¹→∂K, where S¹ is a circle; equivalently, a parametrization on [0,1] has equal endpoints and no other repetitions. The curve is nonconstant and locally polygonal. At a point away from a polyhedron vertex it must become a straight line after local unfolding. At a vertex on the curve, its two incident directions divide the total incident face angle into two surface angles, each required to be at most π. These angles are measured along the surface, not as angles of 3D chords. An ordinary geodesic has angle π on both sides everywhere; the relaxed condition allows a quasigeodesic to pass through a vertex with positive angular defect. The desired output is one curve satisfying all these conditions, not an approximate curve or an existence certificate without a specified curve. A doubled path that retraces itself is not injective and is excluded from this imported strict-simple target.

title: Is minimum-weight triangulation in NP?
importance_reason: Asks whether exact geometric optimization has short certificates despite the algebraic cost of verifying lengths.
formal: Does the following language belong to NP? An instance consists of a finite set S⊂ℚ² of explicitly given points and a rational bound B; it is a yes instance exactly when S has a triangulation whose total Euclidean edge length, counting every edge once, is at most B.
definitions: The input lists n≥0 distinct points (x_i,y_i), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight W(T)=∑_{ {i,j}∈E(T) }√((x_i−x_j)²+(y_i−y_j)²). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality W(T)=B is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if V(x,y) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.
context:
A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) have a single triangular boundary of total length 2+√2. A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.

title: NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds

formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that, for every finite PL-triangulation T of a compact connected three-manifold M, M is closed and admits a hyperbolic metric if and only if there exists a binary certificate w with |w|≤p(|T|) and V(T,w)=1?
definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space M=|T|. The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space H³; for example H³ is the upper half-space {(x,y,z)∈ℝ³:z>0} with metric ds²=(dx²+dy²+dz²)/z². Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.

title: Does bounded neighborhood VC dimension suffice for fast geometric diameter tests?
importance_reason: A proposed structural explanation for fast diameter computation across implicit geometric graphs. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Conjecture 8 asks whether Diameter-Δ for intersection graphs of constant-description-complexity geometric objects always admits a truly subquadratic algorithm when the VC dimension of the radius-Δ neighborhoods is bounded by a constant, in any ambient dimension. The effective object representation, treatment of Δ and allowable parameter dependence still need to be specified for one fully quantified algorithmic statement.
definitions: Given n geometric objects O₁,…,O_n, their intersection graph has one vertex per object and an undirected edge ij exactly when O_i∩O_j≠∅. The input is the object descriptions, so the potentially quadratic set of edges is implicit. Graph distance dist(u,v) is the number of edges in a shortest path, and is ∞ across components. The diameter is max_{u,v}dist(u,v). Diameter-Δ asks whether it is at most the integer Δ or greater than Δ (equivalently at least Δ+1 for finite distances). Define N^Δ[v]={u:dist(u,v)≤Δ}, including v itself. A subset S of vertices is shattered by these neighborhoods if for every A⊆S there exists v with N^Δ[v]∩S=A. The VC dimension is the largest |S| that can be shattered. A constant bound must hold uniformly over growing inputs in the selected class. Bounded distance VC dimension, using all radii simultaneously, is a stronger condition than the fixed-radius version. Truly subquadratic time means O(n^{2−η}) for some fixed η>0, allowing logarithmic factors to be absorbed into a smaller positive exponent saving. Constant description complexity means a bounded number of defining parameters or predicates per object; without further restrictions it does not specify how those predicates are encoded or evaluated.
answer_criterion: Fix the representation and parameter quantifiers, then prove the universal sufficient-condition algorithm or give a counterexample within that model. The time must be truly subquadratic in the number of objects, with the stated uniform exponent saving. Showing tractability for a new single shape family is progress, but does not establish the general conjecture.
statement_review_issue: The source defines low complexity only as constant description complexity. A universal algorithmic statement still needs a specified effective representation/object class and computation model, a convention for whether Δ is fixed or part of the input, and the permitted dependence of the exponent on Δ, ambient dimension and the VC bound. The geometric input must remain implicit; an explicit adjacency matrix would already cost Θ(n²) to read. Choosing a particular semialgebraic representation or a fixed Δ would specialize the source conjecture and is not done silently.
context:
For a fixed vertex v, N^Δ[v] records all objects reachable from it in at most Δ intersections. Bounded VC dimension says these reachable sets cannot realize every pattern on a large collection of test vertices. It limits their combinatorial variety, rather than their sizes.

If all objects intersect one another, the graph is complete and every radius-1 neighborhood is the whole vertex set. Its VC dimension is zero, although the graph has Θ(n²) edges. This is why the algorithm must work from object descriptions rather than enumerate all edges.

The paper gives a subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for boxes despite unbounded relevant VC dimension. Thus unbounded VC dimension does not by itself imply hardness, and an “if and only if” reformulation would contradict a result in the source.

A related framework has time depending on the edge count m for general sparse graphs, alongside stronger results for specific geometric families. Substituting m=Θ(n²) does not produce the desired O(n^{2−η}) guarantee. The extra geometric input structure remains relevant.

The source highlights ordinary disks of varying radii in the plane: their intersection graphs have bounded distance VC dimension, but the paper does not know a truly subquadratic Diameter-2 algorithm for them. This is distinct from the already solved unit-disk case.
why: Seeks a common structural reason that geometric diameter problems admit faster algorithms. A valid general theorem would turn bounds on reachable-set complexity into algorithmic guarantees across shape families and dimensions.

title: Does every point set admit an oriented t-spanner with t < 2?
importance_reason: A specific universal dilation threshold for one-way geometric connections, now settled by a stronger metric-space theorem; its historical value is to distinguish existence guarantees from optimal-orientation complexity. The prior numerical score is preserved.
formal: Is there a real constant t<2 such that, for every integer d≥1 and every finite set P⊆ℝ^d with |P|≥3, some oriented graph on P has oriented dilation at most t? Edges may join arbitrary pairs, with Euclidean lengths, but opposite directed edges on the same pair are forbidden.
definitions: An oriented graph on P has no loops and, for each unordered pair {p,q}, includes either no edge or exactly one of p→q and q→p. A directed walk follows the directions of its edges; its length is the sum of their Euclidean lengths, counting repeated traversals. It is closed if it ends where it starts. For distinct p,q∈P, let C_G(p,q) be the minimum length of a directed closed walk containing both p and q, or +∞ if none exists. Define Δ_P(p,q)=min_{r∈P\{p,q}} (‖p−q‖₂+‖q−r‖₂+‖r−p‖₂), the minimum perimeter of a triangle using p, q and a third point of P. Here ‖x‖₂=√(Σ_i x_i²). Since P contains at least three distinct points, this denominator is finite and positive. The oriented dilation is max_{p≠q} C_G(p,q)/Δ_P(p,q). An oriented t-spanner has dilation at most t. The constant t is independent of the point set, its size and dimension. The target imposes no planarity, sparsity or running-time restriction; choosing an orientation of the complete graph is permitted. A tournament means such a complete orientation. The published solution holds more generally with any metric distance, namely a symmetric nonnegative distance that vanishes exactly on equal points and obeys the triangle inequality.
answer_criterion: The historical assertion is answered positively by the published choice t=5/3. Theorem 6 constructs a tournament with this bound for every finite metric point set. A claim about only average dilation, a prescribed sparse input graph, or a point-set-dependent bound approaching two would have had a different conclusion.
context:
Imagine assigning one-way connections between locations while keeping every round trip reasonably short. The condition concerns a closed walk through each pair, so it controls travel in both directions together. An edge may not be used in both directions; going from p to q and back generally needs a third location.

The reference length is the cheapest triangle through the pair using another point from the same set. For three points, orienting their triangle cyclically gives dilation one: the only directed round trip has exactly the reference perimeter. A transitive orientation of those three points contains no directed cycle and gives infinite dilation. This illustrates why edge direction matters even when every pair is connected.

The original 2025 question asked whether the universal factor could be made strictly smaller than two, including when all pairs were available for orientation. It did not require an optimal orientation or a plane drawing without crossings.

Bhore and coauthors answer this target with factor 5/3 in Theorem 6 of their ESA 2026 paper. Their theorem applies to every finite metric space and supplies a complete orientation. Their Corollary 10 also gives factor 5/3+ε with a linear number of edges in fixed-dimensional Euclidean spaces; choosing a fixed ε<1/3 keeps this factor below two.

Computing a minimum-dilation tournament is a separate optimization question, retained as TCS-1212. A uniform upper bound supplies a good orientation without determining the best one for each point set. The 2026 paper explicitly leaves that optimization complexity open.
why: The historical question tested how much detour is forced by one-way connections when every pair needs a short round trip. The 5/3 theorem crosses its proposed threshold and now serves as a benchmark for stronger dilation, sparsity and optimization questions.

title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
importance_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
focus_reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.
why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.
