title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
importance_reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.
formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.
context:
LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.
why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-09-08: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
working_summary: Learning parity with noise asks for information about hidden binary linear equations when some answers have been flipped. This project asks whether worst-case hardness of the binary nearest-codeword problem implies average-case hardness for a specified low-noise LPN distribution. The chosen regime uses quadratically many samples and a noise rate inversely proportional to the square root of the secret dimension. A reduction must produce that particular random-instance distribution rather than merely another hard coding problem or a different noise level. Such a connection would strengthen the theoretical foundation of low-noise LPN in the way worst-case reductions support lattice-based assumptions.

title: Do arbitrary one-way functions imply one-way functions in NC⁰?
importance_reason: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ circuit family?
definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. A polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ family is generated from 1^n in poly(n) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT gates. title: Unrestricted offline ORAM bandwidth lower bounds
importance_reason: A major lower-bound barrier for oblivious computation, linking memory privacy to fundamental circuit complexity.
formal: Is logarithmic amortized bandwidth overhead necessary for offline oblivious RAM with constant client storage, even when stored words may be arbitrarily encoded rather than merely moved as indivisible items?

working_summary: Cryptographic hardness must occur on instances that honest users can efficiently generate, rather than only on a difficult exceptional input. The cited question asks whether P ≠ NP, or a suitable average-case separation between distributional classes, already implies one-way functions. It also asks about the stronger possibility of trapdoor functions, where secret information enables inversion that remains hard publicly. These targets add progressively more structure to a bare claim that efficient algorithms cannot solve everything. Establishing the implications would connect cryptographic foundations to broad complexity assumptions instead of relying on individual number-theoretic or algebraic candidates.

title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
importance_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
focus_reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.
formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.
why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2013: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions. | 2026-08-19: Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.
working_summary: The quantum PCP conjecture asks whether even a coarse estimate of a quantum system's lowest energy can capture the difficulty of verifying quantum proofs. The system is specified by local interactions, each involving only a bounded number of qubits. The target is hardness for distinguishing two possible ground energies separated by a constant after normalizing the total interaction strength. Normalization prevents a small gap from becoming a constant merely by multiplying the Hamiltonian by a large number. The problem connects robust quantum verification with entanglement, quantum codes, and the limits of approximation algorithms.

title: Does BPP differ from BQP?
importance_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
focus_reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.
formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language L⊆{0,1}* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time C(n+1)^k on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most 1/3 separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on 1ⁿ generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |x⟩, polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |0⟩, and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least 2/3 for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality BPP=BQP would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.
why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.
status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.
progress: 1990s: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with BPP⊆BQP. Wigderson’s Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2 state the model and inclusion. | 1994 conference / 1995–1996 preprint: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms. No unconditional classical polynomial-time lower bound for those tasks follows. | 2019 conference / 2022 journal: Raz and Tal prove an oracle separation BQP⊄PH. This also separates BQP from BPP relative to that oracle, but not in ordinary unrelativized computation. | 2026-08: Bene Watts and Parham publish an unconditional shallow-circuit sampling separation. Its classical resource restrictions and sampling output differ from the unrestricted decision model fixed here.
working_summary: This problem asks whether efficient quantum computation can decide something that efficient randomized classical computation cannot. BPP and BQP both require a reliable yes-or-no answer on every input, with bounded probability of error. Quantum interference gives promising candidate advantages, including the algorithms underlying factoring, but those examples do not establish an unconditional classical lower bound. Separations using special oracles or restricted classical circuits concern narrower comparisons. Settling the ordinary class separation would identify whether quantum computers enlarge the set of efficiently decidable problems at its most basic level.

title: An entanglement entropy area law for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
importance_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
focus_reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.
formal: For every fixed local dimension q≥2, interaction range r≥1, interaction incidence bound g≥1, norm bound J>0, and spectral gap Δ>0, is there a finite constant C=C(q,r,g,J,Δ) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice Λ_L, has unique ground state ψ satisfying S(ρ_A)≤C|∂A| for every A⊆Λ_L?
definitions: Let L≥1 be an integer, Λ_L={1,…,L}² with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of C^q over its sites. Write H=Σ_a h_a, where each h_a is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support X_a⊆Λ_L of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every h_a is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector ψ and its next eigenvalue is at least Δ above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For A⊆Λ_L, let A^c be its complement in Λ_L and ρ_A=Tr_(A^c)(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) and S(ρ_A)=−Tr(ρ_A log_2 ρ_A), with 0 log_2 0=0. The boundary ∂A is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension q^L, which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.
why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.
progress: 2007: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters. | 2021: Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap. | 2022: Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar publish an area law for entanglement spread, rather than von Neumann entropy. | 2022–2023: Anshu, Arad, and Gosset give a nearly linear entropy bound for vertical cuts in locally gapped frustration-free systems. In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) at the end of §4. | 2026-02-05: Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector. | 2026-04-15: Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.
working_summary: An area law says that entanglement between a region and its surroundings grows with the region's boundary rather than its volume. This problem asks for such a bound for the unique ground state of a general two-dimensional local Hamiltonian with a fixed positive spectral gap. Interaction strength, local dimension, and interaction range are held fixed as the lattice grows. Known routes involving frustration-free systems or additional conditions do not automatically establish the unrestricted statement recorded here. A solution would clarify how strongly locality and an energy gap constrain many-body quantum states, without by itself supplying an efficient algorithm to find them.

title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
importance_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
focus_reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.
formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol (P,V) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let p(C) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have p(C)≥2/3 and NO instances have p(C)≤1/3. V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]≥2/3. On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]≤1/3. Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion BQP⊆IP does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’s IP=PSPACE theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove BQP^O⊆MIP^O for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.
why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves this single-prover, information-theoretic question open. The May 2026 trusted-gate result changes verifier resources, and the February 2026 witness-preserving protocol retains LWE. Neither meets this card’s classical-verifier and unbounded-cheater requirements.

working_summary: A classical user would like to check a computation performed by a single quantum device using only classical messages. The honest device must be able to carry out the verification protocol in quantum polynomial time. The difficult requirement is soundness against any cheating device, including a computationally unbounded one. Existing approaches may instead give the user limited quantum capabilities, use separated devices, or assume that a cryptographic problem is hard. The question isolates whether an entirely classical client can obtain unconditional trust in efficient quantum computation under this single-device model.

title: Does NPT bound entanglement exist?
importance_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
focus_reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.
formal: Do there exist finite integers a,b≥2 and a bipartite density matrix ρ on ℂᵃ⊗ℂᵇ such that ρ has negative partial transpose, but ⟨ψ|(ρ^{Γ_B})^{⊗k}|ψ⟩≥0 for every integer k≥1 and every unit vector ψ of Schmidt rank at most two across (ℂᵃ)^{⊗k}:(ℂᵇ)^{⊗k}?
definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by (ρ^{Γ_B})_{ij,kℓ}=ρ_{iℓ,kj}. Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that ρ^{Γ_B} has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is ψ. Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is ρ_W(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d²+αd), where d≥3, −1≤α≤1 and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when α<−1/d, and one-copy distillable exactly when α<−1/2. Consequently the interval −1/2≤α<−1/d consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for d≥3. The endpoint α=−1/2 is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example ρ_W(4,−1/2). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.
why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.
status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

working_summary: Entangled states can sometimes be converted into nearly perfect shared Bell pairs using many copies and local operations with classical communication. Bound entanglement means that this distillation remains impossible despite the presence of entanglement. The question asks whether such states can have a negative partial transpose, a spectral property associated with distillability in simpler settings. Failure of a protocol on one copy or any fixed number of copies does not establish the required obstruction for every number of copies. Resolving the question would sharpen the distinction between entanglement as a property and entanglement as a usable communication resource.

title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
importance_reason: A defining construction problem beyond good quantum LDPC codes, with direct links to local testing, Hamiltonian complexity, fault tolerance and the quantum PCP program.
formal: Do there exist constants r,δ,s>0 and integers w,b≥1, and stabilizer codes Q on unbounded numbers n of qubits, such that Q encodes at least rn logical qubits, has distance at least δn, every listed check has weight at most w, every qubit occurs in at most b checks, and the normalized check Hamiltonian satisfies H⪰(s/n)D_Q?
definitions: Use the Hilbert space (ℂ²)⊗n. On a computational basis bit, X flips the bit and Z multiplies |1⟩ by −1 while fixing |0⟩; Y=iXZ. A Pauli operator is a tensor product of I,X,Y,Z, up to phase, and its weight is the number of nonidentity tensor factors. A listed check Sⱼ is a nonidentity Hermitian Pauli operator with eigenvalues ±1. The m≥1 checks commute, and the group they generate must not contain −I. Their joint +1 eigenspace Q has dimension 2ᵏ, where k is the number of encoded logical qubits. Code distance d is the minimum weight of a Pauli operator that preserves Q but whose restriction to Q is not a scalar multiple of the identity. Checks may be redundant; both the weight bound and the per-qubit incidence bound refer to the listed checks. Define H=(1/m)Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ(I−Sⱼ)/2. For 0≤t≤n, let Q_t be the linear span of E|ψ⟩ over all |ψ⟩∈Q and Pauli errors E of weight at most t, and let Π_t be the orthogonal projector onto Q_t. Define D_Q=Σₜ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(I−Π_t). The operator inequality H⪰(s/n)D_Q means that its difference is positive semidefinite, or equivalently that the corresponding expectation inequality holds for every quantum state. All five constants are fixed independently of n, and k≥rn and d≥δn must hold throughout an infinite family with n→∞. This card uses the bounded-degree stabilizer version of qLTC existence. Checks need not be geometrically local, and no efficient construction algorithm is required.
answer_criterion: Construct or prove existence of an infinite family satisfying all the stated conditions with fixed constants, or prove that every family of stabilizer presentations fails at least one of them. The target requires maximum check weight and qubit incidence to be bounded, not merely their averages. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance does not qualify. Verifying soundness only for some low-weight errors is insufficient: the operator inequality must hold on the entire Hilbert space.
context:
A quantum code is the common accepting space of many checks. Measuring a uniformly selected check rejects a state with probability equal to its expected normalized energy under H. Local testability asks for a robust version of exact membership: a state that requires many local changes to reach the code must violate a noticeable fraction of checks. Constant check weight then makes this a test involving only a constant number of qubits.

Distance from the code must account for quantum degeneracy. A large Pauli operator can be a stabilizer and leave every encoded state unchanged; another can implement a logical operation while still remaining inside the code space. Neither should be called far from the code merely because its written support is large. The spaces Q_t and the operator D_Q measure how many physical qubits are needed to leave the entire code space in each orthogonal error sector. The soundness condition also covers superpositions and mixed states.

A simple classical analogy illustrates the missing property. Consider a chain of equality checks requiring adjacent bits to agree. A string consisting of a long zero block followed by a long one block can be far from either valid repetition-code word while violating only one check. Local constraints and even a large code distance therefore do not by themselves imply robust local testing. The quantum target additionally requires storing a linear number of logical qubits.

Panteleev and Kalachev resolved the existence of asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes: constant check size can coexist with constant rate and linear distance. Their work also establishes good locally testable classical codes. These are two different conclusions. Quantum local testability with constant soundness does not follow by combining the words in the paper’s title; it is the extra property sought here.

Cross and coauthors obtain constant-soundness qLTC constructions with other parameter compromises. One approach has distance growing with check locality; another has constant average locality while some checks and qubit incidences grow. Wills, Lin and Hsieh analyze distance balancing with more general classical ingredients, quantifying the accompanying soundness loss. Such tradeoffs make it important to track the maximum locality, normalized soundness, rate and distance simultaneously.

Dinur, Lin and Vidick’s construction comes much closer: it has k=Ω(n), distance Ω(n/log³n), soundness Ω(1/log³n), and constant check size. Its September 2025 revision corrects the rate analysis by shifting the chain complex. The paper also describes ways to obtain constant soundness, and then linear distance, at the cost of polylogarithmic check size. These variants do not provide all the constants required by this card at once.

The NLTS theorem is another nearby achievement with a distinct conclusion. Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe show that certain good quantum codes yield Hamiltonians whose low-energy states require nontrivial circuit depth to prepare. That theorem resolves a major quantum-complexity conjecture without establishing constant-soundness local testability. A qLTC would give a stronger relation between energy and distance from a code, and could support further work toward quantum PCP; it would not by itself prove the full quantum PCP conjecture.

Li, Li and Liu’s July 2026 revision adds transversal non-Clifford operations to almost-good constructions. For example, their three-qubit controlled-controlled-Z case retains logarithmic losses in distance and soundness. The revision replaces an invalid cap-product argument from April with a substantially different proof using product-expanding local codes. This adds computational functionality while leaving the constant-parameter qLTC question open.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 work uses qLTCs in interactive oracle proofs for QMA, with polynomial communication and polylogarithmically many queried qubits. It illustrates the value of the available approximate parameters. Interaction and a polylogarithmic query budget remain part of that result; it is not a constant-query static quantum PCP or a construction meeting the stronger code parameters here.
why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No bounded-degree stabilizer family with constant rate, relative distance and normalized soundness was located. The corrected 2025 and July 2026 constructions retain inverse-polylogarithmic losses, while constant-soundness variants increase locality or sacrifice other parameters.
progress: 2021–2022: Panteleev–Kalachev construct good quantum LDPC codes and, separately, good classical LTCs. | 2022–2023: Anshu–Breuckmann–Nirkhe resolve NLTS using good quantum codes without constructing good constant-soundness qLTCs. | 2024-10-18: Cross and coauthors publish constant-soundness qLTCs with compromises in distance, rate or maximum locality. | 2024-11-20: Wills–Lin–Hsieh analyze soundness under general distance balancing. | 2025-09-04: The corrected Dinur–Lin–Vidick version achieves constant rate and locality with log³n losses in relative distance and soundness. | 2026-06-08: Sun–Vidick apply qLTCs to quantum interactive oracle proofs with polylogarithmic query complexity. | 2026-07-02: Li–Li–Liu replace the invalid April argument and retain transversal-gate claims for almost-good codes.
working_summary: A locally testable quantum code should reveal a substantial error by checking only a few qubits. The desired family must also encode a linear amount of quantum information and tolerate errors on a linear number of physical qubits. Each check and each qubit's participation in checks must remain bounded as the code grows. These requirements strengthen ordinary good quantum LDPC codes by demanding a quantitative relation between distance from the code space and rejection probability. Such codes would connect robust quantum error detection with the complexity of low-energy states and the broader search for quantum PCP constructions.

title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions — claimed resolution
importance_reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.
formal: Does there exist a family of three-dimensional, bounded-density local Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonians Hₙ and a fixed inverse temperature 0<β<∞ for which the lifetime τₙ(β) of one encoded qubit, under the thermal dynamics below and without intervention during storage, tends to infinity as n→∞?
definitions: The family may use an unbounded subsequence of qubit counts n. Place the qubits in ℝ³, with at most B qubits in each unit ball. Let Hₙ=Σⱼ(I−Sⱼ)/2, where the Sⱼ are commuting nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks, each supported in a ball of radius R, each qubit belongs to at most B checks, and their joint +1 eigenspace has dimension two. B and R are constants independent of n. A Pauli check is a signed tensor product of I,X,Y,Z; X flips |0⟩ and |1⟩, Z changes the sign of |1⟩, and Y=iXZ. Use the following fixed Davies-type thermal generator, in units with ℏ=k_B=1. If Π_E is the energy-E spectral projector of Hₙ, define A_{i,P,ω}=Σ_{E′−E=ω}Π_{E′}PᵢΠ_E for every qubit i, P∈{X,Y,Z}, and energy difference ω. Put gβ(ω)=min{1,exp(−βω)} and Lₙ,β(ρ)=−i[Hₙ,ρ]+Σ_{i,P,ω}gβ(ω)[AρA†−(A†Aρ+ρA†A)/2], with A=A_{i,P,ω} in each summand. Its evolution is Φₙ,β,t=exp(tLₙ,β). Every single-qubit Pauli error is coupled to the bath; energy-raising rates are positive, and attempt rates do not shrink with system size. Choose a completely positive trace-preserving encoding map Encₙ,β from one-qubit states to n-qubit states, with a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse at t=0. It may use a thermal auxiliary state and need not be efficiently preparable. For this fixed encoding, let εₙ,β(t)=inf_D sup_ρ ∥D∘Φₙ,β,t∘Encₙ,β(ρ)−ρ∥₁, where ρ ranges over all one-qubit density matrices, D over recovery channels from n qubits to one, and ∥A∥₁=Tr√(A†A). Define τₙ(β)=inf{t≥0:εₙ,β(t)>1/10}, with infimum of the empty set equal to infinity. Encoding happens before storage and recovery only at the end. This card fixes a stabilizer and thermal-bath model for the broader physical existence question; it imposes neither translation invariance nor a symmetry restriction on allowed errors.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family, one fixed finite β, and encodings with τₙ(β)→∞, or prove that no family in this stated model has that property. A bound exp(Ω(n^η)) for a fixed η>0 would be stronger than required. A lifetime improving only up to a temperature-dependent maximum system size does not suffice. Cooling the bath as n grows, increasing local interaction strengths, slowing error rates with n, enforcing an error-forbidding symmetry, or applying active correction during storage changes the target.
context:
This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime exp(Ω(n^η)) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some η>0. Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.
why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.
status_note: Claimed affirmative resolution in arXiv:2605.10943, 11 May 2026, for passive storage with thermal encoding. Its assumptions and stated theorems were checked, but the full proof was not independently verified. This is not labelled confirmed open. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.
progress: 2010: Chesi and coauthors formulate thermodynamic criteria and relaxation bounds for stabilizer and subsystem quantum memories. | 2016: Brown and coauthors survey passive thermal memories, dimensional restrictions and proposed ways around them. | 2021: Stahl–Nandkishore prove symmetry-protected three-dimensional memory mechanisms with constrained dynamics. | 2026-01-23: The cored-product revision reports finite-size evidence on memories up to 60,000 qubits. | 2026-05-11: Balasubramanian–Davydova–Lin claim an affirmative solution with thermal encoding and stretched-exponential lifetime. | 2026-08-25: Williamson’s layer-code result appears in PRL; its guarantee is partial self-correction over a temperature-dependent size regime.
working_summary: Passive quantum memory aims to preserve an encoded qubit through the natural dynamics of a material without repeated active correction. The question here fixes a nonzero temperature and asks whether lifetime can grow without bound in a three-dimensional local stabilizer system. Protecting a qubit requires retaining phase information as well as distinguishing its classical basis states. The saved card records a May 2026 claimed affirmative construction, while distinguishing its proof claim from an independently verified conclusion. This makes the record a useful guide to the precise thermal model and remaining verification questions rather than an unqualified assertion that the original existence problem is still open.

title: Exact quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel
importance_reason: A benchmark capacity problem connecting quantum error correction, information-theoretic converses and the operational effect of entangled encodings.
formal: Determine Q(q), the unassisted asymptotic quantum capacity of D_q(ρ)=(1−q)ρ+(q/3)(XρX+YρY+ZρZ), for every real q∈[0,1]. Capacity is measured in reliably transmitted qubits per independent channel use, under the coding definition below.
definitions: ρ is a one-qubit density matrix. The Pauli operators satisfy X|0⟩=|1⟩, X|1⟩=|0⟩, Z|0⟩=|0⟩, Z|1⟩=−|1⟩ and Y=iXZ. Thus q is the total probability of a nonidentity Pauli error, each type having probability q/3. For block length n, choose an integer kₙ≥0 and completely positive trace-preserving maps Eₙ from kₙ qubits to n qubits and Rₙ from n qubits to kₙ qubits. Let |Φₖ⟩=2^{−k/2}Σ_{x∈{0,1}ᵏ}|x⟩_A|x⟩_B, and define Fₙ=⟨Φ_{kₙ}|[id_A⊗(Rₙ∘D_q^{⊗n}∘Eₙ)](|Φ_{kₙ}⟩⟨Φ_{kₙ}|)|Φ_{kₙ}⟩. A rate r≥0 is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with liminfₙ kₙ/n≥r and Fₙ→1. Q(q) is the supremum of achievable rates. Sender and receiver have no initially shared entanglement, classical side channel, feedback, or auxiliary quantum channel. Encoding and recovery may be computationally unrestricted and jointly process an entire block. The same q is used independently on every channel use. This definition concerns transmission of quantum states, not merely classical bits through a quantum device.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit determination of the function Q(q) and prove matching achievability and converse bounds: every rate below the proposed value is achievable and no rate above it is achievable, for each q. Evaluating only a fixed block length, identifying only where capacity becomes zero, giving an approximation of unspecified accuracy, or restating the existing unbounded coherent-information optimization does not determine the requested function. The already known endpoints and zero-capacity region must be consistent with the answer.
context:
This channel is a basic model of unbiased qubit noise: a bit flip, a phase flip, or both occur with equal probabilities. Its one-parameter definition hides a hard coding problem. A quantum code must preserve superpositions and correlations with a reference system, which is why the fidelity test in the definition uses half of a maximally entangled state. Correctly transmitting only computational-basis strings would test a weaker, classical task.

Noise conventions differ substantially between papers. In this card q is the total Pauli error probability. A paper writing probabilities (1−3p,p,p,p) uses p=q/3. A paper writing (1−λ)ρ+λI/2 uses λ=4q/3 on the usual mixture range q≤3/4. For example, q=3/4 completely erases the input, even though the channel formula remains a valid quantum channel for all q≤1. The 2026 threshold values below have been converted to q once.

Quantum coding theorems give an exact but unbounded optimization: Q(q)=supₙ max_σ I_c(σ,D_q^{⊗n})/n. Here I_c is the output entropy minus the entropy jointly held by the output and a purifying reference, with entropy S(τ)=−Tr(τ log₂τ). This regularization permits inputs entangled across channel uses. It identifies the mathematical quantity, but does not by itself evaluate this particular function.

Using a maximally mixed one-qubit input gives the hashing lower bound max{0,1−h₂(q)−q log₂3}, where h₂ is binary entropy and 0 log₂0 is interpreted as zero. The expression becomes zero near q=0.1893. Degenerate quantum codes can surpass this benchmark because multiple physical errors can have the same effect on the encoded information. Consequently counting error types as if each required separate correction can underestimate achievable rates.

Agarwal and coauthors’ May 2026 paper searches rank-two input states inside the permutation-symmetric subspace, using representation theory to evaluate many-copy coherent information. It reports a 45-copy numerical positivity threshold p=0.064657, or q=0.193971 here, and explains how degeneracy suppresses the effective environment entropy. This is evidence for better codes and a lower bound on the true threshold, not an optimization over all possible block lengths and states.

Krohn-Grimberghe’s August revision provides an explicit 45-copy state with exact-arithmetic certificates for positive coherent information at q=48717/250000=0.194868. The result extends positivity to smaller q by channel composition and data processing. The preprint distinguishes the threshold printed in the May paper from a stronger state in its authors’ public repository, and bounds both that state and the new witness using certified arithmetic. The certificates are supplied by the author; this review checked the stated bounds and conventions but did not independently rerun the verification artifact.

On the upper-bound side, Q(0)=1 and Q(q)=0 for every q≥1/4. In the latter range the channel is antidegradable: the environment can simulate the receiver’s output. Reliable positive-rate transmission would then permit incompatible copies of unknown quantum information. Between the current positive-capacity lower bound and q=1/4, even the location where capacity vanishes remains unsettled. Determining that location would still leave the exact positive-rate curve to be found.

There are also finer results away from the threshold. Leditzky, Leung and Smith control the gap between single-letter coherent information and capacity at low noise through approximate degradability. Zhu and coauthors optimize channel extensions to obtain tighter upper bounds, with their work presented at TQC 2026. These techniques reduce the gap without proving that a proposed family of codes is optimal at every noise value.

Kondra and coauthors’ August 2026 strong-converse result concerns fidelity decay above capacity for degradable and antidegradable channels. Such a theorem strengthens the operational meaning of an upper bound, but does not supply the unknown capacity curve of the depolarizing channel in its intermediate regime. A full resolution here must match the best achievable rates with upper bounds that apply to arbitrary encodings and arbitrary block lengths.
why: The unresolved communication limit of a canonical quantum-noise model. It tests whether quantum coding theory can turn regularized existence formulas into sharp quantitative limits despite degeneracy and multi-copy advantages.
status_note: Exact unassisted capacity remains open in the 2026 primary literature. The August certificate improves a positive-capacity lower bound, without claiming an exact threshold or capacity formula. All displayed thresholds use total Pauli error q. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

working_summary: A depolarizing channel models a qubit subjected to randomly chosen Pauli errors. Its quantum capacity measures how much unknown quantum information can be transmitted reliably per channel use when many uses are encoded together. The goal is an exact capacity formula throughout the noise range under the unassisted coding convention fixed in the card. Coding across several uses can behave differently from optimizing a single use, which complicates attempts to match achievable rates with impossibility bounds. Understanding this basic symmetric noise model would provide a benchmark for quantum communication and the value of collective error correction.

title: NP outside BQP
importance_reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.
formal: Is NP⊈BQP? Equivalently, is there no uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that decides satisfiability of every Boolean 3-CNF formula with error probability at most 1/3 on each input?
definitions: NP is the class of languages L⊆{0,1}* for which there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when some binary string y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. BQP consists of languages decided by polynomial-size quantum circuit families {C_n} that a deterministic classical algorithm generates from 1ⁿ in polynomial time. The circuits use a fixed finite universal gate set, for example Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, polynomially many qubits initialized with the input x and zero ancillas, and a final measured output bit. Acceptance probability is at least 2/3 when x∈L and at most 1/3 when x∉L. The size bound counts all elementary gates, not only calls to a selected subroutine. There is no advice, postselection, oracle or supplied witness. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. The input length is the length of a conventional explicit binary encoding; malformed encodings are rejected. NP⊈BQP asserts the existence of at least one language in NP outside BQP, rather than merely inequality of the two classes.
answer_criterion: Prove an unconditional separation NP⊈BQP, or refute it by establishing NP⊆BQP. By NP-completeness and closure under classical polynomial-time reductions, the latter is equivalent to putting 3-SAT in BQP. An oracle separation, a lower bound only on unstructured search, an algorithm for a restricted family of formulas, or a conditional hardness statement does not settle the question. A separation from BQP must exclude every uniform polynomial-size circuit family, not just a particular quantum algorithm or architecture.
context:
An NP witness gives a short, classically checkable reason for a yes answer. For satisfiability, that witness is an assignment to the variables. The question is whether the existence of such a witness can always be decided efficiently using quantum computation, even when the witness itself is not supplied. Wigderson lists the noncontainment as Conjecture 11.5 in the inherited 2018 draft.

The distinction between verification and discovery is essential. A quantum computer can certainly evaluate a Boolean formula on a proposed assignment. It can also place assignments into superposition. But a measurement does not reveal a list of the values computed on every assignment. An efficient algorithm must arrange interference so that the eventual measurement supplies the desired decision with bounded error.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms show that quantum computation can exploit special mathematical structure to solve important problems in polynomial time. Their speed comes from extracting periodic information, not from a general procedure for every efficiently checkable witness relation. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so its quantum algorithm does not imply that 3-SAT or all of NP belongs to BQP.

Grover’s search algorithm gives a different kind of advantage: a quadratic improvement for an unstructured search space. Applied to N Boolean variables, the space has 2ᴺ assignments, so the generic search scale becomes 2^{N/2}, with additional polynomial work to evaluate the formula. This is a substantial speedup and remains exponential in N. The distinction is about asymptotic resources, even if that reduction could be valuable on concrete instances.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove a matching black-box obstruction and an oracle separation of NP from quantum polynomial time. Their result excludes a universal shortcut that treats the witness verifier only as an unknown function. An explicit formula reveals more than black-box evaluations: an algorithm can inspect shared variables, clauses and every feature of its encoding. Thus the oracle theorem does not establish the unrelativized separation asked for here.

There is a useful elementary implication. Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, P=NP would put all of NP in BQP. Therefore a positive answer to this card would also prove P≠NP. The converse implication is unavailable: P≠NP alone does not rule out quantum polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems. This helps explain why proving an unrestricted quantum lower bound is such an ambitious target.

The decision version already captures efficient witness finding for SAT. If a bounded-error quantum SAT decider existed, one could repeatedly fix a variable, ask whether the remaining formula is satisfiable, and retain a satisfiable branch. Amplifying the decision success probability makes the probability of any mistake across the polynomially many calls small. Finally, the resulting assignment can be checked classically. This is a consequence of SAT’s self-reduction, not an assumption that a quantum algorithm hands over all possible witnesses at once.

The conjecture also supports hardness results for tasks whose inputs and outputs are intrinsically quantum. In June 2026, Cifuentes proves that an efficient quantum algorithm for detecting a large nonidentity Pauli coefficient of a circuit-prepared state would imply NP⊆BQP. The reduction holds even for pure states and a constant threshold with a promised gap. It transfers the conjecture to a tomography-related task; it does not prove the conjecture itself.

Several nearby questions should remain distinct. BPP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation adds power beyond classical randomization. NP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation can solve every classically verifiable decision problem. Allowing a quantum witness changes the verifier class again, to QMA. Establishing a separation or a speedup involving one pair does not automatically establish the relation between the others.

A resolution would locate a fundamental boundary of quantum computation. If NP⊆BQP, quantum algorithms would provide a universal efficient route to classical constraint satisfaction and its many reductions. If NP⊈BQP, some efficiently verifiable problems would resist even ideal fault-tolerant quantum computers. Neither answer is about today’s hardware capacity: the model already grants arbitrarily scalable, accurate quantum computation with polynomial resources.
why: Determine whether efficient classical verification always leads to efficient quantum solution, a central limit on what quantum computation can achieve.
status_note: No unconditional separation or general quantum polynomial-time SAT algorithm found through 11 September 2026. Black-box lower bounds do not establish the ordinary language-class separation. June 2026 work continues to use NP⊈BQP explicitly as an unproved hardness hypothesis.
