working_summary: This problem asks whether quantum computers still face an unavoidable efficient-computation barrier on some NP problems. An equivalent target is to rule out a bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithm for every instance of Boolean satisfiability. Fast quantum algorithms for structured tasks do not imply an algorithm for general NP-complete search or decision problems. Likewise, a speedup for searching an unstructured list addresses a particular access model rather than the full complexity-class question. A resolution would delimit the reach of quantum computation on problems whose proposed solutions are easy to check classically.

title: Does a quantum witness have more power than a classical witness?
importance_reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.
formal: Is $\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}$? Both classes have a polynomial-time quantum verifier and bounded error. QMA permits a polynomial-size quantum witness; QCMA permits only a polynomial-length classical string. The question concerns the standard classes without an oracle.
definitions: Use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification, completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3, with no shared advice or oracle. Classes here contain promise problems; the witness may depend on the whole input.
answer_criterion: Prove QMA is contained in QCMA, or prove the existence of a promise problem in QMA outside QCMA. A separation relative to an oracle does not settle these unrelativized classes.
context:
A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.
why: This identifies what kind of information might be intrinsically necessary for efficient verification.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2025–2026: A separation relative to a classical oracle is known. The February 2026 paper gives a simpler construction. It leaves the unrelativized class question untouched.
working_summary: A quantum verifier may receive either a quantum state or a classical string as evidence that an input is a yes-instance. QMA permits the former kind of witness, while QCMA restricts the witness to classical information. The question asks whether this change in the form of the evidence changes what can be verified efficiently. Both models already allow quantum computation during verification, so the issue is the additional power of the witness itself. An answer would clarify whether quantum states can serve as fundamentally stronger proofs in the ordinary setting without an oracle.

title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
importance_reason: A foundational computability question about regularized information quantities, separating lack of efficient algorithms from the possible absence of any certified approximation algorithm.
formal: Does there exist a single classical Turing algorithm that, given any effectively described finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channel Φ and a positive rational ε, halts and outputs a rational r satisfying |r−Q(Φ)|≤ε, where Q is the unassisted quantum capacity in qubits per channel use?
definitions: The input includes positive integers d_A,d_B and a program describing the unnormalized Choi matrix J(Φ)=Σᵢⱼ |i⟩⟨j|⊗Φ(|i⟩⟨j|), a matrix of order d_A d_B. On input k≥1, that program must halt and output a rational complex matrix whose real and imaginary entries approximate the corresponding entries of J(Φ) within 2⁻ᵏ. It is promised that the limiting matrix is positive semidefinite and Tr_B J(Φ)=I_A, so it defines a completely positive trace-preserving linear map from d_A-dimensional input states to d_B-dimensional output states. This explicitly specifies “effective description”; finite algebraic matrix descriptions are included. The requested algorithm need only meet its guarantees on inputs satisfying these promises. Memorylessness means n uses implement Φ^{⊗n}, allowing arbitrary joint encoding and decoding across those uses. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary channel is free. Operationally Q(Φ) is the supremum of asymptotically achievable quantum transmission rates with error tending to zero. Equivalently, Q(Φ)=sup_{n≥1} n⁻¹ max_ρ I_c(ρ,Φ^{⊗n}). Here ρ ranges over density matrices on A^{⊗n}; if ψ_{RAⁿ} is any purification and ω=(id_R⊗Φ^{⊗n})(ψ), then I_c=S(ω_{Bⁿ})−S(ω_{RBⁿ}), with S(τ)=−Tr(τ log₂τ) and 0 log₂0=0. There is no running-time bound beyond eventual halting for every valid channel description and every ε>0.
answer_criterion: A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm with a proved finite stopping rule and additive error guarantee for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such approximation algorithm exists in this specified representation. An asymptotic formula without an effective convergence bound, hardness only for polynomial-time computation, or undecidability of a different assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity is insufficient. Undecidability of testing the exact equality Q(Φ)=0 alone would also not disprove computable additive approximation.
context:
Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than ε.

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating Φ independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least 3/4 from capacity at most 1/4, even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.
why: Determine whether the fundamental reliable quantum communication rate is algorithmically accessible even without efficiency constraints.
status_note: No uniform computability theorem or impossibility proof for this finite-dimensional memoryless unassisted capacity found through 11 September 2026. The corrected 2026 paper explicitly leaves the general question open: its quantum-capacity result is QMA-hardness, while its undecidability result concerns a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity.
progress: 2003–2005: Devetak proves a quantum coding theorem yielding the regularized coherent-information expression for unassisted capacity. | 2009: Leung–Smith establish explicit continuity bounds for finite-dimensional unassisted quantum capacity. | 2015-03-31: Cubitt and coauthors prove that arbitrarily many channel uses may be needed before positive coherent information appears. | 2025: Undecidability in Physics reviews the open computability issue and distinguishes memoryful channels and zero-error capacities. | 2026-03-30: Bhattacharyya–Mehta–Zhao’s corrected v3 proves circuit-input QMA-hardness for quantum capacity and undecidability for a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity; ordinary quantum-capacity computability remains open.
working_summary: Quantum channel capacity describes the best asymptotic rate for transmitting quantum information through a noisy channel. This problem asks whether that number can always be approximated by an algorithm from an effective finite description of the channel. The algorithm may be slow, but it must halt and meet any requested rational accuracy. Optimizations involving arbitrarily many channel uses make the asymptotic definition harder to turn into a guaranteed finite computation. Establishing computability or an obstruction would separate the existence of an operational communication rate from our ability to calculate it even in principle.

title: Polynomial-time quantum algorithms for the general hidden subgroup problem
importance_reason: Would extend one of the central sources of quantum speedups beyond the group families currently understood.
formal: Can the hidden subgroup problem over arbitrary finite groups be solved with bounded error using quantum running time polynomial in log of the group order, under the standard efficient group-operation and hiding-function oracle model?
definitions: Let G be a finite group with identity e and H≤G a subgroup. Its left cosets are gH={gh:h∈H}. A hiding function f:G→S is strictly H-periodic when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. The codomain labels distinguish different cosets but have no promised algebraic meaning. The output is a finite list h₁,…,h_r whose generated subgroup equals H, not merely its order or a membership test. Every finite subgroup has a generating set of at most ⌈log₂|G|⌉ elements, so a short output is possible when group elements have short encodings. The standard hiding oracle coherently maps |g⟩|0⟩ to |g⟩|f(g)⟩; with a fixed binary output encoding it can be implemented as |g⟩|z⟩↦|g⟩|z XOR f(g)⟩. Bounded error means that the entire output generates exactly H with probability at least 2/3 on each promised instance. The desired resource bound concerns all computation, including classical preprocessing, group operations, non-oracle quantum gates, measurements and output processing, rather than just calls to f. The precise finite encoding and uniform access to arbitrary G remain unspecified in the source import, as recorded in statement_review.
answer_criterion: The intended positive answer is a uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm with polynomial total cost in log|G|, valid for every group and hiding function in one specified efficient group-access model. A query upper bound alone does not qualify. A negative answer would exclude such algorithms in that same fixed model. The current card retains the missing group-representation specification instead of silently choosing a narrower group family or a stronger oracle.
statement_review_issue: The imported time-complexity question does not specify how an arbitrary group is presented: unique versus multiple element encodings, their length, supplied generators/order information, and the exact coherent group-operation or state-preparation access. The 2004 reference fixes the hidden-function query model and permits inefficient group-dependent preprocessing; it does not supply these missing assumptions for a uniform polynomial-total-time benchmark. A specific group presentation and cost model must be chosen before this broad formulation is marked complete.
context:
The oracle groups elements together by assigning the same label exactly on each coset of H. Consider addition modulo 12 and H={0,4,8}. The function f(x)=x mod 4 is constant on the four cosets and different between them. Outputting the single generator 4 identifies H; listing all twelve inputs or reconstructing the oracle’s labels is unnecessary. In a non-Abelian group, the distinction between left and right cosets matters, so the left-coset convention is explicit.

An element g belongs to H exactly when f(g)=f(e), so a single comparison with the identity’s label tests membership. That test does not by itself find generators quickly: a small hidden subgroup may contain only a tiny fraction of G. The objective is to recover its structure with cost polynomial in the number of bits needed to describe a group element, rather than by scanning every group element.

Ettinger, Høyer and Knill prove that a polynomial number of hiding-function queries suffices for an arbitrary finite group. Their Theorem 1 gives an O((log|G|)^4) bound and also discusses an exact version with arbitrary one-qubit gates. The same paper explicitly says that its classical preprocessing and quantum networks are inefficient. Thus the title’s polynomial query complexity does not settle the total-running-time question. The bounded-error target here does not require the exact gate model from their additional exactness result.

Efficient quantum algorithms solve the Abelian hidden subgroup problem and explain several classic quantum speedups. In August 2026, Morales obtains additional non-Abelian cases: certain semidirect products under bounded-rank and exponent conditions, and quasi-Hamiltonian groups under an input-structure assumption. Those hypotheses do not cover arbitrary finite groups. The dihedral case remains an independently important specialization recorded elsewhere in the atlas.

A multiplication table has roughly |G|² entries, far larger than a polynomial in log|G|. A short generating set with coherent group-operation access is a different input model. Unique element names, knowledge of the group order, and access to uniform superpositions can also change the available operations. The original import names a standard model without spelling these choices out, while its principal reference is designed to count only hiding-oracle queries. The common mathematical task and current research boundary are now stated, but the card remains unfinished until its group representation and cost conventions are fixed.
why: Would extend one of the central sources of quantum speedups beyond the group families currently understood.
status_note: The 5 August 2026 primary preprint explicitly retains the arbitrary finite non-Abelian group question. Polynomial query complexity is established, but no polynomial total-time result was found. The imported group-representation and cost model remains insufficiently specified.
progress: 2004: Ettinger–Høyer–Knill prove a polynomial query bound for arbitrary finite groups while leaving the total computation inefficient. | 2026-08: Morales obtains further non-Abelian special cases with structural and input assumptions; the general case is explicitly still open.
working_summary: Can a quantum algorithm recover a hidden subgroup of any finite group in polynomial total time? The oracle gives the same value exactly on each left coset of the hidden subgroup. The output must generate the entire subgroup. Polynomially many oracle calls are known to suffice, but their processing may be inefficient. The broad import still needs a precise group representation and access model before it is a complete computational statement.

title: A polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem
importance_reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.
formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants C,c>0 such that, for every N≥2 and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of D_N, the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least 2/3 using at most C(⌈log₂N⌉+ℓ+2)ᶜ total operations, where ℓ is the bit length of an oracle value?
definitions: The dihedral group D_N has 2N elements represented as pairs (x,b) with x∈ℤ/Nℤ and b∈{0,1}, and multiplication (x,b)(y,d)=(x+(−1)ᵇy mod N,b+d mod 2). Its identity is (0,0). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer ℓ specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup H≤D_N is hidden by f:D_N→{0,1}^ℓ when f(g)=f(g′) if and only if gH=g′H, equivalently g⁻¹g′∈H. Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle U_f|g,z⟩=|g,z⊕f(g)⟩, usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for H={1}. The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When ℓ is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
context:
Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has H=H_s={(0,0),(s,1)}, with an unknown s∈ℤ/Nℤ. The hiding promise says f(x,0)=f(x+s,1), and each restriction to b=0 or b=1 is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form (|0,x⟩+|1,x+s⟩)/√2 for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(2πiks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity 2^{O(√log N)}. It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length n≈log N: the target here is n^{O(1)}, not 2^{O(√n)}.

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving √(log N log log N). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores exp(O(√log N)) time while using only O(log N) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be N/2, which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.
why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No verified polynomial-time solution is recorded. Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. The review checked these primary statements without independently rerunning the Lean development. The 2022 Moore–Young claim was explicitly withdrawn.

working_summary: The dihedral hidden subgroup problem presents a function that is constant on cosets of an unknown subgroup of a dihedral group. The task is to recover generators for that subgroup using quantum access to the function. The target is a uniform algorithm whose total running time is polynomial in the length of the group description and oracle values. Counting only a small number of oracle queries is insufficient if processing the resulting quantum information is expensive. An efficient solution would extend the reach of hidden-subgroup methods beyond the abelian setting and illuminate connections with lattice-related algorithmic problems.

title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
importance_reason: A central quantum-algorithm target linking graph algorithms, permutation groups and the computational use of entangled states.
formal: Is GI∈BQP? Equivalently, does a uniform quantum algorithm decide, on every pair of finite simple graphs on n vertices given by their adjacency matrices, whether they are isomorphic, with error probability at most 1/3 and worst-case total running time n^{O(1)}?
definitions: A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and has no parallel edges. For equally sized vertex sets [n]={1,…,n}, an isomorphism from G to H is a bijection π:[n]→[n] satisfying {u,v}∈E(G) if and only if {π(u),π(v)}∈E(H) for every u≠v. The input consists of the two explicitly written binary adjacency matrices; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately and empty graphs are handled trivially. There are no promises of rigidity, bounded degree, typicality, or a particular input distribution. BQP means a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits over a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T, acting on computational-basis encodings of the classical input and initialized ancillas, with a measured output bit. There must be fixed constants C,c such that all gates, measurements and classical control can be implemented within C(n+2)ᶜ total elementary operations. The algorithm accepts each isomorphic pair with probability at least 2/3 and each nonisomorphic pair with probability at most 1/3. It receives no nonuniform advice, witness, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle or uncounted memory-preparation service. The target is the decision problem for an ordinary vertex permutation; it is not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory.
answer_criterion: Prove membership by giving a correct uniform quantum algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial total cost, or prove GI∉BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would also answer yes. A separation for a specified Fourier-sampling or sieve model is not a negative answer for unrestricted BQP; an invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic pairs is not a complete positive answer.
context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound exp((log n)^{O(1)}). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |π⟩|πG⟩ is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to Ω(n log n) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to GI∈BQP would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so GI∉BQP would in particular imply P≠NP. The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.
why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ordinary graph isomorphism, or proof of GI∉BQP, was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 correlation tests, state-isomorphism classifications and NPA hierarchy results do not settle this question.
progress: 2005: Aaronson lists graph isomorphism as a target for new quantum algorithmic ideas. | 2005–2010: Coset-state lower bounds establish the need for highly joint measurements in the standard hidden-subgroup approach; the joint journal paper appears in 2010. | 2015–2017: Babai gives a classical quasipolynomial-time algorithm; his January 2017 update repairs the affected recursion and restores the bound. | 28 January 2026: Kar–Roberson–Seppelt–Zeman publish polynomial algorithms for fixed levels of a hierarchy for a different quantum isomorphism relation. | 12 May 2026: Gheorghiu and coauthors classify several group-action quantum state problems, with GI-hardness for the Clifford-group version. | 2 June 2026: Maxwell–van den Hoven–Renema revise their quantum-inspired necessary-condition algorithm; its sufficient full-order version is not efficient.
working_summary: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge. This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs. The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle. Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm. A resolution would clarify whether quantum computation can efficiently handle this central classification problem.

title: The no low-energy sampleable states conjecture
importance_reason: Would rule out a much broader classical description of low-energy quantum states than shallow quantum circuits.
formal: In the perfect-sampling-access model of Definition 5.1 and Conjecture 4 of Gharibian and Le Gall, do there exist a constant k, a family of k-local n-qubit Hamiltonians H_n with ||H_n||≤1, and ε>0 such that for every succinctly represented vector family F there is n₀(F) for which every n≥n₀(F) and every unit vector u∈F_n satisfy u†H_nu>λ_min(H_n)+ε? Here F_n consists of the vectors in F of dimension 2^n. The exact access requirements are expanded below; the numerical machine conventions still requiring specification are recorded explicitly.
definitions: An n-qubit pure state is a unit vector u∈ℂ^(2^n), indexed by binary strings x∈{0,1}^n. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian matrix; its energy in u is u†Hu, its ground energy λ_min(H) is its least eigenvalue, and ||H|| is its operator norm. A k-local Hamiltonian is a sum of polynomially many terms, each acting nontrivially on at most k qubits and as the identity on the rest. The constant k and the polynomial bound are independent of n. No geometric locality or efficient uniform construction of the Hamiltonian family is added to the source’s existence target. The norm bound fixes the energy scale, so multiplying all terms cannot create the required constant gap artificially. For a family F of nonzero finite complex vectors, a succinct representation consists of an injective map rep:F→{0,1}*, one polynomial q and one polynomial-time compiler A. Every u∈F has |rep(u)|≤q(log₂ dim u). On a valid representation A outputs descriptions of a coordinate-query procedure Q_u, a randomized sampler S_u, and m=||u||; on every string outside the image of rep it must reject. For any coordinate x, Q_u returns the complex amplitude u_x, including its phase, in time polynomial in log dim u. S_u produces x with probability exactly |u_x|²/||u||² in polynomial time. The resulting circuit descriptions have polynomial size in log dim u. This is the source’s perfect, ζ=0 access, with no approximation to the distribution or norm. The representation map itself need not be computable from an explicitly listed vector. The same polynomial bounds and compiler apply throughout F; the eventual threshold n₀ may depend on this entire representation family. The assertion tests every unit vector in F_n, not one preselected sequence of easy states. The source counts exact complex additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions at unit cost; this is not automatically a bit-cost sampling model.
answer_criterion: Resolve the stated source-model existence proposition with its ∃Hamiltonian family, ∃ε, ∀representation family, ∃n₀ quantifiers and perfect-sampling plus amplitude-query requirements. Before treating the card as a standalone machine-level benchmark, resolve the numerical conventions recorded in statement_review. Excluding only stabilizer states, Gaussian states or constant-depth quantum preparation does not exclude every family allowed by Definition 5.1.
statement_review_issue: The source uses unit-cost exact complex arithmetic and exact sampling. A fully independent machine-level specification still needs the encoding of complex constants and norm outputs, the circuit instruction set and allowed exact-randomness primitives. The source notes that bit-complexity variants require redefining access; no particular such variant is silently imposed here.
context:
The states |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 both produce a uniformly random bit when measured in the computational basis. Yet for H=(I−X)/2, where X exchanges |0⟩ and |1⟩, their energies are 0 and 1. Their measurement distributions agree while their energies differ. This is why the source also requires access to each complex amplitude.

Listing all 2^n amplitudes would be exponentially long. A permitted description instead has length polynomial in n and supports the prescribed efficient queries and samples. The source further requires a common compiler that rejects invalid descriptions; it is not enough to assert that some sampler exists for each isolated state.

Any particular finite state with suitable numerical data can be given a long description. The conjecture concerns asymptotic families with one polynomial bound, and allows the exclusion threshold to depend on that family. Requiring one fixed threshold to exclude every possible description polynomial at once would change the quantifiers.

The proved NLTS theorem excludes preparation by constant-depth quantum circuits. NLSS instead excludes the specified classical query-and-sampling descriptions. Coble and coauthors exclude stabilizer states and can retain NLTS in the same construction, but stabilizer states form only one class with efficient classical descriptions. Their result does not establish the full NLSS target.

The final source version retains NLSS as open, and the February 2025 fermionic paper excludes a Gaussian subclass while explicitly retaining the general conjecture. This card keeps the source’s exact-arithmetic access convention. Choosing finite-precision amplitudes, approximate sampling or a different randomness primitive requires a separate model decision, so complete machine-level formulation review is not claimed.
why: Tests whether low-energy spaces can exclude every succinct classical description that supports both amplitude queries and exact measurement sampling, complementing lower bounds based on quantum circuit depth.
status_note: The primary formal conjecture and the 2023 stabilizer result were read, and the February 2025 fermionic abstract was checked. No full NLSS resolution was found in searches through 11 September 2026. The source-level conjecture remains active; an independent numerical machine specification is still unfinished. No proof audit was performed.
progress: 2022 / 2023: The NLTS result is proved, as acknowledged in footnote 16 of the final source version; the same note explicitly retains NLSS as open. | 2023: Hamiltonians with no low-energy stabilizer states are constructed; a variant simultaneously retains the separate NLTS property. | 2024-01-04: The final journal version on arXiv states formal Conjecture 4 using Definition 5.1 and perfect sampling access, including coordinate queries and valid-description recognition. | 2025-02-21: A fermionic preprint excludes Gaussian low-energy states and explicitly distinguishes this restricted result from the still-open NLSS conjecture.
working_summary: Can a family of local Hamiltonians keep every classically accessible state a fixed normalized energy above the ground energy? The source’s access model requires exact amplitude queries, exact measurement sampling and a succinct description with recognizable validity. Matching measurement distributions alone does not control quantum energy because phases matter. Known exclusions for stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian states address restricted classes. The mathematical family quantifiers are now explicit, while a complete numerical machine specification remains unfinished.

title: Average-case hardness of multiplicatively approximating Gaussian permanents
importance_reason: Establish a major complexity foundation for a restricted quantum sampling model.
formal: Is multiplicative approximation of the permanent of an independent complex Gaussian matrix, on a sufficiently large fraction of instances, #P-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions as in the Permanent-of-Gaussians Conjecture?
definitions: For X∈ℂ^(n×n), Per(X)=Σ_{σ∈S_n}∏_i X_(i,σ(i)). The entries are independent standard complex Gaussians. The GPE× task receives accuracy and failure parameters ε,δ and should return z with |z−Per(X)|≤ε|Per(X)| on at least a 1−δ fraction of matrices. This concerns the complex permanent itself; hardness of worst-case permanent evaluation or additive approximation alone does not give this claim.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Reproduce the oracle reduction quantifiers, dependence on ε and δ, and discretization of Gaussian inputs and complex outputs from the source before certifying a bit-model statement.
context:
Boson-sampling probabilities are governed by matrix permanents. Average-case hardness addresses whether the apparent difficulty persists on the random matrices relevant to that model.

Aaronson and Arkhipov state the Permanent-of-Gaussians Conjecture separately from their anti-concentration conjecture. The distinction matters: neither the worst-case #P-completeness of the permanent nor an assumption about tiny probabilities establishes the average-case reduction.
why: Establish a major complexity foundation for a restricted quantum sampling model.

progress: 2013: The source isolates the average-case hardness assumption used in its approximate-sampling consequences.

title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
importance_reason: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
formal: For every entangled finite-dimensional bipartite state ρ, do finitely many copies ρ^⊗k and local filters suffice to produce correlations violating a Bell inequality, without an auxiliary entangled state?
definitions: A state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on H_A⊗H_B. It is entangled when it is not a convex combination of product states. Local filters are trace-nonincreasing completely positive maps F_A,F_B applied to the respective k-fold systems before measurement questions are selected; the joint success probability must be positive. Normalize the successful filtered state. Each party then chooses a local measurement from a finite set of positive-operator-valued measurements. The resulting conditional distribution p(a,b|x,y) is Bell-nonlocal when it has no representation Σ_λ q_λ p_A(a|x,λ)p_B(b|y,λ), with nonnegative q_λ summing to one. Such a representation is precisely a local hidden-variable model for finite questions and answers. Local ancillary states and shared randomness are allowed, but no additional shared entangled state is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Entanglement and observable Bell nonlocality are related but distinct resources. This question asks whether repeated access to the same entanglement always reveals nonlocal behavior after local preprocessing.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove an activation result using a suitable auxiliary state. That resource is stronger than additional copies of the given state and is expressly excluded here. Direct one-copy Bell tests also do not settle the finite-copy filtered target.
why: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.

progress: 2012: The source establishes activation with an additional state while distinguishing the unresolved repeated-copy setting.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
importance_reason: Determines the strongest quantum query advantage when the function has no promise, a basic limit on quantum computation.
formal: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
context: The power of quantum information and computation. Qubits, measurements, oracle access, and approximation error must be distinguished.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question compares the power of models or representations. Resolving it would identify whether their difference changes what can be computed, rather than only the implementation cost.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: Query complexity measures how many input bits an algorithm needs to inspect, while allowing other computation for free. This problem compares bounded-error randomized and quantum query complexity for Boolean functions defined on every input. Aaronson's saved survey describes examples approaching a cubic separation and an upper bound with exponent four. The target is the largest possible separation, so finding either more extreme functions or a sharper universal upper bound would address the gap. Requiring total functions distinguishes this question from promise problems, where special input structure can permit much larger quantum advantages.

title: Classical simulation of polynomial-gap local stoquastic adiabatic computation
importance_reason: Determine the computational power of a central restricted adiabatic model.
formal: Can every polynomial-time adiabatic computation described by explicit local stoquastic Hamiltonians with an inverse-polynomial global spectral gap be sampled classically in polynomial time to inverse-polynomial total-variation error?
definitions: A Hamiltonian is stoquastic in the computational basis when every off-diagonal matrix entry is real and nonpositive. The intended input describes a smoothly varying sum of terms acting on a constant number of qubits, an efficiently preparable initial ground state and computational-basis measurement at the end. The gap is the separation of the lowest two eigenvalues of the full Hamiltonian, not only a symmetry-restricted subspace. The intended simulator is uniform randomized classical computation.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Specify Hamiltonian-path encoding, precision, derivative and norm bounds, gap and ground-state uniqueness promises, initialization and exact sampling accuracy quantifiers. The local-input version must be kept separate from oracle-input results.
context:
Stoquasticity removes a sign obstruction that often complicates classical statistical simulation. Whether that suffices for efficient simulation of general explicit local adiabatic computations remains a basic question about the source of quantum computational power.

Bringewatt and Jarret study obstructions based on symmetry sectors and obtain subexponential simulations for those examples. Their result does not establish a general polynomial-time simulation theorem. Oracle-model separations also require care before being transferred to explicitly supplied local interactions.
why: Determine the computational power of a central restricted adiabatic model.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2020: The source simulates a class of previously obstructed examples without resolving the general explicit-local polynomial-time target.

title: Publicly verifiable quantum money from quantum-secure LWE alone
importance_reason: Base quantum unclonability with public verification on a standard computational assumption.
formal: Does polynomial-hard Learning With Errors against quantum polynomial-time adversaries suffice for publicly verifiable quantum money, without obfuscation or any other computational assumption?
definitions: A bank generates a public verification key and a secret minting key. A banknote consists of a serial number and a quantum state. Anyone can verify it using the public key, while a polynomial-time quantum counterfeiter given valid notes should not produce more accepted notes than it received. The intended construction is in the standard model, with no ideal random oracle and no extra trusted setup.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Specify LWE parameters and the full quantum counterfeiting experiment, including minting access, note verification/reusability, correctness error and adaptive adversary access.
context:
Quantum money seeks a publicly checkable object that cannot be copied even by its legitimate holder. Deriving that property from a familiar lattice assumption would substantially clarify its cryptographic foundations.

The cited construction of anonymous public-key quantum money uses additional assumptions, including obfuscation. Anonymous notes and voting are consequences of a stronger construction; their existence under those assumptions does not establish ordinary public quantum money from LWE alone.

title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
importance_reason: Asks whether quantum information can encode useful nonuniform computational advice beyond classical advice of comparable size.
formal: Is $\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}$? Advice for inputs of length $n$ depends only on $n$: a state on $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ qubits on the left, or $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ classical bits on the right. The computation must succeed on every input of that length.
definitions: The quantum computation is uniform and polynomial time, with error at most 1/3 on every input. Advice size is bounded by one polynomial. There is no computability restriction on the length-indexed advice family and no oracle.
answer_criterion: Prove that polynomial classical advice suffices for every language decidable with polynomial quantum advice, or prove a separation of the two unrelativized advice classes.
context:
Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. Instead, the algorithm might use the input to choose which computation to perform with the advice. The open question is whether polynomial-length classical advice can always support an equally effective computation for every input.
why: This distinguishes two basic ways to store auxiliary information for computation. It is different from QMA versus QCMA.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-02-10: The source gives the first separation of these advice classes using a standard classical oracle. It does not claim an unrelativized separation.
working_summary: Advice is information supplied in advance that depends on input length but must work for every input of that length. A quantum algorithm might receive a polynomial-size quantum advice state or only a polynomial-length classical string. The question is whether quantum advice allows it to decide more languages efficiently than classical advice does. Advice is nonuniform and need not be efficiently generated, so the comparison concerns its information content rather than its preparation cost. A separation or simulation would reveal how much computational value can be carried by a reusable description of a length-specific quantum state.

title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
importance_reason: Relates quantum query algorithms to polynomial approximation, connecting two core tools for quantum upper and lower bounds.
formal: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
context: The power of quantum information and computation. Qubits, measurements, oracle access, and approximation error must be distinguished.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question compares the power of models or representations. Resolving it would identify whether their difference changes what can be computed, rather than only the implementation cost.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.

This problem considers partial Boolean functions, whose inputs are subject to a promise. The approximating polynomial must still remain bounded on all Boolean inputs, including those outside the promise. title: Is QMA(2) in BQEXP?
importance_reason: Locating QMA(2) in a standard time class tests the computational effect of unentangled quantum witnesses.
formal: Is QMA(2) in BQEXP?
context: The power of quantum information and computation. Qubits, measurements, oracle access, and approximation error must be distinguished.

working_summary: QMA(2) allows a quantum verifier to receive two witnesses promised to be unentangled with each other. The question asks whether every problem with such a proof system can be decided by a bounded-error quantum algorithm in exponential time. title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
importance_reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.
formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity O(1), completeness at least 2/3, and soundness at most 1/3? The strong access model is defined below. The prover may be computationally unbounded, and soundness quantifies over all prover strategies.
definitions: In each round the prover supplies a quantum register W. The verifier chooses queried positions through a measurement and applies a quantum channel only to those qubits and its private register; query cost counts accessed message qubits, summed over rounds. It returns the entire W register, may send additional classical information, and sends no additional quantum register. It can retain its own private workspace, but cannot retain any part of a prover-message register. The parties have no initial shared entanglement. Total prover-message length counts the full incoming registers, not only queried qubits. This restates the strong model of Definitions 5.1–5.2 and 5.13–5.15.
answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol for every QMA promise problem, or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no protocol meeting all these bounds. Polynomial communication in the weaker general qIOP model does not suffice.
context:
A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.
why: The problem isolates the communication price of an extremely limited quantum verifier. A positive result would eliminate the exponential communication in the present strong construction.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026-01-19: The general qIOP has polynomial communication but uses a polynomial private quantum resource. The strong construction operates on constantly many qubits but communicates $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(n))$ qubits. Question 1.9 asks for polynomial communication.
working_summary: Interactive oracle proofs let a verifier inspect only selected parts of much larger prover messages. This question asks for constant-round quantum versions that verify all QMA promise problems with polynomial total communication and only constantly many queries. The strong quantum access model is part of the target, because different ways of querying quantum messages permit different verification strategies. Soundness must cover arbitrary prover behavior, while the verifier remains efficient and has a constant completeness-soundness gap. The project probes how far proof compression and local checking can extend when the evidence itself is quantum.

title: Oracle separation of BQP from IP
importance_reason: A model-relative separation probing the relation between quantum computation and classical interactive proofs.
formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language L⊆{0,1}* such that L∈BQP^A but L∉IP^A?
definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove BQP^A⊆IP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.
context:
A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.
why: Determines whether classical single-prover verification of efficient quantum computations survives arbitrary oracle access. The distinction is sharper than a quantum speedup over direct classical computation: even an unrestricted interactive helper must fail in the separating world.
status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.
progress: 2021: Aaronson states the oracle separation as Problem 7 and defines the distinction between IP and its efficient-quantum-honest-prover variant. | 2026-04: The preprint A Relativizing MIP for BQP states containment in classical MIP for every classical oracle and explicitly leaves the single-prover oracle separation open. The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.

title: Oracle separation of BQP from efficient-prover interactive proofs
importance_reason: An oracle benchmark for the reach of efficient-prover interactive verification of quantum computation.
formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language L⊆{0,1}* such that L∈BQP^A but L∉IP_BQP^A, where IP_BQP^A requires a polynomial-time quantum honest prover and classical interaction with a polynomial-time classical verifier?
definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover. IP_BQP^A is the subclass of BQP^A whose languages admit such an IP^A protocol with one uniform quantum polynomial-time oracle algorithm as the honest prover. Its total local work and oracle queries across all rounds are polynomial in n, under the same quantum access convention as BQP^A. Only the honest prover is restricted: soundness still quantifies over all computationally unbounded cheating strategies. Polynomial bounds and machines may depend on A and the language, but must work for all input lengths; they cannot depend on the particular input through advice.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and BQP^A language L for which no classical interactive proof has an honest quantum polynomial-time oracle prover. Alternatively, prove BQP^A=IP_BQP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. All negative instances must rule out arbitrary polynomial bounds on rounds and honest-prover work, and the positive alternative must retain soundness against unbounded cheating provers.
context:
A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.
why: Distinguishes the existence of a classical interactive proof from the ability of an efficient quantum device to carry out its honest strategy. It tests whether verification can match the computational resources of the device while retaining soundness against all cheating provers.
status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.

The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.
working_summary: An efficient quantum computation can have a classical interactive proof whose honest prover is too expensive for the quantum device to execute. This problem asks for an oracle relative to which some quantum polynomial-time language has no classical interactive proof with a quantum polynomial-time honest prover. The verifier and honest prover access the same classical oracle, with quantum queries available only to the quantum computation. Soundness must hold even against an unbounded dishonest prover, so computationally sound cryptographic arguments have a different guarantee. A separation would expose an oracle obstruction to classical verification using only the computational power of an efficient quantum device.
