title: Exact quantum fanout in constant depth with unrestricted circuit size
importance_reason: Isolates a basic exact-unitary expressiveness question in constant-depth quantum computation even when finite size and ancilla count are unrestricted. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer d such that, for every n≥1, some finite QAC circuit of depth at most d exactly implements FANOUTₙ on one control qubit and n target qubits, allowing arbitrarily many clean ancillas and no size bound?
definitions: For bits s,x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,1}, FANOUTₙ|s,x₁,…,xₙ⟩=|s,s⊕x₁,…,s⊕xₙ⟩, extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on n+1+a(n) qubits for some finite a(n)≥0. Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over ℂ and generalized Toffoli gates: for any k≥1 distinct controls and a distinct target, |z₁,…,z_k,t⟩ maps to |z₁,…,z_k,t⊕(z₁⋯z_k)⟩. Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase e^(iφₙ), independent of the input state ψ, Cₙ(|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n))=e^(iφₙ)(FANOUTₙ|ψ⟩)⊗|0⟩^⊗a(n) for every unit vector ψ in (ℂ²)^⊗(n+1). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.
context:
On a basis input, the control flips every target when it is one and leaves them unchanged when it is zero. The same circuit must act correctly on superpositions, including inputs entangled with other systems. Agreement only on measured classical outputs would be weaker.

For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|00⟩ yields (|000⟩+|111⟩)/√2. It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

A Toffoli gate may inspect many controls in one layer, but a qubit cannot participate in several gates in that same layer. The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

The ITCS paper discusses approximate implementations and records exact fanout as open even without a size bound. Its known parity/fanout equivalence and later 2026 equivalence results connect the task to other shallow quantum operations, but do not constitute the exact implementation or impossibility theorem requested here.

title: Quantum games PCP with efficient honest provers and short messages
importance_reason: A succinct verification question connecting QMA, entangled games and quantum PCP. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Does every promise problem L=(L_yes,L_no) in QMA admit a one-round entangled multiprover proof with a uniform classical polynomial-time verifier, a constant number r of provers and polylogarithmic-length classical questions and answers, such that: (i) on every x∈L_yes, some polynomial-size quantum witness permits uniform quantum polynomial-time preparation and local execution of an honest strategy accepted with probability at least 2/3; and (ii) on every x∈L_no, every entangled strategy, with no computational bound on the dishonest provers, is accepted with probability at most 1/3?
definitions: Write n=|x|. QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least 2/3, while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most 1/3. In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most O((log(n+2))^a) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state ψ_x, prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state ψ_x is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside L_yes∪L_no. The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.
context:
The verifier has an n-bit instance but exchanges only polylogarithmically many bits with each prover. Quantum information stays with the provers. The task is to check a quantum witness through these short classical exchanges, with a constant separation between acceptance on YES and NO instances.

It is insufficient for a prover to answer quickly after receiving an arbitrarily difficult-to-prepare entangled state. The setup itself must take polynomial time given copies of a polynomial-size witness. Conversely, cheating provers receive no time or entanglement-size restriction.

Very powerful entangled proof systems already exist when honest provers are unrestricted. The 2024 status note explains why these results do not establish efficient-prover quantum games PCP and identifies an error in an earlier claimed QMA construction.

The status note proposes O(log n)-bit questions and O(1)-bit answers. The selected CCC passage explicitly asks for polylogarithmic questions and answers. Resolving this card would settle that weaker efficient-prover benchmark, without automatically establishing the stronger message lengths.

The 2026 paper proves a streaming Hamiltonian verification result. It discusses a possible game application with short questions but polynomial-size answers; that application is not a theorem in the checked passage, and even those parameters would not meet this card’s answer bound.
why: Would connect efficient verification of quantum witnesses to succinct classical interaction with entangled provers. The honest-prover requirement preserves the computational meaning of the witness, which unrestricted entangled proof-system containments do not ensure.
status_note: The full CCC 2026 question and the 2024 status note were checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching efficient-prover protocol or impossibility theorem was located. The stronger logarithmic-question/constant-answer conjecture is distinguished explicitly.

Both questions and answers must have polylogarithmic length, with a constant completeness–soundness gap. title: Are symmetric quantum circuits universal for every finite group action?
importance_reason: A universality question about symmetry as a restriction on quantum computation. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For every finite set X, every permutation group Γ≤Sym(X), and every unitary U on (ℂ²)^{⊗X} satisfying UR(σ)=R(σ)U for all σ∈Γ, does there exist a finite Γ-symmetric circuit C in the gate model below and finitely many workspace qubits Y, initialized and returned to |0⟩, such that C(|ψ⟩_X⊗|0⟩_Y)=(U|ψ⟩_X)⊗|0⟩_Y for every input state |ψ⟩? No bound on circuit size, depth or workspace is required.
definitions: R(σ) permutes the tensor factors labelled by X: R(σ)|a⟩=|a∘σ⁻¹⟩ for a∈{0,1}^X. A finite abstract group acting on X is represented by its image in Sym(X); only this action matters. Circuit wires are W=X⊔Y, with X active and Y workspace. Allowed gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitaries and unbounded-fan-in reversible threshold/equality gates. For S⊆W, target h∉S and integer t≥0, a threshold gate flips bit a_h exactly when ∑_{s∈S}a_s≥t; an equality gate flips it exactly when this sum equals t, leaving all other bits unchanged and extending linearly to quantum states. Layers are sets of pairwise commuting gates; gates within a layer may share wires. A wire permutation acts on a gate by relabelling its target and controls while preserving the one-qubit matrix or threshold value. The circuit is Γ-symmetric if, for each σ∈Γ, some permutation π of W restricts to σ on X and maps each layer to itself as a set of labelled gates. The extensions π need not be selected as a group homomorphism. This is a syntactic circuit condition, stronger than merely requiring its resulting unitary to commute with Γ. Implementation is exact on the full active Hilbert space, with clean workspace, no intermediate measurements or postselection, and no uniformity or finite-angle-encoding restriction on the arbitrary one-qubit gates. An overall input-independent phase can be absorbed into an allowed one-qubit phase gate.
answer_criterion: Prove exact implementability for every finite permutation action and every commuting unitary, or exhibit an action and a commuting unitary that no finite circuit in this model implements. A lower bound only on polynomial-size circuits does not refute universality. Implementing only the invariant-state subspace does not implement an arbitrary unitary on the whole space.
context:
Suppose Γ swaps two active wires. Applying the same one-qubit gate to both wires in a common layer respects that swap. Applying different gates to the two wires generally does not. More elaborate circuits may use extra wires, but every active-wire symmetry must still extend to a relabelling that preserves every layer.

Ancillas are not required to be fixed individually. A swap of active wires may also swap corresponding workspace wires. They begin and end at zero, so they can support a symmetric computation without supplying an asymmetric initial resource.

The full paper’s Theorem 12 proves universality for Γ=S_{n₁}×⋯×S_{n_t}, acting by arbitrary permutations separately inside fixed blocks of wires. This includes the full permutation group S_n. The remaining question allows other finite actions, such as a cyclic rotation of wire labels.

Theorem 3 gives an O(n^3.75)-gate implementation of a permutation-symmetric unitary restricted to the symmetric subspace. Theorem 12 supplies full-space existence for partition symmetries. Neither statement answers universality for every group, and the present question asks existence before asking implementation cost.
why: Would determine whether syntactic symmetry alone limits the quantum operations a circuit can express, even with unrestricted finite resources. It separates a possible expressive obstruction from the additional difficulty of obtaining efficient symmetric algorithms.
status_note: Conference question and full-version Definitions 9–12 and Theorem 12 checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No resolution for arbitrary finite group actions in this precise threshold-gate/ancilla model was located. Results about only local symmetric gates use a different model.
progress: 2025-10-06: The full version proves partition-symmetry universality in Theorem 12 and leaves universality for arbitrary finite groups open. | 2026-01: The ITCS proceedings retain the general-group universality question separately from circuit complexity.
working_summary: A unitary can respect a symmetry even when a chosen gate decomposition does not. This question asks whether every symmetry-preserving unitary has a circuit whose layers themselves preserve the symmetry. The model permits threshold gates, arbitrary one-qubit gates and clean workspace that may also be permuted. Universality is known for independent full permutations within blocks, including the full permutation group. The open target is exact full-space implementation for every finite group action, without a size or depth bound.

title: Cloning random-circuit states without first learning their circuits
importance_reason: A possible computational separation between quantum-state learning and cloning, with cryptographic consequences. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Can one exploit the structure of random quantum-circuit output states to clone them more effectively than known learning-based algorithms, even with subexponential running time and only polynomially many input copies? The source’s algorithm question is parameterized by the circuit ensemble and the desired fidelity and success probability; it does not select a single complete benchmark.
definitions: A sampled n-qubit circuit C prepares the pure state |C⟩=C|0ⁿ⟩. A cloning algorithm receives k copies |C⟩^{⊗k}, with k polynomial in n, and outputs (k+1) registers of n qubits. It receives neither C’s classical description nor a preparation oracle. For output density operator ρ, global squared fidelity with the desired copies is F_C(ρ)=⟨C|^{⊗(k+1)}ρ|C⟩^{⊗(k+1)}. This checks the entire joint output, not each register separately. A high-probability formulation also specifies the distribution of output branches and functions ε(n),δ(n): the source’s No-Cloning assumption says that for every polynomial-time quantum algorithm and polynomial k, the probability of a branch with fidelity at least ε is at most δ for all sufficiently large n. Its probability includes the random circuit and the algorithm’s output randomness. This tail guarantee differs from specifying only expected fidelity. Subexponential time means 2^{o(n)} relative to the number of qubits. The paper offers depth (log n)² one-dimensional brickwork circuits as a motivating ensemble, rather than fixing that as the only allowed family in the selected algorithm question. “Random circuit” must ultimately include a gate-sampling and precision convention.
answer_criterion: First fix the ensemble, copy budget, running time, fidelity statistic and success threshold. Then give and analyze an algorithm meeting that guarantee, or prove an appropriately scoped lower bound. Any claimed improvement over learning-based cloning must have a quantitative comparison; merely omitting a classical circuit description from the output is not such a comparison.
statement_review_issue: A complete algorithmic benchmark still needs a specified circuit ensemble and gate distribution/precision, depth as a function of n, allowed input-copy count, required global-fidelity and success functions, and an objective comparison with learning-based cloning. The phrase “does not learn the circuit description first” describes an approach rather than a formal observable success condition. Conjecture 2 supplies parameterized hardness assumptions, not a unique selection of these parameters for the algorithm question.
context:
For one qubit, a pair of correlated registers can have plausible individual marginals without being two copies of the desired pure state. The global-fidelity criterion checks the entire tensor-product target, including the retained input copies.

Werner’s theorem gives exact optimal worst-case k→k+1 global fidelity (k+1)/(2ⁿ+k) for arbitrary n-qubit pure states. For polynomial k this is exponentially small. title: Does prior entanglement reduce pyramid positional proof systems to PSPACE?
importance_reason: A complexity-class question about the role of prior entanglement in positional quantum proof systems. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: For the source’s pyramid arrangement of verifiers and honest provers, does requiring soundness against malicious provers with arbitrarily much pre-shared entanglement limit the resulting quantum positional proof class to PSPACE? The source asks for this collapse informally; its formal QPMIPˢ definition covers the no-prior-entanglement model, so the modified class and timing conventions still need to be fixed.
definitions: A positional proof places verifiers and honest provers at points p(Q) of a metric space (X,d). A message emitted at time t cannot reach another point before its distance-dependent arrival time. In the formal model, time is discrete, d is integer-valued, the timeout and verifier computation are polynomial in the input length, and quantum messages are passed through local completely positive trace-preserving operations. Malicious strategies may change prover locations while keeping verifier locations fixed and must obey the specified routing and timing constraints. A verifier’s min-ball is B_V={z:d(z,p(V))≤min_P d(p(P),p(V))}. The min-ball condition holds when two such balls are disjoint. In the geometric pyramid illustration, k verifiers lie on a regular k-gon of circumradius R in the plane z=0, another verifier lies at height √(4r²−R²) for r>R, and each of k honest provers lies at the midpoint between a polygon verifier and the top verifier. The balls pairwise intersect but have no common point. PSPACE is the class of languages decidable by deterministic polynomial-space machines; EXP allows deterministic time 2^{poly(n)}. The source’s superscript s means separable initial prover resources and its associated no-PE transmission rules. Arbitrary prior entanglement would permit a joint quantum state across malicious prover locations before verifier challenges, with no fixed finite bound on its dimension; this is a change to the soundness model, not a theorem about the original no-PE class.
answer_criterion: Precisely define the entangled-adversary variant and prove that every language with a proof in that class lies in PSPACE, with the claimed lower inclusion if stating equality; or establish a counterexample under explicitly stated complexity assumptions. Demonstrating failure of the source’s particular EXP construction establishes an attack on that protocol, not a collapse of all protocols for the arrangement.
statement_review_issue: The open passage proposes allowing malicious provers arbitrary pre-shared entanglement, but continues to use the notation defined only for separable initialization and transmission rules. A complete theorem must fix the modified initialization and pre-input/pre-message communication rules, whether honest provers gain the same resource, the precise growing pyramid arrangement and discrete timing implementation, and the acceptance-gap convention. One must also distinguish collapse of the entire resulting proof class from a cheating attack on the one exhibited EXP protocol. The latter alone would not prove a PSPACE upper bound.
context:
If a response must arrive quickly, some distant participants cannot exchange the necessary information in time. Positional proof systems use those restrictions while allowing communication whenever the geometry permits it.

Three disks can overlap in every pair while sharing no common point. The pyramid arrangement creates the analogous difficulty for verifier min-balls: pairwise coordination may be possible even though no single location can answer everyone within the required timing windows.

For the exhibited arrangement, the source proves that classical positional proofs capture PSPACE, while the separable quantum model contains EXP. This is a conditional separation in computational power unless EXP=PSPACE. It does not establish soundness against pre-entangled malicious provers.

Adding an adversarial resource can invalidate a protocol’s rejection guarantee. The question asks whether that change removes the advantage of all quantum positional protocols for this arrangement. It is distinct from giving honest participants more computational power.

The article carefully defines separable initialization, honest and malicious transmission functions, and position-dependent classes. The open entangled variant must say which of these components change before its complexity can be compared with PSPACE.

title: Tight quantum query lower bounds for uniformity testing
importance_reason: A fundamental quantum-query optimality question for distribution testing; the existing numerical importance score is retained.
formal: Does testing whether an unknown distribution p on [d] is exactly uniform or has total variation distance greater than ε from uniform require Ω(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3}, √d/ε}) quantum queries to a synthesizer for p, with success probability at least 0.99 on every promised input? The bound is uniform in d≥2 and 0<ε≤1/4; this explicit small-error range avoids the empty or near-maximal-distance promises implicit in an unrestricted reading of the source.
definitions: Write [d]={1,…,d}, u_d(i)=1/d and d_TV(p,u_d)=(1/2)Σ_i|p_i−1/d|. The algorithm receives d and ε and oracle access to a unitary U_p satisfying U_p|0^k⟩=Σ_i√p_i|i⟩|ψ_i⟩, where each garbage state |ψ_i⟩ is normalized. The extension of U_p away from |0^k⟩ and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of U_p, U_p† or controlled-U_p; intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let Q(d,ε) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with p=u_d or d_TV(p,u_d)>ε, taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap. The conjecture asks for an absolute c>0 with Q(d,ε)≥c min{d^{1/3}ε^{-4/3},d^{1/2}ε^{-1}} throughout the stated parameter range, up to conventional finite asymptotic exceptions.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform two-parameter lower bound in this oracle model, or refute it by a tester with a smaller worst-case asymptotic query complexity in a valid parameter regime. Lower bounds for classical samples, one particular algorithm, constant ε only, or a restricted family of quantum testers do not establish the full claim.
context:
Ordinary sample access reveals only independent outcomes. Coherent access to a sampler and its inverse permits interference between executions. This can reduce the number of calls needed to detect a departure from uniformity; a classical sample lower bound therefore does not automatically apply.

The paper establishes O(min{d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3},√d/ε}) queries. The terms cross at ε=d^{-1/2}: the first governs larger errors and the second smaller errors. The question asks whether any quantum tester can improve this full dependence.

The source recalls Ω(d^{1/3}) queries for constant ε and Ω(1/ε) already on a two-element domain. Knowing both separately does not yield their conjectured joint dependence. For example, at ε=d^{-1/2} the target is Ω(d).

For a string x∈[d]^m, the standard oracle maps |j,z⟩ to |j,z⊕x_j⟩ and defines p_i=|{j:x_j=i}|/m. The authors also conjecture the same lower bound even with this structure available, in the worst case over m and x. This is a stronger claim than the arbitrary-synthesizer target selected here; fixed small m can cap the cost through reading the entire string.
why: Would identify the optimal joint dependence on domain size and accuracy for one of the basic distribution-testing tasks with coherent sampler access, clarifying the extent of quantum advantage over classical samples.
status_note: Conjecture, access definitions, version record and later-result searches checked through 12 September 2026. No matching general quantum-query lower bound was located; classical uniformity and quantum-state measurement results use different access models.
progress: 2025: The TQC paper supplies the matching candidate upper bound and states its optimality as Conjecture 2.
working_summary: A quantum tester must distinguish exact uniformity from a distribution whose total variation distance exceeds ε. It can invoke a coherent sampler, its inverse and a controlled invocation. The best known query upper bound is the smaller of d^{1/3}/ε^{4/3} and √d/ε. The question is whether every tester must pay this cost in the worst case across both parameters. title: Martin’s full conjecture for Turing-invariant functions under determinacy
importance_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
focus_reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.
formal: Assume ZF+DC+AD. Do both assertions hold? (I) Every Turing-invariant function f:2^ω→2^ω is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies x≤_T f(x) on a cone. (II) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump f′ has rank exactly rank(f)+1 in this prewellorder.
definitions: A real x∈2^ω is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write x≤_T y if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and x≡_T y for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when x≡_T y implies f(x)≡_T f(y). A cone above a real a is {x:a≤_T x}. Being constant on a cone means ∃a,b ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≡_T b; the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define f≤_M g by ∃a ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≤_T g(x), and f≡_M g by mutual ≤_M. Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which id≤_M f, where id(x)=x. The prewellorder assertion says that ≤_M is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding [f]. The jump of a real y is y′={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; f′(x)=f(x)′. ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying f(x)≤_T x on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing x≡_T y into indices witnessing f(x)≡_T f(y), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which f(x) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.

The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.
why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.
status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.
progress: 1982: Steel proves Part II for uniformly Turing-invariant functions; the survey records the exact scope as Theorem 1.3. | 1988: Slaman and Steel prove Part I for uniformly invariant functions, the regressive case, and Part II for Borel order-preserving functions. These restrictions are distinct from the full statement. | 2012: Marks, Slaman, and Steel survey the complete formulation under ZF+DC+AD and its connections with countable Borel equivalence relations. | 2023–2024: Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for order-preserving and measure-preserving functions. Their 2024 version explicitly distinguishes the remaining unrestricted conjecture. | 2026: Walsh’s March 2026 Bulletin of Symbolic Logic survey states the full conjecture as Conjecture 6.4 and summarizes the order-preserving partial results in Theorems 6.6–6.7.
working_summary: Turing-invariant functions act on sets of integers in a way that respects mutual computability. Under determinacy and dependent choice, Martin's full conjecture proposes a rigid cone-wise hierarchy for these functions. Its first part says a function is eventually constant in degree or eventually computes its input, and its second organizes the nonconstant behavior with the jump as the next rank. The conjecture would explain why natural operations on degrees appear in a remarkably ordered progression. The reviewed statement includes arbitrary invariant functions, so results requiring uniformity, order preservation, or special definability leave part of the challenge untouched.

title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
importance_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
focus_reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.
formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
definitions: Work in Cantor space 2^N, with coordinates numbered 0,1,… and fair-coin product measure μ. For a finite binary string σ, the cylinder [σ]={X:σ is a prefix of X} has measure 2^{−|σ|}. A Martin-Löf test is a sequence (U_k)_{k≥1} of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs (k,σ), with U_k equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and μ(U_k)≤2^{−k}. A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test X∉⋂_k U_k. A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier q∈[0,2], before seeing X(j). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After X(j) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by 2−q if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. q=1 allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most 1/R. Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.
why: A central equivalence problem for algorithmic randomness: determine whether adaptive computable prediction detects every failure of effective measure-theoretic randomness.
status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

working_summary: Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategies may adaptively inspect previously unseen bits in any order while making fair computable bets. The question asks whether every sequence defeating all such strategies is Martin-Löf random. Martin-Löf randomness instead requires avoidance of every effective sequence of small-measure exceptional sets. Equality would show that flexible computable betting captures the full statistical-test notion of algorithmic randomness. The reviewed model allows partial strategies and unbounded capital success, so limitations for fixed reading orders or weaker betting rules cannot settle the comparison.

title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
importance_reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.
formal: Is every order automorphism of the partial order (Dₜ,≤ₜ) of all Turing degrees the identity? Equivalently, does every bijection π:Dₜ→Dₜ satisfying a≤ₜb if and only if π(a)≤ₜπ(b), for all a,b∈Dₜ, also satisfy π(a)=a for every a∈Dₜ?
definitions: For sets A,B⊆ℕ, A≤ₜB means that an oracle Turing machine with membership-query access to B halts on every natural-number input and decides membership in A. There is no time or space bound. A≡ₜB means A≤ₜB and B≤ₜA. The Turing degree [A] is the equivalence class of A under ≡ₜ, and Dₜ is the quotient of all subsets of ℕ by this equivalence. The relation [A]≤ₜ[B] is independent of the chosen representatives and is a partial order. An automorphism is any set-theoretic bijection of Dₜ preserving and reflecting this order. It is not assumed computable, definable, continuous, measure-preserving or induced by one operation on representatives. The domain includes all degrees, not only degrees of computably enumerable sets or degrees below a fixed bound. The question is interpreted for the actual degree structure in ordinary set theory, for example ZFC.
answer_criterion: Prove that every such bijection fixes every degree, or prove the existence of one order automorphism and one degree that it moves. An automorphism of a proper substructure, a non-surjective order embedding, or a permutation of subsets that fails to descend to degrees is not a counterexample. Rigidity of one cone or of a restricted class of induced automorphisms is only a partial positive result. An independence result should specify the axiomatic base and would settle provability relative to that base rather than assert either mathematical answer.
context:
Turing degrees classify decision problems by what can be computed from an oracle for them. Different encodings that compute one another become one point, and the order records comparative computational power. The rigidity question asks whether this order has any genuine symmetry: could all degrees be consistently relabeled, changing at least one degree while preserving every reducibility comparison? A positive answer would make the entire relative-computability structure intrinsically asymmetric.

Elementary examples illustrate what is already forced. The degree 0 of computable sets is the unique least element and therefore cannot move. The join of [A] and [B] is represented by A⊕B, which stores A on even positions and B on odd positions; because it is the least upper bound, every order automorphism preserves joins as well. These observations do not identify arbitrary degrees, whose patterns of predecessors and successors are far more complicated.

The Turing jump sends [A] to the degree of the halting problem for machines equipped with oracle A. Shore and Slaman prove that this operation is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Consequently every automorphism commutes with the jump, and fixes 0′, 0″ and all finite iterates starting from 0. This is a major restriction, but commuting with an operation does not by itself force a map to fix every argument.

Slaman and Woodin prove that every automorphism fixes every degree above 0″. Their analysis also shows that the automorphism group is at most countable, despite the continuum-sized underlying degree structure. The unresolved region is the complement of that upper cone. It includes degrees incomparable with 0″, not just degrees strictly below it. Thus describing the remaining question as only the interval below 0″ would omit part of the problem.

One possible way to construct an automorphism would be to permute the natural-number coordinates of every oracle set. Kjos-Hanssen rules this out: if one permutation of ℕ induces an order automorphism on all Turing degrees, the induced automorphism is trivial, and the permutation itself must be computable. His result also treats homeomorphisms of Cantor space preserving all Bernoulli product measures. The full question imposes none of these representation or measure restrictions.

Rigidity must also be distinguished from defining every single degree by a first-order formula without parameters. There are only countably many such formulas but uncountably many degrees, so the latter is impossible. A rigid infinite structure can contain elements that are not individually definable: absence of global symmetries is weaker than having a separate finite logical description of each element.

The historical literature includes an announced nontrivial automorphism by Cooper in 1999. Slaman’s survey explicitly reports that its construction had not been independently verified and continues to treat rigidity as open. Kjos-Hanssen’s later journal article likewise states the general question as open. These cards follow the established partial-result literature; an old announcement alone is not treated as a resolution.

This is a foundational computability question rather than an efficient-algorithm problem. Its significance is whether relative computability already determines its own global structure, or whether the degree order admits hidden symmetries that are invisible to all reducibility comparisons.
why: A central structural question about relative computability: whether the ordering of computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. It tests how much mathematical information is recoverable from reducibility alone.
status_note: Literature search checked through 10 September 2026. The checked primary sources explicitly retain general rigidity as open; no later verified resolution was located. The last substantive result documented here is the 2018 journal article, not a claimed 2026 advance. The historical Cooper announcement is distinguished from an independently verified solution.
progress: 1980 and later: Cone-rigidity results culminate in Slaman–Woodin’s theorem that all degrees above 0″ are fixed; the full structure remains outside this conclusion. | 1999: Shore–Slaman prove that the Turing jump is definable from the order, so every automorphism preserves it. | 2008: Slaman’s published survey presents the countability of the automorphism group, rigidity above 0″ and the unresolved general question. | 2016–2018: Kjos-Hanssen excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by integer permutations and certain measure-preserving homeomorphisms; the journal paper appears in 2018.
working_summary: Turing degrees identify sets of integers that compute one another and order them by relative computability. The rigidity question asks whether every order-preserving bijection of this entire partial order fixes every degree. A positive answer would mean that the order structure alone determines the identity of each degree. This is a basic structural question about how much information is encoded by the pattern of computational reducibility. The saved review permits arbitrary set-theoretic automorphisms, so excluding computable transformations or automorphisms induced by a special action on representatives is only a restricted result.

title: Determining the sixth Busy Beaver value BB(6)
importance_reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.
formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$, the maximum number of steps taken before halting by a deterministic Turing machine with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols, and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape. The transition into a separate halting state counts as one step. Thus $BB(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal{M}_6\text{ halts on the blank tape}\}$, where $T(M)$ counts executed transitions and the machine class is fixed below.
definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in T(M). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit positive integer N and prove BB(6)=N: exhibit a machine in the stated class that halts after exactly N transitions, and prove that every halting machine in this class takes at most N transitions. A finite, unambiguous expression using explicitly defined total operations is sufficient to specify N; its decimal expansion is not required. A larger lower bound or the analysis of only some remaining machines does not settle the question.
context:
Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.
why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.
status_note: The primary project pages checked on 10 September 2026 still report BB(6) as unsolved. Lower bounds and holdout counts are attributed to the project; this review did not rerun its proofs or enumeration.
progress: 2025-06: The project credits mxdys with a six-state halting machine establishing $S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 5$. This is a lower bound, not an exact determination. | 2025-09-15; revised 2026-03-23: The collaboration published its proof of S(5)=47,176,870, formally verified in Coq. The result settles the five-state case only. | 2026-08-30: The dated project list records 1,003 BB(6) holdouts after its equivalence reductions. This is a progress report from an informal search, not a certified exact value. | 2026-09-10 status check: The project BB(6) page, revised on 3 September 2026, still lists the value as unsolved. Antihydra remains an example of the unresolved halting behaviors involved.
working_summary: BB(6) is the maximum halting runtime among six-state, two-symbol Turing machines started on a blank tape. The task is to determine this exact finite integer under the saved transition and step-counting conventions. Finding a long-running halting machine supplies only a lower bound; every remaining machine must also be shown to halt within the claimed maximum or never halt. The problem turns the general undecidability of halting into an exceptionally concrete finite classification challenge. The saved review records large candidate runtimes and unresolved holdouts, and distinguishes runtime from the separate Busy Beaver measure counting printed ones.

title: Does Hindman’s theorem imply the ω-jump?
importance_reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.
formal: Over RCA₀, does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA₀⁺? Equivalently, does RCA₀+HT prove that every set X has an ω-th Turing jump?
definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA₀ has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, Σ⁰₁ induction and Δ⁰₁ comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer k≥1 and every coloring c of the positive integers into {0,…,k−1}, there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that c(Σ_{h∈F}h)=i for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump X′ is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The ω-jump existence axiom says ∀X∃Y [Y₀=X and ∀j(Y_{j+1}=Y_j′)], where Y_j={e:⟨j,e⟩∈Y} and ⟨·,·⟩ is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA₀⁺ is RCA₀ plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
answer_criterion: Prove the ω-jump existence axiom in RCA₀+HT, or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA₀+HT in which some set has no coded ω-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA₀ alone, an upper bound of ACA₀⁺, or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA₀; an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
context:
Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA₀ allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The ω-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA₀⁺ demands more set existence than ACA₀. Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the (ω+1)-st jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an ω-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA₀; four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly n≥3 terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no Σ⁰₂ solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA₀⁺. A finite set F is exactly large when |F|=min(F)+1, so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low₂ solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA₀. The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA₀⁺ as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the ω-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.
why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the ω-th Turing jump.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or separation for RCA₀+HT⇒ACA₀⁺ was found in the checked primary literature. The recent variable-word and Carlson–Simpson results have different formulations and do not establish this reversal.
progress: 1987: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA₀⁺⇒HT⇒ACA₀ over RCA₀, leaving the reversal in this card open. | 2012–2014: Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA₀⁺ using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal. | 2017–2020: Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA₀ lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020. | 2018: Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT. | 11 June–2 July 2026: Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength. | 30 July 2026: Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.
working_summary: Hindman's theorem finds an infinite set whose nonempty finite sums all receive the same color in any finite coloring. The question asks whether this principle proves the existence of every set's iterated omega-th Turing jump over RCA0. It measures the theorem's logical strength rather than asking whether the combinatorial statement is true in ordinary mathematics. A positive implication would show that unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity entails a strong closure principle for computability. The reviewed formulation allows sums of arbitrarily many distinct elements, so results for exactly two terms or other restricted variants do not answer it automatically.

title: Universality of Turing equivalence
importance_reason: A classical universality question with consequences for Martin’s conjecture and for the distinction between definable and uniform computational encodings.
formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function f:X→2^ℕ such that x E y if and only if f(x)≡_T f(y), for all x,y∈X?
definitions: The space 2^ℕ consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of ℕ. For a,b∈2^ℕ, a≤_T b means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; a≡_T b means both a≤_T b and b≤_T a. There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel σ-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of X×X and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether E_∞≤_B≡_T for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation E_∞. A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
context:
Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of f(x) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark E_∞. One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group F₂ on {0,1}^{F₂}: two labelings x,y are equivalent when y(h)=x(g⁻¹h) for some group element g and every h∈F₂. This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of 0₂ in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. Let A=[[1,0],[0,0]] and B=[[0,0],[1,0]]. Neither is the zero matrix, but AB=0₂, so the list (A,B) is mortal. Reversing the order gives BA=B, showing that order matters. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over GF(2). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming NP≠coNP, does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.
why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.
