working_summary: Extended Frege adds reusable formula definitions to ordinary Frege reasoning. The question asks whether every Extended Frege proof has an ordinary Frege proof of the same conclusion with only polynomially larger size. Expanding definitions directly can be exponentially expensive, but another Frege argument might avoid that expansion. The comparison tests whether sharing intermediate computations fundamentally increases propositional proof strength. The saved review asks only for existence of short translated proofs, carefully separating this size simulation from a polynomial-time procedure that actually finds them.

title: Superpolynomial AC⁰[p]-Frege lower bounds
importance_reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.
formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies (τ_{p,n})_{n≥1}, constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and n^O(1), such that each τ_{p,n} is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant r>0, infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with MOD_p connectives of τ_{p,n} has total encoded size greater than n^r? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(MOD_p) in Krajíček §5: MOD_{p,j}(A_1,…,A_t) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for 0≤j<p. Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms MOD_{p,0}() and NOT MOD_{p,j}() for j≠0, and all instances of MOD_{p,j}(Γ,A) ↔ [(MOD_{p,j}(Γ) AND NOT A) OR (MOD_{p,j−1}(Γ) AND A)], with j−1 taken modulo p and Γ any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
context:
Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when p=2. Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in AC⁰[p]-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth Ω(w²/log S) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size AC⁰[p]-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as n¹⁰ and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.
why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.
progress: 1988–1994: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo’s 1993 paper gives exponential improvements. These systems lack MOD_p gates. | 2023–2024: Krajíček develops extended Nullstellensatz systems and explains their connection to modular Frege lower bounds; §5 fixes the proof-system presentation used here. | 2025-07-29: Efremenko and Itsykson publish amortized-closure lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth results for resolution over parities. | 2026-01-23: Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish their no-short-proof result for candidate DNFs, first posted in September 2025; unconditional tautologicity remains open. | 2026-02-12: Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov give near-quadratic-depth lifting and a quadratic unconditional size lower bound for parity resolution. These do not settle general modular Frege. | 2026-05-10: Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret release hard CNF instances for the read-once-oblivious algebraic-branching-program fragment of IPS.
working_summary: AC⁰[p]-Frege uses bounded-depth proof formulas that may include modular counting connectives for a fixed prime p. The saved target asks for explicit polynomial-size DNF tautologies requiring superpolynomial proofs at every fixed formula depth. Modular gates can retain counting information that ordinary restriction methods erase. A lower bound would extend the reach of proof complexity beyond the established bounded-depth systems without modular counting. The reviewed record distinguishes logical depth within proof lines from derivation depth and explains why circuit lower bounds do not automatically imply the requested proof lower bound.

title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
importance_reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.
formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every C>0 and c≥1, does some propositional tautology φ have shortest Frege proof size s_F(φ)>C(|φ|+2)ᶜ?
definitions: Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation ¬ and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and A→B by modus ponens. Its last line is φ. There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in φ may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |φ| and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is s_F(φ). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound s_F(φ)≤C(|φ|+2)ᶜ for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
context:
Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |φ|, and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if NP=coNP. Consequently, NP≠coNP would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that n+1 pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, Res(log), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.
why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

working_summary: Frege systems formalize propositional deduction through finitely specified rules and reusable intermediate lemmas. The question asks whether tautologies sometimes require proofs exceeding every polynomial in their own encoded length. It concerns the shortest possible derivation, not the time spent by any particular proof-search strategy. A lower bound would establish a substantial limitation on a familiar model of mathematical reasoning. The saved review notes that powerful counting arguments give short Frege proofs where weaker systems struggle, and that separating Frege alone would not establish NP≠coNP.

title: Do p-optimal propositional proof systems exist?
importance_reason: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation t_Q satisfying P(t_Q(π))=Q(π) for every finite binary proof string π?
definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function P:{0,1}*→TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string π proves formula F when P(π)=F. Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as x₁∨¬x₁. A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on π. The order is ∃P ∀Q ∃t_Q ∀π. No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |π|.
answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.
context:
Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say NP=coNP.

Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from P=NP. Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.
why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
status_note: Primary definitions and the 1989 equivalence theorem were checked, together with February and ICALP 2026 primary sources. The latter retain the propositional optimality questions; their oracle results do not resolve this unrelativized target. A search through 11 September 2026 found no full resolution, and proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 1989: Theorem 2.1(ii) relates polynomial simulation of all propositional proof systems to optimal tautology recognition and finite-consistency proof construction; P=NP implies this existence. | 2026-02-02: Q1 explicitly retains (p-)optimality for TAUT as open. New oracle constructions show barriers for relativizing answers even with assumptions about the polynomial hierarchy. | 2026-07: ICALP work on recursive jump operators gives oracle barriers and results for other languages, while retaining the propositional optimality questions.
working_summary: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system? The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length. Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial. This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology. The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

title: A complete disjoint NP pair
importance_reason: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
formal: Do disjoint languages A,B∈NP exist such that, for every disjoint pair C,D∈NP, there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with f(C)⊆A and f(D)⊆B?
definitions: All four languages consist of finite binary strings. NP means membership has a polynomial-length certificate checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Disjoint means A∩B=∅ and C∩D=∅. The total function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* may depend on (C,D); its running-time polynomial need not be universal across pairs. No requirement is imposed on f(x) when x∉C∪D. Completeness uses one function for both sides, not two unrelated reductions.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
A disjoint NP pair expresses two efficiently certifiable cases that cannot occur together. Complete pairs would provide a universal object for this kind of promise complexity.

Canonical disjoint pairs arise from propositional proof systems, tying the question to proof simulation and finite incompleteness. The existence of a p-optimal proof system would imply a complete pair, but the converse is not asserted. This card asks the pair-completeness question itself.
why: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2017: The paper organizes the complete-pair question and its connections to proof-complexity conjectures.

title: Does Resolution effectively polynomially simulate Extended Frege?
importance_reason: Tests whether conventional proof-size separations remain meaningful when hard instances themselves must be found efficiently.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer s≥1, R(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
definitions: A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation ¬ and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent C∨D of earlier clauses C∨x and D∨¬x. Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), or follow by modus ponens from A and A→B. One may also introduce an extension axiom z↔B, where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here z↔B abbreviates (z→B)∧(B→z). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.
context:
Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

From x∨y and ¬x, Resolution derives y. Together with the clause ¬y, it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.

title: Do symmetric IPS lower bounds imply a symmetric VP–VNP separation?
importance_reason: A structural connection between algebraic proof complexity and symmetric arithmetic circuit classes; existing numerical score retained.
formal: For suitably defined symmetric analogues of VP and VNP, would superpolynomial lower bounds on symmetric Ideal Proof System refutations of unsatisfiable Boolean CNF formulas imply that symmetric VP differs from symmetric VNP? The source poses the development of those analogue classes as part of the question; they have not been specified here.
definitions: A Boolean CNF is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. Over a fixed field K, encode each clause by the product of the factors that equal one when its literals are false, set that product to zero, and add x_i²−x_i=0 for Boolean variables. For example, x∨¬y becomes (1−x)y=0. Let f_1(x),…,f_m(x) be the resulting polynomials. An IPS certificate is a polynomial C(x,y) with C(x,0)=0 and C(x,f_1(x),…,f_m(x))=1 as polynomial identities; an IPS refutation is an arithmetic circuit over K computing C. A group Γ acts by permutations of the x variables and preserves the polynomial axiom set; it then permutes y_i according to the induced permutation of f_i. The circuit is Γ-symmetric when each group permutation extends to a permutation of its gates preserving wires, operation labels and field constants. Polynomial invariance of its output alone is weaker than this circuit requirement. Size is measured by circuit gates with the instance-size floor; a superpolynomial family lower bound excludes any one polynomial bound in encoded formula size. In the ordinary nonsymmetric setting, VP consists of polynomial-degree polynomial families in polynomially many variables having polynomial-size arithmetic circuits. VNP consists of families expressible as a sum over polynomially many Boolean witness variables of such a VP family. How to impose compatible symmetries on these families and on the summation is a missing part of the proposed analogue.

A lower bound for invariant polynomials, for a bounded-degree IPS fragment, or only for Hilbert-like certificates does not automatically establish a lower bound for the full symmetric IPS system.

title: Log-rank conjecture for deterministic two-party communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
focus_reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.
formal: Do there exist universal constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every total Boolean function f:X×Y→{0,1}, on arbitrary nonempty finite sets X,Y, satisfies $D(f)\le C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k$, where r(f) is the real rank of its 0/1 communication matrix and D(f) is its deterministic communication complexity?
definitions: Alice receives x∈X and Bob receives y∈Y. Both know the complete function f and the protocol. They exchange bits interactively; each next transmitted bit is a deterministic function of the sender’s own input and the previous transcript. A binary protocol tree specifies whose turn it is, and every leaf has a Boolean output that must equal f(x,y) for every input pair reaching it. D(f) is the minimum, over all such exact protocols, of the maximum number of transmitted bits on an input pair. The number of rounds and the local computation are unrestricted; protocol description length is not charged. The communication matrix M_f has rows X, columns Y, and entry f(x,y); r(f)=rank_R(M_f) is ordinary matrix rank over the real numbers. The +2 makes the statement unambiguous for rank zero or one. The same constants C,k must work for all matrix dimensions and all functions. There are no undefined entries, input promises, random bits, quantum messages, approximation errors, or restrictions to one-way protocols. Sign rank and approximate rank are different parameters.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most 2ᵈ leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle A×B. Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents M_f as a sum of at most 2ᵈ rank-one matrices. Consequently log₂r(f)≤D(f) when r(f)≥1. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an O(√r log r) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting O(√r) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint revisits the construction without first converting its pointer alphabet to Boolean bits and reports a more precise lower bound Ω((log r)²/log log r). This still has a fixed polynomial exponent and therefore supports no refutation of log-rank.

A recent equivalent formulation isolates the role of cancellation more sharply. Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley show that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of O(r log r) rectangle indicator matrices. The open task can then be expressed as converting such signed decompositions into positive disjoint rectangle decompositions with quasipolynomial growth. This theorem supplies a new formulation, while the needed conversion remains unresolved.
why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.
status_note: Explicitly open in the August 2026 CCC version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley. Checked through 10 September 2026. The established general upper bound is O(√r); recent fixed-polynomial lower-bound refinements and signed-decomposition equivalences do not settle the conjecture.

working_summary: Alice and Bob must compute a total Boolean function while each sees only one part of its input. The log-rank conjecture asks whether deterministic communication is bounded by a universal polynomial in the logarithm of the real rank of the communication matrix. Rank captures linear dependence among rows, whereas a protocol must organize inputs into consistently labeled transcript regions. A positive answer would make this algebraic invariant a remarkably effective predictor of exact communication cost. The reviewed formulation allows unlimited rounds and local computation, and excludes promises, approximation, sign rank, and randomized or quantum protocols.

title: The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
focus_reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.
formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant C>0 such that, for every integer n≥1 and every Boolean function f:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1}, H(f)≤C I(f), where H(f) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and I(f) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n}. For S⊆[n], let χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S}x_i, with χ_∅=1, and let f̂(S)=2⁻ⁿ∑_{x∈{−1,1}ⁿ}f(x)χ_S(x). Put q_S=f̂(S)²; Parseval gives ∑_S q_S=1. Define H(f)=∑_S q_S log₂(1/q_S), with a zero summand when q_S=0. If x is uniform and x^{⊕i} differs only by flipping coordinate i, define I_i(f)=Pr[f(x)≠f(x^{⊕i})] and I(f)=∑_{i=1}ⁿ I_i(f)=∑_S |S|q_S. All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have H(f)=I(f)=0 and satisfy the non-strict inequality.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The Fourier expansion expresses a Boolean rule as a linear combination of parity tests on subsets of its inputs. Squaring the coefficients produces a probability distribution on these subsets. Its entropy measures how dispersed that distribution is; total influence measures the expected size of a subset sampled from it. The conjecture says that the Boolean constraint forces the first quantity to be at most a constant times the second, even though there are exponentially many possible subsets.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy log₂ n but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function g(x)=(x₁+⋯+x_n)/√n, which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

A useful consequence would be spectral concentration: for any 0<δ<1, all but δ of the Fourier mass could be captured by at most 2^{C I(f)/δ} coefficients. This follows by applying Markov’s inequality to the surprisal log₂(1/q_S) of a random spectral subset. It supplies a quantitative connection between stability under individual bit flips and approximation by a short linear combination of parities. The dependence on δ is essential; the claim is not an accuracy-independent support bound.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the conjecture for symmetric Boolean functions and for functions computed by read-once decision trees. Their paper also explains the connection to learning DNF formulas: the conjecture would imply polynomial Fourier concentration for a DNF with polynomially many terms, at each fixed approximation accuracy. This is a structural learning-theory consequence, rather than an assertion that arbitrary Boolean functions become efficiently learnable.

A general bound proved by Han is H(f)≤O(I(f)+∑_i I_i(f) log(1/I_i(f))). The extra term records how influence is distributed across coordinates. It can exceed a constant multiple of I(f), so this does not settle the conjecture. The December 2025 revision adds an acknowledgement of related earlier work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. Bounds on min-entropy concern the largest Fourier coefficient alone and must not be substituted for a Shannon-entropy bound.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s June 2026 revision verifies additional classes, including δ-tribes and functions with specified separation properties. Their method splits on selected coordinates and stops at restrictions already satisfying FEI. It also demonstrates failure of a stronger sufficient inequality when the splitting coordinate is chosen badly. Those examples do satisfy FEI when handled with a suitable coordinate, so they expose a limitation of that inductive route rather than a counterexample to the conjecture.

Slote’s August 2026 preprint disproves a quantum analogue using Hermitian unitary operators with flat, very large Pauli expansions. For the constructed degree-d operators, the spectral entropy grows quadratically in d while the influence grows linearly. These are quantum Boolean functions, not scalar maps on the classical Boolean cube. The result makes the distinction between the two settings concrete and does not provide a classical counterexample.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.
why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 primary paper explicitly retains classical FEI as open and proves only specified classes. The August 2026 disproof is of the quantum extension. No classical resolution was found in the checked sources; the formulation uses Shannon entropy, uniform measure and scalar Boolean functions throughout.
progress: 1996: Friedgut and Kalai propose the conjecture; the historical attribution and its applications are described by O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou. | 2011: The conjecture is verified for symmetric functions and read-once decision trees. | 2023–2025: Han proves a general bound with an additional coordinate-influence entropy term; Combinatorica publication is in volume 45 (2025), and arXiv v2 of 10 December 2025 acknowledges related prior work. | 2026-06-09: The revised González–MacManus–Pereyra preprint proves FEI for new separated classes and δ-tribes; the unrestricted classical question remains open. | 2026-08-02: Slote posts a counterexample to the quantum FEI conjecture. Its operator-valued construction does not resolve classical FEI.
working_summary: A Boolean function has a Fourier expansion whose squared coefficients form a probability distribution. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture bounds the entropy of that distribution by a universal constant times total influence. Intuitively, it asks whether small average sensitivity prevents Fourier weight from being spread across too many descriptions. The bound would connect the spectral complexity of a function with how often changing one input bit changes its value. The saved review distinguishes this classical conjecture from stronger coordinate-wise statements and quantum analogues, whose failures do not by themselves refute the stated Boolean inequality.

title: The Aaronson–Ambainis influential-variable conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for all integers n≥1 and 1≤d≤n and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying 0≤f(x)≤1 for every x∈{−1,1}^n, some coordinate i satisfies Inf_i(f)≥(Var(f)/d)^C?
definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on {−1,1}^n. Write f(x)=Σ_{S⊆[n]} f̂(S)∏_{j∈S}x_j, with f̂(S)=E_x[f(x)∏_{j∈S}x_j]; degree at most d means f̂(S)=0 when |S|>d. Let x^{⊕i} be x with just coordinate i negated. Define Var(f)=E[(f−E f)²]=Σ_{S≠∅}f̂(S)² and Inf_i(f)=E[(f(x)−f(x^{⊕i}))²]/4=Σ_{S∋i}f̂(S)². This is squared L₂ influence, with the factor 1/4 fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because Var(f)≤1/4, fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than (Var(f)/d)^C. Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.
context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider f(x)=1/2+(x₁+⋯+x_n)/(2n). This degree-one polynomial always lies in [0,1], but Var(f)=1/(4n) and each coordinate has influence 1/(4n²). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a log(d)/d fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The accompanying junta theorem approximates restricted functions using few coordinates. Neither assertion directly guarantees such a variable in the original, unrestricted function.

Two recent results clarify the frontier. Blanc and coauthors obtain the desired almost-everywhere classical simulation for a fixed number of quantum query rounds; their exponent depends on the number of rounds. This does not address arbitrary adaptivity or prove the full polynomial inequality. Escudero Gutiérrez, Saucedo and Palazuelos subsequently obtain an optimal root-influence inequality for completely bounded block-multilinear polynomials, improving simulation to allow nonadaptive classical queries for that setting.

The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.
why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.
status_note: The 4 September 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture open. Recent restricted-model and bounded-round results do not prove it; the 2019 general claim remains withdrawn. Checked through 11 September 2026.

working_summary: A bounded low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube describes a real-valued function with controlled algebraic complexity. The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture asks whether some variable has influence polynomially large in the variance and inverse degree. It predicts that meaningful variation cannot be distributed too evenly among all coordinates when the degree stays small. The question matters for understanding when quantum query behavior admits efficient classical simulation. The reviewed record stresses that results for random restrictions, bounded-round algorithms, or completely bounded norms impose additional structure and do not settle the unrestricted scalar-polynomial statement.

title: Mansour’s conjecture with logarithmic accuracy dependence
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C>0 such that, for every n≥1, integer s≥2, Boolean function f:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1} representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and ε∈(0,1/2], some family F⊆2^[n] satisfies |F|≤⌈s^{C log₂(1/ε)}⌉ and Σ_{S∉F} f̂(S)²≤ε?
definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals x_i=1 or x_i=−1; a satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space {−1,1}ⁿ, χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S}x_i, χ_∅=1, and f̂(S)=2^{−n}Σ_x f(x)χ_S(x). Parseval gives Σ_S f̂(S)²=1. Thus ε-concentration on F means that the polynomial g=Σ_{S∈F}f̂(S)χ_S has E[(f−g)²]≤ε. The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all n,s,ε and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible s,n,ε and DNF require more than ⌈s^{C log₂(1/ε)}⌉ coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most ε. A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on ε would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.
context:
A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like n^d. A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability 2^{−w}. Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error 4·2^{−w}. Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows s^{K(ε)} coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for K(ε)=O(log(1/ε)). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were O(log s), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal log(1/f̂(S)²) would capture all but ε of the mass on at most s^{O(1/ε)} coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives s^{O(log log s)} coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to s^{O(log log k)}, where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives (s/ε)^{O(log(1/ε))} concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit s/ε base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.
why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.
status_note: Open in the strong logarithmic-accuracy form stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Fixed-error polynomial concentration, restricted DNF models, and generalized-basis learning results do not by themselves settle this formulation.
