working_summary: A short DNF describes a Boolean function as a small collection of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier representation describes the same function using correlations with parity functions. Mansour's conjecture asks whether almost all Fourier mass lies on a small set of coefficients whose size is controlled by the number of DNF terms and logarithmically scaled accuracy dependence in the exponent. This is a sparsity claim, so a bound on polynomial degree alone does not establish it. Proving the proposed concentration would connect two very different descriptions of Boolean functions and strengthen a central structural foundation for learning DNFs.

title: The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.
formal: Is there a universal constant C>0 such that, for every n≥1, every integer 1≤d≤n and every Boolean polynomial threshold function f=sign(p):{−1,1}^n→{−1,1} of degree at most d, its total influence satisfies I(f)≤C d√n?
definitions: A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with p(x)≠0 at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing x_i² to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on {−1,1}^n, let x^(i) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define Inf_i(f)=Pr[f(x)≠f(x^(i))], pointwise sensitivity s_f(x)=|{i:f(x)≠f(x^(i))}|, and I(f)=Σ_i Inf_i(f)=E[s_f(x)]. The constant C is independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing d=0 adds only these trivial cases. This is the asymptotic influence conjecture, not the disproved claim specifying an exact extremizing function.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal C works for all n,d and all such functions, or show that the ratios I(f)/(d√n) are unbounded over this class. A counterexample to a particular proposed numerical C, or to the original exact symmetric extremizer, does not by itself refute this existential-constant statement. A bound C_d√n with unrestricted dependence on d, or √n times a growing polylogarithmic factor, is partial progress rather than the claimed uniform bound.
context:
A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then I(f)=2D/2^n. The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of C d√n would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with √n; once d≥√n, the elementary bound I(f)≤n already suffices with C=1.

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other n−1 coordinates split evenly, giving I(MAJ_n)=n·binom(n−1,(n−1)/2)/2^(n−1), asymptotic to √(2n/π). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order d√n. Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement used here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives O(d√n). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate I(f)≤√n·(log n)^{O(d log d)}·2^{O(d² log d)} for d≥2. For each fixed d, this is √n times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area BSA(f)=E[√s_f(x)]. The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from I(f)=E[s_f(x)]. A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise s_f(x)≤√n·√s_f(x) yields only I(f)≤√n·BSA(f). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.
why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal O(d√n) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.
progress: 2012–2013: Kane establishes the correct √n exponent up to degree-dependent polylogarithmic factors. | 2017: Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs. | 2018: Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question. | 2022: Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations. | 8 April 2026: Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2. | 27 April 2026: Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.
working_summary: A polynomial threshold function assigns a Boolean value according to the sign of a real polynomial. The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial question asks whether its total influence is always O(d√n), where d is degree and n is the number of variables. Influence measures the expected number of coordinate flips that change the output, giving a discrete notion of boundary size. The proposed bound would limit how irregular a low-degree threshold boundary can be on the cube. The saved review separates this asymptotic claim from the stronger conjecture identifying an exact extremizer, which the cited literature disproves.

title: The Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg evasiveness conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
original_area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A basic lower-bound question about whether symmetry prevents any edge query from being avoided.
formal: For every integer n≥2 and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on [n] to {0,1} that is invariant under every permutation of [n] and monotone under adding edges, is D(f)=n(n−1)/2, where D(f) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n} and U_n={{i,j}:1≤i<j≤n}; a graph is an arbitrary edge set E⊆U_n, with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means E⊆F implies f(E)≤f(F). Invariance means f(π(E))=f(E) for every permutation π of [n], where π(E)={{π(i),π(j)}:{i,j}∈E}. A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in U_n and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output f(E) for every E⊆U_n. The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and D(f) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives D(f)≤|U_n|.
answer_criterion: Prove D(f)=|U_n| for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |U_n|−1. A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.
context:
Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair {1,2} is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning n=p^k for a prime p and an integer k≥1. Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.
why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The October 2025 revision of Elekes, Kátay and Kocsis explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. No later resolution matching the full graph-property model was located. The June 2026 topological counterexample announcement concerns a broader symmetry condition; only its abstract and an in-preparation listing were accessible, so no claim about its proof or graph specialization is made. Source/model review is not an independent proof audit.
progress: 1984: Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant, Theorem 1, establish exact evasiveness for every nontrivial monotone graph property when the number of vertices is a prime power. | 2020-10-23: Aaronson and coauthors, Theorem 5, prove the optimal universal Omega(n) bounded-error quantum query lower bound. This is a separate query model. | 2025-10-20: Elekes and coauthors, version 3, Section 1.1, retain the finite conjecture as open while studying failures of infinite-vertex extensions. | 2026-06-23: Benedetti’s CATA IV abstract announces a counterexample to topological evasiveness. No finite graph-property counterexample is specified in the abstract; the related author publication list still labels the manuscript in preparation at this review.
working_summary: An algorithm learns an unknown graph by asking whether individual pairs of vertices are edges. The conjecture asks whether every nonconstant monotone property invariant under vertex relabeling has some input requiring all possible pairs to be queried. Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free. The example of looking for one edge illustrates how an easy positive instance can coexist with an empty graph that requires a complete scan. The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.

title: A polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication for total functions
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.
formal: For a total Boolean function $F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?
definitions: X and Y are arbitrary finite sets. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits or qubits, and error at most 1/3 is required on every input pair. Public random bits and prior entanglement, respectively, are not charged as communication.
answer_criterion: Establish one polynomial bound valid for every finite total Boolean communication problem, or prove that no universal polynomial bound holds. Promise problems and restricted subclasses do not suffice.
context:
Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.

Alice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.

Totality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.
why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.
status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
progress: 2026: For $F=f\circ\mathrm{AND}_2$, the source proves $D^{cc}(F)=O((Q^{cc,*}(F))^7\log^2 n)$. The polylogarithmic factor and the restriction to AND-composed functions prevent this from settling the general question.
working_summary: Two parties must evaluate a Boolean function when each holds one part of the input. The question asks whether randomized classical communication is polynomially bounded by quantum communication with shared entanglement for every total function. Both models allow bounded error on each input, and their costs count transmitted bits or qubits rather than local computation. A positive answer would limit quantum communication advantages whenever the function is defined on every input pair. The totality condition is central: results for promise problems cannot be substituted, and the polynomial must be universal across all finite domains.

title: Explicit polynomial-separation lower bounds
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: An explicit superlinear or polynomial-gap lower bound would expose a concrete barrier in restricted computational models.
formal: Source target, pending the coefficient convention described below: does there exist an explicit Boolean-function family f=(fₙ), in the book’s NP sense, which has no family of low-degree, low-weight polynomials separating its 1-inputs from its 0-inputs? “Separating” means pₙ(x)≠pₙ(y) whenever fₙ(x)=1 and fₙ(y)=0. The intended small-parameter regime is degree at most d(n) and weight at most 2^d(n), for some d(n)=(log n)^O(1).
definitions: For n≥2, fₙ maps {0,1}ⁿ to {0,1}. The book defines explicitness by a uniform polynomial-time Boolean verifier V and a polynomial q: fₙ(x)=1 exactly when V(x,y)=1 for some binary certificate y of length at most q(n). Thus the family’s accepted strings form a language in NP; merely giving an unbounded-time enumeration does not meet the source convention. A multilinear real polynomial has form p(x)=∑(S⊆{1,…,n}) a_S∏(i∈S)xᵢ, with the empty product equal to 1. It separates fₙ if the two sets {p(x):fₙ(x)=0} and {p(x):fₙ(x)=1} are disjoint; it need not approximate fₙ or classify inputs by the sign of p. In the draft’s literal definition each a_S belongs to {−1,0,+1}, degree is the largest |S| with a_S≠0, and weight is the number of nonzero a_S (degree and weight of the zero polynomial are taken as zero). Small degree/weight means that there exist fixed c≥1 and C≥1 such that, for all sufficiently large n, one can choose pₙ with degree at most d(n)=C(log₂ n)^c and weight at most 2^d(n). The separators need not be generated uniformly. If the literal coefficient convention is retained, a hard family would have, for every c,C and arbitrarily large n, no separator meeting both bounds. The alternative convention suggested by the draft’s addition step allows integer coefficients and counts ∑S |a_S| instead. The source does not clearly reconcile these conventions, so the accepted polynomial class remains a formulation gap.
answer_criterion: Once the source’s polynomial coefficient and weight convention is settled, exhibit an NP family with no separating family in the specified low-degree/low-weight regime and prove the claimed lower bound, or prove that every NP family has such separators. The supplied source currently does not support choosing one of the two conflicting polynomial classes as the final benchmark theorem.
statement_review_issue: The primary draft defines separating polynomials with combined coefficients in {−1,0,+1} and weight equal to the number of nonzero monomials. Its motivating ACC⁰ lemma then adds many such polynomials and calls the sum a ±1 polynomial, although repeated monomials can produce coefficients of magnitude greater than one. It is unclear whether the intended question retains the literal coefficient restriction or allows integer coefficients with weight charged by multiplicity/total absolute coefficient. These are different lower-bound targets. The public errata did not settle the convention; the card does not silently select a correction.
context:
A separating polynomial may assign many different numbers to yes inputs and many different numbers to no inputs. It only has to avoid assigning the same number to inputs with different answers. For example, x₁+x₂ separates two-bit parity: the even-parity inputs have values 0 or 2, and the odd-parity inputs have value 1. No single numerical threshold separates those two sets.

Degree limits how many input coordinates can participate in a monomial. Weight limits the polynomial’s algebraic description according to the chosen coefficient convention. Without coefficient restrictions, x₁+2x₂+4x₃+⋯+2^(n−1)xₙ takes a different value on every Boolean input and therefore separates every Boolean function. The weight convention is consequently central to the question.

The book’s definition asks for membership in NP, expressed by one polynomial-time certificate verifier. It does not require the function itself to be computable deterministically in polynomial time. This distinction is stated in Section 1.5.1 and is part of the recovered problem.

The draft places this question after a claimed easy-separation property of ACC⁰: polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean circuits with AND, OR, NOT and modular-counting gates for fixed moduli. The coefficient inconsistency in that lemma prevents this review from treating the claimed implication as verified for the literal ±1 model.

Adding x₁ to x₁ yields 2x₁, whose coefficient is outside {−1,0,+1}. The draft’s motivating proof sums polynomials but still calls the result a ±1 polynomial. Keeping distinct signed summands would instead produce an integer-coefficient polynomial with multiplicities. This card records the conflict so that the lower-bound target can be fixed without silently changing the source.
why: Studies whether Boolean answers can be encoded by algebraically simple numerical values that keep yes and no inputs disjoint. The source ties the question to restricted circuit lower bounds, but that significance depends on a consistent choice of coefficients and weight; it is not a generic polynomial-approximation problem.
status_note: The intended measure is now recovered, but the coefficient/weight convention requires clarification before a theorem can be certified as matching the source target. Later searches through 11 September 2026 found no directly applicable correction or resolution. The credential-protected second-edition draft was not accessed, and the surrounding circuit lemma was not accepted as proved by this review.
progress: 2012: The public early draft linked from the 2012 book page poses Research Problem 12.31 and supplies the NP explicitness and polynomial-separation definitions. The draft itself is not independently dated. | 2026-09-11: Individual review recovered the missing separation measure and identified the coefficient/weight conflict in the surrounding lemma. Public errata and subsequent-work searches did not resolve that formulation issue.
working_summary: The source asks for an NP Boolean-function family whose yes inputs and no inputs cannot be separated by low-degree, low-weight polynomial values. Separation means that no accepting input and rejecting input receive the same value, rather than that a sign threshold computes the function. The book supplies a precise certificate-based meaning of explicitness. Its early draft conflicts over whether coefficients must remain in {−1,0,+1} or may include accumulated multiplicities. The card now explains the question and its circuit motivation while retaining that coefficient convention as an unresolved formulation issue.

title: Explicit input pairs resistant to partial monotone separation
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
area_label: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
importance_reason: A concrete question about a restricted function family, representation, or resource bound; useful for techniques but narrower than the category's central separations.
formal: Do there exist families of nonempty disjoint sets Aₙ,Bₙ⊆{0,1}ⁿ, each with a uniform NP membership predicate, and an integer-valued function r(n)≥0 with r(n)/log₂log₂n→∞, such that the families are compatible with monotone separation and every monotone circuit separating a 2^(−r(n)) fraction of Aₙ from a 2^(−r(n)) fraction of Bₙ, in either direction, has size n^ω(1)?
definitions: All claims are for integers n≥4, with finitely many initial lengths irrelevant. Explicitness is interpreted for both membership predicates using the book’s Section 1.5.1: there are fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifiers V_A,V_B and fixed polynomial witness bounds p_A,p_B such that x∈Aₙ iff some y∈{0,1}^≤p_A(n) satisfies V_A(x,y)=1, and analogously for Bₙ. This does not require listing exponentially many members. Compatibility with a monotone separator means that no b∈Bₙ and a∈Aₙ have b≤a coordinatewise; equivalently, some monotone Boolean function is zero on Aₙ and one on Bₙ. A monotone circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input variables x₁,…,xₙ, constants 0 and 1, and fan-in-two AND and OR gates, no negations, unrestricted fan-out and one output. Size is its number of AND/OR gates. Write θₙ=2^(−r(n)). A circuit C partially separates the pair if either Pr_{a uniform in Aₙ}[C(a)=0]≥θₙ and Pr_{b uniform in Bₙ}[C(b)=1]≥θₙ, or Pr_{a uniform in Aₙ}[C(a)=1]≥θₙ and Pr_{b uniform in Bₙ}[C(b)=0]≥θₙ. The two probabilities use their separate finite uniform distributions; no condition is imposed on the remaining inputs. Thus the circuit may choose which subsets it separates, and integer subset sizes are rounded up by the displayed fraction inequalities. The required superpolynomial bound means: for every constant k>0 there is n_k such that for all n≥n_k, every partially separating monotone circuit has more than n^k gates. There is no uniformity restriction on these circuits. The growth condition on r means that for every constant c>0, eventually r(n)>c log₂log₂n. No independent time bound is required for evaluating the displayed function r.
answer_criterion: Give explicit membership verifiers for both input families, a function r with the required growth, and a proof of monotone compatibility and the superpolynomial lower bound for every permitted partial separator in both directions; or prove that no such families and r exist. Hardness only for separating all of A from all of B in one direction does not meet the target.
context:
The usual monotone separation task rejects every negative input and accepts every positive input. Here a circuit is allowed to handle only small subsets of each side, and may reverse the output labels. As r grows, the required fractions shrink, so the hardness claim becomes stronger.

Suppose all inputs in A have Hamming weight at least ten and all inputs in B have weight at most nine. The monotone threshold circuit that accepts weights at least ten separates the entire pair in the reverse direction. Regardless of the difficulty of the forward direction, such a pair cannot meet the required two-direction hardness.

For example, r=3 requires correct separation on at least one eighth of A and one eighth of B. A circuit may behave arbitrarily on the rest. This is not a single average-error requirement on the union, where a larger side could conceal failure on the smaller side.

The book relates this robust pair property to lower bounds for circuits containing a limited number of NOT gates. It reports an r of order log log n from Amano and Maruoka’s work and identifies logarithmic r as sufficient for a breakthrough on unrestricted circuit size. Those are dated source statements; the requested improvement is any r growing faster than log log n.

The later negation-width paper controls how many distinct negated variables occur in syntactically produced terms. Its lower bounds do not by themselves exhibit a pair satisfying the two separate fraction conditions here. A bound involving negation width cannot be substituted for the requested r-hard pair.
why: Seeks explicit input distributions for which the monotone lower-bound obstruction survives both severe restriction of the tested inputs and reversal of labels. This robustness is tied to understanding how a limited use of negation changes circuit power, beyond ordinary monotone complexity.
status_note: Book passages and subsequent related literature checked through 11 September 2026. No construction or impossibility result matching the stronger two-direction partial-separation target was located. The search was not exhaustive; no circuit lower-bound proof was independently verified.

The bound is attributed to the draft rather than asserted as a newly verified current optimum. | 2019-03-12: Jukna and Lingas study lower bounds under bounded negation width, a different restriction from the robust pair property.

title: Does the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis hold?
importance_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
focus_reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.
formal: For every real ε∈(0,1), does there exist an integer k≥3 such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and ε, but not on the individual formula. Define sₖ=inf{α≥0 : k-SAT has an O(2^{αn}Lᶜ)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts limₖ→∞sₖ=1; monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of (k+1)-SAT. Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Exhaustive search tries all 2ⁿ assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially 2ⁿ time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A 2^{0.9n}-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds 2^{(1−1/k)n} would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond P≠NP, which by itself allows intermediate running times such as 2^{√n}.

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

title: Can exact weighted all-pairs shortest paths be computed in truly subcubic time?
importance_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
focus_reason: Truly subcubic exact weighted APSP is a central fine-grained benchmark with consequences for a large family of graph and matrix problems.
formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least 2/3? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs O(1), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on O(log n)-bit index words cost O(1). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.
why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is a fixed exponent saving for arbitrary real edge weights; the 2026 node-weighted triangle result does not supply it.
progress: 2010: Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish truly subcubic equivalences between APSP and several path, matrix, and weighted-triangle tasks. | 2013 / 2014: Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved. | 2026-05: Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.
working_summary: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a weighted directed graph. The graph may contain negative edges but no negative cycle. The target is an algorithm with a fixed positive improvement over the cubic exponent in the specified comparison-addition model. Small subpolynomial savings do not meet that target. The question matters both as a basic graph optimization problem and as the organizing hypothesis behind many conditional running-time lower bounds.

title: The Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
importance_reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.
formal: Is it true that for every ε∈(0,1) there is a fixed integer c≥1 for which no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm decides bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors on two lists of n vectors in {0,1}^d, with d=⌈c log₂ n⌉, in worst-case time O(n^{2−ε}) and with error probability at most 1/3 on every input?
definitions: Here n≥2 and the two input lists A and B each have length n; repeated vectors are allowed. The answer is YES exactly when some a∈A and b∈B satisfy Σ_{j=1}^d a_j b_j=0 as an integer sum, equivalently their supports are disjoint. This is not an inner product over the field with two elements. Inputs are explicitly supplied as packed binary vectors. Computation uses a uniform classical RAM with words of Θ(log(n+d)) bits, ordinary constant-time word arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, memory access and generation of a random word. Each program uses a fixed word-length constant; arbitrary-precision unit-cost operations, nonuniform advice and free preprocessing tables are excluded. Reading, preprocessing and all subsequent computation count in the time bound. For fixed ε and c, hidden time constants and the program may depend on these parameters, but not on n. There is no promise on vector weights, overlap or input distribution. Randomness is internal to the algorithm; correctness must hold for every pair of lists.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower-bound proposition, or refute it by exhibiting one fixed ε>0 such that for every fixed integer c≥1 an algorithm A_c meets the n^{2−ε} time and error bounds. This quantifier order matters: the algorithms and constants may depend on c, but the exponent saving ε must work for every c. Giving a different positive saving ε_c that tends to zero with c, shaving logarithmic factors from quadratic time, or proving lower bounds only for restricted circuit models does not settle the proposition.
context:
Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are n² possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on c is the main subtlety. There are already truly subquadratic algorithms for each fixed c, with a saving that can deteriorate as c increases. The polynomial-method algorithm of Abboud, Williams and Yu runs in time n^{2−1/O(log c)} in the relevant large-c regime. This is consistent with the hypothesis: selecting a sufficiently large c can make that known saving smaller than any proposed universal ε. The source is SODA 2015; some later bibliographies mistakenly label it 2014.

Very small dimension permits another strategy: enumerate possible coordinate patterns and aggregate the input instead of considering all pairs separately. The 2026 low-dimensional algorithms achieve a randomized bound of Õ(1.25^d n), with a further reported O(1.16^d n) bound obtained through computer-aided parameter evaluation. These improve the useful range of the pattern-based approach, but their exponential dependence on d becomes a power of n when d=c log₂ n.

For example, substituting c=2 into 1.25^d n gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, n^{1+2 log₂ 1.25}, whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The hypothesis is useful because disjointness can encode compatibility between partial solutions. In the standard split-and-list SAT reduction, each half-assignment produces a vector marking clauses it fails to satisfy. Two half-assignments extend to a satisfying assignment exactly when their vectors are disjoint. Sparsification controls the number of clause coordinates. For the randomized version stated here, the corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a conditional justification; a deterministic-only SAT assumption must not silently be used to exclude randomized solvers.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.
why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.
status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly states the unrestricted OV conjecture as open while proving restricted-model variants. Low-dimensional and average-case improvements do not negate its quantifier order. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2015: Abboud–Williams–Yu obtain dimension-dependent truly subquadratic algorithms via the polynomial method; the exponent saving decreases with the dimension constant. | 2019: Rohatgi develops OV-based conditional hardness for exact Earth Mover Distance, illustrating geometric consequences. | 2024-10-29: Alman–Andoni–Zhang improve average-case OV algorithms; the work appears at SOSA 2025. | 2026-07-01: Dürr–Kipouridis–Lampis–Węgrzycki present Õ(1.25^d n) randomized low-dimensional algorithms at ICALP, with a computer-aided O(1.16^d n) refinement. | 2026-07-26: Choudhury and coauthors establish the logarithmic-dimension monotone-circuit version for the negated predicate and strengthen other restricted-model lower bounds.
working_summary: Bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors asks whether two collections of binary vectors contain a pair with disjoint supports. The hypothesis excludes one fixed polynomial saving over quadratic time across all sufficiently large logarithmic dimension constants. Checking a pair is easy, but identifying a compatible pair among quadratically many possibilities is the bottleneck. Fine-grained reductions use this task to transfer precise barriers to geometric, string, and other algorithms. The saved review notes that subquadratic algorithms at each fixed small dimension are compatible with the hypothesis because their exponent savings can deteriorate as the dimension constant increases.

title: The algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis: the leading exponent
importance_reason: A principal fine-grained benchmark connecting clique detection, matrix multiplication, dynamic data structures, and constraint optimization.
formal: Let τ(k) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let ω be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is liminf_{k→∞} τ(k)/k=ω/3?
definitions: For each fixed integer k≥3, the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on n≥k labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set τ(k)=inf{a≥0: such an algorithm runs in O(n^a) time as n→∞}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have C_k⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed constant C_k; arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For ω, let M(N) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal N×N matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define ω=inf{a:M(N)=O(N^a)}. This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on ω as its exact value.
answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark ω/3. An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every δ>0, there is K such that τ(k)≥(ω/3−δ)k for every fixed k≥K. A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with τ(k)≤(ω/3−δ)k for arbitrarily large k and one δ>0. Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive o(k) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
context:
For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For k=3r, create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are O(n^r) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent ωk/3.

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the n^{ωk/3−o(k)} form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study n→∞ for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, ω is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on ω immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true ω. The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports ω<2.371177, improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is n^k(log n)^{−(k+1)}(log log n)^{k+3}. Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by o(1) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below ω/3. Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.
why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.
status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.
progress: 1985: Nešetřil–Poljak’s grouping reduction gives the matrix-multiplication benchmark, with rectangular refinements for k not divisible by three. | 2021: Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro explicitly formulate randomized/deterministic n^{ωk/3−o(k)} hardness and use it in dynamic formula lower bounds. | 2024–2026: Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve combinatorial clique detection by logarithmic factors; the preprint revision is August 2024 and the Algorithmica version appears in 2026. | 2025: Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß prove exponent-preserving regularization reductions and apply them to Boolean CSP optimization. | 2026-01-23: Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic obtain conditional optimality results for maximum coverage and partial domination using clique and hyperclique assumptions. | 2026-08-17: Dupont and coauthors report ω<2.371177, improving the available clique upper bound through the existing reduction without settling optimality.
working_summary: For each fixed k, graph k-Clique asks whether k vertices are all pairwise adjacent. The reviewed hypothesis asks whether the leading coefficient of the optimal time exponent approaches the matrix-multiplication benchmark ω/3. Grouping a candidate clique into three parts connects detection to multiplication on auxiliary graphs. A lower exponent would change the foundation of many conditional optimality results for other computational tasks. The comparison uses the true matrix-multiplication exponent, so beating an old numerical upper bound or saving logarithmic factors does not by itself refute the hypothesis.

title: The Hyperclique Hypothesis
importance_reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.
formal: For every fixed pair of integers h≥3 and k>h and every constant ε>0, is there no classical randomized O(n^(k−ε))-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most 1/3 on each input?
definitions: The input hypergraph H=([n],E) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of [n]. It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set S⊆[n] of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with O(log(n+2))-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed h,k,ε. Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in O(n^(k−ε)) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least 2/3 for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair h≥3,k>h, one fixed ε>0 and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
context:
A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For h=3 and k=4, a positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes O(n^k) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case h=2 behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at h=3, instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time n^k divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an O(n^3.99) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is Θ(n^h) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because k>h. Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal (h−1)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.
why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.
progress: 2017–2018: Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams develop hyperclique hypotheses, their Max-h-SAT connections and conditional graph-algorithm lower bounds. | 2025: Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß prove regularization preserving fine-grained clique complexity and apply it to Boolean CSP optimization. | 30 March–June 2026: Dudek and coauthors relate the 3-uniform 4-hyperclique hypothesis to arithmetic-progression detection in their STOC 2026 study of algebraic identities. | July 2026: Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß analyze when sparsity helps for hypergraph independent sets and use hyperclique assumptions for matching lower bounds.
working_summary: A clique in an h-uniform hypergraph requires every h-element subset of its vertices to be a hyperedge. The hypothesis asserts that, for fixed h at least three and k greater than h, exhaustive k-tuple search admits no constant exponent saving. Higher-order compatibility cannot be verified merely by checking pairwise adjacency as in a graph. This conjectured barrier supports fine-grained lower bounds for optimization with higher-arity constraints. The saved review fixes randomized classical algorithms and dense inputs, while distinguishing genuine polynomial savings from logarithmic improvements or algorithms benefiting only from sparsity.

title: Can exact edit distance be computed in truly subquadratic time?
importance_reason: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
formal: For the binary alphabet Σ={0,1}, do there exist a constant ε∈(0,1], a constant C>0 and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every n≥1 and every pair x,y∈Σ^n, A outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance ED(x,y) in at most C(n+1)^(2−ε) operations?
definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. ED(x,y) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has w=ceil(4 log₂(n+2)) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo 2^w, integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving ε cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case O(n^(2−ε)) bound for some fixed ε>0 in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.
context:
The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes O(n²) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as n²/log n is smaller than n² but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for n^(2−ε) with one ε>0 that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every δ>0 there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in O(2^((1−δ)N) poly(L)) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation for each fixed η>0, with running time n²/2^(log^Ω(1) n). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on η cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.
why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.
status_note: The checked primary literature gives conditional exact-distance lower bounds and a March 2026 approximation advance. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established deterministic truly subquadratic exact algorithm or unconditional exclusion in this model.
progress: 2015 / 2017: Backurs–Indyk prove a SETH-based obstruction to truly subquadratic exact edit distance; the 2017 full revision also records subsequent developments. | 2015-04: Bringmann–Künnemann establish the conditional lower bound already on binary strings. | 2026-03: A randomized approximation scheme obtains a quasi-polynomial speedup; it does not compute exact distances.
working_summary: Can exact edit distance between two length-n binary strings be computed in truly subquadratic time? Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum. The requested deterministic worst-case bound has a fixed positive saving in the exponent of n. Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved. title: The online Boolean matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
importance_reason: A widely reusable fine-grained hardness hypothesis underlying trade-offs for many dynamic problems; its consequences reach well beyond matrix-vector multiplication.
formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm with a fixed positive polynomial saving in the total time, including preprocessing, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. A subpolynomial saving does not refute the OMv conjecture.
context:
If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.
why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The truly subcubic Boolean online problem remains open; structured-matrix and different-product results require separate assumptions.

These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.
