working_summary: A Unique Games instance assigns labels to vertices, with each edge specifying a permutation relating its endpoint labels. The conjecture asks whether almost satisfiable instances are NP-hard to distinguish from instances with very small optimum value. Although perfect satisfiability can be checked by propagating labels, a small allowance for violated constraints changes the challenge. The conjecture would explain approximation thresholds for many constraint satisfaction problems through semidefinite programming. The saved review emphasizes that hardness with completeness one half does not establish the required completeness arbitrarily close to one.

title: A polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.
formal: Do there exist constants a≥1 and C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most a(log₂(k+2))^C times optimum with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a root r∈V, a nonempty terminal set T⊆V∖{r} with k=|T|, and nonnegative rational arc costs c_e given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset F⊆E such that (V,F) contains a directed path from r to every t∈T. Its cost is Σ_{e∈F}c_e, counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least 2/3 over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of n=|V|, k and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An O(k^ε)-approximation for every separately fixed ε>0, a polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
context:
The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0, from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting ε to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an O(log² k/log log k)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.
why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.
status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly leaves this general-graph question open. The inherited 2024 claim was withdrawn, and its October 2025 replacement is restricted to a special supplied fractional solution; that claim is not counted as an established general result. Planar and quasipolynomial algorithms do not satisfy this card. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1998–1999: Classical directed Steiner approximation algorithms give O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0 in polynomial time. | 2019: Grandoni–Laekhanukit–Li obtain O(log² k/log log k) in quasipolynomial time, with conditional matching-scale hardness. | 2023: Friggstad–Mousavi obtain a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar digraphs. | 2024: Chekuri and coauthors extend planar rooted-network techniques and prove an O(log² k) planar LP gap. | 2024-12-20: Version 2 of Laekhanukit’s initial general claim is withdrawn. | 2025-10-10: Version 3 narrows that claim to access to a relatively integral fractional solution; the record retains its withdrawal comment. | 2026-07-28: Chekuri–Jain obtain planar length-constrained bicriteria approximations and explicitly retain the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic question.
working_summary: Directed Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost directed network connecting one root to every required terminal. The question asks for randomized polynomial-time approximation within a fixed power of the logarithm of the terminal count. Sharing arcs between routes can save substantially, but directionality complicates selecting useful branching structures. A positive result would close a major gap between polynomial-time algorithms and stronger guarantees obtainable in quasipolynomial time. The saved review warns that choosing a shrinking parameter in existing power-factor algorithms can destroy their polynomial running time.

title: The Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
formal: For every rational constant η∈(0,1/2), is there a rational constant δ∈(0,1/2) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with δn an integer, distinguish YES: some S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≤η, from NO: every S⊆V(G) with |S|=δn has Φ_G(S)≥1−η.
definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs G=([n],E), n≥2 and d≥1, given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty S, ∂_G S is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and Φ_G(S)=|∂_G S|/(d|S|). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants η,δ are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For δ=a/b in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since η<1/2; inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each x∈L to a YES graph and each x∉L to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on η and its chosen δ. The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every η by choosing δ and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed η. Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed δ at that η would refute the hardness claim under P≠NP; an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.
context:
Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly Φ_G(S). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

If δ=1/1000, the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.
why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.
status_note: No proof or refutation located through 11 September 2026. The original exact-size regular-graph promise was checked separately from later weighted, volume and randomized variants. The August 2026 least-squares result is conditional on such a variant.
progress: 2010: Raghavendra–Steurer introduce the exact-size expansion promise and relate its hardness to Unique Games. | 2010 / 2012: Raghavendra–Steurer–Tulsiani establish reductions and conditional hardness for Balanced Separator and Minimum Linear Arrangement. | 2026-08: A sparse least-squares lower bound is obtained assuming a randomized weighted exact-volume SSE variant.
working_summary: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size? The target set occupies a fixed fraction δ of the graph, with δ chosen after the gap parameter η. Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set. A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size. Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.

title: The 4/3 conjecture for the metric TSP subtour relaxation
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.
formal: Let Γ=sup_{n≥3,c} OPT_TSP(c)/OPT_LP(c), where c ranges over all metrics on n labeled points and OPT_LP is the subtour relaxation defined below. Is Γ=4/3?
definitions: For V={1,…,n} and E={{u,v}:u≠v}, a metric has c_uu=0, c_uv=c_vu>0 for u≠v, and c_uv≤c_uw+c_wv. Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. OPT_TSP is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For S⊆V, δ(S) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and x(F)=Σ_{e∈F}x_e. Define OPT_LP=min Σ_e c_e x_e subject to x(δ({v}))=2 for every v, x(δ(S))≥2 for every nonempty proper S⊊V, and 0≤x_e≤1 for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against OPT_TSP, an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
answer_criterion: Known constructions establish Γ≥4/3. Thus an affirmative resolution proves OPT_TSP(c)≤(4/3)OPT_LP(c) for every finite metric instance. A negative resolution gives an instance with ratio strictly greater than 4/3, or proves such an instance exists. A supremum need not be attained to make the question meaningful. Improving an algorithm’s upper bound while it remains above 4/3 is progress, not a resolution.
context:
The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor 4/3 says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical 3/2 guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost≤α·OPT_TSP does not establish OPT_TSP≤α·OPT_LP, since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below 3/2, extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound Γ≤3/2−2.18·10^{−34}. The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to 3/2.

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the 4/3 bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are 1/2 or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a 10/7 guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since 10/7 exceeds 4/3, it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of 11/8 on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the 4/3 bound when an optimal solution has at most n+6 nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, ε★>2.05522·10^{−30}, through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to OPT_LP. The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the requested ratio 4/3.

title: Can metric k-Median reach the 1+2/e threshold?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), does a randomized polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation algorithm exist for general metric k-Median that always opens at most k facilities?
definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets C,F⊆V of clients and allowable facilities with C∪F=V, and an integer 1≤k≤|F|. The table is promised to satisfy d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0 exactly when u=v, and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty S⊆F define cost(S)=Σ_{c∈C}min_{s∈S}d(c,s), and OPT=min{cost(S):S⊆F,1≤|S|≤k}. L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed ε the target is one uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε, with constants K_ε,d_ε such that every execution takes at most K_ε L^{d_ε} bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty S⊆F with |S|≤k, and on each input Pr[cost(S)≤(1+2/e+ε)OPT]≥2/3. Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The constants may depend on ε but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0.
answer_criterion: Give the stated algorithms for every fixed ε>0, or rule them out for at least one fixed ε, explicitly identifying any complexity assumption used. This card fixes the yes/no question of approaching the known hardness threshold; it does not additionally require finding a different exact threshold after a negative answer. An algorithm opening k facilities only in expectation, one allowing k+o(k) facilities, or an FPT algorithm with unrestricted dependence on k does not prove the claim.
context:
Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.
why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.
progress: 1998: Feige proves the 1−1/e hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the 1+2/e metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction. | 2002: Jain–Mahdian–Saberi give the classical k-Median lower bound via Set Cover approximation; Theorem 10 states the historical reduction. | 2019: Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li reach 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k, not unrestricted polynomial time. | 2025–19 May 2026: Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time 2+ε approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem. | 10 March 2026: Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting. | 16 July 2026: Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective.
working_summary: Metric k-Median selects at most k allowed facilities to minimize clients' total distance to their nearest selection. The target is polynomial-time approximation arbitrarily close to 1+2/e from above while respecting the facility limit. This constant arises from coverage hardness, rather than from a particular rounding analysis. Closing the saved gap between that threshold and the reviewed 2+ε guarantee would settle a basic clustering benchmark. Algorithms opening extra facilities or exploiting Euclidean geometry do not meet the general metric formulation recorded here.

title: The factor-2 integrality-gap conjecture for the ATSP subtour LP
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
original_area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: Would identify the fundamental relaxation gap for asymmetric travelling salesman.
formal: For every n≥2 and every nonnegative directed metric c on V={1,…,n}, is OPT_ATSP(c)≤2·LP_ATSP(c), where OPT_ATSP is the minimum cost of a directed Hamiltonian cycle and LP_ATSP is the degree-and-subtour linear program defined below?
definitions: A directed metric is a function c:V×V→R≥0 with c(i,i)=0 and c(i,k)≤c(i,j)+c(j,k) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc (i,j) for each i≠j and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. OPT_ATSP(c) is the minimum over all such cycles. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S)={(i,j):i∈S,j∉S} and δ⁻(S)={(i,j):i∉S,j∈S}; for a set of arcs F write x(F)=Σ_(i,j)∈F x_ij. LP_ATSP(c) minimizes Σ_i≠j c(i,j)x_ij over real variables x_ij≥0 subject to x(δ⁺({v}))=x(δ⁻({v}))=1 for every v, and x(δ⁺(S))≥1 for every nonempty proper S⊊V. The degree equalities imply x(δ⁺(S))=x(δ⁻(S)), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. The inequality, rather than division by LP_ATSP(c), also covers zero-cost instances. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is OPT_ATSP(c)/LP_ATSP(c), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed factor-2 inequality for every finite directed metric and every size, or exhibit a finite directed metric with a rigorously proved strict violation. An affirmative answer need not attain ratio 2 on a finite instance: known families approach 2. An approximation algorithm proved only relative to the true tour optimum, or a result restricted to a subset of LP extreme points, does not establish the universal LP inequality.
context:
A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The question asks whether converting the best fractional cost into an actual tour ever entails a factor larger than two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in {0,1/2,1}. An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical 4/3 conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices v₁,…,v_ℓ and arcs vᵢ→vᵢ₊₁, with indices modulo ℓ. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless P=NP, since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.

title: Does W[1] ≠ FPT imply the Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis?
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
importance_reason: A general bridge from exact parameterized hardness to constant-gap approximation hardness. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Assuming W[1]≠FPT, is there an absolute constant ε∈(0,1) such that no deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm can distinguish a satisfiable binary constraint satisfaction instance on k variables from an instance in which every assignment violates at least an ε fraction of the constraints, with k as the parameter?
definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet Σ of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; val(Π) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is val(Π)=1 or val(Π)≤1−ε; no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time f(k)L^C for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to f(k)n^{O(1)} after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here W[1]≠FPT is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no f(k)L^C algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed ε>0 for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of W[1]≠FPT.
answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only W[1]≠FPT as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.
context:
Exact unsatisfiability only says every assignment fails somewhere. PIH asks for a constant fraction of failures on every assignment. If an instance has many constraints, the existence of just one unavoidable violation need not give any fixed gap.

The alphabet is allowed to grow with the input. Exhaustive search takes n^k time, whose exponent depends on k; that is not fixed-parameter tractable. A running time such as 2^{2^k}n^3 would qualify despite its very large dependence on k.

Baby PIH distinguishes satisfiable instances from instances for which even a constant-size list of values at each variable cannot satisfy every constraint. This is a different guarantee from saying that every ordinary assignment violates a constant fraction of constraints.

The Guruswami–Lin–Ren–Sun–Wu theorem derives PIH from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. ETH imposes a quantitative subexponential-time obstruction for 3SAT and is a stronger assumption than the parameterized separation sought here. The February 2026 survey still separates these targets.
why: Would supply a parameterized analogue of the PCP theorem from the standard exact-hardness assumption, giving a common basis for constant-gap inapproximability across many parameterized optimization problems.
status_note: Source definitions, the ETH theorem and the February 2026 survey checked with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No proof under only W[1]≠FPT was located.
progress: 2024: Baby PIH is established under W[1]≠FPT; the full PIH implication is left open. | 2025: The journal version of PIH under ETH records the stronger-assumption theorem, whose preprint already appeared in 2023. | 2026-02: The survey explicitly retains the distinction between PIH under ETH and PIH under W[1]≠FPT.
working_summary: The hypothesis W[1]≠FPT says exact parameterized problems such as k-Clique do not admit fixed-parameter algorithms. The question asks whether it also rules out distinguishing satisfiable binary constraint systems from systems that force a constant fraction of violations. The parameter is the number of variables, while the alphabet may grow with the input. PIH is already known under the stronger ETH assumption, and Baby PIH is known under W[1]≠FPT. A proof of the full implication would provide a broad foundation for parameterized inapproximability.

title: The deterministic k-server conjecture
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.
focus_reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.
formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.
why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary source retains the deterministic conjecture and the general (2k−1) upper bound. The 2023 randomized disproof concerns O(log k), not the deterministic factor k. This card fixes all finite request sequences, identical initial placements, exactly k servers and an additive constant independent of requests; it asks for any deterministic online rule, not specifically WFA.

Movement costs the distance traveled, and the online algorithm does not know future requests. Proving the conjecture would identify the exact price of missing future information for arbitrary metric spaces with equal online and offline resources.

title: A constant improvement over factor 2 for unrelated-machine makespan
importance_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
focus_reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.
formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.
why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
importance_reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance of P|prec|Cmax with an input number m of identical parallel machines, produces a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
definitions: An input specifies n≥1 jobs, a positive integer processing time p_j for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine a_j∈{1,…,m} and a nonnegative start time s_j for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [s_j,s_j+p_j), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge i→j, require s_j≥s_i+p_i. Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=max_j(s_j+p_j); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in Σ_j p_j. The same fixed ε must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule.
answer_criterion: Give one such fixed ε and prove a polynomial-time (2−ε) guarantee for all inputs, or rule out every fixed improvement below two with any complexity assumptions explicitly stated. A bound 2−1/m does not supply a universal ε. Guarantees for fixed m, unit jobs only, special precedence orders, quasipolynomial running time, extra machines or faster processors do not prove the requested statement. A conditional hardness result based on a stronger conjecture must remain labelled conditional.
context:
Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work W=Σ_j p_j needs at least W/m time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax≤W/m+(1−1/m)L, and hence Cmax≤(2−1/m)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not resolve the constant improvement in this question.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take m(m−1) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for m−1 time, and the final job finishes at 2m−1. An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other m−1 machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below 4/3 unless P=NP, leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from P≠NP.

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound (1+n/m)^{O(√(nm))} is subexponential when m=o(n), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.
why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.
status_note: No polynomial-time fixed (2−ε) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here.

title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
importance_reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.
formal: Do a universal integer C≥0 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least 2/3?
definitions: The input is a list of n≥1 rational item sizes s₁,…,s_n∈(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map b:[n]→[k] with Σ_{i:b(i)=j}s_i≤1 for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most KL^d bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least 2/3 over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+O(1) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance C=1, a valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing ε on the order of 1/OPT makes ε·OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as ε shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum OPT_f is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with O(log² OPT) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to OPT_f+O(log OPT_f), and hence OPT+O(log OPT). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of OPT_f would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring Ω(log n). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.
why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. The logarithmic-additive guarantee and recent high-multiplicity/support results do not settle this explicitly listed, randomized formulation.

working_summary: One-dimensional bin packing places indivisible numerical items into unit-capacity bins using as few bins as possible. The reviewed question asks for randomized polynomial time with at most a universal constant of extra bins above optimum. This is an additive guarantee, so the allowed excess does not grow with the size of the instance. It would strengthen approximation schemes whose small proportional errors can still yield many extra bins. The saved review notes that ordinary exact-optimization hardness and a multiplicative scheme do not automatically resolve this stronger additive target.

title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
importance_reason: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret R*(d,T) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in [0,1]. Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
definitions: Let d,T≥1 be integers and B₂^d={x∈R^d:Σ_i x_i²≤1}. A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of R^d satisfying B₂^d⊆K⊆dB₂^d; the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write F(K) for the Borel-measurable convex functions f:K→[0,1], where convexity means f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y) for x,y∈K and λ∈[0,1]. No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes f₁,…,f_T∈F(K), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses X_t∈K, incurs f_t(X_t), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history (X₁,f₁(X₁),…,X_(t−1),f_(t−1)(X_(t−1))). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define R_K(T)=inf_π sup_(f₁,…,f_T) E_π[Σ_t f_t(X_t)−inf_(x∈K)Σ_t f_t(x)], with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally R*(d,T)=sup_K R_K(T), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function g(d,T) and universal constants a,b>0 with a g(d,T)≤R*(d,T)≤b g(d,T) for all d,T≥1. Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate g(d,T) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.
context:
On the interval [−1,1], the convex losses f(x)=(1+x)/2 and h(x)=(1−x)/2 both equal 1/2 at x=0, but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order d^(5/2)√T, apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as d√T. The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in [0,1]; an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.
why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
progress: 2020: A general information-theoretic upper bound O(d^2.5 sqrt(T) log(T diam(K))) is proved for the oblivious exact-feedback model. | 2026-03: The book’s Outlook retains the gap between dimension-linear lower bounds and higher-degree general upper bounds. | 2026-06: Budgeted-perturbation results concern smooth underlying losses, including in the unperturbed case. | 2026-07: The revised two-point strongly convex result has a different feedback and comparator model.
working_summary: What is the optimal expected regret for adversarial convex losses when only one value is observed per round? The learner competes with the best fixed point in hindsight over a known convex body. The losses lie in [0,1] and are chosen before the learner’s random actions, with no smoothness assumption. General upper and lower bounds still have different polynomial dependence on dimension. Two-point, strongly convex, smooth-loss and computational-efficiency results address different guarantees.

title: A constant-competitive algorithm for the general matroid secretary problem
importance_reason: The main unresolved competitive-ratio question for online selection under general matroid constraints.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 such that every finite matroid M admits a randomized online selection strategy which, for every assignment of nonnegative weights to its elements, returns an independent set of expected weight at least OPT(M,w)/C when the elements arrive in a uniformly random order?
definitions: A matroid is a finite set E and a nonempty family I⊆2^E closed under subsets and satisfying augmentation: if A,B∈I and |A|<|B|, some b∈B∖A has A∪{b}∈I. The strategy knows E and I in advance, but not the weights. A fixed adversary assigns w:E→ℝ_{≥0} before the order and strategy coins are sampled. Upon each arrival its identity and weight are revealed. The strategy must accept or reject it irrevocably before the next arrival, keeping the accepted set in I. OPT(M,w)=max_{S∈I}∑_{e∈S}w(e). Expectation includes a uniformly random permutation of E and the strategy’s independent random coins. There is no computation or oracle-query bound; this is the competitive-existence conjecture for the full-information matroid model.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:

formal: Do universal constants C,a>0 exist such that, for every integer k≥2, finite metric space (X,d) with |X|≥k+1, and initial placement of k servers, a randomized online strategy has expected total movement cost at most C(1+log₂k)^a OPT(σ)+β on every finite request sequence σ? definitions: There are k movable servers at points of X; repeated server locations are allowed. Each request names a point of X. Before the next request, at least one server must occupy that point. OPT(σ) is the minimum total movement of a strategy knowing the entire sequence and starting at the same placement. The adversary is oblivious: it fixes σ independently of the online strategy’s random coins. The strategy uses only the prefix revealed so far. No running-time bound is imposed. The exponent a and multiplicative constant C must be independent of |X|, k and the metric.
