Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has Θ(n²) input edges and Θ(n³) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in O(m·a(G)) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity a(G) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order √m, so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent τ, the resulting standard bound is O(n+m^{2τ/(τ+1)}), roughly O(n+m^{1.407}) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent 4/3 in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is {0,3,6}, consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims O(n²) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.
why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.
status_note: No established almost-linear algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem found through 11 September 2026. The 2024 combinatorial proposal is withdrawn. The stated parent-edge rule in the August 2025 linear proposal has the explicit counterexample described above. The separate September 2026 O(n²) claim does not meet the all-density target and is not treated as an established bound.
progress: 1985: Chiba–Nishizeki give O(m·a(G)) triangle listing, yielding linear time for bounded-arboricity families. | 1997: Alon–Yuster–Zwick combine degree splitting with fast matrix multiplication to improve sparse triangle detection. | 2014: Abboud–Vassilevska Williams formulate the no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and derive conditional dynamic lower bounds. | 2024-03-05: Dumitrescu withdraws the claimed faster combinatorial algorithm because its case analysis is invalid. | 2026-07: Kumabe–Uezato use triangle hardness to exclude almost-linear matching for a restricted two-use backreference class, conditionally. | 2026-09-08: A separate Aegypti revision claims O(n²), which is not an almost-linear guarantee for all graph densities; correctness not adjudicated here.
working_summary: Triangle detection asks whether an undirected graph contains three pairwise adjacent vertices. The proposed randomized algorithm must decide this in almost linear time on every explicitly supplied graph. Only existence is requested, so graphs with many triangles do not impose a large-output obstacle. Sparse special classes offer useful successes without covering arbitrary inputs. The challenge is to avoid examining too many combinations of neighbors while still giving a reliable negative answer when no triangle exists anywhere.

title: Seese’s conjecture for MSO₁ and clique-width
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A foundational conjecture asking whether bounded clique-width is unavoidable whenever an entire graph class has decidable vertex-set monadic logic.
formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO₁ satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
definitions: An MSO₁ sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency E(x,y), membership x∈X in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class C, Sat_MSO₁(C) consists of all finite encoded MSO₁ sentences φ for which some G∈C satisfies φ. Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory Th_MSO₁(C)={φ: every G∈C satisfies φ}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in [k], disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width cw(G) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set cw(∅)=0. The conclusion is ∃k∀G∈C cw(G)≤k, with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO₁ satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
context:
An MSO₁ sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO₁ conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO₁ satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether n∈S if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO₁ with the predicate Even(X), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO₁ sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO₁ formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO₁ decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.
why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO₁ decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.
progress: 1991: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO₁ boundary. | 2007: Courcelle–Oum prove that decidable MSO₁ with parity predicates implies bounded clique-width. | 2020–2025: Dawar–Sankaran develop the antichain/minimal-hereditary-class reduction for the stronger grid-interpretation conjecture; preprint 2020, CSL 2022, journal volume 2025. | 2025: Mählmann characterizes bounded shrub-depth through logical expressiveness and records a stronger MSO-dependence conjecture that would imply Seese’s. | 12–26 July 2026: Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk prove bounded clique-width for hereditary 2-WQO classes; the hypothesis differs from decidability of MSO₁ satisfiability.
working_summary: MSO1 permits quantification over vertices and vertex sets in a graph. Seese's conjecture asks whether decidability of this logic over a graph class forces bounded clique-width. The proposed implication connects an algorithmic property of the class's whole logical theory with a finite construction complexity for its graphs. A proof would identify a strong structural obstruction to decidable graph reasoning. The saved formulation imposes no hereditary assumption and excludes edge-set and counting extensions, so results for narrower classes or stronger logics cannot be substituted for the stated general MSO1 question.

title: Exact directed maximum flow in O((m+n) polylog n) time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central static graph optimization primitive with broad algorithmic consequences. The precise remaining overhead separates the established almost-linear breakthrough from the longstanding nearly linear target; this is a general problem rather than a refinement of one fixed algorithm.
formal: For every fixed integer a≥1, do there exist a constant k≥0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_a that, on every directed graph with n≥2 vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in {0,…,n^a}, outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((m+n)(log(n+2))^k)?
definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer f_e to each arc, with 0≤f_e≤u_e and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length B_a⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed integer B_a large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. A_a, k, B_a and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The m+n convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
context:
Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in m^(1+o(1)) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is O(m polylog n).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, exp(√log n) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.
why: Identify whether exact flow optimization with polynomially bounded capacities admits genuinely polylogarithmic overhead over graph input size.
status_note: Primary-source check through 11 September 2026 found almost-linear bounds, not the fixed-polylogarithmic overhead required here. New preprint proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2022: Exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow achieve almost-linear time for polynomially bounded integral data. | 2026-08-18: Li–Wice state an m^(1+o(1)) maximum-flow algorithm, leaving the polylogarithmic-overhead target unestablished.

title: Cereceda's quadratic recolouring conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.
formal: For every fixed d, does the reconfiguration graph of proper (d+2)-colourings of every n-vertex d-degenerate graph have diameter O_d(n^2), where one step recolours one vertex?
context:
No matching Cereceda or general quadratic degenerate-recolouring question was found.

This short research proposal states the target identified in the September 2026 fundamental-problem search. The references give the source models and related results. A full self-contained formulation and detailed progress review remain to be written.
why: The principal structural diameter conjecture in graph-colouring reconfiguration.
status_note: Retained in the source-based research proposal dated 10 September 2026. No full resolution was found in that search; this is not a completed independent open-status review.
working_summary: A recoloring step changes one vertex's color while keeping the graph properly colored. The saved Cereceda question asks whether every pair of proper (d+2)-colorings of an n-vertex d-degenerate graph can be connected in O_d(n²) steps. Degeneracy ensures that every subgraph contains a vertex of degree at most d, providing a natural elimination structure. The challenge is using that structure without forcing an excessively long cascade of recolorings. A quadratic bound would make the reconfiguration space quantitatively navigable, while the saved proposal still requires a fuller source and progress review before becoming a completed card.

title: The vertex reconstruction conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Tests whether a whole combinatorial structure is determined by all of its one-vertex views, with a direct graph-isomorphism connection.
formal: For every integer n≥3 and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality D(G)=D(H) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
definitions: A finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection f:V(G)→V(H) such that {u,v} is an edge of G if and only if {f(u),f(v)} is an edge of H. Write [G] for its isomorphism class. For v∈V(G), G−v is the induced graph on V(G)∖{v}: remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define D(G) to be the multiset {[G−v]:v∈V(G)}, with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus D(G)=D(H) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on n−1 vertices, the number of vertices v with [G−v]=K equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every n≥3, or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with n≥3 and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.
context:
Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If n≥3, every original edge appears in exactly n−2 members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by n−2. Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.
why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026: Dufresne and coauthors (April 2026) and Heinrich and coauthors (May 2026 revision) still treat the general conjecture as open. O’Shea and Wilkins’s 2024 publisher abstract claims a general proof, but its full text was inaccessible and the argument was not assessed here. This conflicting claim is recorded with uncertain status rather than accepted as a resolution. The checked 2026 interval-graph and structured bipartite incidence-deletion results do not establish the full conjecture.
progress: 2022-01-02: McKay’s version 4 reports exhaustive verification for all graphs on 3 through 13 vertices, including stronger reduced-deck checks in their applicable range. The computations were not rerun here. | 2024: O’Shea and Wilkins publish a claimed general proof. Only the publisher-indexed abstract and highlights were accessible in this review; no correctness conclusion is drawn from the claim. | 2026-04-17: Dufresne and coauthors state the full graph reconstruction conjecture as open and explain its invariant-theoretic formulation. | 2026-05-12: Heinrich and coauthors’ revised preprint proves every interval graph of order at least three reconstructible, with a polynomial-time reconstruction consequence. | 2026-06-08: The revised AI-driven proof-search paper states a restricted bipartite incidence-deletion theorem with additional structural hypotheses. It does not claim the general vertex-deletion theorem.
working_summary: The vertex reconstruction conjecture asks whether every finite simple graph with at least three vertices is determined by all its one-vertex-deleted views. The views forget vertex labels but retain the multiplicity of repeated isomorphism classes. Even the edge count and degree multiset can be recovered, while the full arrangement of edges is the unresolved target in current specialist sources. Finite computational checks and a theorem for interval graphs provide partial results. An earlier general proof claim is recorded without validation, and recent structured bipartite results are kept distinct from this full question.

title: Berge–Fulkerson: six perfect matchings covering each edge twice
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A classical exact decomposition conjecture at the intersection of matching theory and global graph structure.
formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list (M_1,...,M_6) of perfect matchings such that for every edge e∈E(G), |{i∈{1,...,6}:e∈M_i}|=2?
definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. The conclusion requires every edge to occur exactly twice, with no omitted edge and no extra coverage. No algorithmic bound is required.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A single perfect matching chooses one incident edge at each vertex. Six such choices would give six incidences at every vertex; the conjecture asks for those incidences to be distributed evenly across its three edges.

The requirement is stronger than merely covering the edges with some collection of perfect matchings. Both the number six and exact multiplicity two belong to the target, and repeated matchings must be permitted.

The 2026 paper distinguishes the finite conjecture and its weaker matching-cover assertions while studying infinite graphs. A statement about a different cover object, such as a cycle double cover, does not establish this exact perfect-matching decomposition.
why: Ask whether every bridgeless cubic graph has a uniform six-term integral realization of its fractional perfect-matching structure.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 primary preprint explicitly states that the finite conjecture remains open. No subsequent resolution was located; proofs in the cited preprint were not independently checked.
progress: 2026-07-31: Magalhães Júnior and Silva explicitly retain the finite conjecture as open while investigating its infinite analogues and their equivalences.
working_summary: Every bridgeless cubic multigraph is asked to admit six perfect matchings. Each edge must occur in exactly two positions of that six-matching list. The matchings may repeat, and parallel edges remain distinct. The target is an exact integral decomposition rather than an approximate or fractional cover. It captures a longstanding structural question about how perfect matchings fit together globally.

title: Barnette’s Hamiltonicity conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A canonical and longstanding Hamiltonicity boundary with direct links between planar structure, graph traversal and drawing.
formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering v_1,...,v_n of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that {v_i,v_(i+1)} is an edge for every i, with v_(n+1)=v_1. The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Hamiltonicity is a global demand: one cycle must visit every vertex. Barnette’s conjecture proposes that planarity, bipartiteness, cubic degree and vertex connectivity together always guarantee this traversal.

The recent approximation result uses a subhamiltonian ordering whose consecutive pairs need not all be original edges. Its 5n/6 guarantee is substantial progress in a relaxed setting, but the missing adjacencies distinguish it from the requested cycle.

The planar dual connects the conjecture with partitions of Eulerian triangulations into induced forests. The 2026 partition paper makes those links precise while continuing to distinguish the unresolved Hamiltonicity assertion.
why: Determine whether four basic structural conditions force a spanning cycle in every graph satisfying them.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The GD 2025 and February 2026 papers explicitly retain the conjecture; no general resolution was found.
progress: 2025: Bekos, Kaufmann and Pfister improve a relaxed subhamiltonian-cycle guarantee to at least 5n/6 original edges; this is not a Hamiltonian cycle in the original graph. | 2026-02-13: Cambie and coauthors restate Barnette’s conjecture as open and study related planar partition problems.
working_summary: Barnette’s conjecture concerns 3-connected cubic bipartite planar graphs. It predicts that every such graph contains a cycle through all vertices exactly once. Every consecutive pair on the cycle must be an existing graph edge. Relaxed book-embedding results may add missing adjacencies and therefore do not settle the conjecture. The question isolates a classical boundary between local structural restrictions and a global spanning traversal.

title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A longstanding and elementary local expansion principle for general directed graphs, with an independent structural research tradition.
formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |N⁺⁺(v)|≥|N⁺(v)|, where N⁺(v) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and N⁺⁺(v) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?
definitions: An oriented graph is a finite vertex set V and an arc set A⊆V×V with no loops and with at most one of (u,v),(v,u) present for each distinct pair. Arc multiplicities are not allowed. N⁺(v)={u:(v,u)∈A}. N⁺⁺(v)={w∈V∖(N⁺(v)∪{v}): there exists u with (v,u)∈A and (u,w)∈A}. Thus a vertex already in the first neighborhood is not counted in the second, even if it is also reachable by a length-two walk. Cardinalities count vertices rather than paths or arcs. A sink has both sets empty and satisfies the inequality. No lower bound on outdegree, connectivity or planarity is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
The first out-neighborhood measures one-step reach. The second counts genuinely new vertices obtainable in two steps. The conjecture asserts that at least one starting point has no decrease in this particular count.

Excluding opposite arcs matters: a two-vertex directed 2-cycle would have a nonempty first neighborhood and an empty second neighborhood at both vertices. The oriented-graph hypothesis rules out this immediate obstruction.

The July 2026 specialist paper retains the general conjecture while treating a strengthening. A separate May 2026 manuscript claims a full solution. This conflict is recorded explicitly; the card does not certify a proof or dismiss the claim without analysis.
why: Ask whether every oriented graph has a vertex whose new two-step reach is at least its immediate reach.
status_note: Claim conflict recorded on 11 September 2026. Glover’s 30 May 2026 version claims a complete proof, whereas Bai–Li–Park’s 24 July 2026 paper explicitly treats the general conjecture as open. Neither acceptance nor correctness of the full-proof claim was established here; the status is therefore uncertain, not certified open or resolved.
progress: 2026-05-30: Glover’s revised manuscript claims a complete proof. This review has not verified that claim or established community acceptance. | 2026-07-24: Bai, Li and Park still explicitly state the general conjecture as open and prove special cases of a stronger matching property.
working_summary: Seymour’s conjecture concerns oriented graphs with no loops or opposite pair of arcs. It asks for a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance exactly two as at distance one. Second neighbors exclude first neighbors and count vertices rather than paths. The statement is a general local expansion principle without degree or planarity promises. A complete-proof claim conflicts with a later specialist paper still treating the conjecture as open, and that status uncertainty is preserved.

title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Connects extremal graph density with the optimal size of sparse distance-preserving structures; consequences extend across graph theory and algorithms.
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.
answer_criterion: Prove the required graph families exist for every fixed k, or refute the universal claim for at least one fixed k. Proving the k=4 case alone would resolve the first unknown case but not the whole conjecture.
context:
High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.
why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The general conjecture remains unresolved; several individual values of k are settled.
progress: 1993: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size. | 2026: Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.

working_summary: The Erdős girth conjecture seeks graphs with many edges despite the absence of short cycles. For every fixed k, the target is arbitrarily large graphs with order n^(1+1/k) edges and girth greater than 2k. Such graphs would match the classical density upper bound up to a constant depending on k. They also force every stretch-(2k−1) spanner to retain all edges, connecting the extremal construction to sharp sparsification limits. The saved review notes that progress for special parameters or fault-tolerant spanner models does not supply the missing high-girth families in general.

title: The list edge-coloring conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Asks whether arbitrary local restrictions on allowed edge colors impose any additional global cost.
formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with |L(e)|≥χ′(G) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with c(e)∈L(e) for every e? Equivalently, is χ′_ℓ(G)=χ′(G) for every such G?
definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map ∂ assigning to each edge e∈E a two-element subset ∂e⊆V. Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer k≥0 let [k]={1,…,k}, with [0] empty; χ′(G), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map E→[k]. A list assignment is a function e↦L(e) where each L(e) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index χ′_ℓ(G) is the least k≥0 such that every assignment with |L(e)|≥k admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree Δ counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.
context:
Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so χ′_ℓ(G) is always at least χ′(G). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every ε>0, all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy χ′_ℓ(G)≤(1+ε)χ′(G). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs K_(p−1) and K_(2p) whenever p is an odd prime; K_r denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are p−2 and 2p−1. These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.
why: The conjecture asks whether local restrictions on available edge colors ever increase the number of choices each edge must receive beyond the optimum with a shared palette. It tests whether ordinary scheduling feasibility is robust to arbitrary per-job availability, across all finite loopless multigraphs.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. Jafari’s 24 August 2026 preprint still leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open and claims results only for two prime-parameter families. No later resolution of the full multigraph conjecture was located. Galvin’s bipartite theorem and Kahn’s asymptotic theorem have narrower conclusions than the target. Recent claims and seminar announcements were not independently proof-audited.
progress: 1995: Galvin proves χ′_ℓ(G)=χ′(G)=Δ(G) for bipartite multigraphs; publisher abstract and Kahn’s discussion checked. | 2000: Kahn, Theorem 1.1, proves asymptotic equality of list and fractional chromatic indices for multigraphs; because the ordinary index lies between them, list and ordinary indices also have ratio tending to one. | 2024-05-21: Molloy’s seminar abstract announces the simple-graph bound Δ+Δ^(2/5) poly(log Δ). This still allows an additive gap; only the abstract was checked. | 2026-08-24: Jafari’s version 1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, claims the conjectured exact values for K_(p−1) and K_(2p), p an odd prime. These partial claims do not cover all complete graphs or all multigraphs.
working_summary: A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to edges that share an endpoint. In list edge coloring, each edge must choose its color from its own finite set of allowed colors. The conjecture asks whether giving every edge as many choices as the ordinary chromatic index always suffices, even with arbitrary list overlaps and parallel edges. It holds for bipartite multigraphs, and a general asymptotic theorem leaves only a vanishing relative gap. Exact equality for every finite loopless multigraph would show that local availability restrictions never impose an additional per-edge palette requirement.

title: Tuza’s triangle packing–covering conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A fundamental integral packing-versus-covering problem tied to two canonical graph optimization tasks.
formal: For every finite simple undirected graph G, is τ_△(G)≤2ν_△(G), where τ_△(G) is the minimum size of an edge set meeting every triangle and ν_△(G) is the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles?
definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices together with all three edges between them. An edge set F meets every triangle if each triangle contains at least one edge of F; equivalently, deleting F makes G triangle-free. Define τ_△ as the minimum cardinality of such F⊆E(G). A packing is a family of triangles whose three-edge sets are pairwise disjoint; triangles in a packing may share vertices. Define ν_△ as the maximum cardinality of a packing. Both values are zero when G has no triangles, including the empty graph. The inequality concerns integral edge sets and integral packings, with no fractional weights and no running-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A triangle packing exhibits many separate obstructions to triangle-freeness. An edge cover removes all such obstructions. Every cover must meet each member of a packing, while taking all edges of a maximal packing gives the elementary factor-three comparison.

Tuza asks whether the covering cost always stays within twice the maximum packing size. Edge-disjointness is essential: the triangles may meet at vertices. The four-vertex complete graph has packing number one and covering number two, so a smaller universal factor is impossible.

Results for dense or bounded-degree graphs and fractional relaxations do not establish the integral inequality for arbitrary graphs. The August 2026 degree-seven manuscript is recorded as a preprint claim rather than an independently verified proof.
why: Establish the proposed sharp factor-two relation between destroying all triangles and packing disjoint triangles.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The 2025 dense-graph paper and 2026 bounded-degree work do not settle the unrestricted conjecture. The new degree-seven result is a preprint claim; its proof was not independently checked.
progress: 2025: The dense-graph paper proves special cases while retaining the unrestricted conjecture. | 2026-08-06: A preprint claims the conjecture for graphs of maximum degree at most seven, a restricted input family.
working_summary: Tuza’s conjecture compares packing triangles with deleting edges to eliminate all triangles. It predicts that the minimum deletion set has size at most twice the maximum edge-disjoint packing. Packed triangles may share vertices, but no edges. The comparison is integral and applies to every finite simple graph. A proof would establish a sharp universal relation between two standard graph optimization objectives.

title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: General Exact Matching is a clean test of removing randomness from algebraic graph algorithms beyond the bipartite setting.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.
answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
context:
Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.
why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 revision of the randomized algorithm and the April 2026 bipartite claim. The revised randomized-algorithm paper explicitly states that deterministic polynomial time remains open. This question allows nonbipartite graphs.
progress: 1987: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms. | 2023: El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open. | 2026-04: Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution. | 2026-08-10: Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using O(n^ω) finite-field operations, where ω denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
working_summary: Exact Matching adds a prescribed red-edge count to the ordinary perfect matching problem. Given red and blue edges, an algorithm must decide whether some perfect matching contains exactly the requested number of red edges. The target is deterministic polynomial time on general graphs. Knowing the smallest and largest achievable counts is insufficient because intermediate counts can be absent. The problem isolates how to enforce an exact combinatorial constraint while avoiding the random algebraic choices used by existing approaches.

title: Neumann–Lara’s planar two-color conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A central directed planar-coloring conjecture linking planarity and decomposition into acyclic subgraphs.
formal: For every finite oriented graph D whose underlying undirected graph is planar, is there a coloring c:V(D)→{0,1} such that neither color class induces a directed cycle?
definitions: An oriented graph has no loops or parallel arcs and contains at most one of (u,v) and (v,u) for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. Its underlying simple undirected graph joins u,v exactly when one of these arcs is present. Planarity means that graph admits a drawing in the plane with edges intersecting only at common endpoints. For a vertex set X, the induced subdigraph D[X] retains every arc of D whose two endpoints lie in X. A directed cycle is a cyclic sequence of distinct vertices with all successive arcs oriented forward. A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed cycle. Color classes may be empty. This is not proper coloring: an arc may have endpoints of the same color provided no monochromatic directed cycle results. The assertion asks only for existence, without an algorithmic running-time bound.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Acyclic vertex coloring permits edges within each class but forbids a cyclic chain of directed dependencies. It is therefore different from ordinary proper coloring of the underlying planar graph.

Li and Mohar settle the case without directed triangles. The unrestricted target includes directed triangles and asks whether the entire graph can still be split into only two acyclic induced parts.

The 2026 partition paper connects this conjecture to planar Hamiltonicity and induced-forest questions. Its formulation on planar triangulations has the same general coloring target, because additional oriented edges can only impose more restrictions and every oriented planar graph extends to an oriented planar triangulation after harmless small cases.
why: Determine whether two acyclic classes always suffice to organize the vertices of an oriented planar graph.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The February 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the general conjecture. The related 2026 list-coloring result for the Erdős–Neumann–Lara conjecture concerns a different assertion.
progress: 2016: Li and Mohar prove two-colorability when the planar digraph has digirth at least four. | 2026-02-13: Cambie and coauthors explicitly state the general Neumann–Lara conjecture as open in Conjecture 3.
working_summary: The conjecture asks whether every oriented planar graph has a two-coloring with no monochromatic directed cycle. Arcs within a color class are allowed, so the coloring need not be proper. Loops and opposite pairs of arcs are excluded. The case without directed triangles is known, but directed triangles are allowed in the general target. The question is a directed analogue of central planar graph-decomposition principles.

title: Is graph canonization polynomial-time reducible to graph isomorphism?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Distinguishes recognizing structural equivalence from efficiently choosing a unique representative of each equivalence class.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a constant c≥1 such that A, given any finite simple undirected graph G, computes a canonical form F(G) in at most O((N+1)^c) steps using the graph-isomorphism decision oracle, where N is the input encoding length and F satisfies the conventions below?
definitions: A graph G on n≥0 vertices is given by n and the symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix on {1,…,n}. Two such graphs G,H are isomorphic, written G≅H, if a bijection between their vertex sets preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency. The oracle takes two graphs in this encoding and returns YES exactly when they are isomorphic. Each oracle answer costs one step; writing the query and all other computation count toward the polynomial bound, so query lengths and number of calls are polynomial in N. Adaptive queries are allowed. The output F(G) is an adjacency matrix of a graph on {1,…,n}, with F(G)≅G. For every pair of input graphs, G≅H must imply F(G)=F(H) as labeled matrices; the reverse implication then follows automatically. Thus one algorithm chooses a single representative for every isomorphism class. No particular representative, lexicographic minimum or vertex permutation is prescribed. The same deterministic machine and polynomial bound apply to all graphs; it has no other oracle or nonuniform advice. The empty graph has the empty matrix as its canonical form.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives such an oracle algorithm and proves its worst-case polynomial running time, isomorphism preservation and identical outputs on every isomorphic pair. A negative answer rules out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with this decision oracle that computes any canonical-form function satisfying these conditions. A reduction that only finds an isomorphism between two supplied graphs does not suffice.
context:
Isomorphism asks whether two presentations describe the same graph after renaming vertices. Canonization takes just one presentation and returns a fixed presentation of that graph’s shape. For example, every relabeling of a three-vertex path must produce exactly the same three-by-three output matrix. It is insufficient to return a different isomorphic matrix depending on the input names. This consistency makes canonical forms useful for indexing and comparing stored structures.

The oracle can compare any two explicitly constructed graphs, but returns only YES or NO. The question grants this ability at unit cost and asks whether polynomially much additional work can select consistent representatives. Finding a vertex matching for one given isomorphic pair has a different output requirement: its choices need not agree across every possible presentation of the same graph.

Babai’s 2019 result gives general graph canonization in quasipolynomial time, meaning exp(O((log n)^d)) for a fixed constant d. It adapts the structure of an isomorphism algorithm and includes additional work to make choices canonical. Having quasipolynomial algorithms for both tasks does not establish a polynomial-time reduction that uses only decision answers.

The ICALP 2026 paper obtains efficient canonical labelling for random regular graphs with high probability and recalls general quasipolynomial bounds. A guarantee for almost all graphs in a random model leaves exceptional and arbitrary input graphs uncovered. The present target is a deterministic worst-case reduction for every finite graph, and remains separate from the unrestricted question whether graph isomorphism itself lies in polynomial time.
why: Distinguishes recognizing structural equivalence from efficiently choosing a unique representative of each equivalence class.
status_note: The reverse relation is open in the checked 2019 primary discussion. The reviewed ICALP 2026 result concerns random regular graphs and does not settle the general reduction. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution; this is not an independent audit of all later work.
progress: 2019: Babai gives a quasipolynomial canonical-form algorithm; the introduction leaves the general converse from efficient isomorphism testing unknown. | 2026: ICALP work gives canonical labelling guarantees for random regular graphs, without a general polynomial reduction to the decision oracle.
working_summary: Graph isomorphism recognizes when two labeled graphs have the same structure. Canonization assigns every presentation of that structure an identical representative. The question asks whether a polynomial-time algorithm can compute such representatives using only a graph-isomorphism decision oracle. General quasipolynomial canonization and efficient results for random graph families do not supply this reduction. A solution must handle every finite graph and keep its choices consistent across all relabelings.

title: Can subcubic subgraphs preserve treewidth within a constant factor?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A structural sparsification principle for a central graph parameter; the gap concerns universal preservation rather than a particular construction.
formal: Does there exist a real constant C≥1 such that every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G contains a nonempty subgraph H with maximum degree at most 3 and tw(H)≥tw(G)/C?
definitions: A subgraph H=(V_H,E_H) satisfies V_H⊆V(G) and E_H⊆E(G)∩{{u,v}:u,v∈V_H,u≠v}. Edges and vertices may be deleted, but no edge is contracted and no new vertex or edge is introduced. H need not be induced, connected or spanning. Its maximum degree is max_(v∈V_H)|{u:{u,v}∈E_H}|. A tree decomposition of a nonempty graph F consists of a finite tree T with vertex bags B_t⊆V(F), such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of each edge lie in a common bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a fixed vertex induce a nonempty connected subtree. Its width is max_t|B_t|−1. Treewidth tw(F) is the minimum width over all such decompositions; nonempty edgeless graphs have treewidth zero. C is independent of G and its treewidth. No bound on the number of vertices of H and no construction-time requirement is imposed.

A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
Treewidth measures how far a graph is from having a tree-like organization. This question asks whether its full scale can always be retained after reducing every vertex degree to at most three.

The known degree-three sparsifier guarantee loses a polylogarithmic factor in treewidth. A universal constant would give a stronger structural witness regardless of the original graph’s density or degree distribution.

The target does not ask for an induced subgraph, a small number of vertices, or a grid minor. These additional output restrictions define different problems; arbitrary subcubic graphs need not have grid structure.
why: Determine whether large treewidth always has a bounded-degree witness with only constant loss.

title: The edge reconstruction conjecture
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A longstanding reconstruction principle that tests how much global graph structure survives individual edge losses.
formal: For every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H with at least four edges, does equality of their edge decks D_E(G)=D_E(H) imply G≅H?
definitions: A finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and parallel edges are excluded. Isolated vertices and disconnected graphs are allowed. For e∈E, let G−e=(V,E∖{e}): deleting an edge retains every vertex, including vertices that become isolated. Two graphs are isomorphic, written G≅H, if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. Write [G−e] for the isomorphism class with vertex labels forgotten. The edge deck is the multiset D_E(G)={[G−e]:e∈E}; each edge contributes one entry, so repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. Deck equality requires each isomorphism class to occur equally often. Entries have no common vertex labeling and do not identify the deleted edge. The question concerns uniqueness from a deck known to arise from a graph, with no efficiency requirement on reconstruction.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all finite simple graphs with at least four edges, or give two nonisomorphic such graphs and prove that their complete edge decks agree with multiplicities. A result for a bounded number of vertices, a promised graph class or decks pooled from multiple graphs does not settle the universal claim.
context:
Think of making one copy of a network for each connection and deleting a different connection from each copy. The copies are shuffled and their vertex names erased. The conjecture says their shapes and repetition counts still identify the original network. For a four-cycle, the deck consists of four copies of the path on four vertices.

The threshold excludes a real ambiguity. A triangle together with one isolated vertex and the three-leaf star are nonisomorphic four-vertex graphs with three edges. Deleting any edge from either leaves a three-vertex path together with an isolated vertex. Their edge decks therefore agree, each containing three copies of the same graph.

An edge-deleted graph has the original number of vertices. A vertex-deleted graph loses a vertex and all edges incident to it. The imported McKay reference primarily studies the latter and its set-deck variant. Calle and Gould give the precise edge-deck formulation used here; retaining multiplicities and isolated vertices is part of that model.

The 2025 K-theory paper reformulates the ordinary conjecture and disproves a stronger statement about recovering several graphs from their pooled decks; it explicitly does not settle the single-graph conjecture. A September 2026 preprint instead studies how few selected entries suffice when the original graph is promised to be maximal planar. Such additional information changes the reconstruction task.
why: A longstanding reconstruction principle that tests how much global graph structure survives individual edge losses.
status_note: The checked 2025 paper explicitly leaves the ordinary edge reconstruction conjecture open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established general resolution; the recent maximal-planar result has a graph-class promise. McKay’s original linked paper is primarily about vertex reconstruction.
progress: 1964: Harary poses the edge reconstruction conjecture, as recounted by Calle and Gould. | 2025: An algebraic reformulation preserves the open ordinary conjecture while a pooled-deck generalization is disproved. | 2026-09: A preprint addresses selected-card reconstruction within the known class of maximal planar graphs.
working_summary: Delete each edge of a graph in turn, erase vertex labels and collect the resulting graphs with repetitions. The edge reconstruction conjecture asks whether this multiset determines every finite simple graph with at least four edges. All vertices survive deletion, and repeated copies of the same graph remain significant. A triangle plus an isolated vertex and a three-leaf star show why a three-edge version fails. Recent algebraic reformulations and results for promised graph classes leave the general uniqueness question open.

title: Is Boolean dimension bounded for posets with planar cover graphs?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A general sparse-structure question linking order representations and reachability information, rather than a finite-family extremal refinement.
formal: Does there exist an integer d≥1 such that every finite poset P=(V,<) with a planar undirected cover graph admits strict total orders L_1,...,L_d on V and a Boolean function φ:{0,1}^d→{0,1} satisfying, for all distinct x,y∈V, x<y if and only if φ(1[x<_(L_1)y],...,1[x<_(L_d)y])=1?
definitions: A finite poset is specified by an irreflexive transitive relation < on a finite set V. The undirected cover graph has vertex set V and an edge {x,y} when x<y with no z satisfying x<z<y, or the reverse relation. Planarity means that this undirected graph has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect; an upward planar drawing of the order is not required. A strict total order compares every distinct pair in exactly one direction and is transitive. The orders L_i need not extend the partial order. Each indicator 1[x<_(L_i)y] is a bit. Both the d orders and φ may depend on P, but the bound d is universal and independent of |V| and the height of P. The least possible number of orders is Boolean dimension. The claim is purely existential, with no algorithmic requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
context:
A family of total orders supplies a short comparison signature for each ordered pair. Boolean dimension asks whether a single Boolean rule can reconstruct the partial-order relation from that signature. The orders are auxiliary encodings and need not respect every comparability.

Blake, Micek and Trotter connect this representation with reachability labeling and prove a constant bound under an additional unique-minimum assumption. That hypothesis is absent from the general question.

The underlying cover graph, rather than an upward planar drawing of the poset, is the specified planar object. Replacing one condition with the other would change the family of inputs.
why: Determine whether planar cover structure permits a constant-size comparison description of an arbitrary partial order.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The unique-minimum theorem and related clique-width results do not resolve arbitrary planar cover graphs; no general resolution was found.
progress: 2022: Blake, Micek and Trotter prove Boolean dimension at most 13 when the planar-cover-graph poset has a unique minimum. | 2026: The clique-width/dimension paper supplies related boundedness results but does not establish the target for all planar cover graphs.
working_summary: The cover graph records immediate comparabilities of a finite partial order. The question asks whether its planarity guarantees a constant number of total orders encoding every comparability. One Boolean rule interprets the pairwise comparison bits from those orders. The orders and rule may vary with the poset, but their number must have a universal bound. The target links sparse graph structure to concise representations of reachability.
