title: Is minimum-color cycle solvable in polynomial time under ETH?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A concise and distinctive optimization problem separating explicit color costs from the broader submodular-oracle setting.
formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) specified below, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,c≥1 such that, for every explicitly edge-colored finite simple undirected graph G, A finds a simple cycle using the fewest distinct colors, or correctly reports that G is acyclic, within C(L+1)^c bit operations, where L is the total input length?
definitions: The graph has vertices 1,...,n, with n≥1. Its explicit encoding lists n and m=|E(G)| in binary, followed by the m distinct unordered endpoint pairs and a color κ(e)∈{1,...,max(1,m)} for every edge, all in binary with delimiters. The coloring need not be proper. A simple cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v_1,...,v_t, with t≥3, whose consecutive pairs and {v_t,v_1} are edges. Its cost is the cardinality of {κ(e):e lies on the cycle}. The output is such a vertex sequence attaining the minimum cost, or an acyclic marker if no cycle exists. L includes every endpoint and color label, rather than an oracle for an arbitrary set function. Here ETH asserts that there is ε>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas with N variables in time 2^(εN) times a polynomial in their binary encoding length. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with at most three Boolean literals. This hypothesis is part of the mathematical setting of the target.
answer_criterion: Working under the stated ETH hypothesis, prove that the required polynomial-time algorithm exists or prove that none exists. An unconditional algorithm with correctness and polynomial bit-cost proof answers positively. A proof that any such algorithm would contradict ETH answers negatively. An obstruction relying only on a stronger unlisted hardness conjecture does not settle this target. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full conditional statement.
context:
Cycle length counts edges, while this cost counts distinct labels. A cycle can repeat the same color on many edges without increasing its cost, so the objective differs from ordinary shortest-cycle problems.

The number of colors in an edge set is a monotone submodular cost. The general submodular-cycle algorithm gives a quasipolynomial upper bound for this explicitly represented problem. Query lower bounds against arbitrary value oracles do not imply a time lower bound for these color labels.

The source explicitly permits an ETH-based negative answer. Accordingly ETH is stated as a standing hypothesis, fixing which conditional obstruction counts. The computational goal remains exact polynomial-time optimization on every explicit graph.
why: Locate the polynomial-time boundary for a simple explicit graph optimization problem with a quasipolynomial general algorithm.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The author’s same-day list still asks the question; no polynomial algorithm or ETH-based exclusion was located. The standing ETH convention makes conditional acceptance explicit.
progress: 2023: Fomin and coauthors give a quasipolynomial algorithm for cycles with monotone submodular costs, including the number of distinct colors. | 2026-09-11: Korhonen continues to ask for a polynomial algorithm or a complexity-theoretic obstruction for explicitly colored graphs.
working_summary: Each edge of an undirected graph carries a color label. The objective is to find a simple cycle using as few different colors as possible. A general quasipolynomial algorithm is known, but a polynomial bound remains unresolved. The card fixes ETH as the standing hypothesis so that an ETH-based obstruction is a precise negative answer. Explicit color input distinguishes this target from lower bounds for arbitrary submodular value oracles.

title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: Exact Matching is a central derandomization test even on bipartite graphs. Its importance remains high while the recent claimed solution is assessed.
formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.
answer_criterion: Establish a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for every bipartite instance, or prove that none exists. The April 2026 claimed algorithm would establish the positive answer if its proof is valid; this catalogue has not independently verified it.
context:
An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.
why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.

Even a small complete bipartite graph can have attainable red counts separated by gaps. This makes the equality constraint stronger than minimizing or maximizing the count. title: Is 3-colorability polynomial-time decidable on diameter-two graphs?
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map c:V(G)→{1,2,3} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv?
definitions: The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.
answer_criterion: Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under P≠NP. A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.
context:
The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.

Bounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.

A tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

The best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to O(n^(1/3) log² n). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.
why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.
status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 version of Murakami’s primary paper. Checked through 10 September 2026; no later general resolution located. Recent algorithms with an additional four-cycle exclusion do not settle this card.
progress: 2013 conference / 2016 journal: Mertzios and Spirakis obtain a 2^{O(sqrt(n log n))} algorithm for diameter two and NP-completeness for diameter three, including triangle-free inputs. | 2019: Paulusma records the diameter-two three-color question as the exceptional unresolved (number of colors, diameter) pair. | 2021 preprint / 2022 journal: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski improve the diameter-two upper bound to $2^{O(n^{1/3} \log^2 n)}$. Their abstract states that polynomial-time solvability remains open. | 2026-07: Murakami proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring for graphs of diameter two with no four-cycle as a subgraph. Sections 1 and 7 leave unrestricted diameter-two 3-colorability open.
working_summary: Three-colorability asks whether vertices can receive three colors with adjacent vertices always different. Here every pair of vertices is promised to have distance at most two. The question is whether this strong proximity condition permits deterministic polynomial-time recognition of three-colorable graphs. Adding a universal vertex cannot directly transfer general three-color hardness because it consumes an additional color. The problem therefore probes a precise structural boundary where very short graph distances may or may not simplify coloring.

title: Polylogarithmic treewidth with forbidden induced minors
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A structural tractability threshold for Hamiltonicity or treewidth would support algorithms for entire graph families.
formal: For every integer t≥2, does there exist an integer c_t≥1 such that every n-vertex graph G with n≥2, no clique of size t and neither Kt,t nor Wt as an induced minor satisfies tw(G)≤c_t(log₂ n)^(c_t)?
definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Write n=|V(G)| and take logarithms in base two. An induced subgraph G[S] retains precisely all edges of G whose endpoints are in S. Kt is the complete graph on t vertices; Kt,t is the complete bipartite graph with two independent sets of t vertices and every edge between the sets. A tree decomposition consists of a finite tree T and bags Bx⊆V(G), one per node x of T, such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every edge occur together in some bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is maxx |Bx|−1. Treewidth tw(G) is the minimum width of such a decomposition. For a concrete wall convention, construct Wt from vertices (i,j), 0≤i≤t and 0≤j≤2t+1: include all horizontal edges (i,j)(i,j+1), and vertical edges (i,j)(i+1,j) exactly when i+j is even, then repeatedly delete vertices of degree at most one until none remain. This is a fixed elementary hexagonal-wall family. Standard wall-size conventions differ by a fixed reindexing; since the source statement quantifies over every fixed t and allows its constants to depend arbitrarily on t, this indexing does not change the family-level claim. An induced minor is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges, with loops discarded and parallel edges merged, but without arbitrary edge deletions. Equivalently, its vertices can be represented by pairwise disjoint nonempty connected branch sets in G, with an edge between two branch sets exactly when their corresponding vertices are adjacent in the induced minor. The clique exclusion is an ordinary clique/induced-subgraph condition; the exclusions of Kt,t and Wt are induced-minor conditions. There is no bound on maximum degree. The constant c_t and the exponent c_t may depend on t, but not on n or G. Allowing separate constants for the multiplier and exponent is equivalent by increasing c_t, since log₂ n≥1. The statement is structural existence of tree decompositions and requests no algorithm for finding them. Restricting to t,n≥2 removes only trivial small or undefined-log cases.

The saved note leaves the threshold as target-dependent and concerns existence, so an efficient algorithm to find the tree would be an additional requirement rather than part of the stated structural question.

title: A minor-monotone parameter characterizing integral Erdős–Pósa duality
area_label: Structural graph theory and graph algorithms
importance_reason: A general structural characterization of integral minor packing–covering duality. Existing numerical score retained.
formal: Historical conjecture, resolved positively: for every fixed nonempty finite graph H, does there exist a minor-monotone graph parameter p_H taking nonnegative integer values such that, for every minor-closed graph class C, H-minor models have the integral Erdős–Pósa property on C if and only if sup_{G∈C}p_H(G)<∞? The same parameter p_H must work for all choices of C.
definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A minor is obtained by deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, with loops removed and parallel edges suppressed. An H-minor model in G consists of pairwise disjoint connected vertex sets B_v for v∈V(H), with an edge between B_u and B_v for each uv∈E(H); its support is their union. Let pack_H(G) be the largest number of models with mutually disjoint supports, and let τ_H(G) be the minimum number of vertices whose deletion leaves no H minor. The integral Erdős–Pósa property on C means that a function f:N_0→N_0 exists such that τ_H(G)≤f(pack_H(G)) for every G∈C. This one f may depend on H and C, but not on the individual graph. A class is minor-closed if it contains every minor of each of its graphs. A graph parameter is invariant under graph isomorphism and is minor-monotone when G′ a minor of G implies p_H(G′)≤p_H(G). Boundedness on C means one finite bound for all graphs in C. H need not be connected. No efficient evaluation algorithm or uniquely prescribed parameter is part of the conjecture.
answer_criterion: The affirmative answer follows from the published finite obstruction-sequence characterization: for the target class of H-minor-free graphs, take p_H(G) to be the largest order of an obstruction in its fixed finite collection of increasing minor sequences that occurs as a minor of G, using 0 when none occurs. Minor monotonicity and the theorem’s excluded-sequence criterion give exactly the required equivalence.
context:
Packing asks for many vertex-disjoint occurrences of H as a minor. Covering asks for a small common vertex set meeting every such occurrence. An Erdős–Pósa function says that bounded packing forces bounded covering throughout a whole graph class.

Choosing a separate arbitrary parameter after seeing C would weaken the conjecture. Here H alone determines p_H, and boundedness of that one parameter recognizes every minor-closed class where the duality holds.

Paul, Protopapas, Thilikos and Wiederrecht give a finite collection of obstruction sequences for every proper minor-closed target class. A minor-closed environment has integral packing–covering duality precisely when it excludes some member of every sequence. Applying this to H-minor-free target graphs yields the conjectured parameter.

Half-integral packing allows each vertex to belong to two chosen models. The source paper’s half-integral results alone do not settle this card. The later theorem characterizes the integral duality required here. For planar H, the classical integral theorem already holds on all graphs, so the constant parameter p_H=0 suffices.
why: Provides a uniform structural explanation for which minor-closed graph classes support integral packing–covering duality for a fixed graph pattern.
status_note: Resolved as a consequence of Paul–Protopapas–Thilikos–Wiederrecht, Obstructions to Erdős–Pósa Dualities for Minors, FOCS 2024, Theorem 1.1 in the full version. Checked the original conjecture, integral EP-pair definition, finite obstruction-sequence characterization and its application to H-minor-free graphs, including disconnected H. This is a published-theorem/model match, not an independent proof audit or proof-assistant certificate.
progress: 2024: The ICALP paper states the minor-monotone parameter characterization as Conjecture 1. | 2024-07-16: The full obstruction-sequence theorem in arXiv:2407.09671v2 yields the required parameter when the target class consists of H-minor-free graphs. | 2024: The result is published at FOCS 2024, pp. 31–52.
working_summary: An Erdős–Pósa property turns a bound on disjoint graph-pattern occurrences into a bound on the vertices needed to hit every occurrence. The conjecture asked for one minor-monotone parameter for each pattern H that recognizes exactly the minor-closed classes with this property. The parameter must work uniformly across all such classes. The same authors’ later FOCS 2024 obstruction theorem gives the required characterization. This settles the integral question, beyond the earlier half-integral result.

title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
importance_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
focus_reason: Dynamic optimality is a central benchmark for adaptive data structures: one simple online BST would compete with every offline BST on every access sequence.
formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
definitions: Keys are [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence X∈[n]*, cost_splay(X;T₀) is the sum of these costs starting from T₀. A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. OPT(X) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds cost_splay(X;T₀)/(OPT(X)+n) for all n, all initial trees T₀ and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost Θ(n), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by O((OPT(X)+n) log log n · log² log log n). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.
why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
status_note: The July 2026 primary preprint gives a growing competitive factor and still distinguishes its theorem from constant dynamic optimality. The primary text and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026; no complete resolution was found in that check. This review does not independently verify the new proof.
progress: 1985 / background: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree. | 2007: Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying. | 2026-07-20: The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.
working_summary: Splay trees reorganize a binary search tree after each access using local rotations. The question asks whether this simple rule is always within a constant factor of the best tree strategy that knows the entire request sequence. An additive linear allowance pays for the initial tree. Frequency and locality guarantees cover useful patterns but do not establish this universal comparison. Understanding this gap would show whether local adaptation can exploit every advantage available to an offline search tree.

title: An explicit static problem requiring superlogarithmically many cell probes
importance_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
focus_reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.
why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.
status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.
progress: 2018: Larsen–Weinstein–Yu cross the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean data structures; the journal version appeared in 2020. This does not settle the static question. | 2025-05-28: Revision 1 of Korten–Pitassi–Impagliazzo improves cell-probe space/time tradeoffs using local PRGs and studies conditional barriers. | 2025-10-22: Ko proves stronger bit-cell bounds for random linear operators, including regimes with superpolynomially many queries. | 2026-03-26: Ko’s preprint claims a nearly log-squared lower bound for dynamic Boolean multiphase problems. No independent proof audit of that claim is supplied here. | 2026-06: Koucký–Loff–Molli–Saks appears at STOC 2026, with conditional natural-proofs barriers and an explicit statement of the static challenge.
working_summary: A static data structure preprocesses a database and later answers queries by reading stored memory cells. This question seeks an explicitly computable Boolean query problem forcing more than logarithmically many reads despite unrestricted preprocessing. The saved formulation fixes short queries, logarithmic word size, near-linear space, and deterministic adaptive access. Free computation between reads makes this an information-access lower bound. Such an example would expose a fundamental limit on making useful information locally accessible through clever storage alone.

title: Can a static dictionary be built deterministically in linear time?
importance_reason: A foundational derandomization question for exact lookup: linear construction, linear storage and constant worst-case queries would give many algorithms an optimal deterministic dictionary primitive. The 2024 and 2026 string-indexing applications show concrete dependencies on dictionary construction costs.
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer d≥1 there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs A_d,Q_d and a constant C_d≥1 such that, for every n≥2, every word length ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉≤w≤d⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, A_d builds a static dictionary in at most C_d n operations and C_d n words of total space, and Q_d answers every membership-and-value query in at most C_d operations.
definitions: The universe is U_w={0,…,2ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs (x_i,v_i)∈U_w×U_w with pairwise distinct x_i and arbitrary v_i; the input order is unrestricted. On query q∈U_w the output is (1,v_i) if q=x_i and (0,0) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved w=Θ(log n) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records (12,5), (47,9) and (103,2) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of n² possible keys occupies n² cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic O(n log n) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general O(m(log log m)²) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to Θ(log m). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.
status_note: The primary dictionary results, later applications and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No complete resolution of the specified logarithmic-word deterministic construction target was found. The accessible 2025 draft Slightly more practical deterministic static dictionaries was also inspected; it contains unfinished statements and does not claim the required linear construction, so it is not used to certify a new bound.
progress: 1999-12: Pagh gives deterministic O(n log n) construction with linear space and constant lookup for w=O(log n); the paper contrasts this with randomized expected linear construction. | 2008: Ružić brings deterministic construction within a log log n factor of sorting time while retaining linear space and constant lookup. | 2024-10-14: The internal-pattern-matching journal paper uses general deterministic dictionaries with O(m(log log m)²) construction and distinguishes restricted small instances. | 2026: Kosolobov’s CPM paper records a construction slowdown when replacing randomized dictionaries in a compressed index. This is an application, not a solution of the present static target.
working_summary: A static dictionary stores distinct integer keys together with associated values and supports exact membership queries. The question asks for deterministic linear-time construction, linear space, and constant worst-case query time on the stated word RAM. All preprocessing work must be included in the construction bound. Random hashing motivates the desired efficiency but does not itself provide a deterministic construction. A solution would give other algorithms a dependable dictionary primitive without making their preprocessing randomized or increasing their asymptotic running time.

title: Data Structure Lower Bound in the Cell Probe Model
importance_reason: Stronger cell-probe lower bounds would advance a general technique for proving data-access limitations.
formal: Data Structure Lower Bound in the Cell Probe Model
context: Computation with limited memory or compressed summaries. Passes, adaptivity, and update models affect the attainable bounds.
why: The significance of this particular question has not yet been individually assessed. The question concerns the cost of a limited computational or informational resource. A sharp bound would separate a limitation of current algorithms from a limitation every algorithm in the model must face.
status_note: Imported from the previous catalogue. Current open status has not been established by a new review.
working_summary: A data structure preprocesses an n-by-n Boolean matrix and then answers matrix-vector products over AND and OR. The cell-probe model counts memory accesses while allowing free computation on the information read. The source asks for a superlinear-in-n query lower bound when the representation stores the matrix with only a small amount of extra space. Existing upper bounds show that this succinct model can outperform straightforward word-RAM expectations. A lower bound must therefore identify information that genuinely has to be fetched, rather than charge for the arithmetic or logical work of computing the answer.

title: Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?
importance_reason: A longstanding concrete stress test for splay-tree adaptivity, already on the elementary deque interface; less sweeping than dynamic optimality.
formal: Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.
definitions: Splaying uses the standard zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rules. Deletions are allowed only on a nonempty tree, and an inserted key must be outside the current key range at the specified end. Amortized cost is a bound on the total sequence, not a worst-case guarantee for each deletion. The initial tree may have any shape.
answer_criterion: Prove a universal O(n+m) total bound for the specified splay implementation, or prove that the ratio between total cost and n+m is unbounded over legal initial trees and operation sequences.
context:
A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.

Deleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. That does not disprove the conjecture, because the initial tree contributes an additive budget proportional to its size. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.

For a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern. A deque workload can switch ends after every operation and introduce new extreme keys between deletions. A bound for one monotone scan therefore does not immediately control this more flexible sequence.

The known total bound has an iterated inverse-Ackermann factor, which grows extraordinarily slowly but is asymptotically unbounded. Removing it would answer a structural question about how rotations reuse earlier work. This is a focused subproblem of the broader study of splaying, with updates included explicitly rather than only searches.
why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.

title: Do pure pairing heaps support O(log log n) amortized decrease-key?
importance_reason: Tests optimality of one particularly simple self-adjusting heap against an established model barrier; a focused algorithm-analysis question.
formal: For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\log N)+K(1+\log\log(N+2))]$? Here D counts delete-min operations, K counts decrease-key operations, and $N\ge2$ is the maximum of 2 and the total number of live items across all heaps at any moment. The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.
definitions: A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.
answer_criterion: Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.
context:
A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.

The pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant. The desired estimate asks whether this sparse restructuring still prevents expensive configurations from being recreated too often.

The operation budgets must be considered together. A sorting sequence already forces substantial comparison work when many minima are deleted, so the logarithmic delete-min allowance is intentional. The unresolved issue is how much additional work to attribute to key decreases while keeping insertions and melds cheap. Using the maximum live population N makes that accounting explicit for a whole finite sequence.

Other self-adjusting heaps already attain the desired decrease-key order. This makes the remaining gap an informative algorithm-analysis problem: is the simpler rule equally efficient, or does its exact restructuring lose something asymptotically? A bound for slim or smooth heaps does not answer this question about pure pairing heaps.
why: This is a precise opportunity to separate an analysis gap from a structural limitation of a simple data structure. Priority-queue costs propagate into graph algorithms, and the problem tests how little explicit balancing information is sufficient for optimal amortized behavior.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July 2026 primary preprint. The displayed bound uses the maximum live population, while the source also develops finer bounds that omit items never deleted. This card fixes one algorithm and one total-cost target.

title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
importance_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
focus_reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.
formal: Does there exist a single deterministic data structure and fixed constants C,c,d>0 such that, for every n≥2, an initially empty undirected simple graph on vertex set [n] can be maintained under any online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, using at most C n^d words of memory and at most C(log₂ n)^c time for each individual operation? Initialization may take at most C n^d time and depends only on n. All connectivity answers must be exact in the word-RAM model specified below.
definitions: An insertion insert(u,v) adds a previously absent unordered edge {u,v}, where u≠v; a deletion delete(u,v) removes an existing edge. A query connected(u,v) returns whether the current graph contains a path from u to v, with connected(u,u)=true. Updates are valid, arrive one at a time and must finish before the next operation is revealed. No future operations or advance description of the sequence is supplied. The data structure must work for every finite sequence, including sequences chosen in response to its previous behavior. The word RAM has word size w=⌈a log₂ n⌉ for a fixed constant a large enough to address its polynomial space. Unit-cost instructions are indirect reads/writes, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient/remainder, comparisons, Boolean bit operations and shifts; arithmetic results stored in one word are reduced modulo 2ʷ where appropriate. Arbitrary-precision computation costs its constituent word operations. All maintenance, rebuilding and query work is charged to the operation performing it. The exponent c is independent of n and of the length or contents of the operation sequence. The graph is unrestricted apart from being undirected and simple; no planarity, bounded-degree or expansion promise is given.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic O(log² n) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve n^{o(1)} worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, exp(√log n) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in m·polylog(m) time, with congestion at most (m/n)·polylog(m), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

A companion SODA 2026 result by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak controls both the time and the number of vertices removed when pruning an expander after one edge deletion. This avoids a large burst of changes propagating through a hierarchy. It is an ingredient in the recent randomized progress; it does not by itself supply the deterministic sparsifier construction needed for the full conclusion.

Known lower bounds do not rule out the target. Pătraşcu and Demaine prove logarithmic amortized cell-probe lower bounds, including for connectivity on disjoint paths. Those results show that dynamic connectivity already has a real information-transfer cost in very simple graphs, but a logarithmic barrier is compatible with polylogarithmic upper bounds. The open issue is whether exact connectivity, deterministic computation and a bound on every operation can be achieved simultaneously.
why: A basic unresolved guarantee for dynamic graph data structures. Connectivity is both a natural maintenance problem and a source of techniques used throughout graph algorithms; combining determinism, exactness and fast individual updates would close a longstanding gap.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The SODA 2026 connectivity paper explicitly retains deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case updates as open. Its unconditional new bound is randomized and expected; its deterministic polylogarithmic conclusion depends on the stated static low-congestion sparsifier construction. Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.

working_summary: Dynamic connectivity maintains whether pairs of vertices remain connected as graph edges are inserted and deleted. The reviewed question asks for deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case time for every operation, with exact answers. Deleting a spanning-forest edge requires quickly finding a replacement across the exposed cut or certifying that none exists. This would combine deterministic reliability with consistently low latency on arbitrary update sequences. The saved review distinguishes amortized guarantees, randomized cutset recovery, and subpolynomial worst-case time from the stronger polylogarithmic bound required here.

title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
importance_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
focus_reason: A central dynamic graph problem connecting approximation, explicit solution maintenance and extremal induced-matching structure.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |M|≥ν(G)/(1+ε) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set [n], n≥2; ν(G) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed ε and constant a≥1, require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm A_{ε,a} such that every sequence of T≤n^a updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most K[n+T(log₂(n+2))^d]. Words have B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least 1−n^{−3}, after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes O(1) time; enumerating all matching edges costs O(n) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on ε and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
importance_reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.
formal: Can an exact minimum spanning forest of a fully dynamic n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights be maintained with polylogarithmic worst-case time per edge update, polynomial preprocessing and space, and high-probability correctness against an oblivious adversary?
definitions: The graph is simple and undirected on the fixed labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, and starts empty. An update inserts one currently absent edge with integer weight in {1,…,n⁴}, or deletes one present edge. Edge weights remain fixed until deletion. A minimum spanning forest consists of one minimum-total-weight spanning tree for each connected component. Break equal-weight ties by the fixed lexicographic order (weight, smaller endpoint, larger endpoint), so the target is the unique forest selected by Kruskal’s algorithm in that order. After each update the data structure must report the edges removed from and added to the maintained forest; on a correct execution at most one edge of each kind changes. These reports specify the entire current forest starting from the empty one. Use a uniform randomized classical word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, standard word operations and random-word generation; all input processing and memory accesses count. For every fixed pair of integers a,b≥1, the target permits a separately tuned uniform data structure and constants K,C≥1 whose preprocessing and space are n^{O(1)}, and for which every update takes at most K(log₂(n+2))^C steps on every execution. For every valid update sequence of length at most n^a fixed before its random choices, all reported forests must be correct simultaneously with probability at least 1−n^{−b}. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on a,b, but not on n or the sequence. This is a Monte Carlo worst-case-time formulation; an always-correct deterministic solution would also suffice. The integer range n⁴ is an explicit specialization, and weights occupy O(1) words. There is no advance access to future updates.
answer_criterion: Construct data structures satisfying the stated bounds for every fixed a,b, or prove the proposition false. Amortized polylogarithmic updates, merely subpolynomial worst-case updates, or maintaining an approximate minimum forest are insufficient. A lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone does not rule out the allowed randomization. A data structure that only stores the graph and postpones finding the forest to an expensive query does not meet the required per-update reporting guarantee.
context:
One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all n−1 tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains O(log⁴ n/log log n) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, exp(√log n) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of n^{o(1)} update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a (1+ε)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to log(U)/ε for weights in [1,U]. The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking ε smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.
why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

The inherited ICALP 2021 link was a mismatched matching citation and is identified as such. Checked through 11 September 2026.
