title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
importance_reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.
formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected polylog(n) amortized update time, worst-case polylog(n) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
definitions: Fix vertices [n], n≥2. Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer λ(G)=min{ |{uv∈E:u∈S,v∉S}| : ∅≠S⊊[n] }. In particular λ(G)=0 for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with Θ(log(n+2))-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant a≥1 as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, U+Q≤n^a, fixed independently of its random bits, it uses O_a(n^b) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is O_a(n^b+U log^c(n+2)); each query takes O_a(log^c(n+2)) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least 1−n^(−3). Initial preprocessing may take O_a(n^b) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of λ(G), n and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.
context:
The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes λ=0 from λ≥1; the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to n−1.

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention λ=0 for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to Õ(m^(11/12)); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of m^(11/12), m^(11/13)n^(1/13), and n^(3/2), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches n^{o(1)} deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to 2^{Θ((log n)^(3/4−η))}, for fixed 0<η<3/4 in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and n^{o(1)} does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a (1+o(1))-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum λ, rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of 1/λ. A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

The reviewed question asks to maintain its exact value under insertions and deletions with expected polylogarithmic amortized updates. title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
importance_reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.
formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
context:
Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.
why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.
status_note: The edge-sensitive target is open in the 2021 source. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate an exact algorithm with the stated sparse update and query bounds. This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.
progress: 2004: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs. | 2021: Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise. | 2024-08-27: Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee. | 2025: Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.
working_summary: Dynamic all-pairs shortest paths must answer exact distances while directed weighted edges change. The reviewed target combines polylogarithmic worst-case queries with amortized update time nearly linear in the edge bound m. It allows polynomial preprocessing and space while requiring deterministic answers. The principal gap is sparse graphs, where updates should cost much less than rebuilding a full distance table. The saved review explains that many distances changing simultaneously is not an impossibility argument, because the oracle may represent those changes implicitly and expose only one queried pair.

title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
importance_reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.
focus_reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.
formal: For every fixed deletion probability δ∈(0,1), is there a constant C_δ≥1 and K_δ≥1 such that every unknown n-bit string can be reconstructed exactly with probability at least 2/3 from at most K_δ n^{C_δ} independent deletion traces, for every n≥2?
definitions: For x∈{0,1}^n, a deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability 1−δ and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let μ_{x,δ} be its probability distribution on ⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k. Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given n, δ and m independent samples from μ_{x,δ}; it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of {0,1}^n, and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and δ must succeed for every x with probability at least 2/3 over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let N_δ(n) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The target is N_δ(n)≤K_δ n^{C_δ} for every n≥2. The constants may depend on δ but not on n or x. The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability (1−δ)^n a trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of Ω(n^{3/2}/log⁷ n) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses exp(Õ(n^{1/5})) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by exp(p^{−7/3}(log₂ n)^c) for an absolute constant c, where p=1−δ. The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since the current card imposes no time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that O(n log n) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly n⁵ is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.
why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?
status_note: The July 2026 quasipolynomial sample theorem supersedes the saved 2025 general upper frontier but does not give polynomially many traces. The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

The question asks whether polynomially many traces suffice for exact worst-case reconstruction at every fixed deletion probability. Survivors lose their original positions, so repeated observations must resolve both symbol values and alignment. A positive answer would close the qualitative gap between polynomial sample requirements and substantially larger general reconstruction methods. The saved review distinguishes information-theoretic sample complexity from reconstruction time and does not treat polynomial lower bounds as evidence against the requested polynomial upper bound.

title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in O(n polylog n) time
importance_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
focus_reason: A central remaining precision–runtime boundary for edit distance, distinct from the established n^{1+ε} constant-factor algorithms and from exact-computation hardness.
formal: Do absolute constants C≥1, K>0 and d≥0 and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤C·ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3 in at most Kn(log₂(n+2))^d time?
definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of n≥1 and two explicitly stored arrays x,y∈{0,…,n²+1}ⁿ. This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in O(log n) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When x=y, success requires D=0. When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as n^{0.9} can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor 2^{Õ(√log n)} in n^{1+o(1)} time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive n^{1−ζ} term in the general guarantee. The exponent ζ and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed ε>0, an O(n^{1+ε})-time randomized algorithm with approximation f(1/ε). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on 1/ε. Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified n^{1+ε} guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed ε=0.01 gives a fixed approximation factor, but n^{0.01} eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing ε as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter η>0, it gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)}n} time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed ε>0 permits a (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0. Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’s O(n polylog n) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.
why: Determines whether a universal constant loss in accuracy makes the basic string-alignment metric computable with only polylogarithmic overhead beyond input reading.

The August 2026 journal publication gives n^{1+ε} time, and the STOC 2026 approximation scheme targets a different runtime–accuracy regime.

The reviewed question asks for a randomized universal constant-factor approximation in near-linear time. The target would estimate global alignment cost without constructing the full quadratic dynamic-programming table. context:
Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a (1+ε)-approximation in n^(2−δ_ε) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in O(n polylog n) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its n^(1+o(1)) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy ε, one algorithm must meet n^(1+η) bounds for every fixed η>0 once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each η, with uncontrolled dependence on η, is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.

importance_reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.
formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), do there exist constants δ_ε∈(0,1), K_ε>0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε such that, for every n≥1 and every pair of length-n strings x,y, A_ε runs in at most K_ε(n+2)^(2−δ_ε) time and outputs an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over {0,…,n²+1}, including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy O(log n) bits. Use a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed ε the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on ε. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, common positive saving for all ε, or efficient procedure generating A_ε is required. Rational ε suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed ε>0 no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in O(n^(2−δ)) time for any fixed δ>0. A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.
context:
Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing ε=0.01 fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired δ_ε must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as n²/logⁱ n, for fixed i, is n^(2−o(1)) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as ε approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized (1+ε)-approximation for each constant ε in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)} n} time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed δ_ε>0. The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed η>0, a constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time. The approximation constant depends on η and is not guaranteed to be 1+ε for an arbitrarily prescribed ε. Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in O(n polylog n) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter ε is fixed before the input length grows; choosing ε below 1/n to force exactness is outside any fixed-ε runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When ED=0 a successful estimate must be zero, and when ED=1 and ε<1 an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.
why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.
status_note: No resolution with a fixed positive exponent saving for every fixed ε was found in the primary-source check through 11 September 2026. The 2026 scheme improves quadratic time by a quasipolynomial factor and does not establish the target O(n^(2−δ_ε)) bound.
progress: 2015: Backurs–Indyk establish a conditional strongly subquadratic barrier for exact edit distance. | 2018-07-20: Rubinstein explicitly asks for (1+ε)-approximation in truly subquadratic time as Open question 2. | 2020–2022: Andoni–Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for each fixed η>0; the approximation constant is not arbitrarily close to one. | 2026-03-31: Mao–Rubinstein give a randomized near-exact approximation scheme with a quasipolynomial improvement over quadratic time, accepted to STOC 2026.
working_summary: Unit-cost edit distance counts the fewest single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform one string into another. The question asks whether every fixed positive ε permits a randomized (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0 on every input pair. Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing that fixed exponent saving. The numerical estimate must have purely multiplicative error even for strings with very small distance, and all preprocessing is included in the runtime. This accuracy target remains separate from TCS-6624, which allows a fixed constant factor but requires O(n polylog n) time.

title: Does the smallest grammar problem admit a constant-factor approximation?
importance_reason: Asks whether a basic measure of reusable string structure can be approximated within a constant, linking compression and approximation complexity.
formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on P != NP should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
context:
A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under P != NP, but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.
why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.
progress: 2005: Charikar and coauthors give an O(1+log(|s|/g*(s))) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below 8569/8568 unless P = NP. | 2020-11 / 2021: Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.
working_summary: A grammar can compress a string by naming repeated pieces and assembling them through acyclic production rules. The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time approximation within a universal constant of the smallest such grammar. The size measure counts all symbols on right-hand sides, including references to other rules. Choosing repeated pieces is difficult because useful substrings can overlap and interact across scales. The saved review separates this constant-factor target from known logarithmic guarantees and emphasizes that alternative grammar-size conventions describe different optimization problems.

definitions: Symbols are integers from {1,…,σ}, encoded in binary; σ and all strings are input. For an empty collection, OPT is zero. The output is an explicit string over the input alphabet, and containment means ordinary forward contiguous occurrence without reversal, reverse complementation or cyclic wraparound. All preprocessing is charged.

title: Can LZ77 random access use linear compressed space and logarithmic query time?
importance_reason: Random access is a basic interface for compressed computation. The linear-space target would remove a persistent overhead for a central repetitiveness measure.
formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to a<b is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use 1+log N at the smallest lengths.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the O(z) requirement.
context:
Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.
why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the July LZ-End result. The stated parse convention, space parameter, and deterministic query guarantee are explicit.
progress: 2019 / 2021: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size. | 2025-05: Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access. | 2026-07: Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic O(z_end)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.
working_summary: An LZ77 parse represents repeated text through references to earlier occurrences, possibly allowing overlap. The reviewed question asks for random character access in logarithmic time using space linear in the number of phrases. The original uncompressed string is unavailable when queries arrive. A solution must navigate arbitrary chains of copied material while keeping every stored shortcut inside the compressed-space budget. The saved record distinguishes ordinary LZ77 from restricted parsing variants and notes that converting to a larger grammar does not automatically preserve the required linear space.

title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
importance_reason: Tests whether a fundamental string task can run at the size of its compressed input, including preprocessing; useful beyond one particular index implementation.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
context:
Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.
why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.
status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 against the original LZ algorithm, the grammar breakthrough, the 2025 seminar question, and later search results. No resolution of this precise LZ-input target was located. The source question is specialized here by making the model and input encoding explicit.
progress: 2011: Gawrychowski gives deterministic O(z(1+log(N/z))+m) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses. | 2021-11: Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain O(g+m) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version. | 2025-05: Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.
working_summary: Compressed pattern matching asks whether an explicit pattern occurs in a text supplied only as LZ77 phrases. The reviewed target is deterministic time linear in the phrase count plus pattern length, with comparable working space. Occurrences can cross phrase boundaries or lie inside copied regions, so isolated phrase inspection is insufficient. Such an algorithm would make search depend on the compressed input rather than the potentially enormous expanded text. The statement includes all preprocessing and allows self-referencing phrases, preventing an uncharged index or an easier parsing convention from weakening the target.

title: Can grammar random access use O(g log g) bits with logarithmic query time?
importance_reason: A basic compressed-space versus access-time frontier at the bit level, relevant to many grammar-based operations. The fixed logarithmic target gives a sharper scope than the broader random-access trade-off landscape.
formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
context:
A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. For example, a short chain of doubling rules can describe an exponentially long string. This difference is why a space bound stated in machine words can hide a substantial overhead relative to the grammar encoding.

To locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.

The April 2026 encoding result improves the grammar representation and keeps logarithmic query time, but retains a g log N expansion-length term. The authors explicitly distinguish their encoding savings from removing that term. Their observation supports treating the latter as a separate question.

ICALP 2026 gives much sharper time-space trade-offs in a broad range of parameters. Its main upper-bound theorem uses a space budget above the g log N scale. Consequently, the optimality statements in that range do not automatically settle the smaller bit budget here. This card fixes logarithmic query time, a binary alphabet, polynomial preprocessing, and explicit workspace rules as a concrete specialization of the seminar’s fewer-auxiliary-bits direction.
why: Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. Resolving this target would determine whether the extra address-length information is an inherent price of efficient access or an artifact of current representations, and would make the distinction between compressed bits and machine words precise.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026 against the April encoding paper and ICALP 2026 trade-offs. This fixes a particular target within the source’s space-reduction question; results using O(g) words must not be read as O(g log g) bits.
progress: 2025: Navarro asks whether efficient grammar random access can avoid the extra space used to store all expansion lengths. | 2026-04-13: Takasaka and I obtain space-efficient SLP encodings supporting logarithmic access; their leading expansion-length term remains g log N in this card’s notation. | 2026 (ICALP): Duyster and Kociumaka sharpen and largely match grammar random-access trade-offs in their stated parameter regimes. Theorem 1.1 assumes a space budget above g log N bits; it does not supply the representation asked for here.
working_summary: A straight-line grammar can describe a string exponentially longer than its own rule list. The question asks for logarithmic-time character access with total storage comparable in bits to the grammar encoding. The representation must be built from the grammar in polynomial time without expanding the string. The obstacle is that navigation often stores expansion lengths requiring logarithmically many bits in the much larger text length. The saved review identifies removal of that length-storage overhead as the issue and distinguishes it from linear-word-space grammar access.

title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.
focus_reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.
formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
definitions: There are m≥1 distinct indivisible items and n≥1 bidders. Bidder i privately knows v_i:2^[m]→Q_{≥0}, with v_i(∅)=0, v_i(S)≤v_i(T) for S⊆T, and v_i(S)+v_i(T)≥v_i(S∪T)+v_i(S∩T) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer B≥1 bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most P(n,m,B) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles S_1,…,S_n and rational payments p_1,…,p_n; unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, u_i=v_i(S_i)−p_i. There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type v_i,v_i′, and every v_{−i}, v_i(S_i(v_i,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i,v_{−i};r)≥v_i(S_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=max Σ_i v_i(T_i), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint T_i⊆[m]. The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.
why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.
status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies O((log log m)²) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. No general constant-factor resolution found through 11 September 2026. The public per-value precision parameter makes the inherited polynomial-communication question explicit in bits.

working_summary: A combinatorial auction allocates indivisible items among bidders whose bundle values satisfy diminishing returns. The reviewed question asks for a constant-factor welfare approximation using polynomial communication and universal truthfulness. Payments must make honest reporting optimal for every fixed random choice, while values may require exponentially large tables to describe completely. A mechanism would show that strategic incentives need not cause an unbounded welfare loss in this communication model. The saved review distinguishes demand queries from weaker value access and universal truthfulness from truthfulness only in expectation.

title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division
importance_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
focus_reason: A central existence question for a strong and widely studied fairness guarantee for indivisible goods.
formal: For every integers n≥4 and m≥0 and every matrix of nonnegative real values (v_ig)_{i∈[n],g∈[m]}, is there a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of [m] such that, for every i,j∈[n] and every g∈A_j with v_ig>0, Σ_{h∈A_i}v_ih≥Σ_{h∈A_j∖{g}}v_ih?
definitions: There are n agents and m indivisible goods, with [0]=∅. Agent i values a bundle S by v_i(S)=Σ_{g∈S}v_ig; values are finite, nonnegative real numbers. A partition consists of pairwise disjoint bundles whose union is all goods; empty bundles are allowed. Every good must be allocated exactly once. There are no payments, chores, probabilistic allocations or discarded goods. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX): the removed good is tested using the values of agent i, not those of agent j. If v_i is zero on all of A_j, there is no inequality to check for that pair. This fixes the EFX convention of Definition 5 and Open Problem 2 of the cited survey. No algorithm, runtime, or restriction to rational or strictly positive values is required.
answer_criterion: Prove that every valuation matrix in the statement admits such a complete partition, or give an instance with n≥4 and finite m for which no complete partition satisfies all the EFX inequalities. The target concerns existence with nonnegative additive values; neither efficient computation nor any stronger fairness or efficiency property is required.
context:
Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called EFX₀. The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete EFX₀ existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. EFX₀ implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.
why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No proof or counterexample for unrestricted nonnegative additive valuations was located. The August 2026 four-agent, at-most-nine-goods preprint is a restricted positive result; the 2026 submodular counterexamples fall outside the additive model. The computational certificate corpus for the small-instance theorem was not rerun.
