working_summary: The problem asks whether every instance with at least four agents and nonnegative additive values admits a complete EFX allocation of indivisible goods. Complete means that each good is assigned to exactly one agent, with empty bundles allowed. For every potentially envious agent i and other bundle A_j, removing any good that i values positively must leave a bundle worth at most i’s own bundle. The statement permits zero values and fixes the positive-good EFX convention, without requiring payments or an efficient algorithm. Universal existence would establish this fairness guarantee despite the inability to divide individual goods.

title: A constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus allocation
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
importance_reason: A major approximation barrier in fair allocation and scheduling, linked by reductions to beating two for unrelated makespan and by relaxation gaps to the limits of fractional methods.
formal: Is there a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least 2/3, every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
definitions: An input consists of n≥1 agents, m≥1 items and an explicit n×m matrix (v_ij) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle S⊆[m] at v_i(S)=Σ_{j∈S}v_ij. An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles (S_1,…,S_n); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is F(S_1,…,S_n)=min_{i∈[n]}v_i(S_i), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within P(L) bit operations, for every random tape, and Pr[F≥OPT/C]≥2/3 on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.
context:
The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value w_j and v_ij is either w_j or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna give an approximation within m^ε for every fixed ε>0, where m is the number of items in this card’s notation. Their approximation–time tradeoff also yields a polylogarithmic factor in quasi-polynomial time. Choosing a smaller fixed ε improves the approximation exponent but increases the polynomial running-time exponent. Letting ε depend on m to try to force a constant factor does not preserve the known polynomial-time guarantee.

Their work also highlights a limitation of a standard configuration relaxation. For a target T, a configuration for agent i is a bundle worth at least T; fractional variables select configurations while respecting item capacities in aggregate. Integral feasible configurations would give every agent enough value. In the general setting, however, the relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by a factor of order √n. The algorithm uses the relaxation recursively on transformed instances, instead of relying on a constant-loss rounding of its original optimum.

Restricted assignment has stronger structure. Haxell and Szabó’s 2025 work improves its configuration-LP integrality-gap bound from 3.808 to 3.534 using topological criteria for independent transversals. This is a bound on the distance between fractional and integral optima in the restricted model. It does not assert a 3.534 algorithm for the arbitrary-value matrix, and an existence argument for a good integral solution must be distinguished from an efficient way to construct it.

There is a striking link with minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter show that a (2−1/α)-approximation for unrelated makespan, for fixed α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for every fixed δ>0. Thus any fixed improvement below two in that scheduling problem would answer this question positively. Their general implication goes in this direction; equivalence is established for a specified two-value case.

Bamas, Morell and Rohwedder’s SODA 2025 result extends the m^ε and quasi-polynomial polylogarithmic guarantees to arbitrary monotone submodular valuations. It uses a recursively structured LP with exponentially many variables and constraints. This broadens the class of preferences that can be handled, while retaining a growing approximation factor even on the additive instances considered here.

More recent constant guarantees also require attention to their input promise. Boehmer’s April 2026 paper obtains value at least 0.4OPT for identical monotone submodular valuations. Identical preferences are a substantial restriction, even though submodularity is more general than additivity. The outstanding question concerns unrestricted disagreement about item values. Settling it would clarify whether balancing heterogeneous indivisible resources admits a constant loss at polynomial computational cost.
why: The central unresolved max-min allocation question: can all agents be protected to within a constant factor when indivisible resources have arbitrary heterogeneous additive values?
status_note: The SODA 2024 reduction paper and SODA 2025 submodular paper explicitly retain the general additive constant-approximation question. Later checked constant guarantees concern restricted assignment or identical valuations, not arbitrary additive matrices. No general resolution found through 11 September 2026. Randomization and simultaneous success for all agents are explicit in this formulation.
progress: 2009: Chakrabarty–Chuzhoy–Khanna achieve an arbitrarily small fixed power of the number of items in polynomial time, and a polylogarithmic approximation in quasi-polynomial time. | 2023–2024: Bamas and coauthors show that any fixed improvement below two for unrelated makespan implies a constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus. | 2024–2025: Bamas–Morell–Rohwedder extend the additive problem’s approximation–time tradeoff to monotone submodular valuations; the work appears at SODA 2025. | 2025-03-27: Haxell–Szabó prove a 3.534 configuration-LP integrality-gap bound for restricted assignment; arbitrary agent-specific values are outside the result. | 2026-04-14: Boehmer obtains a 0.4 welfare guarantee for identical submodular valuations, a different restricted input class.
working_summary: Max-min allocation distributes indivisible items to agents with arbitrary nonnegative additive values. The question asks for a randomized polynomial-time constant-factor approximation to the best achievable minimum agent value. One simultaneous allocation must serve every agent adequately, so favorable expected values alone are insufficient. The difficulty is that agents compete for items whose value can differ substantially between recipients. The saved review separates this general model from restricted assignment, where each item has a common positive value whenever an agent can use it.

title: The power of randomization in truthful unrelated-machine scheduling
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The central randomized counterpart of the resolved Nisan–Ronen conjecture, with a constant-versus-linear gap independent of computational restrictions.
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as m→∞, the function R(m): the infimum worst-case expected-makespan approximation ratio achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms with monetary payments for m unrelated machines and an arbitrary number of indivisible jobs. The infimum ranges over all mechanisms, without a computational or communication restriction. In particular, is R(m)=Θ(1)?
definitions: There are m≥2 machines and n≥1 jobs. Machine i privately knows a vector t_i∈R_{≥0}^n; processing a set S costs it Σ_{j∈S}t_{ij}. Every entry is finite. A direct-revelation mechanism maps reported vectors b=(b₁,…,b_m) to a distribution over assignments σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} and payments to the machines. Jobs are indivisible and every job is assigned exactly once. Let x_{ij}(b)=Pr[σ(j)=i] and let p_i(b) be the finite expected payment to i. Risk-neutral utility is payment minus true processing cost. Truthfulness in expectation means that for every i, true t_i, alternative report b_i and fixed reports b_{−i}, p_i(t_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(t_i,b_{−i})≥p_i(b_i,b_{−i})−Σ_j t_{ij}x_{ij}(b_i,b_{−i}). This is a dominant-strategy condition against arbitrary fixed reports, without a prior on types. The makespan is C(σ,t)=max_i Σ_{j:σ(j)=i}t_{ij}, and OPT(t)=min_σ C(σ,t). For each m, consider a family M=(M_{m,n})_{n≥1} satisfying this incentive condition for every n and report profile. Its ratio is sup_{n,t:OPT(t)>0} E[C(M_{m,n}(t),t)]/OPT(t), and it must also have expected makespan zero when OPT(t)=0. R(m) is the infimum of those ratios. Random assignments may be correlated across jobs. No budget balance, bound on transfers, individual-rationality constraint, anonymity, task independence or efficient representation is imposed. Since only expected utilities matter, payments can equivalently be deterministic amounts p_i(b).
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic scale f(m) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a f(m)≤R(m)≤b f(m) for all sufficiently large m, with matching incentive-theoretic lower bounds and mechanisms achieving the upper scale. A constant-factor mechanism for all numbers of machines and jobs would settle the target as Θ(1). Showing only that R(m) is unbounded would rule out that possibility but would not determine the requested asymptotic order without matching bounds. Restrictions on the mechanism class or input distributions must not be silently added.
context:
A machine has a reason to exaggerate how long jobs take: receiving fewer jobs reduces its work. Payments are intended to counteract that incentive while keeping the overall schedule short. The private information is a whole vector, since a machine may be fast on one job and slow on another. A single speed parameter would describe a different and substantially more structured scheduling model.

The optimization objective creates the difficulty. Minimizing total processing cost can be implemented truthfully by a VCG mechanism, which assigns each job to a cheapest machine. But total cost and makespan differ. The largest load is at most the total cost, while the total cost of an optimal makespan schedule is at most m times its makespan. Thus this familiar truthful rule gives an m-approximation. Without incentive constraints and with unlimited computation, one could simply choose an optimal assignment.

Christodoulou, Koutsoupias and Kovács prove that the factor m is unavoidable for deterministic truthful mechanisms, resolving the Nisan–Ronen conjecture. Their result appeared as a 2023 preprint and in the Journal of the ACM in February 2026. It is an unconditional incentive restriction, independent of computational hardness. The paper’s related-work discussion expressly separates the unresolved randomized setting from this deterministic conclusion.

There are two different ways to randomize truthfully. A universally truthful mechanism draws a deterministic truthful mechanism before seeing the reports. Truthfulness in expectation only asks that honest reporting maximize expected utility; individual random outcomes need not implement truthful rules on their own. Universal truthfulness implies the latter condition, but the definition in this card permits the larger class. Mu’alem and Schapira nevertheless prove a lower bound of 2−1/m even for that larger class.

Randomization already helps when there are two machines. Lu and Yu’s STACS 2008 mechanism is universally truthful and beats the deterministic factor two. Their later WINE 2008 paper gives a truthful-in-expectation mechanism with ratio (m+5)/2 for general m, using a fractional allocation and a suitable rounding procedure. The improvement is substantial in its leading constant, but the guarantee still grows linearly with the number of machines.

The WINE paper also proves a lower bound (m+1)/2 for its task-independent class. A mechanism in the full question may use all reported jobs together and correlate their assignments. Consequently, a lower bound that treats each job separately does not close the gap between the general constant lower bound and linear upper bound. Whether such global dependence can change the asymptotic answer is part of what makes this question interesting.

Expected makespan must be distinguished from the largest expected machine load. Consider m identical machines and m unit jobs. Assigning all jobs to one uniformly random machine gives expected load one on every machine, yet the makespan is always m. Assigning one job per machine has makespan one. Thus the same marginal load target can conceal a factor-m difference in the objective. A truthful fractional solution, or an argument that controls only marginal probabilities, needs a valid rounding analysis before it yields a guarantee for this card.

Fine numerical results for small cases illuminate mechanisms without settling the asymptotic problem. Kuryatnikova and Vera obtain almost matching bounds near 1.505996 for two machines and two jobs within a class of randomized monotone scale-free algorithms. Their paper does not identify the optimal ratio over every truthful-in-expectation mechanism, every job count and a growing number of machines. Both the input restriction and mechanism restriction matter when interpreting the result.

The final question is whether allowing random outcomes fundamentally reduces the price of truthful multidimensional cost reporting. A constant answer would permit useful load balancing despite unrestricted private processing times. A growing lower bound would show that even risk-neutral incentives and unrestricted payments cannot recover the efficiency available to a scheduler who knows the true costs. Matching bounds would quantify that loss as a function of system size.
why: Determine the asymptotic efficiency loss caused solely by truthful multidimensional incentives when randomization and payments are fully available.
status_note: The Nisan–Ronen proof, now published in JACM in February 2026, resolves only deterministic truthful mechanisms. Its randomized discussion records 2−1/m and (m+5)/2 bounds. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted randomized bounds; results for task-independent mechanisms, fractional objectives, Bayesian types or no-payment models do not resolve this formulation.
progress: 2007: Mu’alem–Schapira establish the lower bound 2−1/m for randomized scheduling, including truthfulness in expectation; the full version gives the extended weak-monotonicity argument. | 2008: Lu–Yu give improved universally truthful two-machine mechanisms and a general truthful-in-expectation upper bound (m+5)/2; the linear lower bound in their WINE paper assumes task independence. | 2019–2020: Kuryatnikova–Vera sharpen bounds for a restricted scale-free mechanism class on two machines, including an almost tight two-job calculation; first published 30 May 2019. | 2023-01-27: Christodoulou–Koutsoupias–Kovács post the proof that deterministic truthful scheduling has optimal ratio m, while recording the distinct randomized bounds. | 2026-02-11: The deterministic Nisan–Ronen proof is published online in the Journal of the ACM; its theorem does not cover truthful-in-expectation randomization.
working_summary: Unrelated-machine scheduling assigns jobs to machines with privately known processing times for each job. The question asks for the optimal expected-makespan approximation achievable by truthful-in-expectation mechanisms as the number of machines grows. Random assignments can correlate decisions across jobs while payments discourage strategic misreporting. A constant ratio would show that randomization overcomes the large incentive cost known for deterministic mechanisms. The saved review emphasizes that maximum expected load is different from expected maximum load, and restricted task-independent lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted mechanism class.

title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.
formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most Cn^d queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure μ_i: values are nonnegative, countably additive, μ_i([0,1])=1 and μ_i({x})=0 for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μ_i([x,y]); Cut(i,x,α), with 0≤α≤μ_i([x,1]), returns a point y≥x for which μ_i([x,y])=α. Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require μ_i(A_i)≥μ_i(A_j) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound Cn^d is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
context:
Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely 1/n. The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is Ω(n²) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the Θ(n log n) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to n^{8n²(1+o(1))}. That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to 2^{(8+o(1))n² log₂n}, although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited 2025/2026 average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using n^{O(1)}2^n queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least n^{12} queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.
why: A central information-complexity question in fair division: how many exact preference queries are necessary to allocate an entire divisible resource without envy?
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Polynomial worst-case query complexity remains open. The latest checked general upper bound is the n^{O(1)}2^n protocol reported in the Ye–Bai preprint of 4 September 2026; Chèze’s polynomial result is over random valuation profiles.
progress: 1995: Brams–Taylor give an always-terminating protocol for arbitrary n, without a bound depending only on n. | 2009: Procaccia proves an Ω(n²) query lower bound for envy-free cake cutting. | 2016–2017: Aziz–Mackenzie give a bounded deterministic protocol; the full manuscript’s latest revision is August 2017. | 2022: Brânzei–Nisan study query complexity for approximate fairness and explain the distinction between connected and fragmented exact allocations. | 2023-06-06: Sokolov posts an improved n^{8n²(1+o(1))} query upper bound. | 2025-09-26: Chèze’s article is published online, giving a polynomial query bound with high probability over its random valuation model; journal volume 67 appears in 2026. | 2026-09-04: Ye–Bai post a deterministic n^{O(1)}2^n-query protocol for complete exact envy-free allocation. This reported preprint bound remains exponential.
working_summary: Envy-free cake cutting divides a continuous resource so that nobody prefers another person's share under their own valuation. The reviewed question asks for an exact complete allocation using polynomially many deterministic Robertson–Webb queries. Disconnected pieces are allowed, and local computation between queries is unrestricted. A polynomial protocol would identify a manageable amount of preference information sufficient for exact global fairness. The saved review records a recent single-exponential query upper-bound preprint but distinguishes it from polynomial complexity, approximate fairness, and favorable average-case valuation models.

title: The optimal randomized metric distortion in social choice
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
formal: Determine the exact infimum D* of the universal worst-case metric distortion achievable by any randomized ordinal voting rule, when the rule sees every voter’s full ranking and minimizes expected total distance to voters. The infimum ranges over all rules for all finite positive numbers of voters and candidates, with the model and zero-cost convention below.
definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of n≥1 voters and C of m≥1 candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each v∈V. A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on V∪C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for all points, with a≻_v b implying d(v,a)≤d(v,b). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair (E,d). The social cost SC_d(a)=Σ_v∈V d(v,a), and OPT_d=min_a∈C SC_d(a). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery p=f(E), where p_a≥0 and Σ_a p_a=1. Its expected cost is Σ_a p_a SC_d(a). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define Dist(f)=inf{D≥1: for every E and every consistent d, Σ_a f(E)_a SC_d(a)≤D·OPT_d}, taking inf∅=+∞. This inequality requires zero expected cost if OPT_d=0 and avoids dividing by zero. Set D*=inf_f Dist(f), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
answer_criterion: Give an exact real value or unambiguous exact expression for D* and prove equality: for every η>0 there must be a rule with universal distortion at most D*+η, and every rule must have distortion at least D*. An attained optimum with the matching lower bound also suffices. A numerical interval, a better upper bound alone, or an exact optimum within a restricted family of rules does not determine the unrestricted infimum.
context:
Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively 3−2p and 1+2p. At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.
why: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
status_note: The latest checked preprint, dated 8 September 2026, states upper bound 2.13713 against a general lower bound of about 2.11264. The exact value remains unresolved. These fresh upper bounds were matched to the model but their proofs and computational certificates were not independently audited; no full-resolution claim was found through 11 September 2026.
progress: 2021 / 2022: The former D*=2 conjecture is disproved; a general randomized lower bound approaches approximately 2.11264. | 2025: Tournament and fuller-ranking models are explicitly separated; the source’s numerical gap is now historical. | 2026-08-18: A preprint gives the general upper bound 5/2. | 2026-09-06: The revised random-size-stable-lottery paper states upper bound 2.1441 and a separate family-specific lower bound 2.136. | 2026-09-08: Theorem 1 of a new preprint states the unrestricted upper bound 2.13713; it does not identify D* exactly.
working_summary: What is the smallest universal expected metric distortion achievable from full voter rankings? The voting rule selects a lottery without seeing the distances that produced those rankings. The former value-two conjecture is false, with a general lower bound around 2.11264. A preprint dated 8 September 2026 states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a nonzero gap. Tournament-only and particular stable-lottery lower bounds do not determine the unrestricted optimum.

title: Polynomial-time EFX for three additive agents
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.
formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k≥1 such that, for every finite set of goods and every three nonnegative rational additive valuations, A returns a complete EFX allocation in at most C(N+1)^k steps, where N is the binary input length and EFX has the all-goods convention below?
definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and m≥0 goods indexed by [m]={1,…,m}. The input gives m and each value v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. A complete allocation is an ordered partition (A₁,A₂,A₃) of [m]; bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in {1,2,3}. It is EFX if v_i(A_i)≥v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every i,j∈{1,2,3} and every g∈A_j, including goods with v_i,g=0. The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty A_j gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.
context:
Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

A value as large as 2^L needs only L+1 binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including 2/3-EFX for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.
why: The smallest unresolved computational case for exact EFX after existence for three agents was established.
status_note: The exact polynomial-time three-agent question is explicitly unresolved in the checked 2025 primary paper. The May 2026 work gives relaxed guarantees, not an exact algorithm. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution; no proof was independently audited.
progress: 2020: Complete EFX existence for three additive agents is proved constructively, with a pseudopolynomial algorithm. | 2025: Polynomial-time EF2X for three agents is obtained, while the paper explicitly retains the exact EFX computational gap. | 2026-05: A preprint reports polynomial-time approximate EFX for up to eight agents, a different guarantee from exact EFX.
working_summary: Three agents must receive all indivisible goods under nonnegative additive valuations. An allocation is EFX when removing any one good from another agent’s bundle would eliminate the first agent’s envy. Such allocations are known to exist for three agents, including when values are zero or tied. The question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the binary valuation table’s length. Pseudopolynomial constructions and polynomial algorithms for weaker fairness guarantees do not settle this target.

title: The optimal polynomial-time approximation of EFX
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.
formal: Determine α_alg = sup{α∈[0,1] : there is a deterministic algorithm that, on every finite instance of nonnegative rational additive goods, returns a complete α-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the binary input length}. The number of agents is unbounded and part of the input.
definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 goods and an explicit table of values v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g, with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. An allocation (A₁,…,A_n) partitions [m] into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is α-EFX if v_i(A_i)≥α·v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every pair i,j and every g∈A_j, including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty A_j imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed α in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most C(N+1)^k on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on α, but not on n, m or the valuations. α is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since α=0 is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
answer_criterion: Identify a real a∈[0,1] and prove that a=α_alg: achievable polynomial-time factors approach a arbitrarily closely from below, and no such algorithm guarantees any factor greater than a within [0,1]. An algorithm attaining a suffices for the first part but is not required. A conditional hardness result establishes only the corresponding conditional bound; a guarantee for one fixed number of agents does not establish the universal value.
context:
Higher α means a stronger guarantee, with α=1 giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when α≤4/5. This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor (√5−1)/2≈0.618. Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are (√5−1)/2≤α_alg≤1; the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

The May 2026 preprint reports a 2/3-EFX algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even α_alg=1 would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.
why: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.
status_note: The checked May 2026 primary preprint still gives about 0.618 as the best known general EFX factor. The exact polynomial-time supremum is not identified by the checked sources; searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. No independent proof audit is claimed.
progress: 2020: A polynomial algorithm achieves the universal factor (√5−1)/2. | 2023: The survey retains the gap beyond this general EFX approximation and distinguishes exact existence from computation. | 2026-05: A preprint improves the 2/3-EFX guarantee to eight agents, while retaining about 0.618 as the known general frontier.
working_summary: All indivisible goods must be allocated among agents with nonnegative additive values. An α-EFX allocation lets each agent retain at least an α fraction of the value she assigns to any other bundle after any one good is removed. The question asks for the supremum factor guaranteed by deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for arbitrarily many agents. A general factor of about 0.618 is known, while recent 2/3 guarantees cover only bounded numbers of agents. The computational supremum differs from an existence guarantee and need not be attained by one algorithm.

title: The optimal multiplicative MMS guarantee for chores
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Seeks the intrinsic loss required for fair allocation of indivisible burdens.
formal: Determine the smallest real α≥1 such that, for every finite instance of nonnegative additive chores with any number of agents, there is a complete allocation (A₁,…,A_n) satisfying c_i(A_i)≤αμ_i for every agent i, where μ_i is that agent’s minimax share. Denote this universal factor by α*.
definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 indivisible chores, and finite real costs c_i,g≥0. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆[m] the additive cost c_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}c_i,g; lower cost is better. Let Π_n([m]) be the finite set of ordered partitions of [m] into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define μ_i=min_{(P₁,…,P_n)∈Π_n([m])} max_{1≤j≤n} c_i(P_j). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to Π_n([m]): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when μ_i=0, without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
answer_criterion: Identify a real a≥1 and prove both that every instance admits an allocation with c_i(A_i)≤aμ_i for all i, and that for every β with 1≤β<a there is an instance with no such β-allocation. The lower-bound instances may depend on β; one instance need not attain the worst universal ratio. A guarantee restricted to a fixed number of agents or a special class of costs does not determine α*.
context:
Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and {3,3}; the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus α*≥44/43>1.

Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor 13/11 always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are 44/43≤α*≤13/11, approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a 15/13 multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses 13/11 as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.
why: Seeks the intrinsic loss required for fair allocation of indivisible burdens.
status_note: The checked sources leave a gap between 44/43 and 13/11. A primary preprint dated 8 September 2026 still describes 13/11 as the general frontier. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established determination of the optimal universal factor; restricted-cost results do not settle this question.
progress: 2021: A three-agent, nine-chore example establishes the lower bound 44/43. | 2023: The scheduling reduction establishes the general upper bound 13/11. | 2025: Improved ordinal and personalized-bivalued guarantees concern distinct restrictions or benchmarks. | 2026-09: A comparison-query preprint continues to identify 13/11 as the general multiplicative frontier.
working_summary: Chores are indivisible tasks whose costs add, and each agent prefers a smaller burden. Her minimax share is the lowest worst-bundle cost she can obtain by partitioning all chores among the agents. The question asks for the smallest universal factor by which every agent’s share must be relaxed to make a complete allocation possible. The checked general bounds are 44/43 and 13/11, while stronger guarantees for restricted costs do not close this gap. Determining the factor would quantify the unavoidable fairness loss from indivisible burdens without requiring an efficient algorithm.

title: Competitive equilibrium for almost all budgets with two additive agents
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Tests whether a small asymmetry in purchasing power is enough to recover equilibrium with indivisible goods.
formal: For every m≥1 and every pair of positive additive valuations on m indivisible goods, is the set of positive budget pairs (b₁,b₂) for which no competitive equilibrium exists a set of two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero?
definitions: The goods are M=[m]. For i∈{1,2}, finite real numbers v_i,g>0 define v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g for every S⊆M. Different bundles may have equal value. Budgets b₁,b₂ are arbitrary positive real numbers. A price vector assigns each good a real price p_g≥0, with p(S)=∑_{g∈S}p_g. A competitive equilibrium consists of p and a partition (A₁,A₂) of M, allowing an empty bundle, such that p(A_i)≤b_i and v_i(A_i)≥v_i(S) for every S⊆M with p(S)≤b_i, for both agents simultaneously. All goods must be allocated once. Agents value only their goods: unspent budget has no utility and need not be exhausted. Ties among best affordable bundles are permitted. For each fixed valuation pair, its exceptional set lies in (0,∞)² and must have Lebesgue measure zero, meaning it can be covered by countably many rectangles whose total area is smaller than any prescribed ε>0. The exceptional set may depend on the valuations. The allocation and prices may depend on the valuations and budgets. This is an exact existence statement with no running-time or finite-encoding requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove that the exceptional budget set has measure zero for every finite positive additive two-agent instance, or give one such instance and prove that its nonexistence set has positive two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Failure at a single budget pair, including equal budgets, is insufficient for a negative answer; approximate clearing or a result confined to near-equal budgets is insufficient for a positive answer.
context:
Suppose both agents value one good positively and each has budget 1. At any price at most 1 both can afford and prefer the good, but only one can receive it; at a price above 1 neither can buy it. If the budgets become 1 and 1.01, a price of 1.005 gives a competitive equilibrium: only the richer agent can afford the good. This simple example explains why an exceptional line of budget pairs may be allowed.

The question covers budgets with arbitrarily unequal purchasing power as well as nearly equal ones. It permits a set of failures with zero area, rather than requiring existence at every pair or merely at many sampled pairs. A positive answer would mean that a budget pair drawn from any continuous density avoids the exceptional set with probability one.

Babaioff, Nisan and Talgam-Cohen establish existence for two additive agents with sufficiently close unequal budgets, and generic existence for identical preferences under their stated preference conventions. Segal-Halevi’s account gives almost-all existence with at most four goods and leaves the arbitrary additive case with five or more goods open. Failure examples for more general monotone preferences do not automatically give additive counterexamples.

Budgets represent purchasing entitlements and prices coordinate which bundles are simultaneously affordable. The target retains exact allocation of every good and exact optimality for each agent. Adding utility for cash, allowing unsold goods or replacing each whole good by fractions produces a different market.
why: Tests whether a small asymmetry in purchasing power is enough to recover equilibrium with indivisible goods.
status_note: The checked primary sources explicitly leave the two-agent additive question open for arbitrary budgets and numbers of goods. Targeted searches through 11 September 2026 found no established resolution. Near-equal-budget theorems and results for general monotone preferences have different scopes.
progress: 2017: The generic-budget approach yields two-agent additive existence near equal budgets and for identical preferences. | 2020: The almost-all-incomes paper explicitly retains the open additive case with two agents and at least five goods. | 2021: The original generic-budget paper appears in Mathematics of Operations Research.
working_summary: Two agents use positive budgets to buy indivisible goods at common item prices. Each must receive a most valuable affordable bundle, and every good must be allocated. The question asks whether every positive additive valuation pair has an equilibrium outside a zero-area set of budget pairs. Equal budgets can fail even for one good, while nearby unequal budgets and several other restricted cases are understood. The unresolved target covers arbitrary numbers of goods and budgets that may be far from equal.

title: FIXP-hardness of exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Complete the exact complexity classification of an influential market mechanism with irrational equilibria.
formal: Is computing an exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium for a one-sided matching market FIXP-hard under the standard FIXP reductions?
definitions: There are equally many agents and unit-supply goods with explicitly given nonnegative rational utilities. Each agent has budget one and consumes a lottery totaling one unit. At equilibrium the lotteries clear the market and maximize each agent’s expected utility subject to budget and unit-demand constraints. Exact equilibrium coordinates may be irrational. FIXP is the class of fixed-point search problems defined by algebraic circuits with rational constants and the standard arithmetic/max/min operations.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
statement_review_issue: Copy the equilibrium tie-breaking/minimum-expenditure conventions and the complete FIXP reduction/output model from the source. The informal market equations alone do not specify the exact search reduction.
context:
The Hylland–Zeckhauser market turns random assignment into a pricing equilibrium with fairness and efficiency properties. Exact equilibrium is known to belong to FIXP, while approximation is PPAD-complete.

The source explicitly leaves exact FIXP-hardness open. This is not the already established hardness of approximate equilibrium, nor a claim that every exact output can be written as a short rational vector. An exact classification would identify the real-algebraic difficulty of this central assignment mechanism.
why: Complete the exact complexity classification of an influential market mechanism with irrational equilibria.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2025: The journal version records FIXP membership, irrational examples and PPAD-completeness of approximation while leaving exact FIXP-hardness open.

title: Deciding whether an exact MMS allocation exists
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Distinguishes the complexity of attaining a fairness guarantee from the difficulty of evaluating each agent's benchmark.
formal: Determine the computational complexity of deciding whether an explicitly given finite instance of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations has a complete maximin-share allocation. The number of agents varies with the input. The exact decision predicate is defined below; the classification or bound precision requested by the imported question remains to be specified.
definitions: An input consists of a list of n≥1 agents, a list G of m≥0 goods, and an explicit n-by-m table of nonnegative integers vᵢg written in binary. Input length N counts these lists and all value bits. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆G the additive value vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg, with vᵢ(∅)=0. Let Πₙ(G) be the finite set of labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pₙ) of all goods into n disjoint bundles; empty bundles are allowed. Define μᵢ=maxP∈Πₙ(G) min1≤j≤n vᵢ(Pⱼ). Each agent uses her own valuation for every bundle in this benchmark partition. A complete allocation is A∈Πₙ(G), and the input is a yes-instance exactly when some A satisfies vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ for every i. A zero benchmark imposes the inequality vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥0 and involves no division. Benchmark values are not supplied as part of the input. There are no connectivity constraints, arrivals, transfers, discarded goods or fractional allocations. Computation uses the usual deterministic bit-cost model unless a complexity class explicitly permits nondeterminism or an oracle. The nonnegative rational binary-value version has the same polynomial-time classification: each agent’s row can be scaled by a positive common denominator of polynomial bit length without changing the fairness inequalities.
answer_criterion: Give a proved classification or matching bounds for this exact existence decision predicate, under an explicitly fixed precision and reduction convention. The source import does not yet fix that requested precision, so the card remains an incomplete computational benchmark. Hardness of computing μᵢ, finding an optimal allocation, or solving a constrained variant does not by itself classify this yes/no predicate.
statement_review_issue: The instance predicate and binary input model are now explicit. The imported request for “the computational complexity” does not specify the desired classification or precision: for example, a polynomial-time decision question, completeness under a particular reduction, or matching resource bounds. The checked survey highlights the narrower unknown NP-hardness question, but replacing the full classification request by that subquestion would change its scope.
context:
An agent’s maximin share is what she can guarantee by dividing the goods into n bundles and then taking the bundle she values least. Each agent may prefer a different partition. The question is whether a single allocation can simultaneously meet all these personal guarantees.

For two agents who both value three goods at 4, 3 and 3, each maximin share is 4. Giving one agent the first good and the other the last two meets both benchmarks, although the first agent receives less than her proportional share of 5. Identical valuations always admit an MMS allocation by the definition of an optimal common partition. Consequently, difficulty in computing that partition need not make its existence difficult to decide.

The 2023 survey states that NP-hardness is unknown for general nonnegative additive goods valuations. The existence problem has a Δ₂ᴾ upper bound, also recorded in the 2020 work on the broader graph-constrained model. Here Δ₂ᴾ=Pᴺᴾ means deterministic polynomial time with an oracle answering NP decision questions. This upper bound does not give an ordinary polynomial-time algorithm.

Maximin share and minimax share reverse the order of the minimum and maximum and need not agree. Likewise, computing a fair allocation under an existence promise is a search problem. The August 2026 temporal preprint studies fairness after every round of irreversible arrivals. Hardness in any of these settings cannot be transferred to the static unconstrained existence question without an appropriate reduction.

An exact allocation need not exist when agents value goods differently. Understanding how hard it is to detect existence would separate the cost of evaluating a fairness benchmark from the cost of deciding whether the benchmarks can coexist. It would also clarify when a failure to find an exact allocation reflects computational difficulty rather than an impossible demand.
why: Distinguishes the complexity of attaining a fairness guarantee from the difficulty of evaluating each agent's benchmark.
status_note: Primary-source checks and subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 did not locate a classification of this static additive existence predicate. The 2023 survey explicitly leaves NP-hardness open. Later temporal and pairwise-share hardness claims concern different predicates. The desired classification precision remains an editorial gap; paper proofs were not independently audited.
progress: 2018: The cited paper develops approximation and complexity results for several distinct share notions; its abstract’s minimax-share hardness is not a resolution of this question. | 2020: Work on graph-constrained allocations records the Δ₂ᴾ upper bound for existence and separates it from the harder allocation-computation task. | 2023: The survey explicitly identifies NP-hardness of ordinary additive MMS existence as an open problem. | 2026-08: A temporal-allocation preprint reports hardness under round-by-round fairness constraints, which are outside this static model.
working_summary: Each agent values an indivisible bundle by adding her values for its goods. Her maximin share is the best least-bundle value she can obtain by partitioning all goods into one bundle per agent. The decision problem asks whether one complete allocation gives every agent at least this personal benchmark. Known difficulties in computing benchmarks or finding allocations do not alone establish hardness of deciding their existence. The input and fairness predicate are explicit, while the imported request still needs a specified complexity-classification target.

title: The optimal ordinal MMS guarantee for goods
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: An alternative to multiplicative relaxation that keeps an agent's partition-based fairness standard intact.
formal: For every integer n≥1, determine d*(n), the least positive integer d for which every finite instance of n agents with nonnegative additive valuations of indivisible goods admits a complete allocation A satisfying vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(d) for every agent i.
definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
answer_criterion: Give the exact function d*(n) for all positive integers n, with a universal existence proof at the proposed value and a matching impossibility proof for every smaller positive denominator. By monotonicity, when d*(n)>1 a counterexample at d*(n)−1 suffices for the latter part. An improved upper bound, an asymptotic leading constant, or a result permitting additional copies does not determine the requested exact function.
context:
An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.
why: An alternative to multiplicative relaxation that keeps an agent's partition-based fairness standard intact.
status_note: Primary-source formulation and subsequent-work checks through 11 September 2026 found upper bounds and related simultaneous-fairness results, not an exact denominator function. The April 2026 source still records the n+1 question as open. Mathematical proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2022: The cited matching paper gives the 1-out-of-(2n−2) goods guarantee; its author version corrects a production omission. | 2024-02: Theorem 1 establishes the universal 1-out-of-4⌈n/3⌉ guarantee. | 2026-04: The current simultaneous-fairness preprint still records the n+1 denominator question as unresolved and proves combined guarantees for restricted preferences.
working_summary: An agent’s 1-out-of-d maximin share is the best least-bundle value she can achieve by partitioning all goods into d bundles. The allocation itself still distributes the goods among n actual agents. The question asks for the smallest denominator that guarantees every agent her corresponding share in every additive goods instance. Known bounds allow roughly four benchmark bundles for every three agents, with separate rounding improvements for smaller n. Determining the exact denominator would describe the strongest universally attainable fairness standard of this form.

title: Bounded protocols for connected envy-free proportional cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Asks whether discarded cake permits exact fairness together with geometric simplicity in finite interaction.
formal: For every fixed integer n≥4, does there exist a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol Pₙ and a finite integer Bₙ such that, for every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations and all valid query answers, Pₙ uses at most Bₙ queries and returns disjoint connected bundles A₁,…,Aₙ satisfying μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for all i,j and μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for all i, while permitting unallocated cake?
definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each Aᵢ must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue [0,1]∖⋃ᵢAᵢ may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound Bₙ depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require Bₙ to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all Pₙ.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed n≥4, or prove that for at least one fixed n≥4 no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.
context:
A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length 1/(2n), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact 1/n requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once n≥3. This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is 1/7 instead of the required 1/4. Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a 1/(3n) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all n≥4.
