title: Do EFkX allocations exist for a universal constant k?
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Asks whether a bounded additive relaxation suffices for fairness independently of the number of agents.
formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥1 such that, for every n≥1, every finite set G of goods, and every table of nonnegative additive valuations vᵢ, there is a complete allocation (A₁,…,Aₙ) for which vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥vᵢ(Aⱼ∖S) for all agents i,j and every S⊆Aⱼ with |S|=min{k,|Aⱼ|}?
definitions: For agent i, each good g has a nonnegative real value vᵢg and every bundle B⊆G has value vᵢ(B)=∑g∈B vᵢg; the empty bundle has value zero. A complete allocation partitions all goods into n labeled, disjoint bundles, possibly empty. Each good goes to exactly one agent. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any k goods, abbreviated EFkX: each comparison uses the potentially envious agent i’s values on both sides. The removed set S is hypothetical and is chosen universally, not chosen by the allocation algorithm to make the inequality easier. Actual goods are not removed or discarded. If |Aⱼ|≤k, the comparison is automatically satisfied because its right side is zero; this agrees with treating the source’s k-item condition as vacuous for shorter bundles. Zero-valued goods count as goods and may belong to S. The constant k is chosen before the instance and is independent of n, the number of goods and all values. This is exact existence; it imposes no efficiency requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove that at least one universal constant k satisfies the stated existence claim, or prove its negation: for every integer k≥1 there is a finite additive goods instance such that every complete allocation violates at least one of its required inequalities. A counterexample for one k, or an allocation with a multiplicative factor below 1, does not resolve this quantifier structure.
context:
One indivisible valuable item can prevent exact envy-freeness. EFkX allows a bounded number of items in the envied bundle to account for that discrepancy. It requires envy to disappear even after deleting the least helpful k items from the envious agent’s perspective. The question is whether some fixed allowance works for arbitrarily many agents.

Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 5 and another bundle’s three goods at 6, 1 and 1. Removing its 6-valued good eliminates her envy, but removing either 1-valued good leaves value 7, so the pair fails EF1X. It also fails EF2X: removing the two 1-valued goods leaves value 6. This illustrates why an existential choice of removed goods is a different, weaker condition.

For k=1 this is the usual any-item EFX condition, including zero-valued items. A universal EFX existence theorem would answer this question positively. This card permits any fixed k, so it asks for a weaker universal guarantee. Choosing k separately for each instance, for example as its total number of goods, would make the property vacuous and is excluded.

The AAAI 2025 result establishes EF2X for four agents, in a valuation class that includes additive goods. That is a concrete exact existence theorem. It fixes the number of agents and therefore does not supply the universal constant-k guarantee for unrestricted n.

The May 2026 preprint gives (k+1)/(k+2)-EFkX allocations for every fixed k≥2 and any number of agents. This relaxes the inequality to vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥αvᵢ(Aⱼ∖S), where α<1. Although α approaches 1 as k grows, no finite k in that theorem attains exact fairness. Its negative graph-orientation results additionally restrict who may receive a good.
why: Asks whether a bounded additive relaxation suffices for fairness independently of the number of agents.
status_note: Definition and result-scope checks, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026, did not locate a resolution of exact constant-k EFkX existence for arbitrary additive instances. The current primary preprint is an approximation result, and proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2025-04: Exact EF2X existence is published for four agents, including additive valuations. | 2026-05: A preprint establishes universal multiplicative approximate EFkX guarantees; exact constant-k existence is not established by this result.
working_summary: EFkX compares each agent’s bundle with another bundle after any k of that other bundle’s goods are hypothetically removed. The same agent’s valuation is used on both sides, and all actual goods must still be allocated. The question asks whether one constant k works for every number of agents and every nonnegative additive goods instance. Exact guarantees are known for limited numbers of agents, while a 2026 preprint obtains multiplicative approximate guarantees for arbitrary n. A resolution would determine whether a bounded item allowance can always account for the envy caused by indivisibility.

title: Envy-free proportional cake cutting with free disposal
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Tests whether discarding some divisible resource removes the main algorithmic cost of exact fairness.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n→∞, the optimal worst-case number of exact Robertson–Webb queries needed by a deterministic protocol to return an envy-free proportional allocation among n agents, allowing unallocated cake and bundles that are finite unions of intervals.
definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. Here A₁,…,Aₙ must be pairwise disjoint but need not cover [0,1]; the residue may be discarded. No bound is imposed on the number of intervals per agent except finiteness. Envy is compared only with assigned bundles. Both Eval and Cut calls cost one query, including marks that do not appear in the final allocation. For each n, let Q(n) be the minimum integer B for which a deterministic finite protocol for n agents always returns such an allocation within B queries, for every valuation profile and all valid answers. Known bounded complete-allocation protocols imply that this set of B is nonempty; its least integer is attained. The requested complexity is the asymptotic order of Q(n), with exact fairness on every input and no average-case, error or expected-cost convention.
answer_criterion: Give a function f(n), constants 0<c≤C and n₀ such that c f(n)≤Q(n)≤C f(n) for every n≥n₀. The upper bound must be realized by valid protocols and the lower bound must apply to every valid deterministic protocol in the stated model. Logarithmic or polynomial-factor gaps do not count as matching constant-factor bounds. This card uses the usual asymptotic interpretation of optimal query complexity, rather than asking for an exact integer query count at every n.
context:
An agent should prefer her own bundle to every other assigned bundle, and should value it at least as much as one n-th of the original cake. These are separate conditions when some cake can remain unallocated. For identical uniform valuations, equal bundles of length 1/(2n) are envy-free but fail proportionality.

A value measure can be arbitrarily complicated, so the protocol cannot read it as a finite table. Evaluation queries reveal interval values and cut queries reveal where a prescribed value ends. The cost measures how much exact interaction is necessary; it does not charge the local arithmetic or require the resulting bundles to be connected.

Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded partial-allocation protocol meeting both envy-freeness and exact proportionality, with an exponential query bound. This already ensures Q(n) is finite. Their separate connected-piece result guarantees only a 1/(3n) share and addresses a different output requirement.

The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports n^{O(1)}2^n queries for a complete envy-free allocation. Such an allocation is also a permitted output here, since disposal is optional and completeness implies proportionality under nonnegative additive valuations. The reported bound is an upper bound for this problem, not a matching optimality result.

Discarding some cake may make fairness easier to achieve, but the 1/n guarantee prevents an empty or arbitrarily small allocation. A tight query bound would show whether this freedom substantially reduces the information needed for exact fairness. A lower bound proved only for protocols that allocate everything would need a further argument to cover the more permissive target here.
why: Tests whether discarding some divisible resource removes the main algorithmic cost of exact fairness.
status_note: Model and subsequent-work checks through 11 September 2026 found bounded protocols and the September 2026 single-exponential complete-allocation claim, not matching bounds for this disposal variant. The latter is a preprint and its proofs were not independently verified.
progress: 2016: Bounded protocols are given for partial allocations satisfying both exact envy-freeness and proportionality. | 2026-09: A preprint reports a single-exponential bound for complete allocation, which also gives an upper bound when disposal is optional.
working_summary: A protocol must divide part or all of a cake so that no agent envies another assigned bundle. Every agent must also receive at least one n-th of her value for the entire original cake. The protocol may discard residue and give agents several intervals. Known protocols use a bounded number of exact value and cut queries, and a September 2026 preprint reports a single-exponential complete-allocation bound. The problem asks for matching worst-case query bounds for this more permissive partial-allocation task.

title: Minimum cuts for finite envy-free cake-cutting protocols
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
importance_reason: Separates the complexity of an allocation's geometry from the amount of information a protocol obtains.
formal: For each integer n≥1, determine the least integer c*(n) such that some finite deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol always allocates the entire cake envy-freely among n agents using at most c*(n) final cuts, allowing an agent several disconnected intervals.
definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. The output is a complete partition of the cake into bundles A₁,…,Aₙ. A final cut is an internal endpoint between two positive-length intervals assigned to different agents, after adjacent intervals with the same recipient have been merged. Thus an output with r such successive intervals uses r−1 final cuts; 0 and 1 do not count. Isolated endpoint ownership has no cost or fairness effect. Following the cited Stromquist paper, a point merely queried or marked during the protocol is not a final cut unless it is used as an allocation boundary. A protocol is finite if it terminates after finitely many queries on every profile and every valid sequence of answers. That query count may depend on the valuations and need not be bounded by a function of n; local computation must also terminate. In contrast, the number of final cuts must have the uniform bound c*(n). More formally, c*(n) is the minimum over nonnegative integers c for which such a finite protocol for n agents exists. Bounded complete-allocation protocols show this set is nonempty, so the integer minimum is attained. This question charges output cuts, not evaluation queries, queried marks, or total running time.
answer_criterion: Determine c*(n) exactly for every n, proving both that a finite protocol attains the proposed uniform final-cut bound and that no finite protocol can guarantee a smaller one. A purely existential division with few cuts is insufficient unless a finite protocol can find it. Likewise, an upper bound on total queries does not prove optimality of final cuts.
context:
A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.
why: Separates the complexity of an allocation's geometry from the amount of information a protocol obtains.
status_note: Checked the source’s distinction between queried marks and final cuts and subsequent work through 11 September 2026. No exact all-n minimum for finite protocols under this final-cut convention was located. The September 2026 query bound is a preprint; proofs were not independently audited.

working_summary: The whole cake must be allocated so that every agent prefers her own bundle to anyone else’s. A finite query protocol may give an agent several intervals and may mark more candidate boundaries than it ultimately uses. The objective is the smallest worst-case number of final allocation cuts for each n. Connected envy-free divisions exist, but for n≥3 no finite protocol can always find one. An exact answer would measure the unavoidable fragmentation of an envy-free division that can actually be found by finite interaction.

title: EF1 existence for arbitrary mixed-item utilities
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
area_label: Game theory, social choice and fair division
original_area: Algorithmic game theory and fair division

formal: For every integer n≥3, every finite item set M and every profile of utility functions uᵢ:2^M→ℝ with uᵢ(∅)=0, does there exist a complete allocation A=(A₁,…,Aₙ) such that for every ordered pair of agents i,j there is a set X⊆Aᵢ∪Aⱼ with |X|≤1 satisfying uᵢ(Aᵢ∖X)≥uᵢ(Aⱼ∖X)?
definitions: The n agents are indexed by {1,…,n}. Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when uᵢ(Aᵢ)<uᵢ(Aⱼ). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) for mixed items. If there is no envy, X=∅ works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every n≥3 and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.
context:
With desirable goods, envy can disappear after ignoring a valuable item held by someone else. With burdens, it can disappear after ignoring a costly item in the envious agent’s own bundle. For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

An arbitrary utility can satisfy u({a})=u({b})=1 but u({a,b})=−3. Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.

A positive answer would extend a basic fairness guarantee far beyond additive goods and chores; a negative answer would identify a limit of that guarantee itself.

title: Equilibrium computation for monotone exchange-market utility families
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division

importance_reason: An equilibrium algorithm for an entire monotone-utility class would give a broad tractability result in game theory.
formal: Source target, pending the computational conventions below: can competitive equilibria be computed in polynomial time for exchange markets using any utility family that is monotone in the Chen–Paparas–Yannakakis excess-demand sense? The monotone families here are the complement of the non-monotone families defined below, not all coordinatewise nondecreasing utility functions.
definitions: An exchange market has finitely many divisible goods and traders. Trader i has an initial nonnegative endowment wᵢ and utility uᵢ on nonnegative bundles. At prices p≥0, p≠0, her affordable bundles satisfy p·x≤p·wᵢ, and her demand Dᵢ(p) is the set of utility-maximizing affordable bundles. The aggregate excess-demand correspondence is Z(p)={∑ᵢxᵢ−∑ᵢwᵢ:xᵢ∈Dᵢ(p) for every i}. A competitive equilibrium is a price vector with 0∈Z(p), together with suitable demanded bundles if allocation output is required. The source considers countable utility families U whose members are continuous, quasiconcave and locally nonsatiated: upper contour sets are convex, and arbitrarily close to every bundle there is a bundle of strictly greater utility. Members have binary names and can be applied to selected distinct goods after positive rational coordinate rescaling; U includes a strictly increasing univariate utility. Let M_U consist of finite exchange markets with rational endowments and utilities obtained this way. A market in M_U is non-monotone if, after relabeling goods, there is a strictly positive price vector p and an open neighborhood on which the first coordinate Z₁ is single-valued and continuous, has a continuous partial derivative with respect to the first price, satisfies Z₁(p)≥0 and has ∂Z₁/∂p₁(p)>0. U is non-monotone if some market in M_U has this property, and monotone here means no such market exists. This recovered structural definition does not provide an algorithmic interface to arbitrary named functions. formal: Which restrictions on submodular valuations beyond binary marginal gains permit polynomial-time computation of fair allocations, and which make it intractable? The source particularly asks about three-valued marginal gains and distributional assumptions, across several distinct fairness criteria. A single remaining criterion and valuation model have not been selected.
definitions: There are n agents and a finite set M of m indivisible goods. Agent i has a normalized, nonnegative monotone valuation vᵢ:2^M→ℝ≥0, with vᵢ(∅)=0. Submodularity means vᵢ(S∪{g})−vᵢ(S)≥vᵢ(T∪{g})−vᵢ(T) whenever S⊆T⊆M and g∉T. These differences are marginal gains; binary submodular valuations have gains in {0,1}, while bivalued gains lie in a common set {a,b}. Gains may depend on the items already held. An additive valuation has vᵢ(S)=∑_{g∈S}vᵢ({g}), so its marginal gains do not depend on S. A complete allocation partitions M into bundles X₁,…,Xₙ. Egalitarian welfare is minᵢvᵢ(Xᵢ). Leximin maximizes the vector of utilities sorted in ascending order, using lexicographic comparison. Following the bivalued source, maximum Nash welfare first maximizes the number of agents with positive utility and then their product of utilities. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) requires vᵢ(Xᵢ)≥vᵢ(Xⱼ\{g}) for all i,j and all g∈Xⱼ with vᵢ(Xⱼ)>vᵢ(Xⱼ\{g}). Envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) requires, for every nonempty Xⱼ and each i, some g∈Xⱼ for which that inequality holds. Agent i’s maximin share is MMSᵢ=max_{(P₁,…,Pₙ)} minⱼvᵢ(Pⱼ), over all partitions of M; an α-MMS allocation gives every i at least αMMSᵢ. These criteria are different computational targets. A value oracle answers vᵢ(S) for a queried subset S; an explicit additive input instead lists nm item values. Polynomial query complexity, polynomial bit complexity for a succinct representation, and polynomial time in a full table of 2^m values are not interchangeable. The intended access and numerical conventions remain part of the formulation gap.
answer_criterion: For a specified remaining valuation class and fairness guarantee, prove a precise tractability characterization under a fixed input/access model and explicit hardness assumptions. Existing hardness for maximizing two welfare objectives in the additive ternary subcase is not a classification of all fairness criteria under submodular valuations.
statement_review_issue: The source is a research program across multiple fairness criteria and valuation domains. It does not select the remaining criterion, allowed three-valued or distributional restrictions, exact versus approximate guarantee, valuation representation/access model, or a proposed complete classification. The 2025 ternary additive hardness results settle substantial subcases, but do not specify or settle the entire program. Those choices are required before there is one benchmark theorem to prove.
context:
If v(S)=min{1,|S|}, the first good contributes one and every later good contributes zero. This is binary submodular, even though the value is not a sum of fixed per-item values. Restrictions on marginal gains therefore cover more than additive preference tables.

Leximin prioritizes the least satisfied agent and then breaks ties using the next least satisfied agent. Nash welfare balances a product of utilities. EFX instead compares one agent’s bundle with another agent’s bundle after removal of a good. Efficient optimization of one objective does not automatically give the others.

The 2023 work computes leximin and maximum Nash welfare allocations when positive marginal values are a and b with a dividing b. It also shows that those optima can fail EF1. The arithmetic restriction and the chosen fairness criterion both matter.

The 2025 paper proves APX-hardness of maximum Nash and maximum egalitarian welfare even for additive item values from any fixed {a,b,c} with 0≤a<b<c. In particular, the triple {0,1,2} is already hard. Additive valuations are submodular, so these results obstruct unrestricted exact algorithms for the larger class, assuming P≠NP. They do not settle every EFX, approximate-MMS or distributional question in the seminar contribution.

formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that, given any finite hypergraph H=(V,E) whose vertex–hyperedge incidence matrix is totally unimodular and a strict preference ordering at each vertex over its incident hyperedges, finds a stable matching in time polynomial in the explicit input length? definitions: Hyperedges are explicitly listed nonempty subsets of V. The incidence matrix A has A_(v,e)=1 if v∈e and 0 otherwise; it is totally unimodular when every square submatrix has determinant in {−1,0,1}. Each vertex supplies a strict total order on its incident edges and prefers any such edge to remaining unmatched. With M a matching, an edge e∉M blocks M exactly when every v∈e is unmatched or prefers e to its unique incident edge in M. The promise is total unimodularity, with no bound on hyperedge size; all vertex capacities are one. Input length includes every incidence and preference-list entry. The output is any stable M, without a cardinality or weight objective.

title: Is the matrix multiplication exponent equal to two?
importance_reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.
focus_reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.
formal: Fix the field of complex numbers. Let s(n) be the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit that computes all entries of AB exactly for arbitrary n-by-n matrices A,B. Is it true that $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists C_\varepsilon>0\;\forall n\ge2:\ s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}$? Equivalently, is $\omega=\inf\{\tau:s(n)=O(n^\tau)\}=2$?
definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.
why: Matrix multiplication is a basic operation whose exponent enters many algorithms in linear algebra and graph theory. Determining whether its arithmetic cost can approach the quadratic scale would settle a central question about sharing computation among many related outputs.
status_note: The latest primary upper bound located through 10 September 2026 is the reported omega<2.371177 from August 2026. It leaves the omega=2 question open. The model is exact arithmetic over C; the catalogue has not independently reproduced the numerical certificate.
progress: 1969: Strassen gives O(n^(log₂7)) arithmetic operations, establishing that cubic multiplication is not optimal. | 2018–2019: Alman proves that the universal method applied to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot yield an exponent below 2.16805. This is a limitation of that tensor-based route, not a proof that omega exceeds two. | 2025: The SODA paper More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication gives omega<2.371339 by extending the combination-loss analysis. The original preprint appeared in April 2024. | 2026-08-17: Dupont and coauthors report omega<2.371177. Section 4 describes rounding the optimized parameters to rationals and verifying directed bounds for logarithms; it says the verification repository is being prepared. This catalogue has not independently replayed that certificate. | 2026-08-19: Version 3 of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication incorporates the new optimization bound. The remaining gap to two persists.
