The conjecture is that its circuit size approaches the quadratic output scale, with exponent two. This permits a different algorithm and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Shared intermediate computations already improve substantially on computing every inner product separately, making this a basic test of algebraic efficiency. The saved review describes tensor-method improvements and barriers, while emphasizing that barriers for particular tensors do not constrain every possible circuit.

title: Does the permanent require determinants of superpolynomial dimension?
importance_reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.
focus_reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.
formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence dc_C(permₙ) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every C>0 and integer k≥1, must there be n≥1 such that dc_C(permₙ)>C(n+1)^k?
definitions: The polynomial permₙ(X)=Σ_{σ∈Sₙ}∏_{i=1}ⁿx_{i,σ(i)} has n² algebraically independent commuting variables and degree n; Sₙ is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. Its determinantal complexity dc_C(permₙ) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex m×m matrices A₀ and Aᵢⱼ satisfying the exact polynomial identity permₙ(X)=det(A₀+Σ_{i,j=1}ⁿxᵢⱼAᵢⱼ). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in C[X], for every complex substitution, not only on 0/1 inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.
why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.
status_note: Open in the cited foundational and recent papers; checked through 10 September 2026. This card fixes exact unrestricted representations over C. Symmetric, equivariant, real-field, border, and other-polynomial bounds are not substituted for this model.
progress: 1979: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP. | 2004: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2 using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound. | 2011–2017: Grenet gives a 2ⁿ−1-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open. | 2021: Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound. | 2025: The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open. | 2026: Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.
working_summary: The permanent adds permutation products without the signs that occur in a determinant. This problem asks whether representing it as the determinant of a larger matrix of affine linear forms requires superpolynomial dimension. The representation may use arbitrary complex constants and break all symmetries of the original polynomial. Such a lower bound would separate permanent computation from determinant-like branching programs, rather than automatically from every arithmetic circuit. The saved review places quadratic unrestricted lower bounds beside exponential constructions, leaving a large gap that symmetry-restricted results cannot close.

title: The Shub–Smale τ-conjecture: polynomially many integer roots from short arithmetic programs
importance_reason: A central arithmetic complexity conjecture with a very elementary statement and strong consequences for algebraic P versus NP and constant-free circuit lower bounds.
formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for every nonzero polynomial f∈Z[x], the number z_Z(f) of distinct integer roots satisfies z_Z(f)≤(1+τ(f))^C, where τ(f) is its minimum number of addition, subtraction, and multiplication operations starting only from 1 and x?
definitions: A straight-line program begins with registers containing 1 and the indeterminate x. Each subsequent register contains u+v, u−v, or u·v for two previously available registers; the two operands may be equal. Previously computed registers may be reused without restriction. A designated register must equal f as a formal polynomial over the integers. The cost is the number of arithmetic operations, and τ(f) is the minimum over all such programs. A zero-operation program may output 1 or x. No arbitrary integer constants are supplied: for example 2 must be built as 1+1, and all operations constructing other constants count. Division, comparisons, branching, and exponentiation as a primitive are forbidden. Multiplication counts even when both operands are constants; no bound is placed on intermediate degree or coefficient bit length. This is arithmetic operation count, not bit running time or formula size. Define z_Z(f)=|{a∈Z:f(a)=0}|; repeated roots are counted once. The zero polynomial is excluded. The same universal C must work for all f, regardless of degree, coefficients, or root magnitudes.
answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial bound with one absolute exponent C, or prove that no such exponent exists. A negative answer must yield polynomials violating every candidate polynomial exponent—for example, a family whose integer-root counts grow faster than every fixed power of their exhibited program lengths. One polynomial violating a proposed small exponent, or exponentially many real or complex roots, is insufficient. No uniform efficient procedure for finding the roots is requested.
context:
A short arithmetic program can represent an enormous polynomial. After s squarings, x^(2^s) has exponential degree although its computation has only s operations. Degree therefore gives only the elementary bound z_Z(f)≤2^τ(f). The conjecture says that distinct integer roots are much harder to pack into such a compressed representation than degree alone suggests. Multiplicity cannot replace distinctness: the same repeated-squaring example already has a root of exponential multiplicity.

The restriction to integer roots is substantive. Iterating q_0(x)=x and q_(j+1)(x)=q_j(x)^2−2 uses only a constant number of new operations per stage and gives 2^j distinct real roots for j≥1. Indeed q_j(2 cos θ)=2 cos(2^j θ), so the roots can be written down through distinct cosine values. Thus the unrestricted statement with real roots in place of integer roots is false. Conjectures about real roots of particular sparse sums of products impose additional circuit restrictions.

Shub and Smale connect a polynomial integer-root bound to P_C≠NP_C in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, where exact complex arithmetic has unit cost and branching tests equality. This explains why an apparently elementary univariate question belongs among fundamental complexity problems. The conclusion concerns computation over complex numbers; it must not be silently identified with a proof of Boolean P≠NP.

Rojas develops a p-adic approach, including a reduction showing that a polynomial bound only for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime would already imply the full conjecture. He also bounds rational roots by exp(O(s log(s+1))) in terms of additive complexity s, which charges additions and subtractions while allowing powers and multiplicative structure more freely. This is useful when additive complexity is small; it is not a polynomial bound in the full operation count τ.

The conjecture has consequences beyond the original machine model. Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret recall its implication for separating the constant-free algebraic classes VP^0 and VNP^0, and use it to obtain conditional lower bounds for a variant of the binary value principle in the Ideal Proof System over rational functions. These implications do not establish the conjecture, and their non-Boolean instances do not directly yield Frege lower bounds.

An August 2026 preprint reports exhaustive enumeration through eight operations, using the convention that −1, 0, and 1 are all free. Such a fixed change of constants can be simulated with constant extra cost in the model here, but exact small-length records depend on the convention. The computation is finite experimental evidence and has not been reproduced for this card; it cannot settle the existence of a universal exponent.
why: A precise number-theoretic route to major arithmetic circuit and algebraic machine lower bounds. It probes whether sharing intermediate computations can create many independent integer zeros cheaply, linking computational compression with arithmetic geometry and proof complexity.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The universal integer-root bound remains unresolved in the sources reviewed. The August 2026 census is explicitly a finite computational claim, not a resolution. Full operation count, distinct integer roots, and the exclusion of the zero polynomial are fixed.
progress: 1995: Shub and Smale relate integer-root complexity to the intractability of complex polynomial feasibility and the separation P_C≠NP_C. | 2003: Rojas gives the fixed-prime digit reduction and exp(O(s log(s+1))) rational-root bounds in the different additive-complexity parameter. Neither proves a polynomial root bound in τ. | 2024: Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch, and Tzameret publish conditional Ideal Proof System lower bounds from the τ-conjecture for a binary-value variant over rational functions. | 2026-08-20: Santibañez-Leal’s version 0.03 reports an exact census through eight operations in a convention with free −1,0,1. This finite computational claim is not independently reproduced here and gives no asymptotic resolution.
working_summary: A short arithmetic program can build an integer polynomial from just the constant one and a single variable. The Shub–Smale conjecture asks whether the number of distinct integer roots is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the program length. Repeated squaring shows why the polynomial's degree alone can be enormous despite a compact computation. The proposed root bound connects arithmetic structure to major lower-bound questions by limiting what computational compression can achieve. Arbitrary constants are forbidden and their construction is charged, so changing that convention would change the question substantially.

title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
importance_reason: A basic class equality linking general arithmetic circuits, algebraic branching programs and determinant universality; current symmetry and multilinearity results remain model-specific.
formal: Is VP_ℂ=VBP_ℂ? Explicitly, for every family (f_n)_{n≥1} of commutative polynomials over ℂ with a polynomially bounded number of variables and total degree, if f_n has an arithmetic circuit of size n^O(1), must f_n also have an algebraic branching program of size n^O(1)? The polynomial bounds may depend on the family but not on n; all equalities are exact polynomial identities.
definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output, input gates labelled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, and binary addition or multiplication gates; subtraction is expressible using the constant −1. Intermediate results may be reused without restriction. Size counts gates and wires, with each field constant of unit cost; no division gates are allowed. An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source s and sink t, whose edges are labelled by affine linear forms α₀+∑_j α_j x_j over ℂ. Its output is the sum over all directed s-to-t paths of the product of their edge labels. Its size counts vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients and variable occurrences used in those labels. Layering can be imposed with polynomial overhead but is not required here. There is no width, variable-order, read-once, multilinearity, homogeneity, monotonicity or symmetry restriction. Both circuit and ABP families are nonuniform: no efficient algorithm producing them is required, and complex constants need not have bounded bit descriptions. VP_ℂ consists of the stated polynomial-degree families with polynomial circuit size; VBP_ℂ consists of families with polynomial ABP size and polynomially many variables. Polynomial ABP size already bounds the degree.
answer_criterion: Prove that every family in VP_ℂ admits polynomial-size ABPs, or exhibit a family in VP_ℂ whose minimum ABP size is not polynomially bounded: for every constant c, infinitely many n require more than n^c size. A negative answer must retain small general circuits for the separating family and allow arbitrary complex constants in the competing ABPs. Lower bounds only for multilinear, symmetric, noncommutative, monotone or read-once ABPs do not suffice. Approximation in coefficient space, called border complexity, is a different question.
context:
A circuit can multiply two complicated intermediate results and reuse each of them elsewhere. An ABP has a more linear form of reuse: the polynomial reaching a vertex is obtained by adding predecessor polynomials multiplied by affine edge labels. This is equivalent, with polynomial overhead, to skew circuits, where each multiplication has an input operand that is a variable or constant. The problem asks whether general multiplication and reuse can always be reorganized into this form at only polynomial cost.

The degree restriction rules out an immediate artificial separation. Repeated squaring computes x^{2ⁿ} with n multiplication gates. An ABP with affine labels needs a path of length at least 2ⁿ to produce that degree. This family is excluded from VP because its degree is exponential. The open problem persists when the output degree is polynomial, so a solution must address the structure of efficient computations rather than this simple degree obstruction.

The determinant provides a useful equivalent perspective. Polynomial-size ABPs can be represented by determinants of polynomial-size matrices of affine forms, and the symbolic determinant itself has polynomial-size ABPs. Thus equality would make the determinant universal for all polynomial-degree, polynomial-size circuit computations under polynomial-size affine projections. This differs from the determinant-versus-permanent problem: the permanent is not known to belong to VP, whereas a separation here must already have an efficient circuit on the easy side.

Classical depth reduction supplies a quasipolynomial simulation. If quasipolynomial size is allowed throughout, formulas, ABPs and general circuits compute the same polynomial-degree families. Dutta and coauthors recall this consequence of the Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction in their ITCS 2024 work. What remains unknown is whether the overhead can always be reduced to a fixed polynomial, or whether some efficient circuit computations necessarily resist it.

ABPs also support more algebra than their restricted multiplication rule might suggest. Sinhababu and Thierauf prove that factors of an ABP-computed polynomial have polynomial-size ABPs in characteristic zero. This establishes a closure property that was previously known for general circuits. Sharing factor closure does not establish equality of the models; the June 2026 factoring survey explicitly retains the unresolved chain VF⊆VBP⊆VP.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt’s STOC 2026 work separates symmetric analogues of formulas, skew circuits and general circuits and connects them to graph homomorphism polynomials. These analogues require symmetries of the variables to extend to the computation and measure the largest orbit of gates, rather than simply imposing the ordinary total-size bound. Their separations therefore do not establish VP≠VBP. The work also supplies natural complete polynomial families, potentially useful targets for future unrestricted lower bounds.

A January 2026 paper by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff investigates the min-partition rank method for multilinear ABPs through a combinatorial set-system problem. It recovers a separation between multilinear formulas and multilinear ABPs and studies the potential of the method for stronger lower bounds. The general ABPs in this card can reuse variables along paths and can cancel nonmultilinear terms. A lower bound that forbids those behaviors does not constrain every allowed representation.

A positive answer would show that general efficient algebraic computation can be expressed through path sums and determinants with only polynomial overhead. A negative answer would prove a basic hierarchy inside efficient computation itself. Either result would clarify how much computational power comes from multiplying and reusing rich intermediate expressions, independently of the larger question of whether permanent computation is efficient.
why: One of the central unresolved separations inside algebraic complexity: it asks whether determinant-like path-sum computation captures every efficiently computed polynomial of polynomial degree.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 survey explicitly leaves the VP–VBP inclusion unresolved. STOC 2026 symmetry separations, multilinear lower-bound methods and min-plus-semiring results use different models. This card fixes characteristic zero over ℂ, unrestricted commutative ABPs and exact nonuniform computation.
progress: 1983: Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations; the polynomial-size equality remains stronger. The ITCS 2024 paper reviews this consequence. | 2020–2021: Sinhababu–Thierauf establish polynomial-size factor closure for ABPs in characteristic zero, first in CCC 2020 and then in Computational Complexity. | 2026-01-01: Fabris–Limaye–Srinivasan–Yehudayoff study the power of min-partition rank for multilinear ABPs through combinatorial set systems. | 2026-06: Dwivedi–Pago–Seppelt publish symmetric-model separations and new completeness results at STOC 2026; these do not separate unrestricted VP and VBP. | 2026-06-12: The revised Bhargav–Dwivedi–Saxena survey retains VF⊆VBP⊆VP with no strict containment known, in Remark 7.3.
working_summary: Arithmetic circuits allow intermediate polynomial computations to be reused freely, whereas branching programs represent sums of products along paths. The question asks whether these two models have equal power for polynomial-degree families over the complex numbers when polynomial size is allowed. A positive answer would make determinant-like computation universal for efficiently computed polynomials in this setting. The comparison concerns unrestricted branching programs, with no fixed variable order, width, or multilinearity promise. The obstacle is preserving a polynomial size bound when converting general sharing patterns into path-sum representations, rather than merely constructing some equivalent program.

title: Does the permanent have polynomial-size arithmetic circuits?
importance_reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.
formal: Over the field $\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer n≥1, the polynomial $\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most C(n+1)^k gates? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
definitions: X has n² independent indeterminates and S_n is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families f_n(x)=Σ_{y∈{0,1}^{p(n)}} g_n(x,y), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.
context:
The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.

The permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.

Valiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.

Important partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.

Recent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.
why: This is the central separation question for arithmetic computation. It tests whether summing exponentially many efficiently describable algebraic contributions inherently requires more computation than evaluating one polynomial-size circuit, and organizes lower-bound research across algebra, geometry, and pseudorandomness.
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper still identifies the unrestricted VP-versus-VNP separation as open and explicitly limits its new constructions. No general resolution was located in the status search through 10 September 2026.
progress: 1963: Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion expression gives an exponential-size formula, for example O(n²2^n) arithmetic operations. This substantially improves direct enumeration of n! permutations but remains far above a polynomial bound. | 1979: Valiant establishes algebraic completeness of the permanent over fields of characteristic different from two. Over C this yields the equivalence between polynomial-size permanent circuits and VP=VNP. | 2021: Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds against arithmetic circuits of every constant depth in characteristic zero. Those circuits may have unbounded fan-in, with size accounting for their description; the fixed depth is an essential restriction. The result does not separate general VP and VNP. | 2026-08: Narayanan relates elusive polynomial maps to expansion of iterated sumsets and obtains improved superlinear bounds in certain sublogarithmic-depth regimes. An explicit elusive-curve construction has exponential degree; the paper explains that its parameters do not yet imply VP≠VNP.
working_summary: The permanent sums one matrix-entry product for each permutation of the columns. The question is whether this exponentially described polynomial nevertheless has arithmetic circuits of polynomial size over the complex numbers. Because circuits can reuse expressions and cancel terms, counting its monomials does not establish a lower bound. The problem captures the VP versus VNP question and tests whether algebraically summing efficiently described contributions is inherently expensive. The saved formulation permits arbitrary complex constants but requires exact polynomial equality, so approximation or limits of circuits would address different models.

title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
importance_reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.
formal: Do there exist constants K,C≥1 such that for every n≥1 the symbolic determinant Det_n(X)=Σ_{π∈S_n}sgn(π)∏_{i=1}^n x_{i,π(i)} has an arithmetic formula over the complex numbers with at most K n^C nodes?
definitions: The n² entries x_{ij} of X are distinct commuting indeterminates. S_n is the set of permutations of [n], and sgn(π) is +1 or −1 according to the parity of π. An arithmetic formula is a rooted binary tree. Leaves are labelled by input variables or arbitrary constants from ℂ; internal nodes apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. The output must equal Det_n as a formal polynomial in ℂ[x_{11},…,x_{nn}]. Size counts every node, including each repeated occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subformula. Intermediate results cannot be shared between different parents. Constants are charged unit size, without a bound on their bit description; this is nonuniform algebraic complexity, so no algorithm generating the family is required. Division, comparisons, branching and input-dependent constants are not allowed. Intermediate polynomials may contain higher powers of individual variables and cancellations of those powers; only the final polynomial is required to be the determinant. There is no multilinearity, homogeneity, fixed-depth, monotonicity or bounded-coefficient restriction on intermediate computation. The fixed field ℂ is an explicit characteristic-zero specialization of the inherited question.
answer_criterion: Exhibit polynomial-size formulas with one fixed size exponent for all n, or prove that the minimum formula-size function is not bounded by any polynomial: for every K,C≥1 there is an n for which every allowed formula has more than K n^C nodes. A fixed-power lower bound such as Ω(n³) is insufficient to refute polynomial size. A lower bound restricted to multilinear formulas, noncommuting variables, or bounded depth does not settle this unrestricted commutative formula question.
context:
The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The familiar permutation expansion has n! terms, but this does not prove that every formula is that large. Algebraic identities can compress a sum dramatically, just as a product of short sums can represent many expanded monomials. Conversely, Gaussian elimination is not itself a small formula: its usual presentation reuses entries, performs divisions and selects pivots. Its numerical running time therefore cannot answer the stated symbolic question.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth O(log² n). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size 2^{O(log² n)}=n^{O(log n)}. This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is also a complete problem for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs, whose outputs are sums of products of edge labels along directed source-to-sink paths. Consequently, polynomial-size determinant formulas would imply VF=VBP: every polynomial family having polynomial-size branching programs would have polynomial-size formulas. The larger class VP allows general arithmetic circuits. The June 2026 factoring primer still lists VF⊆VBP⊆VP without a known strict containment and explicitly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved.

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves Ω(n³) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are n² independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power 3/2 in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger n^{Ω(log n)} lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, (x+y)²−x²−y² equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only Θ(n log⁶ n) nonzero entries whose determinants still require n^{Ω(log n)} multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense n²-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.
why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.
status_note: The June 2026 primary survey explicitly retains the question. Sparse and dense multilinear lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted intermediate computations, and recent factoring progress does not furnish determinant formulas. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1984: Berkowitz gives division-free polynomial-size, O(log² n)-depth determinant circuits; unfolding yields quasipolynomial-size formulas. | 1985: Kalorkoti proves an unrestricted Ω(n³) formula lower bound for an n by n determinant, also allowing division. | 2003–2009: Raz establishes n^{Ω(log n)} lower bounds for formulas that remain multilinear at every gate; the original ECCC report precedes the journal publication. | 2019-11-28: Chaugule and coauthors relate formula complexity of Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to the generic determinant. | 2026-06-02: Boyapati–Chillara–Vempati’s sparse-determinant preprint retains the strong multilinear lower bound with Θ(n log⁶ n) nonzero entries; it appears at CCC 2026. | 2026-06-12: The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.
working_summary: The determinant is efficiently computed with arithmetic circuits that can reuse intermediate expressions. This question asks whether polynomial-size arithmetic formulas, whose computation graphs are trees, can also compute it exactly. Each reused subexpression must be copied in a formula, making sharing the central resource under investigation. Resolving the problem would clarify whether a basic linear-algebra operation witnesses a superpolynomial difference between expression trees and circuits. The formulation allows cancellation and arbitrary complex constants, so lower bounds restricted to multilinear, monotone, or bounded-depth formulas do not settle it.

title: The uniform word problem for one-relation monoids
importance_reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.
formal: Is there a single algorithm that, given a finite alphabet A and four finite words u,v,s,t∈A*, always halts and decides whether s and t represent the same element of the monoid presented by ⟨A | u=v⟩?
definitions: A* consists of all finite strings over A, including the empty word ε, with concatenation as multiplication and ε as identity. The presentation ⟨A | u=v⟩ denotes A*/≡, where ≡ is the least equivalence relation containing u≡v that is compatible with concatenation on both sides. Equivalently, s≡t exactly when some finite sequence s=w_0,w_1,…,w_k=t exists in which each adjacent pair is xu y,xv y in either order for some x,y∈A*. The fixed words u and v are literal strings, not variables that can be substituted by arbitrary words. Empty sides are permitted: replacing ε means inserting the other side at a gap in the current string. The alphabet and all four words form a finite explicit input; one may encode A as {1,…,a} and its letters as integers. The requested algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine for all presentations and all word pairs, with no oracle and no unbounded advice. There is no polynomial-time or other prescribed resource bound, but termination is required on both equal and unequal pairs. This is an ordinary monoid presentation. No inverse operation, cancellation law, group axiom or commutativity assumption is present. The presentation itself varies with the input: the card asks for uniform decidability, not merely a separate non-effectively selected procedure for each fixed presentation.
answer_criterion: Construct an always-terminating uniform decision procedure with a correctness proof, or prove that the language of positive presentation-and-word-pair instances is undecidable. One explicit fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem would suffice for a negative answer, but is stronger than is logically required to refute uniform decidability. Enumeration that halts only on equal words, or a procedure whose termination on unequal words is unproved, is insufficient. An exponential derivation-length lower bound is compatible with decidability.
context:
This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

Positive answers are always semidecidable. Enumerate all finite replacement sequences from s and stop if t appears. Every individual stage has finitely many choices, even when one side of the relation is empty. The missing ingredient is an effective stopping argument for negative instances. Seeing no derivation within a long search does not establish inequality when intermediate words may continue to grow.

Length-preserving relations illustrate an easy case. If |u|=|v|, every reachable word has length |s|, so exhaustive search takes place in a finite graph. Unequal input lengths immediately imply inequality. When the relation changes length, that finite-state argument disappears. The question permits enormous running times, so even an impractical computable bound on the needed search would be a meaningful resolution.

Simply orienting a rule toward shorter words need not produce unique normal forms. For the relation baba=aba, the word bababa can shorten through ababa to aaba, or directly to baaba. Neither aaba nor baaba contains baba, so both are irreducible under the shortening rule, although they are equal in the presented monoid. This example shows why termination of one chosen reduction strategy is different from a complete equality test.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family ⟨a,b | baa(ba)^N=a⟩ for N≥2 with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

The inverse-monoid connection is still useful: positive decidability results for the appropriate intermediate class would imply positive results for ordinary one-relation monoids. A negative result in a broader intermediate class need not transfer backwards through that implication. The fundamental goal remains an exact boundary for algorithmic equality under extremely small presentations, with consequences for rewriting systems, normal forms and the ways finite algebraic syntax can encode unbounded computation.
why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?
status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Its inverse-monoid undecidability theorem does not resolve this ordinary presentation problem. Checked through 11 September 2026. The inherited input includes the presentation, so the card explicitly targets uniform decidability and distinguishes it from the per-presentation quantifier.
progress: 1932 and later: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure. | 2021-08-10: Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments. | 2022-09-07: The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure. | 2022-10-28: Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability. | 2026-08-05: Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open.
working_summary: A one-relation monoid allows words to be transformed by repeatedly replacing one fixed word with another in either direction. The reviewed question asks for an algorithm deciding whether two given words become equal under these replacements. Successful derivations can be found by enumeration, but failure to find one does not certify inequality. Decidability would show that even unrestricted length-changing interaction from one rule admits an effective stopping criterion. The saved review notes that finite search works for length-preserving relations, while simple shortening rules need not produce unique normal forms.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
importance_reason: A defining open problem in algebraic computation: randomized polynomial-time search is known, while uniform deterministic polynomial bit complexity remains unresolved even for basic root-finding cases.
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing algorithm that, for every explicitly represented finite field F_q and every nonzero dense univariate f∈F_q[x] of degree n≥1, outputs its complete irreducible factorization using (n+log₂q)^{O(1)} bit operations, with one absolute polynomial bound?
definitions: The field is supplied as F_q=F_p[t]/(h(t)), where p is a binary-encoded prime, h∈F_p[t] is a supplied monic irreducible polynomial of degree e≥1, and q=p^e. These field promises are part of the input specification; no algorithm for constructing h is required. An element is represented by its e coefficients of degree below e, each in {0,…,p−1}. The polynomial f is given by all n+1 coefficients in this representation. Output a unit u∈F_q\{0}, pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials g₁,…,g_r∈F_q[x], and positive integer multiplicities m₁,…,m_r with f=u∏_i g_i^{m_i}. Output order is irrelevant. Arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factors all count in bit time. Repeated factors and characteristic-p inseparability are allowed. The running-time exponent must be independent of n,p,e and f. No randomness, number-theoretic hypothesis, factorization oracle or precomputed field-specific advice is allowed.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives a correct complete-factorization algorithm with the stated uniform worst-case polynomial bit bound for every valid input. A negative answer proves no such algorithm exists in this model; failure of a particular deterministic strategy is insufficient. Polynomial dependence on q or p instead of log q, average-case bounds, fixed-degree results, or conditional algorithms do not resolve the claim.
context:
Finite-field polynomial factorization is a setting where randomization already gives efficient exact algorithms. The desired output has a short representation and is unique up to ordering after normalizing the factors. The open issue is therefore whether random choices are essential for guaranteed efficiency, rather than whether factorization is possible or whether its answer is too large to write down.

The logarithm of the field size is the relevant parameter because one coefficient occupies about log₂q bits. Enumerating all q field elements may be reasonable for a tiny field, but is exponential in the coefficient length when q grows. This distinction is already visible for quadratics over a prime field: the general problem includes finding roots of x²−a modulo an arbitrary large odd prime when a is a quadratic residue.

The field presentation makes a potentially hidden prerequisite explicit. Supplying an irreducible h gives a concrete way to add, multiply and invert extension-field elements using polynomial arithmetic modulo h. The algorithm is not being asked to discover a field representation. At the same time, arithmetic operations are not free: the requested complexity includes their bit cost and must remain polynomial as the extension degree and characteristic vary.

Classical algorithms organize the work into squarefree factorization, separation by irreducible-factor degree, and splitting products whose factors have equal degree. The first two stages have deterministic polynomial-time methods. Randomized equal-degree splitting then completes the factorization efficiently. This organization, surveyed by von zur Gathen–Panario, isolates a concrete source of the derandomization difficulty.

A proposed answer can be checked efficiently without solving the search problem from scratch. Multiplying the claimed factors verifies their product, and finite-field irreducibility tests use modular powering and gcd computations. For a monic polynomial g of degree d, one checks divisibility by x^{q^d}−x and excludes common factors with x^{q^{d/ℓ}}−x for prime divisors ℓ of d. The huge exponents are handled by repeated powering modulo g, not by writing enormous polynomials.

Unconditional deterministic methods do work in time polynomial in n, log q and the characteristic p. Consequently fixed characteristic is already a tractable regime even when the extension field is large. The general obstacle is a large characteristic encoded in only log p bits. Guo’s account records a p^{1/2} dependence up to factors polynomial in n and log q for the best general deterministic methods discussed there.

GRH does not currently remove every obstacle. Evdokimov’s algorithm gives quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, and Galois-theoretic methods obtain polynomial time for certain supplied lifts with controlled groups. Guo’s P-scheme framework extends those special cases and unifies earlier methods. Neither its polynomial-time subclass theorem nor the general quasipolynomial bound is a general deterministic polynomial-time factorization theorem.

The inherited September 2025 paper by Altman changes the averaging question. Starting from one integer polynomial f, it factors its reductions for every prime below a bound N. The average cost per prime is polynomial in the input parameters and the degree m of the splitting field over Q. This gives a strong amortized result when m is polynomially bounded, but m can be as large as n!, and processing all primes below N does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for one arbitrary prime supplied in binary.

Altman also distinguishes averaging over primes from older averaging over input polynomials. A deterministic procedure can run quickly on most randomly selected polynomials and still have hard individual inputs. The present question requires a worst-case bound for every f over every supplied field. Neither kind of averaging can silently replace that quantifier.

Recent multivariate factorization results sometimes suppress the underlying univariate cost in their headline bounds. Chuyoon–Shpilka’s March 2026 paper explicitly restores this dependence in Remark 1.7 and §2.2. Its finite-field subroutine runs in time polynomial in p, log q and the degree; its multivariate theorem includes a factor T for univariate factorization. Specializing the number of variables does not erase that cost.

Umans–Wang’s November 2025 work pursues a different improvement: a number-theoretic conjecture could reduce the degree exponent in fast polynomial-factorization algorithms below the familiar three-halves bound. It also has a separate consequence for deterministic integer factoring. Those are valuable quantitative directions, but the abstract’s deterministic integer result must not be misread as a general derandomization theorem for finite-field polynomials.

The problem is fundamental because polynomial factorization is repeatedly used as a subroutine in symbolic computation and computational number theory. A deterministic solution would make many algorithms independent of randomized splitting choices. A proof that no such solution exists would instead establish a striking separation for an exact algebraic search problem whose answers are efficiently verifiable.
why: A canonical exact derandomization problem in computer algebra, with broad consequences wherever finite-field factorization is used as a subroutine.
status_note: Open unconditionally for all explicitly represented finite fields and dense univariate inputs, based on sources checked through 11 September 2026. GRH alone is not known to give the requested general polynomial bound. Amortization over primes, fixed characteristic, special Galois groups and multivariate bounds retaining a univariate oracle do not resolve this exact question.
progress: 1967–1981: Berlekamp and subsequent randomized splitting algorithms establish the classical framework for finite-field factorization. | 1990: Shoup reduces the characteristic dependence of general deterministic methods to roughly a square root, as reviewed in the later sources. | 1994: Evdokimov obtains deterministic quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, not a general polynomial bound. | 2019–2020: Guo’s P-scheme framework supplies GRH-based polynomial algorithms for additional Galois-group classes and a common treatment of earlier results. | 2025-09-16: Altman gives unconditional amortized factorization over many primes, with dependence on splitting-field degree. | 2025-11-13: Umans–Wang propose a number-theoretic route to better degree exponents in fast factorization; general deterministic finite-field factoring is not resolved. | 2026-03-08: Chuyoon–Shpilka’s sparse multivariate results explicitly retain the univariate-factorization cost and a polynomial dependence on p for the finite-field subroutine.
working_summary: The input is a densely represented univariate polynomial over a finite field whose representation is explicitly supplied. The task is to output all irreducible factors and their multiplicities deterministically in time polynomial in the degree and the logarithm of the field size. This is an exact derandomization question for a central computer-algebra subroutine. The complexity bound must work uniformly across characteristics and extension degrees, with field arithmetic and output writing charged in bit operations. A method relying on randomness, unproved number-theoretic assumptions, or precomputed field-specific advice would leave the stated challenge unresolved.

title: The conjugacy problem for one-relator groups
importance_reason: One of Dehn’s classical algorithmic problems, still unresolved in a basic class defined by a single relation; it tests how far decidability survives beyond word equality.
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, on input a finite one-relator group presentation G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and two words u,v, decides whether some word w satisfies w⁻¹uw=v in G?
definitions: The input consists of an integer k≥1 and three explicitly written finite words r,u,v over the letters x₁,…,x_k and their formal inverses. The group is the quotient of the free group F(x₁,…,x_k) by the normal subgroup generated by r. The relator may be empty, in which case G is free. Equality in the displayed equation is equality in this quotient, rather than literal equality of strings. A conjugating word w may have any finite length. The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine that must halt with the correct yes/no answer for every valid input; the presentation is part of the input. No polynomial-time or other specified resource bound is imposed. This is the uniform decision formulation; a separate algorithm for each fixed group, without an effective way to obtain it from a presentation, is not by itself sufficient.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such presentations and pairs of words, or prove that this input language is undecidable. A one-relator group with an undecidable fixed-group conjugacy problem would suffice for a negative answer. A result only for torsion groups, a decision procedure for word equality, or undecidability of a different equation or membership problem does not settle this question.
context:
A finite presentation describes a group through generators and identities. Here there is just one defining identity, but it can be reused inside arbitrarily long products. The conjugacy question asks whether two elements become equal after a change of reference element: u and v are equivalent when v=w⁻¹uw. It is one of Dehn’s classical decision problems. The 2025 survey explicitly identifies the general one-relator conjugacy problem as unresolved.

Conjugacy is already different from equality in a free group. The words ab and ba are conjugate, since a⁻¹(ab)a=ba, although they represent different free-group elements. At the opposite extreme, the identity element is conjugate only to itself. Consequently, a conjugacy algorithm also decides whether an input word represents the identity, by setting v to the empty word. The reverse implication is the difficult part.

Magnus’s 1932 theorem supplies a uniform algorithm for word equality in one-relator groups. Its inductive approach, clarified through the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, decomposes presentations into simpler group constructions. The corresponding transfer of conjugacy algorithms is much more delicate: the survey gives examples of HNN extensions and amalgams with undecidable conjugacy even though the relevant word problems are decidable. These examples explain a barrier to extending the proof; they are not one-relator counterexamples.

The known word algorithm does at least give a positive semidecision procedure for the present question. Enumerate all finite words w and test whether w⁻¹uwv⁻¹ represents the identity. If u and v are conjugate, a witness eventually appears. If they are not, this search continues forever. A complete decision procedure must also provide a way to terminate on every negative input.

Equivalently, one could give a computable uniform bound on the length of a shortest necessary conjugator as a function of the input length. Such a bound permits a finite search. Conversely, a decision procedure permits computing a bound: enumerate the finitely many inputs of bounded encoding length, identify the positive ones, and search for one witness for each. This observation concerns computability, without claiming that a useful or small bound follows.

The torsion case has been solved for decades. Newman’s 1968 thesis proves decidability of conjugacy for one-relator groups with torsion, including an extended conjugacy problem relative to specified subgroups. Standard presentations for this class have relator R^m with m≥2 and R not a proper power. The spelling theorem controls the possible cancellations strongly enough to support effective arguments. A solution for this class leaves the general torsion-free case to address.

A later structural theorem gives another source of negative certificates in the torsion case. Minasyan–Zalesskii prove that one-relator groups with torsion are hereditarily conjugacy separable: nonconjugate elements in every finite-index subgroup remain nonconjugate in some finite quotient of that subgroup. In particular, for the original group, a finite quotient can witness a negative conjugacy answer.

To see the algorithmic significance, enumerate finite multiplication tables and assignments of the presentation’s generators that satisfy its relator. Each assignment defines a homomorphism to a finite group, where conjugacy can be checked exhaustively. In a conjugacy-separable group, this search eventually finds a separating image for every nonconjugate pair. Run it alongside the search for a conjugator. The argument requires the separation property; finite images alone are not a general-purpose certificate system.

Recent developments illustrate why the exact decision problem matters. Gray–Levine prove undecidability of Diophantine problems in several classes close to one-relator groups, and also obtain undecidability with a fixed subgroup constraint in a one-relator group. General systems of equations, or restrictions on where variables may range, are more expressive than the single unrestricted conjugacy equation on this card. Undecidability for those tasks does not imply undecidability here.

Nyberg-Brodda’s August 3, 2026 preprint goes further: it proves that the unrestricted Diophantine problem is undecidable in certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. Its introduction still explicitly identifies general one-relator conjugacy as open. Undecidability for arbitrary systems of equations therefore cannot be substituted for undecidability of the special single conjugacy equation.

Gray–Reilly’s August 2026 preprint constructs two-generator one-relator inverse monoids with undecidable word problem. It also constructs a two-generator one-relator group with an undecidable prefix membership problem. Inverse monoids are a different algebraic structure, while prefix membership asks about a particular submonoid of the group. Neither result contradicts Magnus’s word algorithm or supplies a conjugacy counterexample.

The significance is a sharp computability boundary inside an extremely economical symbolic formalism. One defining group relation is sufficient to create complicated infinite behavior, yet ordinary equality remains decidable. Settling conjugacy would determine whether this additional existential search can always be controlled. A very slow total algorithm would answer the card; an efficient algorithm for a broad but restricted subclass would be progress without completing it.
why: A central decision problem at the boundary between decidable symbolic equality and existential reasoning in finitely presented algebraic structures.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general conjugacy problem remains open in the checked primary literature. This card fixes the uniform presentation-input formulation. The 2026 undecidability results cited concern different equation, membership or inverse-monoid problems.
