title: The isomorphism problem for one-relator groups
importance_reason: A classical unresolved computability boundary with deep connections to geometric group theory, effective classification and the limitations of presentation-based invariants.
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given any two finite one-relator group presentations G=⟨x₁,…,x_k | r=1⟩ and H=⟨y₁,…,y_ℓ | s=1⟩, decides whether G and H are isomorphic as abstract groups?
definitions: The input consists of integers k,ℓ≥1 and explicitly written finite words r and s in the respective generators and formal inverses. The groups are the free groups on these generators modulo the normal closures of r and s. An empty relator is permitted and presents a free group. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the resulting abstract groups; it need not carry a listed generator to a listed generator, preserve the spelling of a relator, or come from an automorphism of a free group on the given generators. The numbers of displayed generators may differ. The sought procedure is one deterministic Turing machine which halts and answers correctly on every valid pair of presentations. No polynomial-time, elementary-time or other quantitative runtime bound is imposed. There is no promise of torsion, hyperbolicity, nontrivial center, genericity or a supplied geometric decomposition.
answer_criterion: Give a uniform terminating decision procedure for all such pairs, or prove that the isomorphism language on these one-relator presentations is undecidable. A procedure that halts only for isomorphic pairs, or one correct only on a specified subclass or almost all random presentations, is insufficient. Undecidability for arbitrary finite presentations, systems of equations or other algebraic structures must be connected to this exact input class by a valid reduction to count as a negative solution.
context:
A group presentation is a finite description of an often infinite algebraic object. The same group can have quite different descriptions: for example, ⟨a,b | b=a²⟩ and ⟨x | empty relator⟩ both describe an infinite cyclic group. The question is whether one defining relation leaves enough structure to recognize abstract equality of group types algorithmically, even when the supplied generators and words look unrelated.

This is the third of Dehn’s classical decision problems. Word equality compares elements within one fixed presentation; conjugacy asks for a particular kind of equivalence between elements; isomorphism compares the entire groups. Linton and Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the general one-relator isomorphism problem as open, despite broad positive results for subclasses.

The known uniform word algorithm gives a useful positive semidecision procedure. Enumerate possible word images u₁,…,u_k for the generators of G in H and v₁,…,v_ℓ for the generators of H in G. Check that the images satisfy each defining relation and that the two compositions fix every generator. Every check is a finite collection of word-equality tests. If mutual inverse homomorphisms exist, their finite descriptions eventually appear.

The missing part is termination on nonisomorphic inputs. Searching longer for generator images cannot certify that none exist. Equivalently, an effective bound on the lengths of some pair of mutually inverse generator-image tuples, depending only on the input length, would permit a finite search. Conversely, a total isomorphism algorithm would allow such a computable bound to be assembled by checking the finitely many inputs of bounded length and finding witnesses for the positive cases.

Easily computable invariants can reject some pairs. Abelianization, for example, takes the exponent sums of the relator and gives a finitely generated abelian quotient whose isomorphism type can be computed by integer linear algebra. But it is incomplete: the free group on two generators and ℤ² have the same abelianization, whereas one is nonabelian and the other is abelian. The free group is represented here using the allowed empty relator, and ℤ² by the commutator relation.

Another tempting simplification is to ask whether an automorphism of the free group carries one relator to the other, allowing inversion. Whitehead’s algorithm handles the corresponding orbit question. The survey explains that this sufficient condition is not necessary for isomorphism of the quotient groups: the Magnus conjecture asserting such a converse was disproved, and some groups have infinitely many inequivalent one-relator descriptions.

Hyperbolic groups form a large positive case. Dahmani and Guirardel solve isomorphism uniformly for all hyperbolic groups, including those with torsion. Their result also handles peripheral structures and automorphism computations, reflecting how geometric decompositions can organize otherwise unbounded searches. It is a decision theorem, not merely a heuristic for finding likely isomorphisms.

All one-relator groups with torsion are hyperbolic, so this theorem covers that entire subclass. The survey also records decidability for one-relator groups with nontrivial center and other structured families. General torsion-free one-relator groups remain beyond these combined results. Even elementary examples such as ℤ² show that the one-relator condition does not imply hyperbolicity.

Generic-case results explain why many randomly generated instances may nevertheless be tractable. Kapovich, Schupp and Shpilrain establish rigidity for large classes of random one-relator presentations: isomorphism can be forced by simple transformations of the displayed generators and relator. The exceptional inputs are small in a specified distributional sense, but an undecidable set of inputs could still lie among such exceptions.

Kapovich’s August 18, 2026 preprint extends a generic rigidity program to fixed numbers of generators and relators. It gives an algorithmically recognizable generic family and a quadratic-time generic isomorphism algorithm, using small-cancellation stability and rigidity under free-group automorphisms. Its one-relator specialization is relevant progress, while its guarantee remains a generic one rather than a terminating decision procedure for every input.

A different August 2026 result by Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability of the Diophantine problem for certain one-relator Baumslag–Gersten groups. That task asks whether arbitrary systems of equations with coefficients have solutions. It demonstrates that one relation does not ensure decidability of every natural algebraic question. However, it supplies no automatic reduction to isomorphism between two one-relator presentations, so the present problem remains distinct.

A resolution would clarify whether this very economical presentation format has an effective classification in principle. The positive answer could be extremely slow and still be decisive. The negative answer would require encoding undecidable information into abstract group type while retaining a single defining relator—a much more specific construction than demonstrating difficult equations inside one fixed group.
why: One of the central decision problems for finitely presented groups, testing whether a single defining relation permits effective recognition of abstract algebraic structure.
status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform algorithm or undecidability theorem for isomorphism of arbitrary one-relator group presentations was found in the checked sources. The 2026 generic algorithms and Diophantine undecidability result do not settle this all-input isomorphism question.
progress: 1970s: Counterexamples to the Magnus conjecture show that free-group equivalence of relators cannot characterize all isomorphisms; torsion and center subclasses admit positive results. | 2003–2006: Kapovich–Schupp–Shpilrain obtain strong generic rigidity and fast isomorphism algorithms for random one-relator groups. | 2010–2011: Dahmani–Guirardel solve isomorphism for all hyperbolic groups, covering one-relator groups with torsion. | 30 January 2025: Linton–Nyberg-Brodda’s survey records the unrestricted one-relator isomorphism problem as open. | 3 August 2026: Nyberg-Brodda proves undecidability for the separate Diophantine problem in one-relator groups. | 18 August 2026: Kapovich’s preprint extends generic small-cancellation stability and isomorphism rigidity to fixed generator and relator counts.
working_summary: Two group presentations can describe the same abstract group despite using different generators and relations. The reviewed question asks to decide isomorphism between arbitrary finite one-relator presentations. Candidate mutually inverse homomorphisms can be enumerated and checked using the known word algorithm. The missing ingredient is an effective way to stop when no such isomorphism exists. A solution would distinguish complete algebraic types within this concise presentation class, extending beyond equality and conjugacy questions about elements of one already fixed group.

title: The optimal bit complexity of integer multiplication
importance_reason: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n→∞, the optimal worst-case running time for exactly multiplying two n-bit nonnegative binary integers by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine. The target is an attainable asymptotic upper bound with a matching lower bound for every correct machine in this model.
definitions: For every integer n≥1 the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with 0≤a,b<2^n; leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let t_M(n) be its maximum running time over the 2^(2n) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate g(n)>0 means some correct M has t_M(n)=O(g(n)), while every correct M has t_M(n)=Ω(g(n)); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only O(n).
answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate g(n) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in O(g(n)) worst-case time and an Ω(g(n)) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.
context:
For example, 11₂ multiplied by 11₂ is 1001₂: the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes O(n log n) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an s×s binary matrix written row by row. Even a 2×2 matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs Ω(s² log s) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies Ω(n log n) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.
why: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.
status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted multitape lower bound open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching bound or faster general algorithm; the August 2026 OBDD result concerns a different model.
progress: 2021: An O(n log n) deterministic multitape upper bound is published. It does not include a matching lower bound. | 2025-03: A conjectured optimal matrix-transposition lower bound is shown to imply the corresponding multiplication lower bound. | 2026-08: New OBDD-width bounds concern a restricted branching-program model and do not close the multitape time gap.
working_summary: What is the optimal worst-case bit complexity of multiplying two n-bit integers? The model charges individual steps of a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine. An O(n log n) algorithm is known, but only a linear general lower bound is established. A 2025 theorem connects the conjectured matching lower bound to the unresolved cost of matrix transposition. Bounds for restricted branching programs do not determine the optimal cost in this model.

title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture for concise cubic tensors
importance_reason: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.
formal: For every n≥1 and every tensor T∈ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n whose three flattenings all have rank n, is lim_{k→∞} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k)=n?
definitions: R(T) is the least r such that T=Σ_{i=1}^r a_i⊗b_i⊗c_i with a_i,b_i,c_i∈ℂ^n. Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In T^⊗k the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors ℂ^(n^k). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to inf_{k≥1} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k). This is exact rank over ℂ, not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.
why: A structural conjecture about the cost of all bilinear computations, extending well beyond one matrix-multiplication algorithm.

progress: 2024: The source establishes algebraic characterizations and upper semicomputability properties of asymptotic rank; the general conjecture is retained.

title: Unrestricted arithmetic lower bounds for the discrete Fourier transform
importance_reason: Tests whether the central FFT upper bound is inherently necessary in unrestricted arithmetic computation.
formal: Let S(n) be the minimum size of a complex arithmetic straight-line program that computes all n coordinates of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) exactly, in the model below. Do constants c>0 and N exist such that S(n)≥c n log₂n for every power of two n≥N, with no bound on the magnitudes of the constants used in the program?
definitions: For n≥1 set ω_n=exp(−2πi/n), and define DFT_n(x)_j=Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}ω_n^{jk}x_k for j=0,…,n−1 and x∈ℂ^n. This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every c>0 and every threshold N there is a power of two n≥N and a program of size less than c n log₂n. A family using o(n log n) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.
context:
For four inputs, form a=x₀+x₂, b=x₁+x₃, c=x₀−x₂ and d=x₁−x₃. The four Fourier outputs are a+b, c−id, a−b and c+id. Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain O(n log n) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

Dividing all outputs by √n gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is n^{n/2}, whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

The target covers every sufficiently large power-of-two input length and all straight-line programs in the stated model. The FFT achieves this cost by sharing intermediate computations. title: Do single-pair shortest paths require cubic-size min-plus circuits?
importance_reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.
formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
context:
The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. title: Does integer multiplication have linear-size Boolean circuits?
importance_reason: A basic arithmetic operation supplies a concrete candidate for a central circuit-lower-bound barrier. The question is explicitly highlighted in Goldreich’s textbook and retained in Viola’s current manuscript; its nonuniform target is distinct from the catalogue’s machine-time question.
formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and n₀≥1 such that, for every integer n≥n₀, a Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
definitions: The circuit has input bits a₀,…,a_{n−1},b₀,…,b_{n−1}, representing a=Σᵢaᵢ2ⁱ and b=Σᵢbᵢ2ⁱ, and output bits c₀,…,c_{2n−1} satisfying Σⱼcⱼ2ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let M(n) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is M(n)=O(n). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every n₀ there is n≥n₀ with M(n)>Cn. A lower bound c·n with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.
context:
Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

title: Can the shortest addition-chain length be computed in polynomial time?
importance_reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem at the intersection of arithmetic algorithms, circuit reuse and cryptographic exponentiation. Its single-target complexity is repeatedly distinguished from the solved hardness of the generalized problem; it is not a numerical special case of Scholz–Brauer.
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given an integer n≥1 in binary, outputs its exact shortest addition-chain length ℓ(n) in time polynomial in the binary input length?
definitions: An addition chain for n is a strictly increasing sequence of integers 1=a₀<a₁<⋯<aᵣ=n such that, for every i≥1, there are j,k<i with aᵢ=aⱼ+aₖ; j=k is allowed. Its length is r, the number of additions, so ℓ(1)=0. The input is the ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, of length b=⌊log₂n⌋+1. The output is ℓ(n) in binary. One fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine must halt within p(b) steps on every input, for one fixed polynomial p. All bit operations and output writing count. Subtraction, arbitrary constants other than the initial 1, and multiplication of previously formed exponents are not allowed chain operations. Chain entries can be reused arbitrarily. The cost of finding ℓ(n) is distinct from the number ℓ(n) of steps in the chain itself.
answer_criterion: Give such an exact algorithm with one polynomial bound, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An approximation to ℓ(n), a fast heuristic, polynomial time in n rather than log n, or exact results for a restricted family of exponents do not resolve the question. NP-hardness of a multiple-target variant does not establish hardness for this single-target problem. Conditional hardness must retain its assumption.
context:
Exponentiation can reuse powers: multiplying aʲ and aᵏ produces a^{j+k}. Thus a chain specifies a multiplication-only program for an arbitrary formal power aⁿ. Erickson’s notes explain why repeated squaring uses O(log n) multiplications and then ask whether the absolute minimum count can be computed efficiently.

For example, 1,2,3,5,10,15 gives five multiplications for a¹⁵. A convenient repeated-squaring implementation can use six. This small difference illustrates the exact optimization target: the asymptotic order of the chain length is already understood, while selecting its optimal integer value can require much more search.

Each chain step can at most double its largest entry, giving ℓ(n)≥⌈log₂n⌉. Reading the binary digits of n gives a chain with at most 2⌊log₂n⌋ steps. Consequently a shortest chain has O(b) entries of at most b bits. Exhaustive enumeration is finite and yields an exact algorithm, but not a polynomial bound in b.

The decision problem “ℓ(n)≤k?” is in NP: a short chain, together with its predecessor indices, is a polynomial-size certificate. Computing the exact length is equivalent to deciding these thresholds in polynomial time, by searching between the elementary bounds. This observation does not establish NP-completeness.

Koziel and coauthors explicitly distinguish the single-target problem from the generalized task of forming several specified values, for which NP-completeness is known. Their work develops efficient chains for cryptographic arithmetic. The 2025 primary article by Kempes and coauthors likewise describes the exact complexity of the single-target problem as unknown.

The Scholz–Brauer conjecture already appears as TCS-7170. It bounds ℓ(2ⁿ−1) in terms of ℓ(n); even its resolution would not supply a polynomial-time method for finding ℓ(n) on arbitrary binary input. The present algorithmic question has a different conclusion and computational significance.

working_summary: An explicitly represented arithmetic circuit can contain many cancellations, making zero output difficult to recognize from its syntax. The question asks for an efficient deterministic polynomial identity test using that circuit description. Unlike black-box testing, the algorithm may inspect the graph and exploit how intermediate expressions are built.
