title: The capacity region of a general two-receiver broadcast channel
importance_reason: A central multiuser capacity problem with a precisely defined rate region, decades of partial characterizations and recent challenges to the longstanding candidate inner bound.
formal: Determine the weighted capacity F(W,λ)=sup{λR₁+(1−λ)R₂:(R₁,R₂)∈C(W)} for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless broadcast channel W(y,z|x) with rational transition probabilities and every rational λ∈[0,1]. C(W) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, vanishing average decoding error, and no feedback. Require a characterization admitting certified evaluation to arbitrary accuracy as specified below.
definitions: The nonempty finite alphabets X,Y,Z and the full table of nonnegative rational numbers W(y,z|x), summing to one for each x, are explicitly given. Over n uses, the conditional law is ∏_{t=1}^n W(y_t,z_t|x_t). Independent messages M₁ and M₂ are uniform on sets of sizes K₁ and K₂. One deterministic encoder, knowing both messages, sends xⁿ=f(M₁,M₂); receiver 1 observes only Yⁿ and estimates M₁, while receiver 2 observes only Zⁿ and estimates M₂. The average error is Pr[the first estimate is wrong or the second estimate is wrong], averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A rate pair is achievable if there are codes with block lengths tending to infinity, error tending to zero, and liminf (log₂Kᵢ)/n≥Rᵢ for i=1,2. C(W) is the closure of achievable nonnegative pairs. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, secrecy constraint, input-cost constraint or restriction on code complexity. Arbitrary dependence among a codeword’s symbols and time sharing are allowed. C(W) is compact, convex and downward closed; its support values for all rational λ determine it. Rational channel laws make the evaluation task a finite-input question.
answer_criterion: Give a matching achievability and converse characterization together with one terminating algorithm that, on input (W,λ,p), where p≥1 is an integer, outputs rational ℓ≤u with u−ℓ≤2⁻ᵖ and ℓ≤F(W,λ)≤u. No efficiency bound or single-letter restriction is imposed. A finite-dimensional formula with justified auxiliary-cardinality bounds, or a multiletter characterization with an effective certified convergence bound, would qualify. A bare limit over all block codes, an unevaluated regularization without an error bound, or numerically close inner and outer estimates does not. A proof that such uniform certified evaluation is impossible would instead settle the computability obstruction to this formulation.
context:
A broadcast channel has one transmitter that knows both messages and two receivers with different observations. This differs from an interference channel, whose transmitters know separate messages. The difficulty is to use one sequence of transmitted symbols for two purposes simultaneously: some structure can help both receivers, while other structure must carry information tailored to only one. A capacity region records all achievable tradeoffs, not just the best sum of rates.

The two point-to-point capacities alone do not determine this tradeoff. If a noiseless binary symbol X is delivered identically to both receivers, each receiver separately has capacity one, but independent private messages must satisfy R₁+R₂≤1. If X instead consists of two bits and each receiver gets its own bit, the region is the square 0≤R₁,R₂≤1. Both examples have the same individual capacities and different joint possibilities.

Marton’s coding method introduces auxiliary random variables describing private and shared layers and uses correlated codebooks to coordinate their information. Its inner region is achievable, so it gives a lower bound on capacity. For important structured channel classes it is exact, but neither efficient evaluation of that inner region nor optimality on those classes determines the general answer.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite auxiliary-cardinality bounds for Marton’s region, turning the previously unrestricted optimization into a computable finite-dimensional problem. They also show that Marton’s inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region differ for some channels. A gap between an achievable region and an outer bound alone does not reveal which bound is loose; it is not evidence that an intermediate numerical value is capacity.

There is already an exact multiletter perspective: applying Marton’s construction to successively larger product channels and regularizing recovers the operational capacity region. Geng, Gohari, Nair and Yu develop this approach and establish new special cases. The obstacle in the present formulation is a certified finite answer: an asymptotic union without an effective convergence guarantee does not tell us how many channel uses must be examined for a requested accuracy.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s August 2026 preprint claims strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton region. It first finds a ternary-input example with a fixed-input-distribution advantage for two-letter coding, supported by interval-arithmetic bounds. A separate constraint-removal construction then produces a finite unconstrained channel with M(W⊗W)>2M(W), where M is Marton’s maximum private-message sum-rate. The unconstrained example has an enlarged alphabet; the result should not be stated as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample.

That claimed inequality means a two-use code can beat the one-letter inner bound after normalizing rates per use. It does not compute capacity: further block lengths may improve the region again, and a matching converse is still needed. The paper explicitly retains the general capacity question as open. Its numerical certificates and auxiliary construction have not been independently rerun as part of this card.

On the converse side, Gohari, Liu and Nair’s ISIT 2026 work introduces two auxiliary receivers to strengthen outer bounds. These are hypothetical observers used in the proof, not additional terminals allowed in the communication model. Their reported bounds improve the sum-rate upper bound for examples such as the binary skew-symmetric broadcast channel, while still leaving an inner/outer gap.

Finding globally optimal numerical values is also separate from deriving the correct region. Dou and coauthors develop Blahut–Arimoto-style methods for evaluating inner and outer bounds, with convergence statements tied to the optimization’s structure. Such methods help explore examples, but convergence to a local optimum or to an optimum of an unproved bound is not a capacity theorem.
why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.
status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general capacity question remains open in the checked primary literature, including the August 2026 paper. That paper’s narrower Marton-suboptimality claim is identified as a preprint result; accepting it would not solve the full characterization or certified-evaluation task.
progress: 1979: Marton develops the general achievable region based on correlated auxiliary codebooks. | 2009–2012: Gohari–Anantharam prove finite cardinality bounds and computability of Marton’s inner region, while exhibiting gaps from a known outer region. | 2014: Geng and coauthors study product channels, regularization and new classes where Marton is optimal. | 2024-02-20: Dou and coauthors publish numerical algorithms for inner and outer bounds; these evaluate bounds rather than settle their tightness. | 2026: Gohari–Liu–Nair obtain stronger outer bounds using two auxiliary receivers, with strict improvements on example channels. | 2026-08-20: Huang–Liu–Liu post a claimed counterexample to one-letter Marton optimality, first with an input-distribution constraint and then on an enlarged unconstrained channel. The full capacity region remains unknown.
working_summary: A broadcast channel sends one transmitter's input to two receivers with different noisy observations. The reviewed question seeks the exact private-message capacity region together with certified evaluation to arbitrary accuracy. One codeword must simultaneously carry information useful to each receiver, creating tradeoffs not determined by their individual capacities. A full characterization would resolve a fundamental multi-user communication problem beyond particular channel families. The saved review describes gaps between inner and outer bounds and an unverified 2026 claim that two-letter coding can outperform the full one-letter Marton region.

title: The Li–Li undirected multiple-unicast conjecture
importance_reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.
formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
definitions: Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities c_e>0, and let (s_i,t_i), i=1,…,k, be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source s_i initially knows its own message M_i, uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every t_i must recover M_i for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let X_{u→v} be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge {u,v}, and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale b>0, the code supports r∈R_{≥0}^k when H(M_i)≥b r_i for all i and H(X_{u→v})+H(X_{v→u})≤b c_{uv} for every edge. Define C(G) as the closure in R^k of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define R(G) by nonnegative real path flows f_{i,P}, for simple s_i-to-t_i paths P, satisfying Σ_P f_{i,P}≥r_i and Σ_{i,P:e∈P} f_{i,P}≤c_e. The target is C(G)=R(G) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
answer_criterion: Prove C(G)⊆R(G) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
context:
Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send x⊕y; a receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small K_{3,2} example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is 3/4; their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed 3/4. The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an Ω(n log n) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.
why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.
status_note: The August 2026 primary papers explicitly leave the general conjecture unresolved. This card fixes causal zero-error coding with entropy capacities and closure of rates, as in the cited formal model. Restricted topology results, multicast gains and alternative error conventions are distinguished. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.
progress: 2004: Li and Li formulate the undirected no-coding-advantage conjecture, as recorded in the subsequent primary literature. | 2005: Jain and coauthors prove that the four-session K_{3,2} example has coding rate equal to routing rate 3/4. | 2017: Braverman–Garg–Schvartzman show that any constant strict advantage amplifies to a polylogarithmically growing gap. | 2019: Afshani and coauthors derive conditional multiplication-circuit lower bounds from the conjecture. | 2025-06: Vamsi–Thakor analyze specified asymmetric demands in layered networks. | 2025-10-21: Braverman–He give superconstant undirected multicast gaps; the unicast conjecture is explicitly left open. | 2026-08-06: Liu–Que–Li–Li report metric-based proofs for further network classes, including at most five terminal locations. | 2026-08-06: A separate session-interaction framework reduces the conjecture to a property of all irreducible cores; it does not establish that property universally. Its manuscript corrects a quantifier in the conference definition to require one common witnessing solution.
working_summary: In an undirected communication network, routing sends independent messages along paths and may split each message among several routes. Network coding additionally allows intermediate nodes to combine information from different messages. The Li-Li conjecture says that coding does not enlarge the achievable rate region for independent unicast sessions beyond fractional multicommodity routing. The saved formulation uses zero-error causal coding and one shared capacity budget for both directions of each edge. A proof or counterexample would determine whether coding provides a fundamental throughput advantage in undirected networks after routing has already been optimized globally.

title: The exact capacity of the binary deletion channel
importance_reason: The canonical capacity problem for synchronization errors, connecting coding, information theory, sequence reconstruction and the structure of optimal input processes.
formal: Determine the capacity function C(δ) of the binary independent deletion channel for every fixed δ∈[0,1], in bits per input bit, with matching achievability and converse results.
definitions: For input x=x₁⋯x_n∈{0,1}^n, retain each bit independently with probability 1−δ and output the retained subsequence in its original order. The receiver sees the subsequence and its length, but neither terminal sees the deletion locations; there are no erasure markers, substitutions, insertions, feedback or side channels. Both terminals know n and δ. A block code consists of deterministic maps Enc_n:[M_n]→{0,1}^n and Dec_n:⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k→[M_n]. Its average error is Pr[Dec_n(Y)≠M], where M is uniform on [M_n] and Y is the channel output on Enc_n(M). A rate R is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with liminf_{n→∞}(log₂ M_n)/n≥R and average error tending to zero. Define C(δ) as the supremum of achievable nonnegative rates. Encoding and decoding have no computational or storage restrictions. The parameter δ is fixed as n grows. Equivalently, Dobrushin’s coding theorem gives C(δ)=lim_{n→∞} C_n(δ), where C_n(δ)=(1/n) max_{P_X on {0,1}^n} I(X;Y), with base-two mutual information. These C_n are normalized per input bit; the random output length is not the normalization. The endpoints are C(0)=1 and C(1)=0.
answer_criterion: Give the exact capacity curve, with codes approaching the proposed rate from below and a converse showing that no higher rate has vanishing average error, for each fixed δ. The displayed multiletter limit already defines and characterizes the quantity; simply restating it is not a new determination of capacity. A capacity result at one interior parameter, a finite-block numerical interval, or a finite-order expansion near an endpoint is valuable partial progress rather than resolution of the whole curve.
context:
A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity 1−δ. Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so C(δ)≤1−δ is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The basic coding theorem is known. Optimizing mutual information over distributions on n-bit inputs and letting n grow gives the operational capacity. Moreover, C_n(δ)−log₂(n+1)/n≤C(δ)≤C_n(δ). Thus the issue is not the absence of a definition or an approximation scheme in principle. The finite optimization has 2^n possible inputs, and its rapidly growing size obstructs useful evaluation at large block lengths.

The input bits should not automatically be assumed independent. Correlations can make runs of equal symbols easier to identify after deletions. Run-based constructions choose a distribution on run lengths and analyze how deleted runs disappear and neighboring surviving runs merge. Rubinstein and Con optimize such distributions to prove C(δ)>0.1221(1−δ) for every 0<δ<1. This establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the parameter range.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove C(δ)=1+δ log₂ δ−A₁δ+A₂δ²+O(δ^{3−ε}) for every fixed ε>0 as δ tends to zero, with explicit constants A₁≈1.15416377 and A₂≈1.67814594. They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports C(δ)≤0.3578(1−δ) for δ≥0.64. These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

The half-deletion point illustrates the remaining gap. Rubinstein and Con report an achievable rate above 0.104075, while the 2026 upper-bound table gives 0.1896. A universal lower bound proportional to 1−δ is useful for the whole curve, but it can be weaker than a pointwise run-length optimization. These different types of statements should therefore not be collapsed into one purported best numerical bound for every parameter.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the exact Shannon capacity requested here.
why: The simplest channel with hidden synchronization errors still lacks an exact nontrivial capacity formula. Resolving it would establish how much information is fundamentally lost through missing alignment.
status_note: The 2026 primary sources retain a gap between achievable rates and converses. The August half-deletion improvement is recorded as an unreplicated preprint claim, not an exact-capacity solution. Checked through 11 September 2026.
progress: 1967: Dobrushin establishes a coding theorem relating operational capacity of synchronization channels to normalized multiletter mutual information. | 2013: Kanoria–Montanari determine the small-deletion expansion through the δ² term and input processes achieving that order. | 2023-05-11: Rubinstein–Con improve run-based achievable rates and finite-channel numerical converses; their universal lower bound is 0.1221(1−δ). | 2026-04-07: Pinto–Ribeiro improve computer-assisted upper bounds, including 0.3578(1−δ) for δ≥0.64 and a reported 0.1896 upper bound at δ=1/2. | 2026-08-03: Chen posts a claimed certified lower bound C(1/2)>0.11032415. The preprint and its limits are recorded; the numerical certificate is not independently reproduced in this review.
working_summary: The binary deletion channel independently removes transmitted bits and hides their original positions. The question asks for its exact capacity as a function of deletion probability, measured per input bit. Missing alignment makes this harder than an erasure channel that marks where losses occurred. Matching achievable rates and converse bounds would quantify the fundamental cost of synchronization uncertainty. The saved review describes finite-block optimization, run-based coding, and remaining numerical gaps, while recording a recent lower-bound claim as unverified and separating transmission capacity from trace reconstruction.

title: Do binary codes beat the Gilbert–Varshamov rate asymptotically?
importance_reason: Determine whether the basic random-coding benchmark is an intrinsic binary information limit.
formal: Do constants δ∈(0,1/2) and η>0 and binary codes C_n⊆{0,1}^n for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least δn and log₂|C_n|/n≥1−H₂(δ)+η?
definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. H₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t). The constants δ and η must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
context:
The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.
why: Determine whether the basic random-coding benchmark is an intrinsic binary information limit.
status_note: Source-backed open target. The source and relevant later-work search were reviewed on 11 September 2026; this is a bounded literature review, not a proof that no resolution exists.
progress: 2025: The materials distinguish the existential binary rate-distance gap from explicit construction and list decoding.

title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
importance_reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.
formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given n≥1 and rational coefficients (a_S) for nonempty subsets S⊆{1,…,n}, always halts and decides whether Σ_{∅≠S⊆[n]}a_S H(X_S)≥0 holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. X_S is the tuple (X_i)_{i∈S}. Its Shannon entropy in bits is H(X_S)=−Σ_x p_S(x)log₂ p_S(x), with 0log₂0=0. Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in [0,1] summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict ≥0 and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.
context:
For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with 2^n−1 coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is H(X₁)+H(X₂)−H(X₁,X₂)≥0. Conditional mutual information is H(X₁,X₃)+H(X₂,X₃)−H(X₃)−H(X₁,X₂,X₃)≥0. Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.
why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.
status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.
progress: 1998: Zhang–Yeung’s first non-Shannon inequality shows that the elementary Shannon proof system is incomplete, as recalled by the inherited source. | 2013: Kaced–Romashchenko distinguish conditional and unconditional inequalities and their behavior on entropic versus almost-entropic points. | 2020: Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu establish co-r.e. upper bounds for validity of unconditional and certain more general information constraints. | 2023: Li proves undecidability of conditional information inequalities, network coding and conditional-independence implication; the premise-free question remains separate. | 2024: Hannula classifies several restricted semantic and syntactic versions and explicitly states the general information-inequality decision problem as open. | 2025-09-28: Csirmaz’s revised exploration compares major inequality-generation methods and records open completeness questions. | 2026-03-03: E. P. Csirmaz–L. Csirmaz revise their five-variable work, giving two infinite inequality collections and an enumeration procedure within the proposed method.
working_summary: An information inequality is a linear combination of joint entropies asserted to be nonnegative for all distributions. The question asks whether an algorithm can always decide validity when the coefficients are rational and finite alphabet sizes are unrestricted. Standard Shannon inequalities certify many cases but do not describe every valid entropy inequality. A decision procedure would clarify the limits of automated reasoning about information, with implications for coding and database bounds. The saved review notes that invalidity can be semidecided and that undecidability results with conditional premises do not automatically settle this unconditional problem.

title: The capacity region of the general two-user interference channel
importance_reason: A canonical unresolved network-information-theory model in which independent communications compete through interference.
formal: Determine the capacity region C(W) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-user interference channel W, with independent private messages, separate encoders and no feedback, using the average-error operational model below. The additional requirement intended by “determine” or “characterize” remains to be specified: a general limiting formula is already known.
definitions: Let X₁,X₂,Y₁,Y₂ be arbitrary nonempty finite sets and let W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂)≥0 sum to 1 over (y₁,y₂) for each input pair. At block length n≥1 the conditional output distribution is the product over t=1,…,n of W(y₁,t,y₂,t|x₁,t,x₂,t). A code has positive integer message counts M₁,M₂, deterministic encoders f_i:{1,…,M_i}→X_i^n, and decoders g_i:Y_i^n→{1,…,M_i}. Messages U₁,U₂ are independent and uniform on their respective sets. Encoder i knows U_i only, and receiver i observes only Y_i^n and must reconstruct U_i. Both codes and W are known in advance to all terminals. There is no feedback, message cooperation, shared entanglement, common message, input-cost constraint or extra communication. Private means individually intended; secrecy from the other receiver is not required. The average joint error is P[g₁(Y₁^n)≠U₁ or g₂(Y₂^n)≠U₂], averaged over both uniform messages and the channel law. Its convergence to zero is equivalent to convergence of each receiver’s average error to zero. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with n→∞, joint error tending to zero and liminf (log₂ M_i)/n≥R_i for i=1,2. C(W) is the closure in R² of all achievable pairs. Rates are bits per channel use. Arbitrarily large codebooks and unlimited computation are permitted; this is a capacity question, not an efficient encoding question. Maximizing error over message pairs defines a different convention and is not imposed.
answer_criterion: The operational object C(W) is defined, but a completed benchmark criterion must specify the required representation or evaluability of its general characterization. Any proposed capacity theorem must prove both that all rates in its stated region are achievable and that rates outside it are impossible for every channel in the stated family. Merely repeating the operational definition or the known unrestricted information-spectrum formula does not identify the missing intended advance; the source must determine the additional requirement.
statement_review_issue: The source asks to “characterize” the capacity region but does not specify what form of answer would improve on the existing operational definition or general information-spectrum formula. A finite-dimensional single-letter expression, a computable approximation procedure with a certified error bound, and an unrestricted limiting formula are different requirements. The source does not select one or prescribe encodings for numerical evaluation; choosing one here would create an additional mathematical target.
context:
There are two senders and two receivers. Each sender has its own message, but both inputs can affect both outputs. If instead both receivers see only X₁ XOR X₂, the two separate one-bit messages cannot both be recovered at a total rate above one bit per use. The tradeoff between the two rates, rather than either isolated link’s capacity, is the object of interest.

A code uses the channel many times and permits a small probability of decoding error. title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
importance_reason: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
formal: Do there exist constants r∈(0,1], δ∈(0,1/2) and A>0 such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with k≤n≤k/r, an encoding C:{0,1}^k→{0,1}^n, and randomized local decoders Dec_i for i∈{1,…,k}, satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word z∈{0,1}^n differing from C(x) in fewer than δn positions, and every requested index i, Dec_i with oracle access to z outputs x_i with probability at least 2/3 while making at most ⌈A log₂(n+1)⌉ bit queries on every execution.
definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is k/n and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants r, δ and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple (x,z,i); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.
context:
A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses 2^{O(√(log n·log log n))} queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

importance_reason: The basic unresolved limit of compressing correlated information without coordination between encoders.
formal: Determine R_p(D₁,D₂) for every pair of correlated finite-alphabet discrete memoryless sources, reconstruction alphabets and distortion functions in the model below. definitions: Fix nonempty finite sets X₁,X₂,Ŷ₁,Ŷ₂, a probability mass function p on X₁×X₂, functions d_i:X_i×Ŷ_i→[0,∞) with finite values, and thresholds D_i≥0. The pairs (X₁,t,X₂,t), t=1,…,n, are independent with common law p. A length-n code consists of positive integers M₁,M₂, functions f_i:X_i^n→{1,…,M_i}, and a joint decoder g:{1,…,M₁}×{1,…,M₂}→Ŷ₁^n×Ŷ₂^n. Write (Ŷ₁^n,Ŷ₂^n)=g(f₁(X₁^n),f₂(X₂^n)). Encoder i sees only its own source block; descriptions reach the decoder without transmission errors. Codes are deterministic, agreed in advance, and there is no interaction or decoder side information. For ε>0 a code meets rates R_i and distortions D_i within ε when (log₂ M_i)/n≤R_i+ε and E[(1/n)∑ₜ d_i(X_i,t,Ŷ_i,t)]≤D_i+ε for both i. R_p(D₁,D₂) consists of nonnegative pairs (R₁,R₂) for which such codes exist for every ε>0 at all sufficiently large n. This includes limiting boundary rates. Expectation is over the source pairs. Computation and codebook size are unrestricted; rates count bits per source symbol.

context:
Two sensors can observe related data without seeing each other’s recordings. Their common decoder can exploit correlation, while each sensor must choose its description from its own recording. For identical fair binary sources and zero Hamming distortion, sending the first recording at one bit per sample and sending nothing from the second sensor suffices. For independent fair bits, those same rates cannot reconstruct the second recording. Hamming distortion counts the fraction of incorrectly reconstructed symbols.

Higher distortion permits less accurate reconstructions and potentially lower rates. The target is the entire set of feasible pairs of description rates for fixed tolerances. It neither requires exact recovery of every block nor merely asks for the smallest sum of the two rates. A useful exact theorem must match an achievable region with a converse excluding every other pair.

title: The capacity region of the general two-way channel
importance_reason: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.
formal: Determine the capacity region C(W) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-way channel W with independent messages and causal adaptive encoders as defined below. definitions: Fix nonempty finite input sets X₁,X₂ and output sets Y₁,Y₂, and numbers W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂)≥0 summing to 1 over the output pair for each input pair. A length-n code has positive integer message counts M₁,M₂ and independent uniform messages U_i∈{1,…,M_i}. At time t=1,…,n, terminal i transmits X_i,t=f_i,t(U_i,Y_i,1,…,Y_i,t−1), where f_i,t is deterministic. Given both messages and the entire preceding history, the output pair at time t is sampled according to W at the current input pair. Both inputs are selected before either current output is observed. Terminal i uses a deterministic decoder g_i(U_i,Y_i^n) to estimate U_(3−i). Average joint error is the probability that at least one estimate is wrong, over the messages and channel outputs. A nonnegative rate pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if codes with block lengths tending to infinity have joint error tending to zero and liminf (log₂ M_i)/n≥R_i for both i. C(W) is the closure of these achievable pairs in R². R₁ measures communication from terminal 1 to 2, and R₂ from 2 to 1, in bits per channel use. Codes and W are known in advance. There are no other communication links or shared random seeds. Local computation is unrestricted.

title: Is the Shannon capacity of a finite graph computable?
importance_reason: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer k≥1, A on input (G,k) halts and outputs integers a and b>0 with |a/b−Θ(G)|≤2^(−k)? No bound on running time is imposed.
definitions: Encode G with vertices {1,…,n}, n≥0, by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For m≥1, the strong power G^⊠m has vertex set {1,…,n}^m. Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either x_j=y_j or {x_j,y_j} is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; α(H) is its maximum cardinality, with α of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define Θ(G)=sup_{m≥1} α(G^⊠m)^(1/m). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as m→∞, and 1≤Θ(G)≤n; set Θ(G)=0 when n=0. The desired output approximates Θ itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.
context:
Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity √5. For nonempty graphs, log₂Θ(G) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of C₇ is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
importance_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
focus_reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most C·ε^{−c} vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let P_F contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define dist(G,P_F) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in P_F on the same vertex set, divided by n²; define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of min{n,s} distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when G[S] contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers C,c≥1 such that for every rational ε∈(0,1), every n≥1 and every G with dist(G,P_F)>ε, this tester with s=⌈Cε^{−c}⌉ rejects with probability at least 2/3. It automatically accepts every graph in P_F. The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy ε are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in P_F can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small ε. Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being ε-far means that a positive ε fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an ε fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on ε, but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding C₄, its complement and C₅, although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.

Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.

Induced C₄-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.

Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced C₄-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in 1/ε.

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.

title: Does polynomial testability imply polynomial distance estimation for dense graph properties?
importance_reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.
focus_reason: A universal polynomial tester-to-estimator implication would convert robust graph-property recognition into quantitative distance measurement across the dense model.
formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with P_n nonempty for every n≥1, does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in 1/ε, independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-ε distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
definitions: P_n is a nonempty subset of graphs on [n], invariant under vertex permutations. For n≥2, dist(G,P)=min_{H∈P_n}|E(G)△E(H)|/binom(n,2); for n=1 it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer t≥2, with ε=1/t, and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each G∈P_n with probability ≥2/3 and rejects each G with dist(G,P)≥ε with probability ≥2/3; no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants C,a≥1 with at most Ct^a adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants C′,b≥1, using at most C′t^b queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with Pr[|q−dist(G,P)|≤1/t]≥2/3 for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative q_P(poly(ε)) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are ε-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has Θ(n²) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on ε. The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether q_P(ε) can be replaced by q_P(poly(ε)); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.
why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

title: Query complexity of directed acyclicity testing with bidirectional access
importance_reason: A sharp testing or correction bound for a specific distance, property, or sampling regime.
formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n→∞ for each fixed degree bound d≥1 and fixed rational ε∈(0,1), the minimum worst-case number Q(n,d,ε) of incidence-list queries needed by an adaptive randomized two-sided-error tester to distinguish acyclic n-vertex digraphs from digraphs more than εdn edge deletions away from acyclic, when every indegree and outdegree is at most d and both incoming and outgoing queries are allowed.
definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set {1,…,n}; opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index i∈{1,…,d}; it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and ε are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v₁,…,v_k, k≥2, with arcs v_i→v_(i+1) and v_k→v₁; acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let τ(G) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is ε-far if τ(G)>εdn. Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least 2/3 and reject each ε-far graph with probability at least 2/3. There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational ε; there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested Θ bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and ε. One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound F(n,d,ε), a uniform tester using O(F) queries, and a matching Ω(F) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed d,ε in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on d,ε, but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.
context:
A long directed cycle can remain invisible in a small explored neighborhood. The tester sees only chosen incident edges, so even the ability to move both forward and backward does not directly reveal whether some distant portion closes a cycle.

A directed cycle on n vertices becomes acyclic after deleting one arc. Its normalized distance is 1/(dn), so for fixed positive ε and large n it is outside the promised far case. Property testing asks for reliable rejection only when many arc deletions are unavoidable.

The source records an Ω(n^(1/3)) query lower bound for adaptive two-sided testing at suitable fixed parameters. Reading every outgoing list uses at most nd queries and determines the whole graph. The gap between such lower bounds and the linear bound motivates the sharp query question.

The 2023 model comparison distinguishes access to both directions from access only to outgoing arcs. A lower bound against the less informative oracle cannot automatically rule out an algorithm with incoming queries.

Yoshida’s preprint states stronger one-sided and two-sided lower bounds when queries only reveal outgoing neighbors and indegree is unrestricted. These hypotheses differ from the fixed bidirectional bounded-degree setting of the original question.
why: Measures how much local information is needed to certify the absence of global directed cyclic structure up to a proximity promise. It would clarify the power of adaptive two-direction exploration in sparse directed graphs.

The card explicitly chooses query complexity as the measure of the source’s best-algorithm question. The 2026 paper was checked at introductory-statement level, not independently proved.

title: Sample stretching and the meaning of independent synthetic observations
importance_reason: A specialized problem or research direction in the saved collection; the category review places it behind broadly reusable primitives and general model separations.
formal: Given k independent observations from an unknown discrete distribution p on a domain Ω, what is the smallest distortion ε for which an algorithm can output k+1 independent observations from a distribution p′ with dTV(p,p′)≤ε? The intended dependence of p′ on the input data, the independence convention and the accuracy guarantee remain to be specified.
definitions: A discrete probability distribution p on a finite or countable set Ω assigns nonnegative masses p(x) summing to one. Total variation is dTV(p,q)=(1/2)∑_{x∈Ω}|p(x)−q(x)|. The k input observations X₁,…,X_k have joint law p^⊗k, meaning Pr[X₁=x₁,…,X_k=x_k]=∏ᵢp(xᵢ). A sample transformation sees only these observations, the known domain and k, and may use private randomness independent of the input. It has no further sampling access to p. One possible literal output requirement is: for every p there exists a fixed q_p with Law(Y₁,…,Y_{k+1})=q_p^⊗(k+1) and dTV(p,q_p)≤ε, where the law averages over both input samples and private randomness. A different requirement allows a random distribution Q inferred from the data and asks for conditionally iid outputs given Q, together with a specified probabilistic accuracy guarantee for dTV(p,Q). The latter generally gives a mixture of product laws after averaging over Q, not a product law. Yet another condition, used in sample amplification, is dTV(Law(Y₁,…,Y_{k+1}),p^⊗(k+1))≤ε. Here distance is on Ω^(k+1), whereas the original source compares distributions on Ω. These three formulations must not be identified. For a finite domain Ω={1,…,n}, any resulting optimal distortion would be a function of k and n; the source also allows a general discrete domain.
answer_criterion: After fixing the source’s intended output and accuracy conventions and the domain class, determine the optimal distortion as a function of the parameters, with matching attainable upper and universal lower bounds, or with a proved infimum if attainment is not required. Results for a different joint-output or conditional-independence guarantee do not settle the chosen target.
statement_review_issue: The phrase “some p′” must be quantified: is it fixed for each unknown p and algorithm, or may it be random and depend on the observed sample? In the latter case, independence may be conditional on p′ or on the data, and the bound on dTV(p,p′) needs an almost-sure, expected, or fixed-confidence convention. These requirements are inequivalent. The domain class and whether the optimum means an attained minimum or an infimum must also be fixed. The later amplification definition is precise but is a different target and cannot silently replace this one.
context:
Let X be a fair bit and return (X,X). Each output separately is a fair bit, but the pair never equals (0,1) or (1,0). Independent fair bits have positive probability for both outcomes. Correct one-coordinate distributions therefore do not guarantee independent synthetic observations.

Suppose a random Q is a point mass at zero or a point mass at one, each with probability one half. Two draws from Q are independent after Q is fixed, but their unconditional law is again the pair (X,X). This distinction matters whenever the output distribution is learned from a random input sample.

The 2024 paper makes the entire synthetic dataset statistically close to fresh independent samples from p. Its definition measures one total variation distance on the product domain. The original stretching question instead asks for independent samples from a nearby marginal p′, so amplification theorems cannot be imported as a resolution without reconciling the requirements.

If the nearby distribution itself is random, an expected accuracy bound, an almost-sure bound and a high-probability bound ask different things. The original short contribution does not choose among them. This card exposes that choice instead of giving the impression that every interpretation has the same answer.
why: Investigates what genuinely new statistical information can be supplied from a fixed dataset. Independence is central: synthetic observations can have plausible marginals while substantially overstating the effective amount of data.

title: Is private PAC sample complexity polynomial in VC dimension and log-star Littlestone dimension?
importance_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
focus_reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.
formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most 1/10 and confidence at least 9/10, while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set {0,1}^X of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target h∈C and distribution D on X, with probability at least 9/10 over m independent draws x_i from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most 1/10. Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector (h(x))_{h∈C} can be identified, giving at most 2^|C| cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.
why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.
